product_title: Creative Muvo 10 Portable Wireless Bluetooth Speaker with NFC
review_headline: Amazingly good sound quality for the money.
review_body:
For the asking price ($79.99 MSRP), the Creative Muvo 20 Portable Wireless Bluetooth Speaker is very functional (some might say that it \\"just works\\") and sounds incredibly good. I've paired it with a Kindle Fire HD, Dell Venue Pro Windows smartphone, Windows PC and even my OUYA. Pairing with all devices is a cinch (at least if you've ever paired anything before) with no \\"missed\\" pairing attempts at this point, even when previously paired with another device. Range is also very good. Paired to the Fire HD, I left the Muvo 20 in the kitchen, turned it up and then started walking the Fire HD around the house, even on to the back porch. I don't have the largest home, but at no point was the connection lost. The Muvo 20 kept blasting away the Ramones the entire time. Battery seems to be good (I've never actually let it run all the way down, instead opting to charge it via Micro USB between listening sessions) and the ability to use it to charge other devices is a nice bonus.

Sound quality is also very good and the volume is more than loud enough to do my old-school punk justice, as well as keep my daughters dancing to their favorite music in the next room. I've queued up classical, folk, rock, bluegrass, jazz, some country, you name it, and all sounded great. Granted, I haven't turned it all the way up (no need) and there's not a whole lot of bass coming out of it (some, just don't expect too much thump), but the Muvo 20 has more than met the expectations that I had for it. I'm sure some audiophiles will scoff at that and point out any number of 'superior' units that cost several times the price, but for those who don't have to have the latest and have a more constrained budget, the Muvo 20 will more than likely do justice to whatever you want to listen to.

Update: 7 months down the line and the Muvo 20 is still going strong. Battery life is downright great (I can't remember the last time it actually went dead on me) and I've moved it to work where I can actually crank it up. Most of the music I listen to (old-school punk) tends to be loud and decidedly lo-fi, and while this works great for that, some of my coworkers have used to to play some of their tunage and the audio quality is more impressive than I would have known. It's still not great for low, low bass, but it handles the highs and middle range with great clarity, even at higher volume levels. Bluetooth range really depends on what you're using to transmit to the Muvo, but that's not its fault. My Windows phone stays connected at over 30 feet and through a wall, but the cheap Bluetooth USB adapter that I use on my desktop doesn't fare nearly as well (much to my disappointment...I have over 40GB of music on that thing). product_title: FiiO X5 High Resolution Lossless Music Player
review_body:
If you plan on using it to listen to music and only that then this is a great player. If you actually need the software to do stuff then you might run into some problems. Sometimes it's a bit slow when changing songs. The user interface is disgusting and a pain to use, but a huge improvement over the fiio x3. I noticed that the wheel spins easier after using it quite a bit so it might be overly sensitive later on. Seems like and ipod copy except for the buttons. There's only a hi/lo gain, no medium, and it's in the software instead of a switch. HO is at the top so when you take it out of your pocket it'll be facing the wrong way. If you plan on using it at your desk with headphones then the cables will pull down on your player and make it turn. Not good for the headphone plug/jack.
There's a bug where sometimes music plays from the player while used as a USB DAC so you get 2 songs playing at once. You stop this by turning off the music first then plugging in the USB again. Not sure what happened there but it only happened once and never happened again.
It can't read my cue sheets for some reason, and instead of playing the song without the cue sheet, it crashes instead. My sansa clip reads it without problems and skips the tracks perfectly when I click the next button. The cue sheet and the audio file have the same name so I'm pretty sure it wasn't my fault especially since the clip can use it.
There's also background hissing for low impedance, sensitive IEMs,so se846 users, stay away.
There were too many problems for me to deal with so I ended up returning it. Fiio products have good hardware for the price, but the software/design is a joke.

product_title: Logitech 915-000162 Harmony 700 Rechargeable Remote with Color Screen (Black) [Discontinued by Manufacturer]
review_headline: Setup could be improved... and a few tips if you buy this.....
review_body:
This does work well, but, here are some tips which will help you once you get it.

To initialize the unit, you'll need the serial number and make/model for all of your gear. Best to take pics of your units using your phone in advance so that you can zoom in and type it into the software which configures the unit. Once that's done, the setups can be just a bit confusing if you happen to have an HDMI switch and don't use the source selector on your TV. So, tip #1, if you have an HDMI switch, when you configure the TV for input on an action, just pick the source the HDMI switch feeds, typically HDMI1. In another step, pick which of the HDMI switch settings matches the configuration.

Tip #2, and this is important, is to be sure you remove the little plastic protective cover from the infrared cover on the remote itself. That's at the bottom (facing you) not the top. If you do not do that, then the remote will operate improperly, missing steps.

Finally, tip #3, this unit will send commands to each unit in a sequence, so, when you press, for example 'Watch TV' keep the unit pointed at your gear until it is all done. That doesn't take long, but, if you press it then put it down, it won't finish.

As for the unit itself, if a particular action doesn't work, you can press HELP and you'll be walked-through a fix.

I'm giving 4 stars only because of the setup; it is one a geek will love, but everyone else may struggle with. So, if you're up for using USB ports on your computer, downloading control software, entering information by hand and then configuring actions, by all means get it. On the other hand, if you're not, look into a unit which provides a list of device IDs you can look up instead.p right, then pick a button, it works. I wish the instructions just said that.

product_title: Brainwavz M5 In Ear Earbuds Noise Isolating Earphones stereo Headphones
review_headline: Good performance at a budget price
review_body:
These are not the best-sounding earbuds I have, but the sound quality is well above what I have come to expect at the sub-$40 price level. It puts out a pretty clear sound with nicely defined mid and upper ranges. The bass is decent – not all that rich, but it rounds things out nicely. The quality gets a bit harsh and clipped at loud volumes but, at normal listening levels, it performs quite well.

Comfort is also better than the typical budget set of earbuds. It comes with a variety of silicon tips (S/M/L) plus foam tips (the Comply foam). The foam tips work best for me – they hold tight, are comfortable, and provide the best sound isolation of any of the tips. They do take a bit of time to get used to since they feel different than the customary silicon tip. But, once they mold themselves to your ears, they feel and work very well.

It comes with a well-made case and a shirt clip. I don’t have much use for the clip, but the case is very handy to have.

On the downside, the build quality of the cords is on the thin side, and they don’t have as sturdy of an anchoring that I’d like to see. The 3.5mm jack was also somewhat fussy, producing a lot of static when I first used it. It appears there was a loose connection since pressing on the jack cut the static way down. It still occurs, but only when it is bumped hard while plugged in. Still, these issues could have been solved by heavier gauge cables and more robust connectors. I realize these are budget ‘phones, but even at this price point the cables and connectors should be better, so I’m dropping the rating one star due to that.

Overall, a great set for the price. Well worth considering if you want good sound but want to keep the price reasonable. The cord issues make these best suited for non or low-active work (e.g., not the best pair to get if you’re a long-distance runner).

review_headline: Impulse purchase at great price, worth it with a annoying flaw
review_body:
Some of the reviews on this product make it seem like this is a horrible radio. Its not. Its quite above par. Not stellar, but definitely better than most radios. I wouldn't say get this if the price is quite a bit more than the regular PAL, because the Bluetooth (BT) function (which is the main difference) is really annoying with iOS devices.

The Good:
Fully charged battery lasts quite a long time between needing to be recharged
Finish is gorgeous for being plastic, even though its not classy as all the other Tivoli radios, it holds its own quite well.
It feels sturdy and has a great heft
Sound is excellent. I'd say I like it better than my Model 10 stereo setup

The Bad:
Power cord has a huge transformer (aka wall wart), but luckily, you don't have to keep this plugged in all the time

The Ugly:
Here's where I knock off a star. I would consider dropping it two stars, but for the price I paid, I'm not going to be mean:
The Bluetooth function with iOS 7.x devices isn't ready for prime-time.

It took a few times to initially pair my iPhone 5S with the PAL BT. But once set up, then anytime I switch the PAL to BT mode, it does NOT automatically connect (it should if only one device has been set up with PAL).
And when you try to manually connect, there's more than 50% chance it won't connect the first time. You have to keep going to iOS BT settings and clicking on BT devices to force it to connect. You are lucky if it connects second time.
I'm hoping this is a iOS issue, so that a software update could fix it. But if its is issue specific to PAL BT, then we are out of luck :(

I love the radio and for the price I paid, I have no regrets. But if you are on fence between the regular PAL and the BT PAL, I suggest stay with the regular one, unless the BT version is significantly cheaper.

product_title: Logitech Harmony Smart Control with Smartphone
review_body: Logitech has hit a home run. Very easy to set up either through web site or smart phone app.  Remote uses RF to communicate with the Logitech hub.  The smart phone communicates with the hub via your wireless internet router.  From there the hub sends out IR signals to your electronic equipment.  If the hub is within the same compartment as your electronic equipment, then they will receive the IR signal appropriately.  However, if some of your equipment is on another (solid) shelf or on the other side of a solid wall within your equipment enclosure, then the IR signal will be blocked by the solid wall or shelf and therefore will not reach your other equipment.  Logitech provides for this contingency by enclosing one mini IR Blaster.  This is attached to the back of the hub with a wired connection.  You then run the wire into the section of the cabinetry holding your other equipment.  When the hub receives the signal from the RF remote, or the smartphone via your wireless network, it sends out the appropriate IR signals from the hub and also the mini IR Blaster so that all of your equipment gets an IR signal.  If you have more than one area of your cabinet that contains your equipment, then you will need to purchase an additional mini IR Blaster from Logitech to cover these areas.  (The hub has two attachment areas for mini IR Blasters.) You only need one IR source per cabinet area no matter how many pieces of electronic equipment you have in any one area.  The IR signals emitted from either the hub or the mini IR Blaster are strong enough to bounce off the walls of the enclosure and get to each piece of equipment.  It just cannot go through solid material.  So Logitech has you covered if your equipment is contained within 2 or 3 separate areas within your entertainment center.  If you have more than 3 separate areas then this particular solution would not work.  When the hub is in communication with your home network, the light on the front of the hub is green.  Whenit has lost connection to your home network, it is red.  The only problem I have encountered is that occasionally when the hub light is green the RF remote will not work.  Unplugging the power to the hub for a few seconds and then reattaching the power forces the hub to "reboot" and re-establish the connection.  This is not a problem for me, because the hub is sitting on top of my center speaker of my 5.1 speaker system on an open shelf which is easy to get to.  Might be a problem if access to the hub is difficult.  Other than this minor inconvenience, we love the setup.  My wife loves only using one remote.  My setup is a Samsung Plasma TV (PN58B560T5FXZA), Pioneer AV Receiver/amp (VSX-33), Dish Network Sat/DVR (ViP 722K), and LG Blue Ray Disc Player (LG BD570).  Logitech maintains a huge database of IR remote controller settings for almost all makes and models of electronic equipment.  If you by chance have a piece of legacy equipment that is not in their database, the Smart Controller can "learn" the IR signal from your existing remote.  I have not had to use this feature, though.  I have used several different Logitech remotes in the past, but I like this solution much better.

product_title: J-Tech Digital Hdmi Audio Converter Adapter
review_body:
I bought this hoping it would enable me to hear an HDMI component on zone 2 of my receiver.

For whatever reason receiver manufacturers allow only 2-channel, analog audio to be played on other zones. Digital audio such as optical and HDMI can only be played on speakers A and B in the main zone.

The product description says this device simultaneously outputs HDMI and 2-channel, analog audio on the RCA outs. But, the owner's manual says if 5.1 audio is going through the HDMI, no audio is output to the RCA outs. So, the RCA outs only work if the HDMI is set to 2-channel audio. This limitation defeated my purpose, as I wanted to connect the converter box, throw it behind my receiver and forget about it. I don't want to constantly switch the button on the converter box.

In the end I returned the box and gave up on using zone 2 (as I have had to do in the past). I went back to the speaker A and B configuration. The primary limitation of this configuration is that A and B must have the same source. The concept of zones is to have different sources. But, until manufacturers start supporting digital audio on the zones, I for one am going to be stuck with one source on speaker A + B.

product_title: In-Line Attenuator 3 dB (1)
review_body:
After calling my cable provider numerous times for extremely poor internet service and even a tech came out- who said the lines were fine, tech checked the signal on his laptop, I was still having dropped signals, no internet or it was very very poor connectivity. I had my Airport Extreme router hooked up to it. They kept saying that the Airport was the main issue, clearly there was nothing wrong w/ it, I even did factory resets on both the modem and router. I got fed up and started researching. I learned about attenuators and down stream power signals. My Channel power levels were fluctuating from +4- +6dBmV on all channels 1-8 (SB6141), so I decided on a 3dBmV attenuator. Power levels are now zero to +1 and I have fantastic Internet performance. The power signals are supposed to be as close to zero as possible or else you will get poor quality internet connection. Disappointing that the provider did not offer this option, but of course why would they want to spend $7-8 dollars extra on a customer for a small part to easily fix your line?

Four stars as I could not track this item during delivery. Otherwise great DIY fix, check your power levels as there are different levels of attenuators.

product_title: SoundMAGIC E10 Noise Isolating In-Ear Earphones
review_body:
I'm picky about how my music sounds, the problem is I don't have disposable income to devote to audio equipment. With a long international flight coming up, I needed a new pair of earphones that are comfortable and sound great for less than $50. These headphones are a home run!

Included is a nice crush-proof case and 7 pairs of silicone tips. This is the first set of earphones I've owned that really fit comfortably, without some 3rd party replacement tips. The build quality is really nice; the cable is firm and does not tangle easily. Microphonics have not been much of an issue for me, a huge upgrade from other earphones I've owned. The included cord clip definitely helps keep everything on you.

Sound quality is outstanding for the price. I immediately noticed that some of my music tracks were poor quality, and this was just off of my ipod, no high quality amplifier or DAC involved. On better quality music, vocals are very clear, highs are very crisp, mids are very well produced, and the bass is nice and tight. I wouldn't say these are good for bass-heads, but if you enjoy music that isn't usually bass-heavy, these will be great.

The noise isolation is great. I used these on a very long flight and was able to almost completely block out the sound of the plane. I also use these at my desk when I want to ignore conversation around me and focus on getting things done.

All in all, an excellent value!

product_title: Koss KSC75 Portable Stereophone Headphones
review_headline: The undeniable king of value in headphones
review_body:
I've owned a wide variety of headphones in my life. Ultimate Ears, Shure, Etymotic, Sennheiser, Grado, etc. These Koss headphones are just remarkably good for the price. They cost about 1/10th as much as entry level IEMs but sound only marginally worse. They have ruined every other budget headphone or earbud for me.

I've been running with these during marathon training. They probably aren't really made for this, but whenever I try another pair of headphones (e.g. yurBuds), the sound quality is so lacking that I wind up back with the KSC-75s. I am sure I am greatly reducing their life this way, but they are just about ideal for running outdoors: they let enough ambient noise in, they stay in place, the sound quality is excellent, and my ears don't hurt after hours of wearing them. I'm sure they are nowhere near sweatproof, but at $10/pair (as they frequently are on Amazon), I just load up and then figure it's not a huge deal to go through a pair now and again.

The only thing that they really lack is a mic/pause/next feature for music. That is the one thing I miss that yurBuds or others offer.

The wire, like many wired headphones, might eventually become finicky. I just bought more of these because the wire on my 6 year old pair was causing erratic loss in one ear. Even still, it only happens sometimes and that's after months of significant running mileage.

Just a great, great headphone for the price. I will still use my Ultimate Ears or Shure IEMs for listening sessions or on the plane, but the Koss phones are my go-to for outdoor workouts and other situations where I don't want or need full isolation.

product_title: Polk Audio AM5119-A Buckle Headphones
review_body:
So, I just got these in the mail today(March 7th, 2014). This is my first impression, and as such I will hold back from commenting on the audio quality until they've gotten a chance to break in. I will post an update at a later date. Also, I have owned and used the Sony MDR-7506 headphones for about 8~9 years (still working great), so I will be drawing from that experience, and making some comparisons.

First, about the fit and finish. They are a beautiful and solid product. The leather appears to be genuine, it's soft, and very attractive. I think these will hold up well over time.

Second, concerning comfort. These are not the best in terms of comfort. However, they are most certainly not the worst either. Compared to the Sony MDR-7506, they fit tighter and are heavier. If you're using them for more than an hour, you will probably start to feel a bit uncomfortable.

Third, about sound isolation. These are not \\"noise canceling\\" headphones. However, because of their tight fit, they do isolate the music quite well. I cannot hear the voice of someone right in front of me while the music is playing. In this regard, the tight fit does offer some benefits compared to the 7506 headphones.

Fourth, about the cord. The connection to the headphones is a 2.5mm jack, not a standard 3.5mm jack(1/8\\"). So, if you are thinking of upgrading to a higher quality cable, you will need a 2.5mm to 3.5mm cord. Since I already had a good 3.5mm microphone cable(http://www.amazon.com/ProX-Cables-XC-MM05-Performance-Interconnect/dp/B00B1VFLLK/ref=cm_cr-mr-title), I purchased a simple 2.5mm to 3.5mm adapter (http://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B00CXX8748/ref=oh_details_o04_s00_i00?ie=UTF8&psc=1), which actually made a bigger difference than I anticipated. You will, however, lose the remote control capabilities(volume control, track switching, etc) with mac products if you decide to go this route.

Summary: These are excellent headphones in terms of build quality. The audio is also very good, even right out of the box. As they break in, I expect them to develop even more clarity. For now, that's all I'm going to say.

product_title: Pro-Ject Debut Carbon Premium WITH Ortofon 2M RED Turntable
review_body:
I already own a vintage Elac Miracord 50 H II that I purchased new in Germany. It is still in excellent condition, but I decided it was time to update to a more modern and cleaner looking turntable for my system. I chose the Pro-Ject Debut Carbon over the Music Hall models (it seemed like almost a coin-toss decision).

The turntable arrived on-time and excellently packaged. Unpacking and setup was extremely easy (did get a bit frustrated with the fishlne anti-skating weight, but I'm over it now). I had placed the first vinyl LP on the turntable about 20 minutes after it arrived (\\"Big Towne 2061\\" by Paris to be precise). I expected the turntable to play at least as well as my Elac Miracord, and did it ever. Over the past several days, as the cartridge was breaking in, the sound exceeded my expectations. My Pro-Ject Turntable does not have any of the hum noise reported by some customers (I did change to upgraded cables during assembly just in case though).

If you are looking for a reasonably priced, quite excellent, turntable this is one to consider. I'll probably add the ceramic platter soon, but other than that it is good to go, and looks fantastic.

review_body:
I thought I was ordering two different styles of glasses - as shown in the photo on the product page. But instead I got two pairs of the clip-on style glasses. Which is actually fine with me - the clip-on pair was the main reason for me placing this order.

The glasses I got are well made, and they work fine with the 3D images I've tried them out on (haven't tried them with any 3D videos yet though). They should last a long time - but keep in mind that they don't look like they would stand up to a lot of physical abuse. Except for the main metal clip, the rest of the glasses are made of plastic. I could see these getting easily broke if someone were to sit/step on them.

I tried these on a couple different pairs of eyeglasses and they fit pretty good. The clip portion does rest on the lens, but the prongs are padded with rubber so that shouldn't be a problem with occasional use.

All-in-all I'm happy with these glasses.

ETA: Noticed reading some of the other reviews that there are comments about the colored lenses seem a bit dark - my guess for that is the thickness of the plastic - I measured it to be a bit over .05\\" in thickness. Compared to the thin colored film used for typical cardboard 3D glasses, that is pretty thick. Thicker colored plastic would result in the glasses being a bit more dark.

ETA2: Something I overlooked at the time of purchase. This order was suppose to ship free - but I had it sent to my PO Box and didn't notice that a shipping charge was applied because of that. Totally my own fault - usually when that happens I use my work address instead. Just thought I would mention it to keep anyone else from making that mistake.

product_title: Pioneer SP-SB23W Andrew Jones Soundbar System
review_headline: Bluetooth broken on #1, but third unit received is wonderful
review_body:
Original review: Ordered on March 13th, received unit with November manufacture date on March 14. Bluetooth on sub-woofer fails! (Pioneer just finished telling me that Amazon was no longer selling defective units!) Ordered a replacement, but Amazon says no way to have distribution center send me one with the Bluetooth in place. Guess I order one every single day until I deplete the supply of old ones in the warehouse that serves my area. (It's good I have Prime!) Please comment if you have a better plan.

March 24th update: I ordered a replacement from Amazon and also bought one from BestBuy. Bluetooth worked flawlessly on the BestBuy unit, but the speakers in the soundbar sounded tinny and thin in all three settings (dialogue, movie, and music). I took it back. The following day my replacement unit arrived from Amazon. They had replaced a defective unit with a November date with a unit that also had a November manufacture date despite my request for a more recently manufactured unit! I set it up quickly, fully expecting it to be unsatisfactory. Surprise! It sounded absolutely terrific and the bluetooth worked flawlessly.

This weekend, my neighbor brought over his new $1,500 plus Paradigm soundbar and woofer to see if the difference was worth $1,1100 to him. In a blindfold A/B test, he thought the Pioneer Soundbar was actually the more expensive Paradigm.

Verdict: Buy the Pioneer SP-SB23W if you have a high tolerance for stress and can be patient. My new rating of four stars is generous given that only one of three units worked properly. Pioneer should recall those units they know to be defective. Posting the problem on the website, without issuing a recall creates terrible PR for what actually is an excellent unit.

Pros : They look neat. The pads are comfy. STRONG signal - I went a room and a half away while paired with iPhone, and not so much as a stutter. If you're only going to use these to listen to bass-heavy music on one device, I suppose they'd be okay. But for my purposes, NOPE.

product_title: Sennheiser HD 800 Reference Dynamic Headphone
review_body:
This is Sennheiser's highest-end headphone. They are open, so sound comes out and outside sound comes in to some extent. In terms of sound decay and imaging, these headphones are top notch, especially the imaging, which some say no other headphone can match. These headphones have a bright sound signature. The soundstage is also top notch. These are the most open-sounding headphone I've heard (and I've heard many headphones). The bass is not very strong but relatively tight. The bass isn't \\"missing\\", it's just not as powerful as some of the other headphones out there. In other words, for bassheads this is a no-go. The bass is very tight, but there's just less of it. The sound is very detailed, but in some of the higher frequencies, the treble is over-done a little bit. Look into EQing this if it bothers you. You can also boost the bass if it suits your bassy tastes. However, EQ only goes so far. It's best to pick a headphone that has a sound signature you want.

These require 300 omhs and I recommend an Objective DAC + Amp combo. Please make sure you take time to adjust the headphone to the shape of your head both for comfort and audio reasons. Speaking of comfort, these are quite light and comfortable. The clamping force is very low. Any lower and they'll just fall off your head, and that would be no good. Earcups are very large, and even with huge ears they will fit just fine inside the cups. Padding is soft. Cable is quarter inch and braided. It exhibits no microphonics.

Yes, these are great audiophile headphones, but I'm not giving a 5/5 because they are big budget monsters. If I could give 4 and a half, that would be a definite consideration. Also, please don't read Amazon reviews like they are all valid. The z2300 from Logitech gets what, 4/5, 5/5 average reviews? Make sure you listen to the headphones before buying them unless you are really THAT rich and you just want some new toys. Stop handing out 5/5s on reviews, guys.

Please note that these are very revealing and analytical headphones. If you want to mix music, these look like a very strong contender. If you have music with subpar quality or mixed in a less-than-ideal way, it will show up in your listening experience. While this speaks to the accuracy of these headphones, some audiophiles actually prefer a different experience geared towards making the sound pleasant rather than extremely accurate. You still have the brightness issue however.ry revealing and analytical headphones. If you want to mix music, these look like a very strong contender. review_body:
Let me start by saying I am not a expert in sound systems. I am just an average Joe, who likes the sound quality of my tv programs and music to be better than what you can get coming from the speakers built into the tv. I have had inexpensive external speakers connected to 3 of my TV's for several years now - and for the most part, I have been quite satisfied with the sound of the 3 systems. The external speakers I have been using are the type that have a powered sub woofer and 2 satellite speakers hard wired to the sub woofer - similar to pc speakers. They sound good, but the length of the hardwired speaker wires is too short. Thus you cannot get quite enough speaker separation to fully enjoy the stereo separation. I decided to take a step up and buy the Boston Acoustics speaker system [B. A.] to give me better separation and hopefully better sound.

Well I got the better stereo separation, and that was nice.

But I did not care for the sound very much. I like a very clean, normal sound when I am watching TV or listening to music. I did not get that with the B. A. sound system. It appeared as though they were using some reverberation technology to "enhance" the sound. The reverb or echo effect did not sound normal. It produced a sound effect that was not normal watching tv or movies. That may be the effect that some people enjoy while watching movies - but not me. While listening to music, the reverb effect was not as noticeable, but the music was not clean. It was kinda muddy. I had the B. A. Sound system set to the 'movie' setting while watching movies/tv and set to 'music' while listening to music.

One last item. I have a Vizio Smart TV with a remote that uses an IR/Bluetooth signal. This is the one with the slide out QUERTY keyboard [VUR10]. I was unable to get the B. A. dongle to learn my remote -- even with the help of the 30 day technical help personnel. It was obvious that the dongle would not recognize the signal coming from my remote. So if you have a Bluetooth remote -- beware!!

review_body:
MAXELL UR-120 Blank Audio Cassette Tape -4 pack (Discontinued by Manufacturer) by Maxell.
Maxell is an excellent audio tape, and I have not had any problems with it. Beyond that, both blank and prerecorded audio cassette tapes are getting harder to find as the audio cassette as a recording medium has pretty much faded from consumer use, and is now mainly used as one of the backup mediums in computer centers. Making personal recordings of elderly family members, and recording radio programs, are fast becoming the only consumer uses of audio cassette tapes, which many manufacturers no longer produce. I think one very important factor that many are unaware of is that these earphones need a break in period just as the original S4's did. This break in will "season" the sound of these tiny speakers. You will notice a world of difference in sound quality if you will just do the following:
Plug in your earphones to a good CD player and adjust the volume to about half the sound level you listen to at the highest volume you prefer, say my loudest volume would be 18 on my portable CD player so I set the volume to 9 and let them play for about 40 hours at this level. This break in period is essential and as I said you'll notice a world of difference after you do this.

Front - 2 Venturi 820

product_title: Bose Solo TV Sound System
review_body:
Since my wife was wanting a stand to raise our TV in the bedroom a little higher, I decided to try the Bose Solo since I wanted to improve the sound quality.

Set up and installation was easy using the optical cable and our 32" LCD fits perfectly on top.

Now, the sound quality is remarkable!

We have the volume set at a reasonable level and the quality of sound is a major improvement over what the TV speakers produce. As a matter of fact, set at the same level that we normally listen to our TV at, we can hear voices more clearly, other sounds and even background music that we could not hear before is very noticeable now.

Another nice thing I have found with this unit is when my wife is watching TV in our bedroom, I can not hear it in my office across the hall (25' away) any more than I could hear the TV speakers. The sound is very directional which is an extremely nice feature since I do not have to worry about closing the door when I am on business calls.

If you are looking for a surround sound or something that is more theater like, this is not the unit for you and is best suited for someone who wants improved sound quality at low to normal volume levels.

One word of advice after installation, turn your TV speakers off or the volume all the way down to prevent any unwanted reverberation and echoes.

product_title: Bose QuietComfort 20 Headphones
review_body:
These headphones are perfectly suited for someone doing a lot of travel. I've owned other noise canceling earbuds, and while good, are not in the same class as these for the noise cancelling alone. They work very well on the plane and are almost scary good at cancelling out road noise. I've worn them walking to work on a busy road and I can hardly hear the cars when I switch noise cancelling mode on. I would only do that for novelty purposes. Which brings me to my next favorite feature, aware mode. This is great when you hear the flight attendants getting giving a message. Press one button on the microphone and it uses the microphones in the earbuds to amplify the outside noise. This makes it nice so that you don't have to pull the earbuds out to hear the announcement.

They are comfortable to wear; however, on flights longer than 4 hours I did take a couple breaks from them. It is nice that the headphones still work when the battery is out, although the sound quality is much better with the noise cancelling on.

The sound quality is the best of the headphones I've ever owned, but some audiophiles may prefer a non-noise cancelling earbud. In a noisy environment, I don't think you can get much better. One note for those that haven't used noise cancelling headphone before, they are great at blocking out background noise, such as a jet engine, but sounds like people talking will still be heard. If you're trying to use these where there are people talking, play some light music and you won't hear them.

product_title: Coby Micro MP3 Player with LCD Flash Memory MP301 (Black) (Discontinued by Manufacturer)
review_headline: These Coby MP301 players are worth their weight in gold as long as you follow simple guidelines to protect them..
review_body:
OK... I read where people beat up on some of these products because they can be easily broken but as far as the electronics go, these players will give you a long hard use service life if you take care of them. I use mine every day and I know all of the weak points and the strong points on these little buggers. On a side note, The ear buds they supply are perfect "crap" and I only use them as an emergency back-up ear bud replacement until I can either repair or replace my good ear buds..

The strong point is you will get thousands of hours of playing time out of these little mp3 players before either the buttons wear out or the memory dies in them. The two main weak points are the audio jack and the battery cover and there are a few simple guidelines to follow that will all but eliminate those weaknesses.

Weak point: The battery cover can be lost if you are not careful so just use a tiny piece of clear tape once you load the battery into it and that issue is forever solved. The second issue is the audio jack on the mp3 player itself will break if you put the player into your pocket and sideways pressure gets applied to the jack as you walk or get into or out of a car which will break it loose from the circuit board and cause either one or both channels to die so either put it in a top shirt pocket or if you want it on your side, use an old cell phone holster and let it ride there so you can wear it on your side. This is how I use mine when I am wearing a shirt without pockets.

One more thing too. I normally repair my own ear buds since the wires tend to break at the jack and if you are a technical person and you use a big replacement jack to fix your ear buds or if you purchase headphones with a large jack you must be careful not to put pressure on it and break the input jack on the mp3 player. I have done this in the past but luckily I work in the electronics repair industry so I repaired mine but you may not be that fortunate. Once again, these players will play for thousands of hours before they physically wear out. One more thing... Invest into rechargeable batteries with a charger. I normally get 10 hours play-time on a single charged battery. The investment is well worth it. On an ending note: I don't always drink beer, but when I do, I prefer Dos Equis and you should too.... Stay thirsty, my friends.

product_title: Logitech Harmony Smart Control with Smartphone
review_body:
Logitech has done a good job simplifying the tangle of remotes that most people have to live with. I had an earlier Harmony remote for several years and liked it, but after a while the charging base stopped working and it got all sticky... Oh well. I used a Tivo remote for a long time then a cheap universal after I dumped to Tivo for a TWC DVR. I recenlty purchased a new TV and decided to try the latest Harmony.

The description of this remote is really all about the smart phone app, which is flashy but is only part of the story. The best feature is the control module which is a puck that sits on your shelf and blasts IR signals to all your devices. The phone app communicates with the puck over WiFi. Setup is easier than I remember, and is all done in the app. You need your model numbers of course, but once you have them setup its easy to to create the expected activty shortcuts which allow you to tap "Watch TV" and have all the devices turn on and switch to the right inputs on their own. The new puck means that you don't have to point the remote at the right place so all devices get the signals, a big improvement. Once setup you can use the phone app to control just about anything. It works pretty well once you get used to it, and the app will keep your phone from locking while you use it. I do sometimes have trouble connecting the app to the puck and I have to turn my WiFi on the phone off/on to get it working.

As I shopped around looking at indoor antennae I discovered that they have changed over the years from the old rabbit ears I used to use. After checking for the best type for my distance to transmitter, it seemed the small thin flat ones were recommended. How could such a small antenna work I thought, but for the money it was worth a try. Surprise! This AmazonBasics antenna outperforms my old rooftop antenna! I have it placed on top of a wall unit about 7 feet from the floor. I am getting 75 channels with an average signal strength of 85%; VHF and UHF. I might add that I am about 25 miles from the Chicago transmitters. I'm having the new roof installed tomorrow, and I am happy to say it will no longer be a curiosity.

product_title: Definitive Technology Mythos ST-L SuperTower with Built-In Powered Subwoofer - Each (Graphite Silver)
review_body:
Granted that these are the most recent addition to the Def Tech Mythos lineup, still there should have been more press, reviews and YouTube videos of this product. I am surprised that a brilliant product like this has so little coverage. So I decided to write this review. I will dispense with technical details for now - I will add those later when I have broken them in a bit more. I just got my speakers a few days ago.

I started to search for new speakers that were in the $5000 - $7500 range. I wanted a 2.0 system with no frills and pure musical sound. I researched for many months and visited at least ten hi-fi equipment stores in DC, NY and Chicago (Fortunately I travel a lot on work - no I did not do it just for the speakers). I listened to Martin Logans and found them fatiguing - they are highly accurate but their brightness can be tiring. I gave the 800 series of Bowers and Wilkins a good listen - excellent midrange for vocals but I would have had to spend at least $10,000 for the 803 to get what I like. Anything below that was lacking in bass although soundstage and image were excellent. I listened to the gorgeous Sonus Faber Olympica III but again, it would have set me back by $13,000. I listened to the Wharfedale Jade series but they are massive speakers with sound not that different than the B&Ws. I even heard the highly acclaimed KEF LS50s considered to be the most accurate speakers produced recently - and they were good but highly directional and good just for a small room.

After all this I realized that accuracy was not what I was looking for - it was richness and musicality. I wanted to enjoy the wine and not dissect every detail of its aroma, texture and color. I was under the influence of pretentious audiophile reviews and consequently looked for only the things that they looked for. Fortunately I snapped out of it and realized that all that mattered was what sounded best to me. How does it matter if it sounds good to some audiophile sitting in his mom's basement testing speakers all day, every day? The only speakers I would listen to are the ones I buy. It is a very personal decision.

And then I listened to the Definitive Technology STL Towers. I had heard that Def Tech had released these speakers recently so I decided to go to a local Magnolia store and give it a listen. It was love at first note. I took my own CDs - Dark Side of the Moon, Joni Mitchell's Turbulent Indigo, Sting's Nothing Like the Sun and Etta James' Greatest Hits. The more I heard the more I was amazed and impressed. I switched between B&Ws and Martin Logan and the STLs and the STLs outperformed by a big margin. The soundstage was vast, I could almost picture the different instruments in different parts of the room. The bass was rich, not overwhelming, and very well integrated - unlike a subwoofer that plays a bit aloof from the main speakers. I sat there and listened for two hours. These were albums I have been listening to for the last twenty years since high school but they seemed new and fresh - I was thrilled. When I played How Do You Stop by Joni Mitchell, even the chatty sales guy stopped talking and heard the entire song staring at the speakers all the time. At the end of the song he looked at me and said - Wow!! - and it was, like a private audience with Joni Mitchell.

These are great lookers too. I got the graphite version and they look gorgeous. They are tall and slender but very substantial in weight - you will need help. I have them hooked to Peachtree Nova Preamp and 220 watt power amp. My main input is the Oppo 105D blu ray player that has a Saber DAC, which is brilliant. Your input and amp will matter. My entire setup cost me roughly $10K. Definitely get good cables - I can't stress that enough. I am using the STLs as home theater speakers as well, with an Epson 5030 UB projector. I don't miss a center channel. The STLs are phenomenal and cover the entire range and have two inbuilt 1200 watt subs that give you the rumble in the movies when you need it. And when you want them to play music, they oblige willingly like a personal DJ.

These are great all round speakers that balance accuracy, musicality, warmth, depth and looks. They fill my 13 x 20 room with wonderful sound that brings a smile to my face every time. I love these speakers. Good job, Def Tech. You deserve a lot more press coverage and five star reviews.

UPDATE: November 2015

I posted a separate update review under the Black version of the speakers (I don't know why they have them categorized separately). My last review was about my buying process and how I chose the ST-L towers. This is a follow up after owing these speakers for one and a half years.

I had bought these towers a few days after they had just been released. I had gone to my local Magnolia AV and compared them to other leading speakers, mainly Martin Logans and B&W 803s. I recently went back to browse and listen to the 803s again. They sounded boxy compared to the ST-Ls. Now that might offend B&W faithfuls but I personally feel that the 803s sound hollow and you can tell that the sound is coming from two speakers. Comparatively, ST-Ls are invisible. The sound seems to come from the wall behind them and there is no hollowness or boxiness that would indicate that the sound is being produced by a couple of speakers. As I have mentioned in my other review, Martin Logans sound too bright to me so they are not for me.

Now that I have broken in my ST-Ls I find them very pleasing, warm and transparent. There are no artifacts and midrange is especially realistic. A lot has been written about the bass these speakers can produce but it is important to know that the bass is deep and natural, not big and boomy. So if you're looking for window shakers, then you're missing the point. These speakers are very flexible, will rumble for those explosions in movies, and will sing when it comes to music, all while sounding understated and refined. You end up paying attention to the sound than to the speakers, although they are great lookers.

It will take a bit longer than other speakers to break them in as they are sealed in metal bodies and sound tight when new. You also need more power to drive them so bigger amps will release their potential. I use a 220W per channel Peachtree. They top out at 350W but you could use amps more powerful. It is the lack of power that is likely to damage your speaker than more power.

I am very happy that I bought these speakers and continue to be amazed with their performance. Just like a museum's architecture shouldn't compete with the exhibits, these speakers don't compete with the sound for attention. That is being invisible. I have not felt the need to add a subwoofer in a 15x20 room. Def Tech is not as big as B&W who have a marketing machine behind them so Def Tech doesn't get as much publicity as it should. I have not heard the other Def Tech speakers but the ST-Ls outshine speakers twice their price.

In the end, it is a personal decision. Go listen to them and take your time. Take your own CDs or records that you love and see how they sound. Don't let reviews guide you too much. product_title: (Create a generic Title per Amazons guidelines)
review_headline: Powerful sound, great mic, and all in a nice compact package!
review_body:
I received my SHARKK Bluetooth speaker yesterday and I've got to say that I'm really very pleased with the quality and build of it all.

Let me start off with a bit of a background. I was looking for a portable bluetooth speaker with a good mic that I could use for conference calls as I'm often traveling to new locations and don't always have the luxury of a dedicated landline. My primary concern was the quality of the mic and speaker for calls, and of course the overall size of the speaker, I did a lot of research online and decided that Jawbones were out as they're just too big for me still. I wanted a speaker that wasn't any bigger than the palm of my hand. That helped to narrow down the options, and the 2 top contenders seemed the be the SHARKK speaker and Anker's new Cube speaker. Since I'm a geek, I ended up getting both to try them out side by side. The SHARKK came fully charged with a 3mm audio cable, mini-USB cable, and a nice carrying bag to keep everything in.

I ran both the SHARKK and Anker speakers through the following tests:
1. SIZE: Held the speaker in the palm of my hand
2. BLUETOOTH CONNECTION: Connected bluetooth speaker to my LG G2 phone
3. SPEAKER CLARITY: Played a song at low, medium, and high volume via bluetooth from my LG G2
4. MAKE CALLS: Made a call out from my LG G2 and spoke at a distance of 1 ft, 2 ft, and 3 ft away.
5. RECEIVE CALLS: Received a phone call and picked it up from the speaker while still playing music

Here were the results:
+ SIZE: The SHARKK was definitely smaller than the Anker in terms of physical size, but both felt like they were comparable weights. The SHARKK seemed to have a better build quality as it had a nice metallic casing that felt sturdy, whereas the Anker felt somewhat plasticy in comparison despite it's larger physical size.

| = | BLUETOOTH CONNECTION: Both the SHARKK and Anker were equivalent here.

| + | SPEAKER CLARITY: The SHARKK and Anker were both very impressive in terms of the volume coming out of them given their small size. I'd actually say the Anker may have been a little louder, but the richness of the treble and bass of the SHARKK just made it sound so much better.

| + | MAKE CALLS: Both speakers worked fine when dialing a call out, and the call volumes were pretty comparable. That being said, the SHARKK had a significantly better mic sensitivity. I was able to speak from a distance of 1 ft., 2 ft., and 3 ft. away while still being clear and heard fine by the other party on the line. The Anker was barely able to pick up my voice at a distance of only 1 ft and it constantly had a strange buzzing noise that the other party on the line noticed (in some cases it completely drowned out my voice) ... this may have been due to a defective product, but it was disappointing nonetheless.

| + | RECEIVE CALLS: The SHARKK again was the victor here. Both speakers were able to pause the music when I picked up the call via the speaker button, and resume the music when I ended the call via the speaker button. However, in the case of the SHARKK, when I received an incoming call, the SHARKK would actually say the number of the caller whereas the Anker would just give a generic sounding ring.

The SHARKK blew the Anker speaker out of the water for most of the tests. I would buy this speaker again in a heartbeat. The only downside that I can think of is that when you power up the phone it makes a loud initialization noise and speaks. You can lower the volume of the speaker globally, which in turn lowers the tone and voice volume, but it would be nice to be able to configure the volume of the initialization separate from the normal volume of the speaker itself.

Overall, if you're looking for a small speaker with exceptional sound output, quality build materials, and a strong mic, then the SHARKK is for you.

product_title: Bravo Audio V2 Class A 12AU7 Tube Multi-Hybrid Headphone Amplifier
review_body:
You will not find a better amp for the price. This little amp is pretty bare-bones. It has RCA inputs as well as a 1/8" input. It has a volume knob, 1/4" output and an on/off switch. It uses a 12AU7 tube and is pretty powerful.

The stock tube it comes with is complete crap. It has no bass at all and really sounds pretty terrible. First thing I would do is buy an old NOS tube off of ebay. Skip the new tubes on here and go with something vintage. Personally I've used a 1956 GE that sounded great as well as a blackplate RCA (preference being the RCA). A new tube can be had for $10-$15 shipped depending what you want. I would go USA made as the quality is still good but the price isn't as high as tubes made in the UK, Holland, and Germany. Look for a long blackplate tube, which would be ideal.

Overall this amp is awesome as long as you change the tube.

product_title: Brainwavz Hi-Fi Noise Isolating Headphones
review_headline: A solid performing set of headphones that did not disappoint.
review_body:
[[VIDEOID:mo3IPS0DNFFNHMI]]I found these to have great, overall sound quality. With its 6W of power, the 40mm dynamic drivers are capable of handling the deep bass I used to test these with. Distortion wasn't an issue at all and the mids, highs and vocals rang through crystal clear. These hold up nice to all of my genres of music.

In my video review, I go over many of the features, so I won't cover all of them here. The thick, lightweight aluminum, adds to the durable feel they have to them. These are solidly built, with great attention to detail. Being on the heavier side, weight in at around 12oz, I was worried about head/neck fatigue, but I'm glad to report it wasn't an issue.

The plush, cushy ear pads and head pad are very welcoming. I didn't notice any pressure points on my ears or head, even after sustained use. Unlike other headphones I've tested, the sliding side adjustments for the ear pads on these, allow for small, incremental movements which make a distinct \\"click\\" while adjusting. This softly locks the preferred position into place. Some headphones simply slide into place, and after long use I would have to be readjust them. That's simply not the case with these.

I love that it came with three different cables for all of my listening scenarios (2 diff length flat wires and 1 round wire with remote controls). The airplane adapter was great also and I haven't seen that option in other headphones).

ISSUES?
Well not really. However, as is the case with most over-the-ear cans, expect to have some hot ears after prolonged use. Personally, this is a compromise I'm willing to make in order to get the proper noise-cancelling along with the channeled music that I'm after. Also, at full volume, you may notice some \\"leakage\\" of sound, in quiet environments, but it's not intolerable and definitely not out of the ordinary.

The HM9's are a solid performing set of headphones that did not disappoint.

product_title: AmazonBasics Ultra Thin Indoor HDTV Antenna
review_headline: Better than rabbit ears... most of the time
review_body:
Bought this antenna to replace the rabbit ears I have used since cutting the cord. As other reviewers have indicated, your mileage will vary. In my case, I'm about 10 miles away from the broadcast towers, and placed the antenna against a window facing the towers with overall good results.
- Reception: Good on Hi VHF (ch 7 - 13), excellent for UHF (ch 14 and on). Here in Costa Rica, we have both digital and analog broadcasts, analog channels come in with very good picture quality particularly on UHF. As for digital, solid signal most of the time, but I still get some audio cut offs on some channels and video quirks on one, which is why I took a star off.
Some have asked about Lo VHF reception, the antenna does pick analog channels but just barely, I don't believe it would work for digital broadcasting if that is your case.
- Appearance: Better looking than rabbit ears for sure, and easier to place, but you may still want to conceal it a bit if possible. Due to its shape its quite easy to place it against a wall or even flat on the ceiling. Keep in mind that while it is flat, it is rather large - bigger than an letter-sized sheet of paper.
- Bottom line: I recommend this antenna for people that are looking for something better than rabbit ears and can't go with an outdoor antenna. Take your time to find a good reception spot - the antenna comes with a fairly large cable so it shouldn't be that difficult.

product_title: Sennheiser On-Ear 926MHz Wireless RF Headphones with Charging Cradle
review_body:
I got these to listen to my movies while the kiddos are sleeping, but unfortunately they don't work well for that. The way they handle input volume is bizarre: the headphones automatically adjust volume to ensure the sound isn't too loud or too quiet.

I watched The Dark Knight Rises, which is a typical action movie sound-wise, and the headphones were constantly changing volume on me, to the point where I missed half the dialog. In short, when an explosion or other loud noise happens, the headphones go really quiet, making any dialog afterwards inaudible. Turning up the headphones doesn't really work, because the volume slowly goes back up to normal, making the next explosion ear-shattering for the moment it takes the headphones to go quiet again.

I use these now for playing video games - the effect is still there but it isn't as disruptive in most games. With the base only a few feet away from my head, there's no hiss that I notice.

product_title: Yamaha YAS-152BL Soundbar
review_body:
This Yamaha 152BL is the second soundbar in my house and I've used it for about one month. My first soundbar that I use in my basement AV setup is a Sonos so that it is connected wirelessly to all my other Sonos speakers (totally awesome by the way). But Sonos commands a big price premium for their strong wireless technology so the Sonos soundbar set me back about $700.

So now I'm using this Yamaha on a second TV and it's a nice unit, particularly for $300 and sounds about the same to my layman ears as my Sonos soundbar. The Yamaha was very plug-and-play easy for my situation - just plug the optical cable from the soundbar into the tv and that's it (other than also plugging it into a wall outlet). The Yamaha and tv are then in synch on audio except the soundbar speakers are much better / more powerful than the wimpy stock speakers that need to fit inside a flat panel tv. One tip I almost always forget after setup - once you're using the soundbar be sure to go into tv menu and turn those speakers off so they don't muddle the bar's superior sound.

Like I mentioned I think the Yamaha's sound is good as far as soundbar's go (ie; way better than stock tv speakers). Soundbars will never be the true 7.1 surround sound because the soundbar is physically only in front of you. Most soundbars will attempt to extend some surround sound aspect and I think this Yamaha does as decent a job as any (eg; when I'm watching some scenes I do hear some sound coming from far left or far right of tv). And while soundbars will have better bass than stock tv speakers they will also never replicate the bass of a 35 pound dedicated subwoofer. BTW, this Yamaha soundbar (like my Sonos) has a jack for a dedicated subwoofer for the true bass-heads. Also this soundbar has other output speaker jacks so several rear speakers could be connected to increase surround sound aspect.

As for bluetooth, I tried it with my phone to see if it worked and it did as wasfairly easy to use. But I have a bunch of bluetooth speaker devices and I've given up on the hassle of fiddling with them individually (hence the inspiration for me to blanket my house with sonos speakers that can all play in synch with one touch).

Overall in summary I think this Yamaha soundbar is a solid value at $300 and I've had a good experience with it thus far - 5 stars from me in consideration of price/value.

- appear to be VERY sturdy considering I've used them daily for many months, not always gently, and they've lasted beautifully; looking at mine you cannot tell they are used!

product_title: Mohu Leaf 30 TV Antenna, Indoor, 30 Mile Range, Original Paper-thin, Reversible, Paintable, 4K-Ready HDTV, 10 Foot Detachable Cable, Premium Materials for Performance, USA Made, MH-110583
review_body: Recently decided to stop the basic cable I was getting after ***ca$$ decided to make me use a silly descrambling device that downgraded the signal to non HD and made the picture look terrible.  So I read the reviews for this and ordered it.  It arrived today and the picture looks pretty good.  I did  buy  the 2-port Bi-Directional Cable TV HDTV Amplifier Splitter Signal Booster with it after seeing 1 or 2 Mohu Leaf Paper reviews suggest it (written by some of the more technically able reviewers here and very much appreciated).  I assume the amp is working to give me extra clear signal.  I only have one thing to add.  Initially upon installing it, I attached the Mohu and amp splitter directly to the downstairs TV.  The connecting cords are thick coaxial cable (coax). The living room has a recessed area for a TV with the cable outlet in the back.  The initial setup was unruly and had  coaxial cable coming out of the drywall enclosure leading to the leaf that was placed at the highest point. (My better half wouldn't approve of it) I briefly thought about trying to drill holes for the coax but that seemed like too much work.  Luckily, I looked upstairs out the different coax outlets and realized the house had extra coax outlets installed in most of the rooms.  The builders had been kind enough to label the cable they ran.  The basement was equipped with a bigger beefier signal amp/splitter for the house.  I looked for an unused coax outlet on the second floor upstairs, connected the Mohu to the signal amp and then connected the amp to the outlet. In the basement, I took pictures of the existing setup and found the CATV/antenna signal-in coax (this is the large AMP splitter to feed the entire house coax).  The outside cable feed is split for 1 line to cable modem and the other line to the CATV/antenna signal-in.  I disconnected the cable coax signal coming from the splitter (signal to cable modem intact) and attached the well labelled cable connecting to the coax outletI had attached by Mohu/amp setup and viola,  I have broadcast HD signal piped throughout the house coax outlets (except for the cable I used to send the signal down to the basement, but the bidirectional amp has extra outlets anyways if I needed it.) The best part is no messy dry wall mistake cleanup.  Even on the second floor of my house, the Mohu isn't perfect and some lesser channels still need adjustment.  Now I have to record how I did this so I can reverse it if we move out or restart cable television. Also need a few smaller coax cables since the coax distance up stairs is short for where I am placing things.  I assume this setup can be done with rabbit ears.  This antenna is a bit wide so the wife still notices it a little bit.

product_title: Sennheiser On-Ear 926MHz Wireless RF Headphones with Charging Cradle
review_body:
I thought maybe 5 stars was too much as i kind of just bought these without checking around
I took one star off because the phones fit lightly enough so that i have to get used to them slipping off my head when i bend down a bit. You train yourself to be prepared for that. The first time you do that it is a trauma. So one star off for a heads up. Besides i don't really believe in 5 starring everything that comes around. 4 stars rocks in my rating system

A while back i had read all the customer reviews for the Sens all the way up to $300 phones and then burnt out on the whole thing as I just didn't know how much money to spend for what i wanted.

(problem is stores don't supply demo models anymore its all online and i really cringe to think i may have to order and send a few sets back just to audition them. stupid waste. So i gambled with the Sens and I won big time)

Some time later I bit the bullet and got the lower priced model I did not shop much I figured the Sens would do the job.

they did these replace my 12 year old falling apart JVCs for double the price same quirk in that when the signal you are listening to stops (as in say, a single youtube music clip) after a while if there is no signal you get a loud hiss. if you are listening at a safe proper level it isn't overpowering. the jvcs didn't come CLOSE to these at double the price (for the 12 year old price of the js)

I find the controls to be superior to what i have had before, and after a bit of orientation i have NO trouble switching the unit off with my left thumb when i know the signal stopped. I am also having a minimum of trouble on the right hand distinguishing between the volume wheel and the tuning wheel (which doesn't need adjustment once its set for my proximity) I think i will tape over that. but the operation experience is SMOOTH.

the unit is very comfortable although not completely transparent, the flaw being as above with the slipping. but the sound. I have very old burnt ears and the clarity of these phones enables me to enjoy a good balance of the dynamics of the program signal without having to crank too high up (as i had to do with my old phones) and that causes problems with my nerve damage in my ears.

They sound great and i am not going to knock myself out trying to find a comparison - certainly a $300 or so pair is going to be too much diminishing returns so i wouldn't bother. They can't sound THAT much better for triple the price. At least not for my old ears.

Best purchase i have made of this type in many a year. Excellent overall. I really don't like giving 5 stars for items like this, I took one off mainly for the slippage, which as i said, one familiarizes and then they are trained to be aware and take precautions.

Solid, well enough build for the weight and price, and the recharge feature where you hang up on the base works well with a minimum of fiddling. (although i did get a pack of AAA Eneloops to have just in case i forget to hang them up.)

Highly recommended product, the idiosyncrasies and shortcomings are minimal and can be lived with nicely I don't think there is a headphone anywhere that isn't going to provide a few nits.

Smooth Product, Big delivery - Sennheisers ROCK!!

product_title: Emergency AM/FM/WX Crank Radio 20-576
review_body:
It's a nice little radio. Options for battery or crank, with AM/FM and all the weather bands. Reception is very clear even with the antenna down, and even better with it up. I tested the USB charger and it seems to work well. The flashlight is pretty weak but will do for a little light in an emergency. You would probably want a separate flashlight, though, with a broader beam and more power. The case feels a little cheap, but at this price point it's actually sturdier than I expected. Cranking doesn't give you much juice but five minutes of cranking got me about the same amount of time of radio playback. I think it's probably much more practical to use the battery option instead until/unless you run out of batteries, but it's certainly good to have the crank for back-up.

I'd been waffling on buying a crank radio/charger for awhile to keep around in case of an extended power outage, and for the price I couldn't turn this one down. I wish it had solar, but for less than a third of the price of its cheapest competitors, it's a very nice radio.

review_headline: Lots of great features, a couple of pretty bad points.
review_body:
This is a great alarm packed with a lot of cool features. The description adequately covers all the good points, so I'll focus on the negatives.

One slight negative is that the automatically set time is off by about a minute. I'm not sure if this is because it's syncing off of an incorrect clock or else it's not correcting for transition time. I didn't take any stars off this because I've never had a clock with auto-set so I don't know if this is just par for the course. Bottom line: you can set it yourself if you want to need it to be more accurate, it just would have been nice to have near atomic clock precision.

The other slight negative is the fact that the interface is unintuitive. We'll get used to it, and the manual is fine, so I'm not going to deduct anything for this either (although I might drop it from a 5 to a 4 if I was otherwise inclined to rate it a 5).

The two main negatives are:

1. The primary display is too bright. It's not too bad if it's not pointing directly at you, but it definitely adds a significant amount of light pollution at any angle.

2. It's impossible to mitigate 1 and still be able to read the clock from bed. The display isn't readable from a lower angle.

I think if 1 and 2 were independent of each other I'd probably rate it a 4, but they really snowball into making the clock significantly less than ideal unless the time happens to be compatible with seeing the projection (which isn't intense enough to be visible past a few inches except in dark conditions, which is probably a good thing so I didn't mention it as a negative)
