product_title: Sewell Direct SW-29863-12 Deadbolt Banana Plugs, 12-Pair
review_body:
I purchased these thinking that they are the best thing out there according to the favorable reviews. First of all, if you look carefully at the pictures, you will notice that the tip is made in two parts: the solid center shaft on the base of which the wire is pressed, and the spring type tip made to fit snugly into the speaker or receiver binding post. The spring type part of the tip is loose and swivels onto the center shaft part and remains loose even when inserted into the binding post. When playing high SPL, especially when low sub frequencies are present, you can head crisp spark like sounds which are not part of the music. When I removed the banana plugs they were all loose, the spring type parts of the tips had collapsed to the size of the binding posts' holes and do not resume their original shape. Therefore there is NO spring to the material used. This means that they can only be used once comfortably tight. Whenever they are removed, they have collapsed to the size of the binding posts they were in, and if you insert them again, they no longer hold snugly. I returned to bare wires, and the snap, crackle, and pops disappeared. Secondly, The two parts between which the wire is squeezed, when bottomed at the threads, can only be used for 16 gauge and larger wire, the teeth leave too much gap to adequately tighten an 18 gauge wire, barely enough for 16 gauge. In the future I will first read the unfavorable reviews to see what can be expected from the products I purchase. On the other hand, Amazon is the WallMart of the internet stores. If a product does not perform as it should, you can always return it for exchange or refund.

July 2015, After all is said and done, after a couple of years, just a few units have given me problems. On average, (90%) these units do perform quite well; to the exception of when you use them in subs that can take 1,500 Watts or more at low impedance (2 Ohm), they tend to crackle due to vibrations or simply due to arcing between the two parts of the plug. All in all, they are quite good for everything else below these powers.he two parts of the plug. All in all, they are quite good for everything else below these powers.

The touchless navigation worked very nicely, the tankbot would avoid any large objects like a desk, box or hands. However every so often it would bump into a wire or try to drive over something small and end up easily flipping over. Though for the price it sells for (~12.50) the touchless navigation worked very well.

However, I was somewhat disappointed by the smartphone controlled capabilities. If you plan on getting it, I suggest going to the app store and downloading it before purchasing it so that you can get a feel of how "limited" the controls are. The most disappointing part of the remote is that the tankbot is IR controlle, which means that the bot has to be within line of sight in order to control. The IR eye is located in the front of the robot which I find to be very inconvenient because in order to get a good signal going, it has to be facing you.

Overall this product is very easy to play with and sets up nicely. Finding a USB power port isn't that hard now-a-days. An idea to increase the range of the tankbot would be to buy IR repeaters, but they're fairly expensive to buy, so for now I'll let the bot roam aimlessly around my room.

Another thing to add, this toy does well on both solid floors and carpets. Furs and hairs from the carpet don't latch onto the wheels (a common problem among wheeled toys)

product_title: HomeWorx HW-150PVR ATSC Digital TV Converter Box w/ Media Player & Recording PVR Function / HDMI Out
review_body:
Update 12/26/13: I purchased a new antenna with more umph, and WOW! I went from about 21 channels to 39 channels. This unit gets more stations than my tv tuner. I am getting channels in that are so far away, they are not even listed as local stations in my newspaper. I'm sure it's due to the antenna, however this unit is tuning more than the tv.

Update 9/22/13: The units are coming out with a newer FW version than the originals. My box had FW V3, I updated it to V10. If your box comes with V8, you do not want to update to V10. The V8 is for the new remote layout. The V10 is for the old remote layout. People with V8 upgraded to V10 are having problems and have to go back to V8 FW. Also, although QAM is not supported, they do have a QAM FW for both the old and new remotes, V12. You can get it from their forums.

Update 9/11/13: I bought a URC-WR7 universal remote that works great with this box. The Homeworx has some buttons that are not on the URC remote, however the URC does have 4 favorite buttons as alternatives. If you look at the Media sonic forums, Logitech Harmony supports this unit as well.

Original review: I originally purchased this unit about 6 weeks ago and had problems. I emailed customer support at Mediasonic and they responded back very quickly. I was able to return the unit easily. I decided to wait to buy again until after the release of the newest firmware (FW) upgrade and see what kind of reviews it was getting. I checked the Mediasonic forum on their website as well as the AVS forum. Finally decided time to try again and I'm glad I did.

After purchasing the 2nd unit, I have no problems. Customer support released a FW upgrade very quickly after customer feedback. It has fixed all of my problems. It works great to pause live tv and recording shows. EPG in my area is only 12hrs, but it works.

Some discrepency about watching one channel and recording on another. My original unit would do it about 1out of 10 times. So far, my current unit has no trouble. This is related to pressing the record button and then turning to another channel. I have not tried it yet during a scheduled recording. According to Mediasonic the unit only has 1 tuner and shouldn't be able to do this. They say the adverts and printed materials were misprints and need to be fixed. I have not heard about anyone else having problems with this. Mine works.

I \\"cut the cord\\" from cable tv a year ago, but really missed being able to pause live tv and record shows. I primarily stream programming and movies now, a lot cheaper than satellite and cable. I bought a TiVo about 6 months ago and just feel it's not worth the money for OTA tv only. Now that I have this unit, TiVo is gone. This is my sole unit, on my sole tv, in my family room. The entire family uses it. No regrets.

This is a very basic DVR, no wifi/internet. No apps. It is not an all in one solution. I have a Roku for that. It is a great tuner and dvr. Picture is just as clear as if the antenna was going straight to my hdtv. I have a 750gb USB powered external hard drive attached and have not had any problems. Time is from the channels and displays in military time.

UPDATE: After playing around with the unit I have a revision to the record one channel while watching another. If you use the RF out and set the unit to \\"loop through\\" you can record one channel and watch another (through the tv input) without any problem. You just need to change the input on your tv.

However, if you are recording a channel, say channel 32-1, then you can change to other subset channels on the unit like 32-2 or 32-3, and continue to record your original channel 32-1. It will not allow you to record 32-1 and change to channel 41-1 on the unit. It will give you the choice to stop recording or leave the channel where it is and continue to record. This occurs regardless if it is a scheduled recording, or I just press record and then change channels.

Daylight Savings Time is fixed, as well as some scheduled recording issues as far as I can tell.

product_title: Technics SA-DX930 Audio/Video Receiver (Discontinued by Manufacturer)
review_headline: Would be better if they were built properly.
review_body:
This isn't a bad receiver. The biggest problem with this unit, as you will read, is heat. While it's not uncommon for units to create heat when pumping out the sound, the problem is that these units are hit and miss as far as being put together properly.

I picked up a used unit, and the first thing I did was to take it apart. Since I'm an Electronics Technician, I figured I could deal with the heat issue. Heat is generated by two power ICs and two transistors. The heat is supposed to be transferred to the heat sink in the middle. The problem is that whoever was putting these together, didn't understand the basic concepts behind why they were doing what they were doing. (Made in Malaysia)

When I went to unscrew the power ICs from the heat sink, the screw had no torque on it at all. I could have unscrewed it with my fingers - literally. That's problem number one. Problem number two is that they used WAY too much compound between the heat sink and the components. As many people will know, the compound is meant to make sure the two sides meet. Sometimes surfaces are uneven, so compound fills in the gaps. It's not meant to be lathered on. (Anyone who has put on their own CPU heat sink will know exactly what I am talking about.)

Bottom line is that this was an overload waiting to happen. I was lucky in that the user of this unit hardly used it and never at loud volumes.

After I scraped off all the old compound, I put on a skim coat of Arctic Silver, then screwed back on the components. This time I used my ratchet and properly torqued the screws so that maximum contact with the heat sink.

With that done I went about dealing with the fan. Another issue with this unit is that the fan only comes on when you turn the volume up past a certain level. So at lower volumes the unit will cook with heat. My solution was to remove the stock fan and then put on a 120mm to 80mm reduction fitting and then slap on anice quiet fan that could move some decent air. If you do this, remember you want the fan EXHAUSTING air. Never point it inside. Aside from pumping in dust (have you looked behind your receiver lately?) the other issue is the air at the back is usually warmer. I had to use my own mini-power supply to power the fan, which I plugged into the switched outlet on the back so it would come on and off when the unit was turned on and off.

Important note: While you can take off the stock fan from the chassis, you can NOT disconnect it. I checked the schematic in the service manual, (also tested this) and if you disconnect the stock fan the microprocessor will detect there is no fan running and trigger an overload shutdown when you turn the volume up past the point where the fan would normally turn on. So you need to keep the fan running. I'd suggest you screw it onto the front of the heat sink. If you look closely you will see there are mounting holes for an 80mm fan. Perhaps they intended to have a fan mounted there but then decided to relocate it to the rear of the unit. (which was a wise move) However, if you do mount the fan up front, you'll need to make an extension for the fan cord. Either way, so long as the fan works, the unit won't cut out.

With these changes made, I can crank the unit up and it pumps out the volume with ease. Yeah it generates heat, but it's all safely exhausted. The case stays cool and I can feel the warm air being exhausted.

The only thing I wasn't too keen on was the sound output in two-speaker stereo mode. It was lacking in base and treble, so I had to crank both dials all the way up to make the sound quality reasonable. What would be easy to do would be to buy an equalizer and then hook it up via the tape monitor. Then, pressing the tape monitor button would enable/disable the equalizer.

I would caution anyone who wants to buy this unit, if they don't have the ability to deal with the poor heat sink installation and/or add an active fan. I've heard many people who haven't had their units last very long because heat fried the power ICs. If you can get this unit cheap, and you can mod it, I'd say buy it. If you can't, then you may want to avoid it.

product_title: Sony HTCT260 Sound Bar Home Theater System (Discontinued by Manufacturer)
review_body:
My wife and I aren't audiophiles but we watch a lot of DVD movies and appreciate good sound quality. Our old 5.1 system was showing itself inadequate for our needs so my search began for an inexpensive replacement. After much research (plus a few questions here) I decided upon the Sony HTCT 260 based upon reviews here and elsewhere.
Ordered it here at Amazon and it arrived *much* sooner than anticipated (in fact, days before the optical digital cable I ordered at the same time).

As mentioned here many times before, setup was very easy. I used my existing coax digital audio cable as my ordered optical digital audio cable hadn't arrived yet. As it turns out, my Samsung HDTV is so old that the optical audio digital output is disabled when using HDMI for DVD-in making the coax connection my only usable option (yay for multiple options!) although the optical audio digital still makes a marked improvement when listening to standard TV output.

Difference in audio quality between the HTCT 260 and our old system is night and day! Our 20x15 front room wasn't conducive to a good 5.1 setup so for our needs a soundbar works just as well despite the lack of true surround sound.
What we wanted in a new audio system was clarity, depth and more bass. The HTCT 260 really delivers on all counts.

I test an audio system by listening to a scene that's complex and varied. There are a few scenes in \\"The Avengers\\" that work well, allowing me to determine not only what sounds are rendered (few? many? all?) but are they also clearly distinguishable. By going over the same scene multiple times after altering the HTCT 260's settings/tones/levels I could tweak the output to best suit our particular needs. The subwoofer & overall volume can be overwhelming in as small a room as our front room but that's easily dealt with by dialing it down to give us a solid bass presence and deep booms without knocking the windows out of their frames.

My SonyDVD player remote is nearly identical to the HTCT 260's remote so there is some confusion if I'm not careful, but I am glad it uses AA batteries instead of the usual AAA's (I have rechargeables for both sizes but AA's last much longer) and it had no difficulty recognizing my Samsung HDTV. If only the HTCT 260 remote's Bluetooth controls could also function for our DVD player!

If you want all the bells & whistles along with true 5.1/6.1/7.1 Surround Sound then look elsewhere. However, if you want quality sound at a budget price then give the HTCT 260 a *very* hard look. Despite the lack of HDMI and/or EQ (which we don't really need), I give the HTCT 260 5 stars for value & sound quality at a surprisingly low price.

product_title: Etymotic Research MC5 Noise Isolating In-Ear Earphones
review_headline: Really nice sounding headphones for under $100
review_body:
Sound: What the MC5 does best is reproduce the sound accurately. This does mean that the bass isn't as in your face as a lot of other headphones under $100. What you do hear is clear highs and mids with a lot of detail. I listen to a lot of ambient music, and with the MC5, the (HD like) sounds make me more emerge into the music. I also can pick up more details in the music with these headphones. Since the bass isn't so overwhelming, listening to EDM is a different experience. Some people might not like listening to such bass heavy music with these headphones, but I find that it's not really that bad. Over time I got used to the different listing style with EDM. Also to add as others have said, it really sounds like the music is coming from your head.

Comfort: This is really the issue with these headphones. You have to try the different tips to find which one is comfortable to you. I really like the foam tips. I find that they are the best in terms of Noise isolation and comfort. I can listen to hours comfortable with the foam tips. All the other tips just were not comfortable to me or didn't do as good job block noise. It's nice that they add so many options to try to find what works with you.

Noise Isolation: I can only talk about the foam tips as they are what I use. When you have the music on, it's like the whole world is gone with the only sound is the music playing. So be careful for traffic and other things of that nature. Also what I found is I missed phone calls because I can't hear the phone ringing. What is still noticeable is the wire sounds (the sounds when the wire rubs on your shirt). I only really notice this when listing to audio books and other quieter tracks.

Durability- My first MC5 lasted about 2 years and 8 months before the wire covering stared to expose the wires. Which is average life for headphones

So would I recommend these headphones? Yes, I would. The sound is very accurate and it does block external sounds.

review_headline: Great sound - Customer Return is top notch

Now the replacement process:
- I contacted JLabs and sent them a picture of my earphones. ... That's it. Easy!

This compared to other companies:
- Skullcandy has a lifetime warranty and I've used this about 5 times now. You need to mail in the headphones, so basically I've spent an extra $30 for replacements. Most of their headphones last me about 3 months.
- Shure has a 2 year warranty. I replaced it once and then the now the same issue is happening, it will cost $70 to replace.
- Bose - 1 year warranty. Since my headphones were out of warranty, it cost $70 + shipping to replace them. Also their replacement cable wiring broke on me as well.
- Seinheiser - 1 year warranty. Need to ship in the headphones.

Not bad. Let's see how my new pair of JLabs holds up. Thanks!

Update:

product_title: Sony MDRZX100 Headphones
review_body:
I go through headphones very quickly (three or four pairs in the last year). I've had these for a week, and they've been excellent (I have high-hopes for their lifespan).

Pros:
> The speakers can swivel and rest flat. Last week, I worked parking cars in a large field lot, and could listen to music without having to compromise my hearing.
> Despite being able to use them as small neck-speakers, they are also very loud when worn over the ears without having to be turned up all the way. The sound-quality when wearing them is clear and even works with bass-heavy* songs.
> Sturdy design. The cord, the sliding head-pieces, and the earpieces themselves; all seem to be made out of durable well-put-together materials. I've yanked and tripped and smashed them and they're still in excellent shape.

Cons:
> Because the ear-pieces rotate flat (and only in that one direction), storage is limited to "flat" rather than any other position. But, really, that's probably the better storage position anyway.
> Sleek, white, "modern" design means that any dirt, or wear, is immediately visible (but I knew that when I ordered them).

Overall: Great pair of reasonably priced headphones.

*These are not bass-heavy headphones, and don't act as such. You still can't get the clarity of bass that you would with higher-quality (and considerably higher-priced) headphones, or speakers (with a subwoofer). But for what they are: I'll take it!

EDIT (4 months later):
>>I haven't scuffed these, and it's been over 4 months now - so my "con" about them being all sleek and white has been debunked.
>>I walked around in a rainstorm with these, and they still work fine (I was a bit concerned).
>>The covering over the ear-pads has ripped around the inside speaker. This hasn't bothered functionality, but I fear it means they will deteriorate faster than I had wanted.

EDIT (1/27/2015 - Approximately 2.5 years later):

product_title: Arrowmounts AM-P18B Articulating Wall Mount for 37 to 60 Inch Flat Panel TVs AM-P18B/37-60 Black
review_headline: Good looking mount, bad packaging & unforgiving install
review_body:
I replaced a fixed mount with this full motion mount to make it easier to watch TV in the kitchen and breakfast table. Let me say that once I got it installed, it is working as expected. Getting it to that point was a journey.

First, it came in shoddy packaging. The shipping box was ripped and the manufacturer's external packaging left something to be desired. Upon opening the boxes, I found screws rolling around loosely and felt the mount pieces were not secured well in the box.

If this is your first time to install a mount, the directions are worthless. A single sheet only provided a list of the parts and some arcane pictures of how to drill into studs. There were no verbiage or pictures on which screws to uses, how to use the spacers, or what to do if your studs are spaced farther than the mounting plate.

Yes, my house is from an era when building standards were not in place so the spacing between studs was closer 21 inches. The mounting plate does not span 21 inches. I think it was 18 or 19 inches...make a note to measure your stud spacing prior to buying or you will have to improvise.

Here is what I did to improvise. I have some left over plywood from some cabinets I built. I cut it down to span the stud gap and doubled up with two layers. I screwed the plywood into the studs then mounted the plate to the plywood. I was able to align the mount with one set of screws going into the studs. My TV is fairly light so I am pretty confident that this will hold well. Take into account the weight of your TV if you decide to go this route.

One last thing to note, there did not seem an easy way to separate out the articulating arm from the mounting base. It would have made installation way easier to separate the arms as the unit is heavy. I ended up extending the arms then resting it on my shoulders while I screwed the bolts in. Again, planning helps in this regard as i had measured and drilled the holes prior to placing the plywood on the wall.

in the end, what should have taken about 30 minutes to mount ended up taking about three hours. Plan ahead to make sure you have the right product for your situation and hopefully things will go smoother.

product_title: Bose QuietComfort 20 Headphones
review_headline: Slightly better NoiseCancel than the QC-15 but…
review_body:
When I first saw this I was excited, because the QC-15s have a few cons (Bulkier, doesn't work without battery). So this was like the best of passive noise canceling (like my -now stolen- etymotic) plus Bose's active noise canceling tech, which, at least on the QC-15 is superb.

I am an Android user (and have a series of iOS + Apple products like this very Macbook Air). I develop software so I need iPhones, iPads and Androids.

When I got my QC-15, I remember going to an App Store with my MBAir to try whether the mic would work when connected in the computer. It did, so it was awesome, because I could use it to Skype with people without using the integrated mic in the computer while wearing the awesome headphones.

I later gave my QC-15 to a very good friend who couldn't afford them and decided I was eventually going to buy new ones.

I finally got these new QC20. As an Android user, I picked the Android version. That was my first mistake.

I'll summarize the pros/cons:

Good Things:
- They are light and very portable. The battery doesn't really bother much (but it has a few caveats).
- Moderately easy to fit and less tiring (for me) than the full in-ear-canal (Etymotic stuff). I flew 16 hours straight and they didn't really cause a major problem (tho I could feel them by the end).
- Easy to sleep with these on a plane while tilting your head. Still some vibrations can be heard, but with the others is really hard for obvious reasons.
- The USB charging is nice (Boeing 767-400 have USBs on every seat so you can watch the TV while not draining your battery).
- The new "Aware Mode" is also a nice thing, but on a plane it will not necessarily be loud enough to hear a person talking to you. You have to turn it on-off when you want to use it, because when that is on, the cancelled noise is nowhere near as good as when it's off.
- The sound is good, but these are not top of the end headphones. The idea is for sound to be acceptable in noisy environments. It's certainly not the best sound you can get, but it will be probably the best isolation in certain environments. And the combination of both is extremely decent.
- You can use them even when turned off as regular headphones.
- The cable is nice and doesn't create the annoying sound (known to Etymotics and such) when hit by objects or your own body.

Now the Bad things:
- With the 3 sizes (S-M-L) ear tips, you might not find an appropriate one for your ear size. Mines (I was using Med) would slowly pop out after a few hours. Not a big deal, but I wish Bose would offer more choices (Like Etymotic does).
- The battery is not heavy, but heavy enough to cause disconnects if it hangs from a loose plug (like on a plane where the plug is abused a few times a day).
- The position of the battery in the "cable" is a win-loss situation. Sometimes you feel like it's great and sometimes you wished it where somewhere else.
- The Amount of cable after the battery could use a few more inches (it's really really short) so you have to basically "stick" the battery with your phone and every time you hold your phone, you have to hold the battery or it bother you all the time
- The Android/Windows version only comes with 1 button (plus the button to activate aware mode). The button serves as a play/pause on any app that is registered to operate with media buttons (most should anyway). But it has no volume controls (lame). The iOS version of these controls in the QC15 work on Android (the volume doesn't but the play pause does, so you get the same functionality). On the plus side, the QC15 buttons (for iOS) work with a Macbook so you get a Mic, mute, volume keys and this is why I'm returning my QC20. I use a Macbook Air and I need the headphones + mic for Google Hangouts or Skype. It doesn't work for some reason. The MIC works on my Nexus 4 tho (but no mute which would have been great).
- Since the buttons are not interchangeable (like in the QC-15), you're stuck with what you got. I'd get the iOS -EVEN- if you have an Android device (don't know about Windows).
- The tips (rubber?) are very weird and fit ok, but they are "fragile" (I almost broke one trying to remove it) DON'T PULL. Read instructions.
- For obvious reasons, you can't detach the cables and use the noise cancel feature alone (like in the QC-15)

Conclusion:
These are great headphones if you travel a lot (especially on short trips where you don't carry a lot of stuff and you have limited space in your bag). They win the size war vs. the QC-15.
I've compared the noise cancellation inside a 737-900 mid-flight side by side. I asked a fellow passenger for their QC-15 and tried one after the other for a couple of times. The sound isolation is pretty much the same, I'd say the QC20 have a little but more mugginess to voices because they are somewhat in-ear and provide more passive isolation. But the "real" engine noise was cancelled by both in a very similar way. If anything, the QC20 wins by a small margin.
The sound quality is hard to compare (especially in a plane!) but with the QC-15 I had to turn my volume all the way up. With the QC20 it was 3/4 (for the same volume experience). I don't know if this was because of the battery or what.
All in all, these are expensive headphones that I can only recommend if you travel a lot and don't want to carry extra batteries or don't want to deal with the "big" QC-15.
The battery is not replaceable so I guess that could be a factor. It lasted through two flights: 8 + 4 hours with no problem whatsoever, but then again, Bose claims 16 hours.

So… which one do you get?

It really depends. If you're looking for portability, you won't look back, the whole thing is really light for what it does!
If you hate in-ear stuff, go QC-15.
If you want sound quality, get an AudioTechnica or similar :)
If you don't mind carrying AAA batteries around and want to use the noise canceling feature without carrying a cable and stuff, the QC-15 can do it.
If you need Macbook (Air/Pro) microphone compat, get the iOS version (even if you have an Android phone). Note: I haven't tested the QC20 iOS version, but I did have the QC15 iOS version and it works on both android (as a mic+play/pause) and on Mac (as Volume+mic+play/pause). The volume controls won't work on Android and that's why the presumably sell two versions, so you don't get controls that don't work… I assume the QC20 will have a similar behavior. But you should dbl-check.

I will be personally getting the QC15 again instead of these (which I am returning as we speak).

What would I like to see improved?

More ear tips
Ability to detach the whole battery thing and use them as regular earphones.
Volume buttons for Android (that also work on Macbooks!)
Battery should be replaceable, otherwise you're going to have to throw the whole thing away in a few years.
Better price, 200 dollars would be better.ut no mute which would have been great).

product_title: Pioneer SC-1523-K 9.2-Channel Network A/V Receiver
review_headline: Feature rich, excellent sound and some surprising gaps...
review_body:
Nine month update:

While the fundamental areas of attention (both the positive ones and those that are not so much) in the original review (below) remain intact, the selling price of the this receiver has dropped considerably since it arrived on the market. These make its obvious shortcomings less glaring. Assuming the price stays in the three figure range, I'm bumping this from three stars to four stars. While you could never go wrong selecting this receiver, you'll need to reinvest some of the resulting savings from recent discounting into add-on hardware if you want either Bluetooth or WiFi capability.

-----

Original review:

When offered the opportunity to review the SC-1523-K, I couldn't wait to try it out. I've been on an audio (and later, audio/video) upgrade trajectory since Jimmy Carter was president, and have delighted in the incremental changes that arrived with each upgrade process. And even though my electronics budget has grown over the years, the price of this receiver is still several times more than I would normally consider spending (even if I can afford a little extra extravagance now).

Here's what quickly became apparent about this model: while long on functions and features, serious gaps are apparent in the user interface (and at least one absent input) that will come as a big surprise to anybody parting with the premium price of this receiver.

The issues begin as soon as you open the box. The enclosed documentation consists of a quick start guide, a guide to avoiding speaker wiring shorts, a generic safety sheet and warranty information. Conspicuously absent: a printed user guide. Yes, it's downloadable from Pioneer as a .pdf. The user guide is 131 pages long, the features are many, and this should have been included has a hard copy in the box so users aren't forced to refer to a display device. This is an unacceptable omission for a device this feature dense and this pricey.

The SC-1523-K arrives \\"network ready\\"; it can be connected directly to a wired LAN out of the box. Want to connect wirelessly? Fine, but according to Pioneer you'll be doing so *only* via the Pioneer AS-WL300 adapter, and you'll be adding almost another Benjamin (plus!) to your purchase price. You can also add Bluetooth connectivity. Of course, this will also require *another* proprietary Pioneer adapter, and you'll get to part with another Benjamin to do so. Please not that some users have had success with non-Pioneer network/Bluetooth adapters, so your experience could vary (but don't look to Pioneer for a list of supported/compatible adapters from non-Pioneer sources; you'll have to locate this on your own).
Many inexpensive electronics components arrive with either WiFi or Bluetooth (and in some cases, both) integrated , and I can certainly find less expensive AV receivers with *both* types of connectivity built in. That one of these capabilities was not included in this device --which touts interactivity and network capabilities-- is surprising.

Want to provide input from a standard 3.5mm stereo output adapter (like you might use from an iPod or a smartphone?). You won't be doing so with this receiver. My current 2-year old Sony A/V receiver, which cost a fraction of what this model has such an input...

The SC-1523-K includes a claimed \\"interactive\\" set-up (Windows CD included; Mac users will have to download for their systems) as part of its \\"AVNavigator\\" software package. Be prepared. The software is not especially intuitive, and you'll still be referring regularly to the user manual (on your display device, since it's not available as a printed document).

The components I hung from this machine are very basic compared to its full capabilities (a simple 2.1 (stereo with subwoofer) audio system, cable/DVR and Blue-Ray player inputs, all feeding a single HDMI output to a television.

Both the front panel controls and the remote are overly complicated and very non-intuitive. The remote has more than 60 buttons (some mulch-functional, all the same color and most the same size) crowding its surface, and you won't be figuring it out without frequent trips to the user guide (remember...it's a .pdf...so I hope you haven't turned off your display device yet!). Neither will you be reading the miniscule labels in the light of room dimmed for movie watching.

The volume display is in an arcane dB scaling. Why Pioneer chose this instead of a progress-level minimum/maximum indicator is anybody's guess.

Users of surround sound speaker systems will get to use an included calibration microphone to balance the levels of their speakers (a use case I was unable to test).

Once you get past these deficiencies --and for me, some are deal-breakers when it comes to long-term usability--you'll find many features: up to 9.2 speaker inputs, speaker bi-wiring, supplementary amplifier integration, HDMI inputs aplenty (9!), USB inputs, RCA inputs, optical inputs and 3 HDMI outputs. It will provide power to deliver sound worthy of whatever source or speakers you place in the stream.

Finally, when you're ready to move this into place: bring a strong friend. It weights 39 pounds...much more than even vacuum-tube analog HF transceivers I used in the navy in the last century. This is not a criticism, but a heads up: some people may need help carrying or moving this.

In short: Lots of features and capability, lots of mass, and some surprising gap areas in a premium priced A/V receiver.

In short: Lots of features and capability, lots of mass, and some surprising gap areas in a premium priced A/V receiver.

Finally: this item has dropped in price considerably since its release. The usability issues that nicked it two stars remain, but its faults seem less grievous when the pricing is displayed with just three figures.

I have a Macbook Pro purchased in mid-2010, and this product worked for me. Two adjustments I had to make:

- In order for my TV to display my computer screen and in order for my computer to detect the TV, I had to perform the following steps:
1. In Display Preferences, click on \\"Detect Displays\\".
2. Then immediately connect the adapter cable.
If I performed the steps by doing (2) then (1), then I would have the issue where my computer did not detect the TV. I had to perform the steps in order, (1) then (2).
- After my computer has successfully detected the TV, I would go to Sound Preferences to make sure the sound output is the TV and not my Macbook's speakers. This only needs to be performed the first time you hook up to your TV.

Once I made the above two adjustments, everything worked great! Video quality and sound quality are both excellent.

Then I actually read the speaker's user guide and moved the speakers forward (3 feet from the wall behind, 2 feet at either side, 6 feet in between) and moved my chair forward a few feet. THAT'S when these speakers shined. Upping the amp and finding the right position made these speakers go from being a lateral move from the Energy RC-70s to a major improvement. product_title: Sony SRF-M37W Walkman Digital Tuning Weather/FM/AM Stereo Radio (Black)
review_body: I own 3 of these now. The oldest one is about 10 years old. The markings are worn off of the face, the belt clip broke, and the battery door is barely holding on, but it still works great! They get excellent reception and an alkaline battery (AAA) will last at least 40 hours of continuous use. I use one 5 days a week, 8 hours a day at work. They're plenty tough. I have another at home for chores like mowing the lawn. The third is for backup and because it seems that whenever I find a product that I really, really like, they go away. Expect to replace headphones from time to time. If you're gonna be moving around and catching the wires on stuff, buy cheap headphones, because I've yet to see a set at any price that will survive such conditions for very long. Rechargeable AAA batteries are a good idea if you're going to use it a lot and they work as well or better than alkalines in this radio. The lock feature is very nice and helps keep it tuned while you're moving around. Also, the rotary volume adjustment is a convenient feature as I prefer it to buttons when I need to get the volume down in a hurry (like when the boss or a coworker is addressing me). The volume works even when the lock feature is on. The volume is loud enough that I can hear it through foam ear plugs (headphones are NOT ear protection and earphones can be a safety hazard in some environments). The belt clip is removable and the radio will fit in a shirt or pants pocket. It's about the size of a pack of non-filter cigarettes. The digital tuner is nice because you don't have to search for a frequency. Just set it, lock it, and if you lose the signal there's either interference or you're out of range. No guesswork like with a dial tuner. Hope this review helps.

product_title: Soundbeats Seasky 3.5mm Plug In-ear Earphone with Microphone & Volume Control for iPhone, iPod, iPad Best Seller
review_headline: Enhanced bass?!  Panasonic RPHJE120K sound better and are cheaper.
review_body:
My last experience with earbud headphones was not very good - I couldn't get them to stay in at all - so I didn't want to buy a nice pair. When I saw that even the cheapest ones now included multiple rubber tips, I thought I would give it a try again. I bought a few sub-$10 earbud headphones to try out. I typically use pro grade over-the-ear Sennheisers for audio, but wanted something lighter. So far, I've just tested these and the Panasonic RPHJE120K earbuds. These Seasky headphones say \\"Enhanced Bass\\", but they had almost no bass response whatsoever. The mids are muddy, and the upper frequencies are very dominant. On tracks with a bunch of treble, the Seaskys lose all definition and it turns into a very irritating white/pink noise wash. Almost headache-inducing. EQ didn't seem to help any.

The Panasonics were a few bucks cheaper and have tremendously better sound quality. On certain tracks, I even had to EQ the bass down with the Panasonics, but for most modern rock/pop stuff the extra bass was nice. The Seaskys were packaged better - in a nice black box that was easy to open. The Panasonic ones came in a plastic clamshell that was designed by sadists. I had to use very sharp scissors to open them and I still was cussing the packaging. I thought I was going to short out the cord before I even tried them on because the packaging was pinching the headphones. The Seaskys medium rubber tip fit best for me, and it was ever-so-slightly more comfortable than the medium tip on the Panasonics. It was easier to change the tips on the Seaksys because the driver post is round, whereas it is elliptical on the Panasonics.

But since I will only open the package and change rubber tips ONCE over the lifetime of the headphones, the vastly superior sound quality of the Panasonic headphones made them a no-brainer over the Seaskys. I'm honestly shocked by the difference in sound quality between the two since they're in the same price range and havethe same size driver, etc. I'm not even sure I would be willing to use the Seaskys as a backup pair for audiobooks...I definitely would not use them for any type of music.

review_body:
This is a direct comparison between the two soundbars my husband and I recently tried, and why we kept the Yamaha YAS-101. I don't want to go on and on, so suffice to say the Yamaha wins, hands down. After trying and returning three (3), yes three! different JBLs, (same model) thinking each one was defective, we concluded that it was the unit in general that just wasn't performing to the standard we were expecting, given the brand and the many positive reviews we'd read beforehand. We then purchased the Yamaha, and have been extremely pleased with its performance in every way. First of all, the big negative with JBL is the remote control. It's cheaply made and works only intermittently (at best) - very frustrating. The light indicators (such as they are) are located on top of the unit, making it difficult to see when one has the thing positioned on a mantle above the TV. Granted, ours is an unusual configuration, but that's another story. The lights on the Yamaha are on the front of the soundbar and very easy to see and monitor; and said lights are much more functional than the JBL's. They actually \\"tell\\" you what's happening when you're using the remote. Dolby is better on the Yamaha. It has Dolby Digital and Dolby Pro-Logic. (We weren't receiving Dolby Digital when it was connected to the TV, but took some online advice I found and reconnected from DirecTV box to sound bar, using the optical digital cable, and we're now getting Dolby Digital for all broadcasts. HDMI cable is from TV to DirectTV.) Re: sound...with boosted bass (subwoofer) set at highest level, great sound for a small to medium sized room - far superior to TV speakers (and the JBL) which, after all, is why most of us buy this in the first place.

Bottom line - unless Bluetooth is important to you (wasn't for us, since we have internet music through our audio receiver and built in ceiling speakers), buy the Yamaha. Dollar for dollar and the MSRP dollars are the same for these two models, you're getting a much better engineered, better looking, all around better unit with the Yamaha. And guess what? THE REMOTE WORKS! - consistently and well. After about 6 weeks of JBL frustration, we're now very happy campers!

review_headline: Hate Apple!  Love this iPod classic!
review_body:
It's definitely a love/hate relationship with Apple products. I don't like iTunes. (Yes, I prefer to manually manage my content, thank you. No, I do not want you to decide what songs I would like based on my current selections, thank you. No I do not want you syncing all of the content on the entire computer, thank you.)

But if I can get past the aggravation of being treated like a moron in the name of sales, this little media player is just right.

I started out with an iPod nano that I got free using some AmEx points, and used that daily during workouts.

Got hooked. With a pair of Bose headphones, the sound was spectacular. Workouts sped by.

After a couple of years, when the battery on the nano started to die a bit, i decided to upgrade to something that had a bit of a screen and more storage space for podcasts and video bits. No way did I ever think this system would put out the bass like it does. Once I got the levels set on all my speakers, I cranked the volume just to see what it would do. I was rattling the windows on the second floor of our house, and I was set up in our basement! It was Awesome! Just by adding this subwoofer, my electronic kit was louder than my acoustic drum set and sounded twenty times better! I couldn't believe it! And if that wasn't enough, recently I purchased a 2008 Dodge Grand Caravan SXT. The sound system was extremely lacking bass. Since I was broke after buying the Van, I was looking for anything I might already have that would do the job. I noticed that my van is equipped with a power converter so you can plug things in from your home like an air compressor or digital game, etc. When I saw this, I figured what the heck!, why not try plugging the Yamaha sub in and see what happens. Well, again, Holy $&^*&%!!!! It literally shakes my van! I don't need to buy anything else except maybe upgrading the stock 6x9 speakers. I don't need to buy an amp or subwoofer enclosure or any wiring kit. All I had to do was plug this in and run an audio signal to it. That was it! Now I have an extremely loud sound system in my Van! Freakin' crazy! Everyone I've showed it to has been in disbelief. I love Yamaha products and the SW315 is definitely one of their best. Buy it, you'll love it!!!

product_title: Clip Plus 4 GB MP3 Player (Black)
review_headline: Great bang for the buck. (when working properly)
review_body:
I was looking for an inexpensive MP3 player and it was between this and an iPod Shuffle.

I do have other Apple products (iPhone and iPad), but for a simple MP3 player I ultimately chose the 4GB Sansa Clip for several reasons:

-It has a screen. I want to listen to specific songs or albums depending on the mood I'm in, and it's much easier to navigate through your collection than it would be on an iPod Shuffle.
-With 4GB, the Sansa Clip has twice the storage space than Shuffle's non-expandable 2GB.
-It has an expandable memory slot. Amazon currently has 16GB MicroSD cards for $11 and 64GB cards for $49, so it can potentially hold a lot more of music.
-The Sansa Clip is $20 cheaper than the Shuffle.
-You don't need an application (like iTunes) to copy your songs onto the Clip. The instructions tell you to install Rhapsody, but I never bothered to. Simply copy files into the \Music\ folder.
-Although I never use it, it has an FM radio tuner.

As for the Sansa Clip itself, I'm very happy with it so far. Haven't had any crashes or battery issues yet like other reviewers have.

UPDATE: Only a few months after purchase, I've had many issues with my unit. On an almost daily basis, it just stops playing music and I have to cycle the power. A few times, it wouldn't turn on until I did a reset (hold down the power button for 30 seconds). Unfortunately, I am living abroad so the 1 year warranty is pointless while I'm away from the US.

review_body:
I spent a lot of time researching cable for my home theatre set up in my new home. I had previously purchased AudioQuest cables to run my two front mains, but they were a bit short after the move (always buy longer than you think you will ever need as they say). Anyhow, I just refused to pay that much for cables again. Most articles that I have read (that seem to be unbiased) said that a good quality 12GA copper cable would power just about anything. I came across this and decided to give it a try.

I am using a Denon 4310 (yes, I know, it's older) powering Definitive Technology Mythos ST's front mains, Mythos Ten center, Mythos Gem XL's for rears, and also a couple of small Polk Audio for height channels left and right. I am using this wire to power the front mains and center only. The only reason that I am not using this for the other speakers is that 1. I needed smaller diameter cable to run under carpet and 2. all the other speakers are small and unpowered. The main focus for this wire was for the front mains (R and L) as those have powered subwoofers in each of them, so I wanted a good thick cable to carry all the signal for the low, mid, and highs to these speakers. I am not using a separate subwoofer as the ST's do a great job of providing room shaking bass by themselves (not that I WOULN'T add a sub at some point...).

Anyway, after all was said and done, I could not hear any audible difference between this wire and my previous AudioQuest cables. The only place I noticed a difference was in my wallet. The other cables ran $150 for a pair of 10lf cables. This is a 100lf spool for about a third of the price! The cable was surprisingly easy to bend and cut for such a thick wire. Installation was a breeze! I terminated with Sewell Direct banana plugs and everything went smooth.

I highly recommend this cable for your audio needs! I still have over half of my spool left and am glad to have the extra cable!

product_title: Parasound - Zdac - Digital to Analog Converter - Black
review_body:
Being an analogue enthusiast for nearly 40 years, I decided to upgrade my computer audio so I put together a modest package from Audio Advisor and since I live in the middle of nowhere I decided to trust their salesperson and get everything at once. I got the ZDAC in silver, a pr. of Audioengine A5+ speakers in bamboo (with table stands), 2 Pangea Signature power cords, and a single 8ft. Kimber 8TC spkr cable (to run to the right speaker). I had some Acoustic Zen WOW and Kimber Silver Streak interconnects and a Tara Labs USB cable laying around so I went to work breaking in the system and using JRiver Media Center as the media source for my FLAC collection which is extensive. BTW the ZDAC and powered speakers plugged directly into a Maestro wall outlet (I can't tell you how important this is!!). First impressions were good as the combination produced a very detailed sound that was a bit lightweight in image density compared to my dedicated analogue system with a Rega RP6 Van Den Hul cartridge OTL tube mono-blocks, Sound Lab electrostats etc. But I was taken back by the musicality of the system and thought it just right for a computer. I did prefer the warmer midrange of the copper WOW interconnects compared to the Kimber silver. Next I contacted The Cable Company and they sent me 5 different USB cables and a couple of 75ohm cables (including the Black Cat SilverStar)to compare. I ended up picking the Cardas Clear USB as it was the clear winner, with the Black Cat a distant second. In my set-up the Cardas had real synergy with the rest of the components. After a few weeks of listening I then added my Hsu Research VFT-2 MK4 sub to the mix and as long as I kept the volume on it pretty low, it added nicely to the mix. Next I tried some different power cables, notably the Shunyata Venom-3 and found it so lacking in bass that I sent it back. The point of this review is this: I can now listen to digital music with real enjoyment. My favorite Diana Krall recordings sound nice a relaxed and while her image is not nearly as large or palpable as my expensive analogue system, she is right there with me, just the way I want, centered nicely between my (2) 27\\" computer monitors. There isn't much depth but that's not what I was looking for in a computer audio system. A friend brought over a couple of his DAC's for comparison last week including the diminutive Dragonfly, one from Arcam, and one from Creek. I am happy to report that they all sounded pretty good, and I could easily live with the Arcam rDAC. Together my friend and I have a gazillion hours of live Phish recordings that we can now jam out to so that is great!
For someone who despised digital for decades I am happy to report that the new breed of DAC's can put a smile on this old face. If you get a ZDAC, experiment with cables, especially power cords as they make a real difference. And don't forget to upgrade your wall outlet or you will truly miss out on the fun. Hope you find this helpful.

product_title: Onkyo TX-NR626 7.2-Channel Network Audio/Video Receiver (Discontinued by Manufacturer)
review_headline: Runs hot, interface needs some work
review_body:
Overall I'm very happy with it. The size and design is about as expected for an A/V receiver. I chose this model in part because of the powered zone 2 which I use for the patio speakers. Unfortunately it does run a little hotter than I expected, I'm concerned about leaving it in an enclosed cabinet area and it obviously isn't very small or sleek so putting it out to be seen is less than desirable.

One complaint is the interface. It displays on your TV and you can use SiriusXM, Spotify and others over your home network. Unfortunately they're pretty basic. The SiriusXM application does not support the more recent "MyXM" streaming or on demand content. I'm OK with this, but if you use any of their mobile or web applications you'll miss those features. Second the Spotify app is very simple, you can search, play a playlist or play from a starred list. I do not see any options to use the "radios" in Spotify and when you're using a playlist there is no sorting, shuffling, etc. available.

So, overally, very good with basic access to Sirius, Spotify, etc. but the applications are missing features available on other platforms.

review_headline: Amazing sound, beautiful design, great price.
review_body:
I could not be more happy with this product. Over the past few months I have been on a mission to find the best sounding wireless audio dock/bookshelf speaker system. I have bought and returned the Soundfreaq Sound Platform 2, Bose SoundLink, Jawbone Jambox, and Sonos Play: 3. This Samsung system not only sounded MUCH better than all but the Sonos, but is easily the most attractive of the bunch. It looks simply stunning on my living room end table

The sound quality of this dock matched only by the Sonos Play: 3 which costs $150 more. I decided that I would rather get basically a year of Spotify free than a negligible boost in sound quality. This unit fills my living room, kitchen, and dining room with wonderfully clear and beautiful music from any of my iDevices or Galaxy S3. I never use the built in dock but is a nice touch should you need it.

Setup was easy for me but could be somewhat complicated for the non-tech savy, but trust me, it is worth every bit of effort.
If I had to come up with one criticism, it would be the ability to change the "Bass" setting. It doesn't sound bad, but I am a minimalist, just set the unit up to sound great out of the box, don't let the user ruin all of Samsung's hard work by fiddling with the EQ.

You will not find a better sounding system in this price range, period. Trust me, I tried.

Here is the radio I purchased from Amazon.com in Oct. 2011. I am returning it to you. I will tell you why.

3. Emergency band...(after small quake)

Apparently I was wrong to think this radio would be a good choice for any of my minimal needs.
I would like to return it for a refund. While it is true I've had it since Oct. 2011

I should have read the 37. ONE Star (Amazon.com) reviews..saying exactly what I've just written...but I was, like others, blinded by the image, and great writing about this inadequate radio.

review_body:
Pros: Small, good construction, decent power especially for a portable device, and lots of input options. The use of a removable standardized battery is great too. Battery life is also very good, I've been able to get about 4 hours at nearly full volume (36 out of 40) without it shutting down. Excellent price. Comes with everything you need except a USB charger but those are a dime a dozen now. My wife loves it to take into the bathroom for shower music (but not in the shower itself, obviously) ...

Cons: Sound quality is just OK. It's quite clear but the shape of the unit makes it difficult to produce low frequencies, so don't expect much in the way of bass. The frequency response is also peaky in some areas, so it's not what I'd call an audiophile system but it is truly great for less than $40. The shape, though excellent for desk environment, can be difficult to deal with in a portable situation. It's easy to carry but sometimes tough to fit in a small bag.

So would I buy it again? Absolutely. I was in the process of building myself something similar but this is far more flexible and sounds good enough to be acceptable. If you're looking for a desktop/laptop speaker for office background listening, a "booster" for the laptop sound system for traveling or presentations, or a way to turn your smartphone into an occasional boombox, this is a great buy. Does it compete with the $200 units? Nope. Does it compete with the $80 to $100 units in stores? Most definitely and at half the price.

For reference, I'm an audio nut and a pc/network tech, so I'm decently informed on this subject. My home system includes brands like Velodyne, Magnepan, and Luxman. My car stereo carries Alpine, Eclipse, and JL Audio. I know good sound when I hear it.

product_title: Wi-Fi Music Player with 3.5-Inch Color Display
review_body:
I don't know why it took me so long to get an internet radio- I found this radio to be easy to set up although a touch cumbersome due to needing to enter data such as wifi access codes by scrolling through an alphabet on the screen with a dial. The sound is reasonable for a small speaker and is helped by tweaking the bass upward a touch. The volume knob is the black knob on top which looks somewhat like a stubby antenna and strangers to the radio rarely could figure out how to change the volume on their own. I also found the iphone app to be useful and easier to use than the radio itself or the remote control it comes with. Sadly after a week or so the radio began to have troubles hooking into my wifi and would frequently rebuffer and restart songs. Soon after, it also began to make a strange warbling sound for about 30 seconds and be unresponsive to any controls until it shut itself down and restarted with a message about reinitializing network access and I sometimes would have to reenter wifi information to get it to log on to the internet. The episodes of failing to connect started infrequently but soon were occurring a couple times an hour. My home wifi is cable modem based and none of my computers, tv's, or other electronics have any problems even when streaming video so problems with my wifi setup seemed unlikely. Contacting customer service got a response about hard rebooting and reentering all the data again which did not fix the problem so I was given an address to mail in the unit for warrantly repair. I paid my 18 dollars to UPS to ship and got a notice when it arrived and the repair has taken just a bit over a week and I was notified the unit is on the way back to me so I will have lost about 3 weeks of use. I will update the review once I get a chance to use the unit again. I like the radio but looking through all the reviews there does seem to be a not uncommon amount of units out there which have the same problems.

10/2/13 UPDATE

After sending in my radio for warranty work I received a replacement in the mail. Once going back through the setup (10 minutes) I have had no further problems. The radio is back to being on all the time and I don't know how I survived being in our kitchen without it. I will up my stars to 4 with the one star subtraction due to the slightly wonky input style when setting up and the sound which is good but not great (but really what I expect in a small unit like this)

product_title: AmazonBasics HDMI to DVI  Adapter Cable - 9.8 Feet (3 Meters)
review_headline: Don't buy this cable if you want it to carry an audio signal.
review_body:
This cable is HDMI to DVI-D, meaning it only carries digital signals, but it is dual-layer, meaning it can carry two video signals. If you want it to carry an audio signal also you want it to have a DVI-I connector, which carries both HD digital video and audio. It should have two separate sets of 9 pins plus two small pins on each side of the large flat pin. This way it can connect to a screen with built in speakers -- either a TV or computer monitor -- and the quality will be the same as if the screen had an HDMI input.
You can see pictures at

product_title: Munitio Billets Earphones with 1 Button Universal Mic Control
review_body:
OVERALL:

Sound 8.5/10 Very good soundstage for such a price and a tremendous bass to boost.

Design 9/10 This is subjective to the individual but I liked the design a lot.

Durability 8/10 Sturdy light aluminum enables these to take a bit of a beating.

Comfort 6.5/10 Nothing great, but you won't notice them unless you think about it.

The good:

-One of the best contenders for an IEM for this price; money well spent.

-Sound quality: Great highs. The sound signature of these is like a V. You can really hear the highs with these more-so than I had anticipated. The mids are decent as well, though for $70, despite being nothing to scold at, it's nothing to really praise, either. Detailed bass. The bass isn't like the V-Moda IEMs or iBeats I've owned before. The bass is punchy and actually allows you to hear the mids and highs a lot better, though some of it still bleeds out into the mid range, but nothing I can really complain about for how immersive yet accurate the bass is.

-Build quality: It's very light-weight despite being pretty darn durable. I dropped a textbook on them and no damage whatsoever was done. The cord is also nice; smooth rubber makes it resistant to getting tangled all the time.

-Design: I really liked the 9mm design. It was originally what attracted my attention. I got the black ones and they're a nice metallic dull color.

The bad:

-In the details it was supposed to come with 3 sets of red eartips and 3 sets of black. The case included only the black ones. This is just a small annoyance. The eartips go in your ear and will never be seen by you or anyone else while you're using them so it doesn't really matter what color they are since the material and size are the same. I'm not going to hold them accountable; this is more for letting others know the updated specifications of the item.

-Bass may be a little overpowering forgenres that are not already bass-oriented. To fix this, you can just mess with your EQ settings a bit and it'll be fine.

Nothing extraordinary:

-Comfort: It fits well enough, better than conventional earbuds by far, but that's to be expected from any pair of earbuds $50+.

-Mic: I hope you didn't buy these for the mic. I sure didn't. But I went ahead and tried the audio on it anyway. It's mediocre at best and annoying to use at worst. I would just use it as a pause and play button. (I plugged it into an iPhone and pushing the button toggled the music on and off)

product_title: B&O PLAY by BANG & OLUFSEN - Earphones Black
review_headline: Fantastic for a year then died
review_body:
These are literally the only headphones I have ever owned that I never had to fiddle with during any type of workout. I put them on once and they stay put through cardio, weights, running outdoors etc. Ear buds I typically have to re-seat every couple minutes at least.

For all the people complaining that they have trouble keeping them in their ears I really feel bad for you since these aren't designed to fit in the ear. God that must hurt jamming these into the ear. They are supposed to sit outside the ear canal.

The sound is superb in the mid-highs but very little base mostly because again these don't seal the ear canal.

Unfortunately this is where the good ends.

As other reviewers have pointed out the wire to the connector is very thin and is a direct input as opposed to angled like most headphones. What this means is that the wire takes an inordinate amount of abuse and since it is delicate to begin with doesn't last nearly as long as headphones in this price range should. Once the wire is frayed you will lose one or both speakers making these useless. I found this out the hard way today as I had to say good-bye to my beloved B&O's. Really a shame that such a well crafted headphone would have such a fatal flaw.

Doubtful that I am going to replace this pair with another since it doesn't appear they have made any improvements to the wire and connection.

Back to constantly fixing ear buds I guess.

Other reviews have mentioned a loud whooshing noise in wind, which I haven't noticed. It was fairly windy yesterday and I could hear it but it didn't seem any different than other headphones.

You can hear some ambient noise but not a lot, so I do hug the side of the trail to avoid getting run over by a bicyclist.

Overall, great purchase and well worth the money!

product_title: Skullcandy Aviator (Discontinued by Manufacturer)
review_body:
The Skullcandy Aviators are better than anything else in the price range. The sound quality is amazing, even better than many $300 headphones. I can hear every high and low in the music. These are great for every genre, and I listen to many different genres. The bass is very good, but not too heavy. Some headphones, like beats and the Skullcandy Skullcrushers overdo the bass. These headphones get it just right, so you can hear all ranges of low notes. I couldn't ask for headphones with better bass or sound quality. They are very comfortable, almost as much so as Bose. The ear cups look small, and are smaller than most other over-ear headphones, but they are just as big as you need them to be. product_title: Panasonic Lightweight Headphones with XBS Port
review_headline: Shockingly good. High quality sound regardless of price---which happens to be dirt cheap
review_body:
I have used these headphones for years, for listening to music on numerous systems, hooked up to a desktop stereo as well as a laptop computer. I own more than one pair, use them constantly, and did not think much about them. They were cheaper than dirt and did the job.
But in hindsight, and now that I have devoted a bit more time evaluating many other headphones, I took these outstanding Panasonics for granted.

Their sound is exceptional. They should not be disrespected or dismissed. They blow away inexpensive headphones that look similar to it. And shockingly, they blow away many full-sized headphones,including some that cost 20 times more, $100 and up, particularly in terms of treble clarity.

This may seem like a bold claim, but I stick by it: these are better than many headphones on the market. Yes, it makes sense to maintain reasonable expectations (these are, after all, under $10 headphones) but the RP-HT21s far---far---exceed these expectations. In addition to being among my go-to headphones for daily use, they are so good, I use them to test audio gear, and as a reference versus other headphones.

The RP-HT21s offer clear, crisp, well-defined mids and sparkling highs. Wonderfully bright and airy, no muddiness or veil. In fact, the treble is so good that I include these among my treble reference headphones when testing and comparing other headphones. It leans towards cool rather than warmer, in tone. The sharp clarity is this set's strength. The bass is tight, clean and solid. It is not boomy, loose nor overwhelming in quantity but enough for any music.The imaging is extremely clear. These little headphones even offer a bit of soundstage with good imaging and separation.

Again, keep in mind that the drivers are small. Don't expect a big picture or full sound like that offered by full-sized cans, but if you appreciate the sound of clean, brighter headphones (Grado, AKG, Beyerdynamic), you will like what the RP-HT21s offer within its capabilities.

The drivers are 30mm. They are fairly easy to drive: low impedance (24 ohm) but sensitivity is medium (100 db). I find that I have had to turn them up a minor notch or two for volume.

They are ideal for use through smaller sources, but I find that they sound just as fine over larger stereo systems. I tested them through various sources, and they sound great through all of them, small as well as bigger. They are good without EQ. With EQ, they can be fine tuned to even more impressive levels. Bumping up the bass a few notches, and the treble just a bit (I love detail) can really transforms the RP-HT21s into the surprise performers. They also respond well to amping. Just be careful not to blow them out.

These super light portables are ideal for indoor listening. For outdoor use, they are certainly portable, but they are open air. These are on-ear headphones---as in small drivers right on the opening of your ear. There is no real seal. Which means that you will also hear everything in the room around you, no isolation. If you are type that listens outdoors at high volume, a set of full sized closed headphones would of course be better. These are best at low to medium volume, they struggle a bit when cranked up. For quieter listening, the Panasonics make me very happy.

The fit can start out a bit tight, very snug on the head, but they break in, no problem. They are comfortable on the ear, and I often prefer them to full-size headphones that can get hot. The foam covers are replaceable, but the headphones are so cheap, it makes more sense to just buy a whole new set if the covers wear out.

I am finding that good versions of these types of headphones have become more difficult to get, and these Panasonics really are far better than the Maxell HP-200 and other terrible cheapie throwaways; the ones that look similar, and are sold with computer equipment and given away on airplanes. They are vastly superior to cheap ear buds and IEMs. They beat or compete admirably against portables such as the Koss Porta Pro, Koss KSC75 (which costs more than twice as much), and the Sennheiser PX100 and PX100 II, which are ten times more expensive.

The L-shaped plug and cord are of better quality than the flimsy wires you might find on other phones in the same bottom end price range.

The RP-HT21s get my vote as the best sounding dirt cheap headphones out there. And they may also be the cheapest good headphones out there, too. These are under $10 headphones, capable of real surprise. So cheap, you can try them without guilt. And if you love them like I do, own many pairs.

review_headline: Great sound. Good fit is a MUST!
review_body:
If you can normally get a good fit out of other earbuds and generally get them to stay put, these are for you! If you're like me and have trouble with earbuds slipping out, then look elsewhere.

Just as expected after reading multiple reviews from this website and others, It took a few minutes to get a decent match of hooks & buds paired up to get a good fit. These are great sounding headphones that produce a deep bass that are great for working out in the gym.

But, after a few weeks of wearing these, I've noticed the bad (for me at least). These earbuds, although have a good fit initially (first few minutes of wear), still tend to slip out of my ear canal while running. Once you lose that good fit, you lose sound quality. I would have to push the buds back into my ear every 2-3 minutes to reestablish that good sound/fit.

I should say that I love the sound quality of ear buds, but this being my third set (1st were no name brands, 2nd were skull candy), I have yet to find an earbud that will stay in during my workouts. It could very well just be a problem with the shape of my ear/ear canal and I may need to move on to an over-the-ear type headphones rather than earbuds.

***UPDATE***
Dropped from 3 stars to 2 starts. My reason being is that the earbud rubber cover would come off extremely easily. It started on only one side and I figured it was just because of sweat. Now anytime I remove one of the earbuds from my ear I'm stuck having to catch or \\"fish-out\\" the rubber cover out of my ear. I also noticed the speaker is able to be angled in your ear canal. This sounds good on paper, but the slack needs to be taken up or removed from the where the cord comes from the bottom of the earbud; if you tug on the cords, it immediately changes the angle of the speaker in your ear canal which causes it slip out easier and/or lose that tight fit as mentioned before.

Definitely would not buy again.

product_title: iLuv  Syren NFC-Enabled Bluetooth Portable Speaker
review_headline: Petite Size - Decent Sound - Good Value
review_body:
There are many, many Bluetooth speakers on the market. This SYREN from iLuv is one of the less expensive ones and it a tad larger than some of the smallest. Its unique design does a good job of producing very decent small-area sound. It connects easily, is remembered by connected devices and is a nice addition to a desk where the music from your iPhone (or other Bluetooth enabled device) is meant to be heard by only those in the immediate area. This SYREN does precisely what it claims, although there is one error in the Amazon ad page: It does not run on AC. There is no AC adapter. The only power/charging method available is via a USB port. I have used this speaker for 8 hours straight and it was still playing perfectly when I turned it off. I charge it overnight so it is full and ready for the new day at work where I also take advantage of the speakerphone capacity that works quite nicely. When a call comes in, the music playing stops and people on the other end tell me that my own voice comes through loud and clear.

The design is both sleek and mildly flawed in that the four control buttons (On/Off, VOl +, Vol - and Phone answer/pair) are on the backside of the unit - as is the power plug port and the charging indicator light. This is awkward as the unit has to be picked up and moved around to manage its functions. There is a small light on the bottom-front that indicates that it is turned On.

I have replaced a much larger Bluetooth speaker at work with this SYREN. The larger one has bigger speakers and is powered by AC. However, in my 10' X 14\\" office, the volume of the SYREN is more than adequate and the battery life is long enough that the lack of an AC charging capacity really doesn't matter. I do think, however, that the Product Page should be corrected.

All in all, I like this speaker a lot. It's small stature allows me to easily place it in different spots around the office and the speakerphone functions really do come in handy. For the cost, this is a very reasonable option for anyone looking for a reliable, small but decent sounding Bluetooth speaker/speakerphone.ndy. For the cost, this is a very reasonable option for anyone looking for a reliable, small but decent sounding Bluetooth speaker/speakerphone.

Great sound, you can tell the noise cancellation is working, especially in loud areas like the gym. I've also taken a few calls with them and people cannot tell the difference between using my iPhone mic and the headphone mic, awesome feature that most other products do not offer.

Compared to other headphones out there, these are probably the best ones for the money and even the style. I own the Motorola S305 (total garbage and a high price), the Sennheiser PMX (decent, sound doesn't compare and sort of an uncomfortable fit), Philips ActionFit (decent sound, very uncomfortable, hurt my ears) and I purchased the Kinivo headphone about two months ago. These seem to be an upgraded version of the Kinivo (which I also really like), just better in all respects - design, sound, quality of the materials (love the buttons) and the battery deserves its own review! I've been using these for over 40 hours now and NO charge yet! Still going. Amazing.

Summary:

1. Great sound, great design, the battery lasts forever, noise canceling mic is on-point, they turn heads, people ask me what I'm wearing - just a great product. 5-stars! And the price couldn't be better, ordering another pair for backup or if I lose this one (I tend to misplace things). Highly recommend it.

review_headline: Product has been revised, now is flimsy. Will not hold a 50" plasma's weight.
review_body:
This is a completely different product than the one listed. They revised it to cut costs and now it's flimsy. Brackets come in multiple lightweight pieces. It's impossible that Cheetah really believes the bracket you hang the TV on could hold 165 lbs. My 50\\" plasma weighs 97 lbs and when we went to hang it, it started bending the thin metal bracket before we even let it hold all the weight. That's not surprising, considering I can easily bend the bracket with my bare hands, and I don't even lift, bro.

It's really shady that they completely changed the mount and kept the same model number. The old version clearly had 1 piece heavy duty brackets to connect the mount to the wall on one end, and the TV on the other. Save yourself some grief and go with another brand. This will not hold your TV.

Update: I was contacted by Cheetah, and they say they have asked for the new model back from Amazon and asked Amazon to only sell the old model. Apparently the reviews got through. It sounds like they are scrambling to fix the problem, which is encouraging. If you order this product, I would certainly make sure that the one being sent is the old model that matches the pictures here on Amazon. They also offered me a discount on my next Cheetah mount, which I certainly appreciate. If I see that this problem gets solved, I may give them another chance, since their older customers seemed satisfied.

review_headline: These head sets are great for the price
review_body:
As I've gotten into longer distance running, I needed a pair of headphones that would stay in place in spite of the amount I sweat. I don't like anything bulky that wraps around my head, and for years had used a pair of Sennheiser sport earbuds at the gym. Moving into distance running led to them no longer staying in my ears, so I went looking for a replacement pair.
I bought the monster isport headphones after doing a fair bit of research, and they suit my primary goal - they stay in my ears. As others have said, finding the right combination of sizes on the various pieces is a pain and takes a while. I completed two runs before I found the "just right" fit. The downside is that they're just not as comfortable as my old Sennheiser's. I'm okay with that, because they stay in place and I wear them only when running, but if you're an audiophile, you may want to keep looking. The sound quality is also not anything special, but again, I wasn't looking for that when I purchased them.
Overall, if you're looking for headphones specifically to put up with high intensity activity, these fit the bill. I haven't had them long enough to truly know, but the construction seems sturdy and able to withstand the beating of a good workout. That said, I will be keeping my Sennheiser's handy for anything that doesn't involve a lot of movement.
