review_headline: Looks good, works great, sound is impressive
review_body:
Purchased this player to replace an older JBL unit. Always liked the JBL sound on the older unit but because of the iPod connector weakness of design, that connector ultimately failed. All attempts to repair the old JBL were to no success even though I have a lot of experience in electronic repair. The cost of the OnBeat Xtreme were off putting to start but reviews seemed strong so ultimately we took the plunge and have now had this unit for about a month or so.
Features are very good and the sound quality is impressive for a portable player. It works well for those wanting nice background music source but the price for this JBL doesn't warrant a background music player of this quality in my opinion. However, if you wish a player that will deliver into a large room or wishing to listen to your favorite music at concert hall sound levels, this is a good use for the JBL OnBeat Xtreme.
The fixed equalizer settings seem to fit the ambient environments quite well. Access to this feature is a little tricky but instructions are helpful to realize this feature. Generally, it is a twiddle free device. How it is set up and delivered is well done.
It looks good and the quality is apparent so use in any room is acceptable.
Finally, the arrangement to support the connector to the iPod, iPhone or iPad is significantly improved over the previous JBL design. I am pleased with this arrangement but am certainly more careful when making these connections on the Xtreme.

review_headline: Great method to start my Windows Home Server located in a remote area!

product_title: iHome Portable Rechargeable Stereo Speaker System
review_headline: Good enough for a speaker in its price range
review_body:
With the idea of replacing an old speaker system I used for my bedroom I decided to order the iHome Portable Speaker System. I incorrectly assumed I would be able to use it as a docking station for my iPhone, my bad for looking at the picture and not reading the product details. Hopefully you will read this and that will not happen to you.

Since this is not a charging dock, the small ledge on the front only serves to place your device in it. Since this is a portable speaker, it is not really a safe thing to do if you are planning to move the speaker around. If you, like in my case, intend to use this as a stationary device, this detail may not be an issue then.

The first thing I noted when opening it is that it uses a micro USB cord to recharge the battery, there is no power cord (at least not included in the box) so if you do not have a computer or similar device running when you need to charge the speaker, this may be a huge inconvenience. In my case, I planned to plug this to a power source and use it in my bedroom, with no computers around I preferred to avoid the hassle and use it on my desk in my office instead.

How does it sound? Acceptable, nothing more. While the iHome provides a clear sound, it does not deliver sound powerful enough to be used on open spaces or parties, it is more like a small convenient device to be used in a small or closed space, like a kitchen, an office, you get the idea. Since there is no dock, the iHome uses an AUX cable (included) to plug in your devices, which pretty much makes it a universal speaker, which is good.

If you are looking for a powerful device to play your tunes this may not be the best option. If what you need is a small portable device that uses an AUX input, well, I actually own a better choice than this one, the [[ASIN:B00A0JUO48 X-Mini UNO XAM14-GM Portable Capsule Speaker, Mono, Gun Metal]] is smaller, looks great and provides a very good sound experience for its size, with the downside of also needing a micro USB cord to charge its battery. If the small ledge to place your device is a must have, then the iHome may be your best option.with the downside of also needing a micro USB cord to charge its battery. If the small ledge to place your device is a must have, then the iHome may be your best option.

product_title: Sanyo NEW 1500 eneloop AA Ni-MH Pre-Charged Rechargeable Batteries
review_body:
We've got a baby on the way and it seems like half of the baby stuff we have needs a battery of some sort. I picked up this pack to save money over the long term but also to help the environment. Throwing away batteries, when you could just recharge them, seems like such a waste and not very responsible when bringing a new little person into the world. That's it for the environment lecture.

One of the cool things about these batteries is that they have a slow discharge rate so you can charge them and use them months later with little drain on the overall power. It also means that you can put these batteries into gadgets that you use less often with out them draining too quickly (flashlights, remotes, etc) This feature also means that the batteries arrive precharged so you can use them right out of the box.

One of the big pluses is the C and D spacers. Some of the new baby things take C and D so I put in the AA with the spacers and was good to go.

The charger is small and unobtrusive, and charges pretty quickly. And again, you can keep these charged and ready to go so although the charger only handles 4 at a time, it shouldn't be difficult to keep a good number of batteries ready to go.

The case holds everything snuggly and is a nice small size and easy to store. Great for keeping track of everything.

As for the batteries performance, I bought an OEM version of this product about 5 years ago and have been using the 4 AA's in Xbox controllers. Those batteries have been recharged dozens of times and have often gone months without use. I have had no problems with them and they continue to charge well and hold their charge for considerable use (and non use).

My one piece of advice on these would be to buy more batteries then you may think you need. I had looked at getting a 4 or 8 pack or the smaller case, but now that I have the Super Power Pack, it's easy to find things that require batteries. The sooneryou invest in rechargeables the more money you'll save; and with the Eneloops said to last 1500 cycles you can save a lot of money and save a lot of waste.

So, an iPhone with the IHeartRadio app and the Bose SoundLink have become our favorite way to listen.

The sound, of course, is all-Bose: ear-opening fidelity from an eye-poppingly small box. Bass and treble in balance instead of exaggerated, and a natural vocal presence that literally puts the on-air talent in the same room with you.

When we first used the SoundLink to listen to streaming web radio, it had a tendency to drop out for several seconds at a time. The sound was also marred by annoying ticks and pops. The solution: bypass the Bluetooth and use an ordinary 3.5mm male-to-male audio cable connected between the iPhone's headset jack and the SoundLink's AUX port. The Bluetooth and WiFi don't interfere with each other, and the show goes on.

review_headline: Proof that not all HDMI cables are created equal

Proof that not all HDMI cables are created equal

Seriously, wow. I've never experienced such a shoddy cable. Switching electrical appliances or devices in my apartment were sufficient to cause this cable to cause drop outs of signal that required manual wire manipulation.

product_title: Monster NCredible Npulse Headphones
review_body:
I have had the opportunity to review 2 pairs of headphones recently for Amazon. One was this pair, the Monster NCredible NPulse and the other was [[ASIN:B0092T864W Yamaha PRO 400 High-Fidelity Over-Ear Headphones (Piano Black)]]. They are both great headphones. Here's my thoughts on why you might choose one over the other.

Price: The Monster headphones are $50 cheaper.

Contents: For $50 more, the Yamaha headphones come will a hard shell carrying case, 2 different cable lengths and an quality adapter so you can plug into both small and large jacks. The packaging on both was nice, but the Yamaha was more substantial.

Comfort: This was a toss up for me as each of the headphones had a pro and a con. The Yamaha headrest was more comfortable to me and I preferred the way that the ear cups fit (they actually enclose my ear). The Monster ear cups were not large enough to cover my ears and sat on top of them. This is not comfortable with earrings. My ears are on the small size of average, so I wasn't expecting this. The Monster headphones did fit my head better than the Yamahas. The Yamahas are meant for a large head.

Sound: Both pairs are great. If you want Bass - lots of Bass - go with the Monster. For pure, clean, well balanced sound - go with the Yamaha.

Feature: The Monster headphones have a \\"DJ\\" feature where you can flip up one side to listen to outside noise while keeping the headphones on. I found this to be a useless feature because it wasn't comfortable to flip up the ear cup.

product_title: Clip Plus 4 GB MP3 Player (Black)
review_body:
We own two of these. One was a gift to our elementary-age son, and he was pretty happy with it, so when my old player finally gave up the ghost, I purchased a second Clip+ for myself. As the happy owner of a Sansa Fuze that took years of abuse and kept working long after it should have ceased to function, I expected a similar simple and reliable performance from the Sansa Clip. What a mistake! The sordid details:

I learned immediately that the Clip does not play well with Macs (nor, as it turns out, PCs - more below). Two things happened every time I plugged either Clip into my MacBook. First, all files were instantly wiped, including the few songs it originally came with; and second, only some of the songs I reloaded onto it actually played. The Clip's screen would cycle rapidly through the titles of the rest without any sound and then turn itself off. There was no rhyme or reason to which files played successfully and which did not. Sometimes, a song title would show up twice on the same playlist; one would play and the other wouldn't.

Well, okay, be that way. I'll just use a PC for charging and syncing MP3 files - which worked fine until four days later, when the Clip decided it wasn't going to turn on anymore, no matter what. It took a fifteen-minute troubleshooting session with Sansa online support to solve that puzzle. Then all was fine for another week until the power button inexplicably jammed and wouldn't function (the player was never dropped or handled roughly). I figured my Clip was a lemon; bad luck but probably uncommon. So I gave up on it and borrowed my son's, which he was no longer using.

Using a PC, I loaded 102 MP3 files onto his Clip and immediately encountered the exact same problem with some songs playing and others just rapidly cycling through the titles, followed by the Clip shutting itself off. "Okay," I thought, "I can cope with this; even if I can't listen to half of my music files, at least thething plays the other half." But then the Clip began showing an error message stating "Not enough space for music DB. Please free 90MB." This made no sense whatsoever on a 4 GB player with only 102 MP3 files, including the ones that appeared to be titles only. But once the message popped up, it was all over. The player locked up completely and had to be forced off (power button held down for 30 seconds). It also stopped charging when plugged to any computer. I found many web sites with instructions for fixing this error (learning in the process that it is widely considered to be "the error from hell"), but they all require me to access the Clip's settings files from my PC or Mac - which I cannot. None of the four computers that we own will recognize my son's Clip when I attach the USB cable. I know it's receiving power, though, because the same error message pops up on the screen again as soon as it's plugged in - and then it freezes up and has to be forced off. Again. It's maddening!

My husband has been pressuring me to get an iPod for my upcoming birthday. I've resisted the idea thus far because, in theory, the $40 Clip should completely meet my needs. All I want is a basic player for listening to MP3 files, for crying out loud, and that's exactly what the Clip is made to do. But sadly, neither of our two Clips can manage that basic task. I wish Sansa still made the Fuze; that thing was amazing. After three years of heavy use, the case was cracked and deeply scratched, the screen showed nothing but a blur of colors, and the slide power button was broken. But, by golly, if I kept it charged, it synced whatever I told it to and played on. And on.

I NEED music to accomplish many things. If my lawn is overgrown, the house badly needs vacuuming, or the garden is weedy, it's because there's no functioning music player into which I can plug myself. I've gone to ridiculous lengths to troubleshoot these two players, wasted a lot of time, and suffered much aggravation, to no avail. I am still without music. Sigh. It's back to Amazon for our two Clips and back to the drawing board for me.

product_title: Bose CineMate GS Series II Digital Home Theater Speaker System
review_body:
I literally spent a couple weeks going back and forth at a best buy comparing these speakers to the Onkyo LS3100 as I feel those speakers are one of the top competitors for 2.1 home theatre speakers. First off, if you're mostly looking for convenience over sound, the Onkyo is the way to go. With bluetooth connection you can very easily play sound from your phone, computer, etc. The speakers automatically turn on with your tv (when connected) and sync with the volume control. However, the sound quality is noticeably worse than Bose Cinemate. I compared them side by side with various genre's of music and movies. The Onkyo's are just not very clear, they have a very noisy, trebley sound to them. The subwoofer is maybe, Ok, it does get pretty boomy and distorted at times.

The Bose Cinemate's on the other hand are very clear, though do tend to lean more towards the treble side, which is generally made up for with the subwoofer. But even then, there are some mid's missing from the sound. Also to note, for the gigantic size of the subwoofer, it's not specifically loud. Maybe I don't have it in the best location of my (11'x12') room but it needs to be at least half way up to make any impact. Pretty clear subwoofer, no distortion or booming sounds.
For my size room the volume is more than enough. Although when tested at high volumes the sound definitely does not hold up. It'll get distorted and lose its clarity. But that is only for large rooms, otherwise it is plenty loud. Moreover, the spatial sound of these 2 speakers are Fantastic. It really does have the best surround sound for a 2.1 speaker system. Movies sound great with these. The sound is spread very clear and the panning is amazing. Almost sounds like real surround sound. And because they're 2speakers music sounds great as well, which doesn't usually stay together with 5.1+ systems. The only complaint with movies is that explosions and other loud sounds like breaking glass, for instance, is specifically loud and somewhat distorted. I understand dynamic during movies, but they can be a tad loud and a bit distorted, not full and clear like the rest of the sound.

Lastly, concerning the convenience compared to the Onkyo LS3100. There is no bluetooth so either you're hooked up thru optical or stereo. In my case, I'm hooked up thru both. I have the optical cord in my tv and a stereo in my computer. If the tv is on, the optical cord will always take over and be used as the default source (obv optical sounding somewhat noticeably better than stereo). Using this setup I can listen to music/watch movies on my computer, and because i have an hdmi connecting my computer to my tv I can drag a movie to my tv and switch the speaker output to \\"hdmi\\" which will go thru my tv, and thru the optical cord. Apple Tv would probably be easier where you can watch whatever's on your computer thru your tv without a cable. The universal remote is great, it easily synced to my Samsung tv and panasonic dvd player. Has all the basic controls needed for both systems. And the volume on the remote always controls the speaker system so there's no need for any other remote unless you're using an Apple remote to control a movie on your computer (or apple tv).

---Also to mention, one thing that bothers me is that the sound levels are controlled in such small increments. It really takes a lot of clicks to turn volume up or down... Random point, if you're concerned about electricity/leaving electronics on, the system automatically turns off after 15min of no signal from sources so if you fall asleep watching movies/listering to music, etc. it will turn off when the movie/music is done playing. And it's extremely easy to turn on, idk why ppl complain. You hit the tv power button then the main (bose) power button for speakers. Not complicated or time consuming.---

Overall, if you want pretty great sound and can spend $100 more than the Onkyo LS3100, get this system. Sound is always better over convenience and even then the only real advantage is bluetooth. $600 for these speakers, in my opinion, is pretty steep for the sound quality, but it's probably the best deal over buying 2.1 speakers + receiver. I know ppl think that setup is way better but for the convenience of an easy setup and less space taken it's worth it, esp if you're gonna end up paying $600+ anyways for speakers and a receiver. If you're an average sound thriving consumer these are more than fine for sound quality. I'm a long time musician and I have good enough ears to be able to tell accuracy and quality of sound.

product_title: Heatshield Products Combo AN Wrench46
review_headline: Great sound, extremely rugged, nice size, just perfect!
review_body:
My wife and I are avid campers, boaters, sailors, kayakers, and eat outdoors every evening in the summer. We love music, and I have about 3,000 songs on my Android smartphone. I have tried about 10 or 12 different portable speakers, most of which are in a storage box in a closet because they just weren't worth using. Many of those used a headphone jack connection, because Bluetooth speakers until recently didn't have the power, battery life, or sound quality I wanted.

I bought my wife a Jambox speaker and she loved using it in the kitchen, so I got her another one for her desk at work. However, the hard plastic case of the Jambox slides around if we try to use it in the boats, and when we get splashed, it isn't waterproof.

I was intrigued by the design of Pyle Sound Flow speaker and decided to try it. I couldn't be happier! The rubber housing keeps it from sliding around on the dash of the motor boat in choppy water or on a table in the sailboat while heeling, and the hanging loop lets me hang it inside the cabin of the sailboat or from the ceiling light-hook loop of our tent. While I don't plan to test its waterproof capabilities by taking it to 130' while scuba diving, I am confident that it will survive even heavy splashing while using it in either the power or sail boats, or in a kayak. The switches are rubber coated for protection as is the entire housing.

The unit is quite a bit heavier than a Jambox, but about the same size. The weight helps keep it in place, especially with the gripping rubber housing. It comes with a 3' USB charging cord. I initially charged it from my laptop, but on the boat, I use a USB adapter in the boat's dashboard DC plug, so I can charge it while playing music on the dash of the boat. [[ASIN:B00AWUDDWK ReVIVE PowerUP 3P Universal Car Charger & DC Splitter Adapter w/ Dual USB Rapid Charging Ports for Phones, MP3 Players, & More DC-Powered Devices]].

I use my Xoom with Navionics software fornavigation, and also have my smartphone with me at all times while boating, and this device connects effortlessly via Bluetooth to either device. So, I can easily play stored music and playlists from either device, or can use my 4G to stream my Pandora \\"stations\\", or my YouTube music video playlist through this powerful little speaker. The possibilities are endless.

Sound quality for this size speaker is the best I have found. It is rich, with a strong but not over-powering bass. Highs and mid-range are also excellent, and it puts out a deep, rich stereo sounds that sounds great even over the noise of my twin outboards.

Some reviewers reported a weak, 5' Bluetooth range. Pairing it with my Motorola RAZR Maxx HD phone, it stays connected up to about 20' away. When I go beyond that range and lose the connection, it seamlessly and instantly picks back up as soon as I am in range again. That is more than enough range for using it in any of my boats, camping, eating outdoors, or even in the house in most situations.

You won't be disappointed with this speaker. You can get even better sound by spending another $200 on a Bose, but I would never take a Bose camping or boating. For a rugged, waterproof, great sounding outdoor wireless speaker, this is the way to go.

product_title: Yamaha RX-A1030 7.2-Channel Network Aventage Audio Video Receiver
review_body:
I owned previous generations of Yamaha. My last receiver was their pre-RX, pre-Aventage line. I sold it to a neighbor after a decade of flawless service (actually 10 years of constant power on!). I owned the esoteric multi-thousand dollar separate combos of other manufacturers, prior to Yamaha. Those expensive units reliability was always in doubt. They almost were impossible to have fixed, and just as impossible to afford to have fixed.

This present Yamaha puts my whole system together, putting all my HDMI inputs through a processor for video and audio. The result is a an excellent picture and audio, no matter the source. The surround effects are very accurate. The theater and decoding choices are many, with all sonically pleasing.

Tied a Sharp 70\\" LED screen to the output of the Yamaha's HDMI. Even Netflix type sources look like Blu Ray. Its amps went to Tannoy studio monitors and a double 10\\" commercial subwoofer. All components are now rigidly controlled by the high Yamaha standard that are applied by the 1030.

As I suspect compromises at lower entry levels of any manufacturer, I can highly recommend only the upper line of Yamaha.

ADDENDUM: Please note, that, during your audio setup, using their YPAO(tm) R.S.C. (Reflected Sound Control) Sound Optimization with Multi-point Measurement, it will set your subwoofer all wrong, that is it will be hardly heard at all. Other Yamaha owners using YPAO have already noted this problem. So, for the sub to be accurate, you must set it's own level at minimum before starting (-6 to -12). This is so the YPAO detects it, but just barely, and then gives it the go ahead for a Yamaha +10db. After all is set and saved, you can return to the sub and adjust its level higher (for the urban, disco, rock levels that you prefer). Actually even movie soundtracks will present as thin, without punch, unless you do the previous.

product_title: FiiO E6 Portable Audio Headphone Amplifier
review_headline: FiiOE6 unleashes potential of AKG K242 and the IPod - I now take these puppies for long walks
review_body:
I am reviewing the AKG K242 along with the FiiOE6.

I plugged-in this power hungry 91 db AKG unit to my ipod's headphone jack and as expected from the AKG's specs and the notoriously bad equalization of the Apple Touch Ipod, sound produced was very restrained. A number of users warned of this so I ordered my AKG with an inexpensive EiiO6 headphone amp.

The K242 delivered 300% better at line level boosted by EiiO E6 portable headphone amp. With this low cost combination, program material was freed IPod's wimpy built in equalizer. The AKG K242's great potential has been tapped for portable use!!
I also own a Grado SR80i which is more efficient at 99 db and am happy to report that it also greatly benefits from the amp.

The AKG plays loud enough out of Sony Walkman MP3 and the sound quality is good straight from device. However, I bet it will sound better at line level + FiiO6 + L5 Line Out Dock (LOD) Cable For Sony Walkman. I can't wait for my order (I am getting another EiiOE6 for it)

Some may complain about the AKG K242's 10 foot chord but a belt clip GPS case solved the mobility issue. I walked 5 miles yesterday with the entire package - AKG, EiiO6, L9 LOD in the GPS case and it was bliss!!

The EiiO6 manufacturer's claim of 10 hours use per charge is true for this brand new unit. It took approx 45min-1 hour to charge from a USB port. I wonder how long the lithium battery will last ... anyway I am endorsing this model because of its performance and low replacement cost.

product_title: PNY Smart Active High Speed HDMI to HDMI Cable in White C-H-A10-A16-A
review_headline: Amazing Price, Excellent Quality, Use to Show iPad Movies on Flat Screen TVs
review_body:
First, if you've priced HDMI cables lately, you'll know that they're expensive--and the longer they are, the more expensive they are. So this cable is impressive for the price alone.

Second, it gives you excellent HD transfer rates and quality--which means your shows and DVDs will look awesome.

Third, it's really long. Sixteen feet long, in fact.

The problem with other HDMI cables is that they're quite thick and bulky, and they're much more expensive in general.

This cable could be used for anything requiring a long HDMI cable, but the application that I'm using it for is to play movies, Netflix, and YouTube off my iPad to a large flat screen TV. In fact, I bought this cable specifically because I wanted a thinner (smaller form factor) cable for travelling. I take this cable with me in my briefcase so that when I'm in hotels I can watch Netflix on the hotel's TV--and I can comfortably lie on the bed and have access to my iPad's controls. In order to do this you'll need an iPad HDMI adapter like these (depending if you have a lightning connector or not):

http://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B007IRBNRW/ref=oh_details_o07_s00_i00?ie=UTF8&psc=1

http://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B009WHV3BM/ref=oh_details_o07_s00_i02?ie=UTF8&psc=1

This cable + iPad + adapter = you can play/show all your iPad media on your flat screen TV.

***Note that is cable is directional--meaning that you have to be careful to plug the correct end in your "source" and the other end in the TV. Each end is labelled, so just plug it in right and everything will be good.***

Let me know if this was helpful!

product_title: JVC Noise Cancelling Headphones - Black
review_body:
I bought these headphones for use on a series of multiple cross-country flights (6 round trips in 2 months), and for a recent vacation flight to Africa. I've tried a few low cost noise cancelling earbud and headphone solutions prior to this but they all disappointed. I was not willing to spend $300 on the leading brand, but I feel these JVCs are a good compromise between price and performance. They don't eliminate *all* noise (my wife says they don't do much for her on BART) but they do a great job of reducing the low pitched drone of jet engines during flight. So instead of turning up the volume to try and drown out background noise, you just turn on the Noise Cancelling and enjoy your music or movie. BTW the Noise Cancelling also makes the music sound better and makes spoken dialogue clearer and easier to understand. After trying these headphones out on BART, my wife was skeptical until she tried them on an airplane with me while watching a movie. She then took the headphones from me and wore them the rest of the flight!

The single AAA battery in the right earphone lasts for many hours and is easy to replace. The headphones are comfortable (I wear glasses) even after being worn for many hours. The removable cable plugs into a deep socket in the left earphone, as others have mentioned this deep socket may make future cable replacement somewhat of a problem. However I've found a cord that fits and it's right here on Amazon! [[ASIN:B004G7SDES StarTech.com MU6MMSRA 6 feet Slim 3.5 mm to Right Angle Stereo Audio Cable - M/M]]

The headphones come with a study hard shell carry case that zippers up around the outside. Inside is a zippered mesh pouch that can hold the removable cable and some extra batteries.

I now take these JVC headphones with me on all my flights. All in all I feel this product is a good buy, and I am very satisfied with my purchase.

product_title: Denon AVR2112CI Integrated Network AV Surround Receiver
review_headline: Sounds great. Connectivity is a joke. Airplay = useless.
review_body:
Let me start off by saying that this receiver sounds incredible. We have it connected to some vintage / 80s Paramount floor speakers & the sound blows away anything remotely close to what we paid for it. It has plenty of inputs for just about anything you'd need. The user interface is workable, not the best looking by any means (I'm a designer, so I'm picky about that stuff) but it works. The Audyssey technology seems to work pretty good. It's pretty easy to hook up / connect to your network, which has to be ethernet because there's no wireless.

Now let me get griping. DO NOT BUY THIS FOR THE AIRPLAY FEATURE, IT'S WORTHLESS. We're an Apple household so this was a major selling feature for me. When (if) it works, it seems to work ok. It cuts out pretty often on my wife's MBP & iPhone 4s. My phone / computer / iPad seem to work pretty good, WHEN YOU CAN GET IT TO CONNECT. I'd say that getting iTunes to see the receiver as an option works about 1/6 tries, maybe less. Today I hooked up the audio out jack on our Airport Express because I was tired of playing Russian Roulette to see if the receiver decided it wanted to be visible. I've tried restarting, resetting, restarting the computer / iTunes / Airport Express, etc. Nothing seems to work. As I type this I'm listening to music through it, played through the connection on the Airport Express & the Denon isn't on the iTunes output options. So frustrating, Airplay is 90% of the reason I chose this receiver.

In short

The Good
----------------
Sounds incredible
Easy setup
Plenty of inputs for just about anything you'd want to connect
User Interface looks ugly but it works pretty good
Network connection is fairly simple to setup & hooks right up to Pandora
Audyssey feature / setup is easy & works good
The remote is easy to setup & seems to control most things (not our dinosaur ReplayTV but I didn't expect that)

The Bad
----------------
No WiFi - you'll need an ethernet connection or Airport Express type device to connect to network
Two HDMI outs would have been nice

The Ugly
----------------
AIRPLAY is worthless! If it decides to show up, it cuts out constantly. A much better route is hooking up to the audio out on the Airport Express that you need to connect the receiver to the network anyways.

product_title: Sony Portable NFC Bluetooth Wireless Premium Speaker System
review_body:
This portable BT speaker is better than I expected. It is very solidly constructed, is easy to set up (push two buttons) and has fantastic sound. It is a relatively heavy speaker case, but it's so solidly built that you are almost glad it weighs as much as it does.

My wife and I recently moved and decided not to have a TV in the bedroom. When we watched video on the iPad or phone, we had to listen to the items' speakers which are like the ones on the transistor radios from the 1960s (yep, I'm that old). I got tired of that, went portable speaker shopping on Amazon and came upon this gem of a product.

I have a keen ear for sound quality, and had never bought a portable BT speaker before. I've always heard that the quality of sound transmitted via BT is of inferior quality compared to wired speakers. I play streaming movies and TV from both my iPad and Samsung S4 phone, and the sound is rich, full-spectrum and virtually distortion-free on this speaker. You can really \\"feel\\" the base. The choice of three equalizer settings, although limited, does help the sound quality for the environment in which the speaker rests. It lasts for many hours on a single charge. Only complaint: The bluetooth connection notification beep is very loud.

Bottom line: Good luck finding anything wrong with this product. It rocks!

product_title: Sony MDR Premium Over The Head Headphones
review_headline: Great for tunes, musical instruments, etc.
review_body:
My husband and I have put these headphones through the paces by listening to pop music, oldies, hip-hop, etc. as well as hooking them up to our electric musical instruments with headphone jacks, and they have performed extraordinary well across the board. The subtle melodies of early Bee Gees tunes shined through just as well as Lana Del Rey songs.

We have a pair of Sony extra bass headphones and were really disappointed that those sacrificed overall quality in favor of the bass. These headphones cost approximately 3x the selling price of those, and the extra money is worth it as these have rich bass and treble for a variety of sounds.

My husband now uses them exclusively when playing his electric keyboard and really loves the tone. He also prefers the open cavity on these headphones versus the solid muff on many units as it allows for comfortable wear for longer periods of time while also helping to seal off most outside noises. The band is also adjustable which allows for achieving a near-perfect fit.

The headphones ship with two cables to attach from the headphone to your headphone jack. One is a four-conductor connector for iPods and other Apple devices while the other is a standard three-conductor connector for everything else. The cables and the phones both store nicely in the included carrying case which has a leather feel but is undoubtedly imitation. The headphones also ship inside a deluxe Sony box with an interior molded to hold the phones securely during shipment. You may prefer to keep the headphones in here versus the bag.

All and all, I don't think the sound could be improved upon much in a headphone pair at this price point, and these seem to be sturdy enough to last for a very long time.

product_title: Apple iPod touch (5th Generation) NEWEST MODEL
review_body:
I've tried every music player out there: Samsung Galaxy Player, Zune, and a few others, but the latest iPod touch continues to blow those devices out of the water. Even though I'm an Android user, this device is far more superior when it comes to portable computing. I mainly use it for music, but every other function built into it still has an advantage over whatever else is available. Sure, its got some flaws such as the closed Apple environment, but adapting to it doesn't take too much time if you're coming from the Android or Windows environment. I've been using the iPod since the classic and it still serves as my number one multimedia device (other than my smartphone).

App store: 5/5 - a plethora of apps in the App Store
Battery life: 5/5 - Considering you only use what you need and keep the brightness to a tolerable level, the iPod can go up to 4 days without charging.
Portability: 5/5 - It's lighter than its predecessor and thinner: makes it a great device to carry around!
Camera: 4/5: Apple still needs to improve the iPod touch camera as it is only 5MP, but the video shooting quality is great: 1080p video!
iOS environment: 4/5 - It's still a pain to turn off features that are only needed temporarily (WiFi, Bluetooth, Brightness, etc), by going through a bunch of screens....this is where Android stands strong, however iOS 7 seems very promising to change all this!
Multitasking: 4/5 : Another area where Android stands strong, as multitasking on this is still tedious to get to by double clicking the button.

Did I forget anything? I think this is by far a superior device, but be aware that Apples competitors are catching up in almost every aspect of the device. I do hope that Apple continues to improve its iPod Touch line! I would definitely recommend this to any family or friend who want portability, top notch functionality, and an environment they feel comfortable with!

product_title: Cheetah Mounts APDAM2B Dual Articulating Arm (20” Extension) TV Wall Mount Bracket for 32-65” TVs (many up to 75” or more) up to VESA 600 and 165lbs, including a Twisted Veins 10’ HDMI Cable and a 6” 3-Axis Magnetic Bubble Level
review_body:
Incredible value for the money. Here are the pros/cons:

Pros:
- Comes with A LOT of mounting hardware, including spacers and screws you might need for the back of your TV.
- Comes with 6 wall screws and 4 masonary/drywall anchors, which was helpful because I could only hit one stud in the middle so I put 2 anchored screws on each side.
- Dual arms inspires a lot of confidence
- Incredible range of motion on my Panasonic Viera 55" LCD
- Really wide plate for hanging the TV allows about 8" of left/right adjustment, so you can hit wall studs and still center the TV where you want it
- The TV plate (what the TV actually hangs from) can be rotated/adjusted several degrees, which is awesome because getting the wall plate mounted perfectly level is difficult. I recommend removing the plastic washers and replacing/supplementing them with the locking "teeth" washers included in the box.
- Really high quality HDMI cable included. Runs 3D perfectly.
- Allows multiple options for running cables through the wall and the mount

Cons:
- It tilted my TV down several degrees, but I used the included spacers and longer screws to fix the issue and it points straight ahead. May just be the design of the back of my TV.
- The arms are really tight out of the box and are difficult to extend all the way out. It looks like you can loosen them a bit with a socket wrench (NOT in the instructions), but I dared not try with my $1,800 investment hanging from them. I can still easily get it 8" away from the wall and turn it a good 15 degrees. I recommend standing on the wall mount and pulling/adjusting the TV plate before mounting, this seemed to loosen them up a bit.

All in all, I don't think you can get a better mount for the money in terms of quality, design, and extras (screws, hardware, etc.) You won't be disappointed!

product_title: Sony STR-DN1040 7.2-Channel Network A/V Receiver (Built-in Wi-fi & Bluetooth)
review_headline: Great Sound and Amazing Connectivity Options
review_body:
Updated 6/16/2013 original post 6/3/2013
Great news first you can stream your music files on Android Phone over wifi(like Airplay though not as good) using AirTwist(from DoubleTwist for 5$). More on this below in the File Steaming section.

I am a first time buyer of A/V receiver. I researched a lot about the receivers for about a few weeks i was actually looking at the DN1030 and I had the following wishlist of features in the order of priorities.

1. Builtin/Cheap Wifi(~20$)
2. Stream Audio from Android/Airplay
3. USB In front for FlashDrive with Charge Power >500ma
4. 2 HDMI OUT
5. 2 Digital Audio In
6. MHL in front(powered HDMI in other words)
7. ARC(Audio Return Channel)
8. Passthrough Input Change while in Standby
9. Preout (totally optional as I know it adds to price significantly. NOT available on DN1040)
10. High HDMI Count

Due to price and desired features limitation my research was focused mostly on Sony, Onkyo and Yamaha. The top contenders were Onkyo and Sony with Onkyo leading with its TX-NR616 ($349 + 25$ Wifi Dongle) and Sony DN1030 was next.

DN1040 sounded good but it was too expensive that I did not even consider it in the features matrix. Luckily last week I saw a deal on Rakuten.com (formerly Buy.com) that was only 449 for DN1040. I checked my feature list and all the top 8 parameters as well as number 10 were a go on this one and added Bluetooth which was not even in my feature list. So I pulled the trigger immediately. And boy am I glad that I did!
(Add 6/10) One other important reason why i bought this is because the STR-DN1030 came out on the top in the mid range receivers in the CNET Review last yr and many other websites recommend it.

My Setup:-
Speakers: [[ASIN:B001202C44 Energy 5.1 Take Classic Home Theater System (Set of Six, Black)]] (i paid 299$)
Speaker Wire: [[ASIN:B0029HHIDY RCA AH16100SR 100 Ft. 16-Gauge Speaker Wire]]
Banana Plugs: [[ASIN:B006U3O566 Sewell Direct SW-29863-12 Deadbolt Banana Plugs, 12-Pair]](26$ NOTE: Cannot use banana plugs on the speaker side without Speaker mounts)
Speaker Mounts: [[ASIN:B002WNAFSU Videosecu 6 Black Satellite Studio Speaker Mounts / Brackets for Walls and Ceilings 1UP]] (needed some grinding to fit the speaker but works great for the price)

My Amazon Reviews:
Speakers : http://www.amazon.com/review/R25L9POODXC2X8/ref=cm_cr_rdp_perm
Mounts : http://www.amazon.com/review/R2GPNDBZ7HSVSV/ref=cm_cr_rdp_perm

Initial Setup:-
Was a breeze just power up the system and it asked you about the setup of the speakers and network, And does a quick 2min speaker audio configuration using the bundled mic and you are ready to use it. Most of the features like Airplay, DLNA just work out of the box without any changes to the system settings. Looks great too especially compared to the 1030 this one has much better looks and works great the two big dials looks nice and the buttons are kind of invisible as they almost the same color as the front panel. The UI is pretty simple almost too simple i would have preferred a little more control especially with the HDMI options etc.

Remote:-
I got the remote to work with my LG 42LH90 TV using the code 503 and Also by LG Bluray Player with code 337. Though a little confusing the remote works okay once you get a hang of it. One major drawbacks i see of the remote is that it cant be used in a truly universal mode i.e you cant control the BD player without having the receiver wakeup. However you can control the TV with out waking the receiver. I have a feeling that it is probably me that is not able to use the remote correctly. Will revise my review as soon as i figure that out.

File Steaming:-
I have used Doubletwist/Airtwist for a few days works pretty well and reliably each time from 2 different Android Devices. But couple of issues to use this you have to enable AirTwist which is heavy on WIFI, depending on how much wifi drains your device battery the runtime of the phone can be less than halved. The worst part is that double twist does not have an option where it only enables airtwist when playing music to External Speakers it has to be switched on/off manually and you know how that goes.
There is another app to use the Airplay Feature of the receiver but primarily for people who are ready to root their devices it is AirAudio on Google Play Store i only tried the free version without rooting and works like charm. Still considering rooting for this. If you want to try it please read the complete play store description of the app beware some devices can get temporarily bricked because of the app. The advantage here (i.e if you root) is you can use any music player or video player and it works. Also appears this following app works similar to the above AirAudio App it is called Airplay on Android AOA Service.
On a personal note first time in 2 yrs i am unhappy about being on android the reason is Airplay. Google seems to be working on an Airplay like protocol and system level support for external playback thing but it is probably a few months and a couple of updates away for all current devices.
To conclude its seems the best way(power and functionality efficient) is to have the tunes stream from a home media server using sony network media app.

Apps:
Apple iOS Remote Apps: Media Remote App + Network Audio Remote App (compatible with iPod touch, iPhone, and iPad; requires iOS 4.3 or later)
Android Remote Apps: Media Remote App + Network Audio Remote App (compatible with Android 2.2-up)

Bluetooth:
The blue tooth does work very well too. The pairing is real easy and audio quality seems to be good as well. One thing I liked about their implementation of BT is that you can skip track from the remote. But i personally prefer file streaming compared to bluetooth as the audio quality is better that way and also your phone doesnt need to stay in the range radius for the bluetooth to work.

Music on USB:
I used a USB flash drive and this feature works fine with it. Though i think it could be a little better like faster UI and remember where it was previously on the directory. Also if you hook up your iphone or android it has a 1A at 5V rating for charging.

To wrap up:
The setup was easy everything just works. Looks great and works great. The UI is pretty simple almost too simple if you ask me. The Android Remote App works fine. Streaming from android works flawlessly with double twist (DLNA). I paired it with Energy Take Classic 5.1 the audio is great (I am not qualified to do a comparative study here) and the connectivity option are amazing this is something I can certify Sony has basically thrown in the kitchen sink (well in the world of AV Receivers don't compare it with sonos) with Wifi/Bluetooth/Airplay/DLNA and combine that with Net Streaming Option (Pandora, Slacker Sony Unlimited Music etc)
The only complains I have so far is too few options/granularity when controlling connectivity, more Audio Streaming Options, Video streaming (netflix et all but 59$ roku can fix it). All in all I think it is an amazing receiver (especially for what I paid) will add more details as I explore them.
All in all i am very happy with my purchase especially give the deal that i got.

If you are shopping for a receiver you should also check out Sony STR-DN840 the network features are same.
CNET, whathifi, and crutchfield already have professional reviews of 1040. And crutchfield has a ton of tech spec.

Features yet to be evaluated
Standby power
Sony Network Media Remote App(this is different from the remote control app)
Standby Switching of Inputs
MHL (BTW it has 1A at 5V rating like the USB)

review_headline: Pretty close to the best bass!

The simple:

3. Lights are super cool - no gripes here.
4. Wires - comes with the extra wire for your computer for input, but the bad thing is that the main cord is not replaceable. This kind of makes sense because it's a computer headphone, but it still bothers me.
5. The headpiece itself is super comfy - at least for my head. Have insomnia? No problem. Turn up the bass while on your pillow and fall asleep.

Disclosure: this is a sort of cut-n-paste, duplicate review as I had already submitted a review for the 1-female to 2-male \\"Y\\" connector.

Yes, you can find cheaper. Personally, I can't stand cheaply made RCA \\"Y\\" adapter cables that cost a dollar or three. Other then they don't float your boat and no, the cheaper versions do not float my boat, there's no good reason to not use the cheaper versions as they work equally as well. But pride of ownership demands I use something better and Mediabridge products do exactly that.

I agreed that interconnects don't have to be expensive and I find these cables hit the middle ground perfectly as they're not what I consider to be expensive nor are they what one might call cheaply made and they're definitely less expensive then the \\"Monsters\\" being sold at big box electronic stores.

The cables look great and when in hand, my first impression was, how professionally made this product felt. The cables are heavy duty, with color coded molded ends that are gold plated to reduce corrosion. The cable's \\"Y\\" is reinforced and overall the set has a nice, heavy, professional quality feel that tells the purchaser, they made the right decision.

The overall length of the \\"Y\\" adapter is fifteen inches.

In the simple, these are well priced, Prime Membership delivered, quality made, professional looking, \\"Y\\" adapters that expectedly will last for years if not outlive the purchaser of these cables. I've had a couple of these for a few months now and have used them for connecting/disconnecting a Home Theater based subwoofer system (I move the subs around a lot) and they're what I consider to be a \\"GREAT!\\" product, at an excellent delivered price that from personal experience, I feel completely comfortable recommending for stage or home use.

Hope the above helps with your buying decision.

product_title: Sony MDRZX100 Headphones
review_headline: Sony MDR-ZX100 ZX Series Stereo Headphones (blue) - Excellent price and sound!
review_body:
For the price, these headphones are fantastic.

As a birthday gift for our son, a few weeks ago we purchased some fake Dre Beats headphones and they broke right away (plus their sound was crappy)... but not these Sony headphones, they sound excellent and are very comfortable to wear. We ordered a black pair of these to replace those other bad headphones, and our son has been extremely happy with them as a replacement gift.

I 'borrowed' them for a few hours and listened to some good old fashion rock (Aerosmith, Green Day, Creed,...) and can totally attest to the fact that these headphones provide deep bass, good midrange and very good treble sounds. In addition, the unit is fairly lightweight so you really do forget about them being on. I wore them for about an hour at a time and they never got hot or uncomfortable to my ears.

What is also very nice is that, unlike those fake Beats, other people around you can't hear your music... and believe me, I cranked up the tunes a bit. These headphones did a good job of blocking out external noise so I heard nothing but the music (even when my son supposedly kept hollering at me to give the headphones back to him)...

The headband was quite comfortable to me; adjustments were easy to make and they stayed in place without any problem. The cord is about four feet long, which is more than we will ever need.

So... since I liked them so much, and also since I have to participate in webinars and telephone conference calls at work (and those calls can get loud when on speakerphone), I ordered these blue headphones just to take to the office. Hopefully my boss won't notice the playlist that pops up on my laptop during lunchtime!! :)

If you are looking for a very affordable headphone option that is comfortable to wear and provides good sound quality, we totally recommend these headphones.

Go for it.

product_title: MEElectronics Sport Fi S6 In-Ear Sport Headphone System with Armband
review_body: When I first received these headphones I thought they were great, very comfortable with the different size ear pieces included.  After about 1 month of use the wire connecting to the audio plug started to get a bit weak or worn, no connection loss but was very loose at that area.  The bass response from these headphones are great for a sub $50.00 set of quality headphones I just want to say.  After about 4 months of use the earpieces started to get loose like the audio plug still not a big issue just some minor adjustment and the fit is as good as ever.  Now about a month later the audio plug connection has gotten loose enough that signal is being lost from the right earpiece occasionally. The memory wire around the earpieces is very loose and does not try to stay in shape 100% of the time, again not a very big issue.  The problem is after about 6 months of use the connector where it plugs into the audio port has gotten so loose that signal is dropping from the right earpiece and then the left so it sounds like the channels are bouncing from one earpiece to the other rapidly.  It makes it almost impossible to listen to anything on thses headphones now as the sound just jumps 2 or 3 times a second from mono in one earpiece or the other. If they would have lasted longer than 6 months i would have given these a 5 star review. Other than the shorts that developed and the wires loosening they are great headphones.

product_title: Koss Pro-4AA Studio Quality Headphones
review_headline: Used a pair of these for YEARS!!!
review_body:
These phones are absolutely amazing. I no longer own a pair of these (I have a smaller pair of Koss headphones), but had them from 1979 and finally updated them about 10 years later. Now, the plus is that they block out sounds very effectively. Cueing up a record was easy in a noisy environment (yes, I used records mostly at that time LOL). The problem with me was that I have a large head and they tend to squeeze a bit. But they didn't move. Also, if you're in a warm (or hot) area and perspiring, your ears can get pretty wet in you can't take them off...no breathing under these things.

One warning: the bass can be so strong (you don't HAVE to have your audio adjusted like that), it can actually make your ears hurt and you don't even realize how loud it is since the sound is so clean. Please be careful.

The reason I finally got rid of them (gave them away) is that the ear cushions had hardened due to age. I think at that time, the cushions were hard to come by, and rather expensive. Decided to just stop using them instead.

Buy these...if you find them comfortable, you'll like 'em.

product_title: Yamaha NS-AW194 Indoor/Outdoor 2-Way Speakers
review_headline: Some distortion on the high notes when turned up
review_body:
I'm using these INDOORS in an open floor plan great room/dining room/kitchen. They produce more than enough sound but I recommend you mount them on the walls for the best sound. When set on carpeting, the bass is too muddy. Besides, they are designed to be mounted on the walls and brackets with tightening knobs are furnished. Neither speaker wiring nor bolts to mount the brackets to your wall are included.

I like to be able to hear the words to the music and the crisp high notes as well as some bass. However, if you crank them up to the volume you'd be using around a pool outdoors, there is some slight distortion from the tweeters. I don't notice it myself INDOORS unless I crank them up loud enough to irritate my neighbors.

The best location for these is definitely not on the floor and I've found so far that the closest to ear level, maybe 5 or 6 feet high, mounted on the wall seems the best for the best quality sound. Currently they are on a glass shelf on my TV stand placed horizontally. They aren't meant to be placed that way, as the sides are rounded and they would rock back/forth if touched, but sound-quality is fairly good that way. The Yamaha nameplate on the speaker can be turned vertically or horizontally depending on which way you have the speaker situated.

product_title: JBL Portable Stereo Speaker with Wireless Bluetooth Connection
review_headline: Hands down... best value at this price point.
review_body:

I eventually made my way to Best Buy to really test their stock out, pairing my phone with one speaker after another. I tried the Jawbone Soundbox, Beats Pill and anything else they had for $200 and under. What floored me with the JBL Flip was the price point... $99. If it sounded even remotely good and could satisfy my music needs within my humble apartment, I was in.

I wasn't disappointed.

I'll say this. If you are in the market for a superior bluetooth speaker and really want the best, and can drop $300 without a thought, go with the Bose SoundLink. It's the best. It's what you want. It's loud, the clarity at high and low frequencies is what you've come to expect from Bose products. Buy that.

However, when you get to slightly lower price points the differentiation becomes the actual hardware, more than anything. There are great options at $199, but I can say without a doubt, if you drop $100 on the JBL Flip, you won't be disappointed. It is absolutely the best value bluetooth speaker on the market right now.

product_title: FiiO D3 (D03K) Digital to Analog Audio Converter - 192kHz/24bit Optical and Coaxial DAC
review_headline: Excellent Addition to Any MEdia Computer.
review_body:
If you are really into audio and you bought a new pair of decent speakers, such as studio monitors, for any use, especially with a computer, you owe it to yourself to purchase one of these. Putting this DAC between your computer and your speakers will result in much higher quality audio. You will hear many more details in your music and you will hear everything at a higher quailty. Higher end speakers, anything that wasn't a no name brand purchased at big lots or another bargain section, are capable of playing better quality audio than your computer can feed them, this product will not make your audio sound as good as it ever could but for only $28 it is a huge upgrade.

I myself was skeptical about purchasing one of these as just about every reviewer was using these just as a way to hook a new T.V. to older sound systems. I purchased a set of Yamaha HS50m studio monitors to listen to my music on and I had them hooked directly to the computer through my headphone jack, since I was waiting for this DAC and the mini toslink cable to come. I hooked this DAC into my computer using a mini toslink to toslink, Apple iMac only has mini toslink, and then I used a HOSA dual quarter inch to RCA to go from DAC to my speakers. I instantly noticed a huge improvement in my sound quality. Having listened to songs just as We're Gonna Make This Day (Feat. Massif), and Overnight by the Zac Brown Band as well as Southern Comfort Zone, Beat This Summer, Pressing On A Bruise by Brad Paisley and finally Lullaby by Nickelback, I noticed a huge difference in amount of quality and detail as opposed to juat using the studio monitors. This product is well worth the $28 dollars you will spend on it.

Only one downside, which is with any system that utilizes toslink, you lose the ability to control the volume with your computer, you can still control it in each application or on the speakers themselves. This DAC doesn't have a volume for output. It is only a minor issue in myopinion and the trade off is well worth what you will gain.

review_body:
These are solid cables. And, when I say solid, I mean difficult to bend. I've noted the recent trend to build cables with an extra, braided jacket and have not been impressed with their usability in consumer or professional settings. (I'm a former professional audio engineer and present-day film and video production pro.)

These heavy, braided jackets are designed to reduce cable twisting and thus prevent the interior conductors from being twisted and broken. However, the connector is seldom oriented ideally for the device into which it will plug and one must often wrench the cable around to plug it in. That torsional tension is then translated directly to the connector and socket for the entire time it is plugged in. In addition, should you be working with small clearance around the device socket, any bend imposed from external objects is also translated to the connector.

In general, I plan to avoid purchasing braided-jacket cables in the future.

review_headline: Attach a Blu-Ray Playe to an Old TV
review_body:
A couple of weeks ago I nabbed a superb deal on a refurbished Sony Blu-Ray player. Unfortunately for me, I didn't bother to check the ports and jacks that the player was equipped with, and thus was extremely surprised when I was confronted with an HDMI and digital-audio coax jacks. That was it.

The problem lay in that, while my TV had a DVI jack and thus could be paired to the player via an HDMI-to-DVI cable, this solution didn't transmit audio. My TV lacked any sort of digital audio input option, and thus a solution needed to be found. A quick web search told me that I needed a little adapter box to solve my woes, and that's when I came across the little device you're reading this review about. All it does is convert digital PCM audio (with input options of copper coax or fiber-optic) to analog (using "RCA" style red-and-white cables).

While I could have saved a few bucks ordering this from the world's favorite online auction site, I had a lot more trust in Amazon and their absolutely epic return policy. (Super-fast shipping didn't hurt.) Ordered this little guy, it showed up a couple of days later, and about thirty minutes later my new Blu-Ray player was completely installed and streaming HD video from YouTube. Audio was crystal clear, with no white noise or audio defects whatsoever, unless the player was turned off but not the TV. (Then there was white-noise.)

NOTE: I had to set my player's audio output to be transmitted in PCM format. Until I did that, the box didn't seem to be doing anything. (Or maybe I was doing something wrong.)

Setting the hub up on the network (great, yet another device hanging around my router, just what I need) was pretty straightforward.
Transferring the content from previous remotes was a blast (open up myharmony.com in a browser, NOT the device software you have installed on your computer)

The battery looks to be an improvement. No more charging constantly.

Cons:
Figuring out how to get the battery out (just in case) was a bit tricky. Took me a few minutes to figure it out

The app (for iOS) is, well, pretty bad. I can't count the # of times I tried to delete a 'button' and it just wouldn't work. Same with moving, or adding a button. At one point, I had to close the app out, because device functions were all greyed out when trying to add something. Could select device, but not functions in it.

VERY little control over functionality on the actual remote. For example:
I have an entertainment center that contains a Wii, PS3, 360, Tivo, ATV, TV and home theater system. One of the frustrating things about these devices (going back to even the 880) is that the system won't always pair up automatically. It'll turn on the PS3, the stereo, the TV, but have the TV on a different HDMI setting than it needs to be, the stereo on a completely different one, etc. I have a button to deal with this on the One. product_title: Yuin G1A Earphones
review_headline: High end clip-on headphone. Can it be?
review_body:
The Yuin G1A. You can say that these are the most high end clip-on headphones in the world. That sounds like hyperbole, but it's true. Clip-ons don't really have much of a market for audiophiles, and are content with staying relatively on the domestic market, and/or for physical activities. With a small niche market, the Yuin G1A sits comfortably as the most expensive and highest regarded clip-on headphone.

I am a huge fan of clip-ons. They don't hurt my ears like IEMs. They stay in place no matter what I do, short of literally touching them. They are small enough to lay down with. After a few days of adjusting to how clip-ons feel on your ears, they may as well be the most comfortable headphone design ever made.

It helps that my first experience with clip-ons was with the Koss KSC-75, which for a mere $10-$20, should be in every audiophile's inventory. The KSC-75 hits well above their price range, is extremely comfy, pleasing, and just... legendary.

My 2nd taste of clip-ons headphones was with the rare and mature KSC-35. The KSC-35 is older than the KSC-75 and discontinued everywhere, but can be bought directly from Koss on their website. The Koss KSC35 sacrifices just a little comfort in place of more musicality and warmth compared to their cheaper, and more common sibling. It's also now sold for 3x the price of the KSC-75, though I personally don't believe they should be priced so high, despite my overwhelming love for them.

So how does the Yuin G1A stack up next to the budget conscious Koss offerings? Does the overall package justify the huge price difference? Let's find out.

The package is quite small. A nicely designed cardboard box, with a nice presentation. Doesn't look as generic as the Koss packaging. Upon opening the package I am greeted by the sleek Yuin G1A.

Build Quality: The 'cups' have a sexy, brushed metal finish to them, which immediately puts it well above the KSC-35 and 75 in aesthetics. With that said, that really is the only physical aspect I find superior to the Koss clip-ons. Everything else is so ridiculously similar to the Koss clip-ons, they may as well have been made by the same OEM. The cable's only difference is that the two sides merge further down the line, making it easier to wear the G1A behind the neck, so you can take them off and let them rest on your shoulders/chest, which isn't that easy to do with the Koss clip-ons due to how close the clip-ons are to where the cables merge.

The build itself is... well, it doesn't inspire confidence. The clips are plastic (a very comfortable curved plastic), which seem like they won't take a beating the way the KSC-75's silicone/metal clips, or the sharper, stronger plastic on the KSC-35 would. The cable is quite frankly, sad. It is essentially the same thin, flimsy cable found on the Koss clip-ons. My KSC35's cable is already pulling away from the drivers, and I have feeling the same would probably happen to the G1A's cables.

The good thing about the Koss clip-ons is that their ugly 'hubcaps' aren't luxurious, so I doubt you'd fear messing them up. They are rugged to say the least. On the other hand, you have the G1A with it's amazing brushed metal finish, which might be just as sturdy, but I'd be scared to just toss them in a bag in fear of scratching them or leaving any marks whatsoever. The fact they are $150 further enhances my fears of treating them with wild abandon like I'd do with the Koss clip-ons. In the end, they are expensive, yet very cheap feeling other than the back cover. Very disappointing overall. It's fine with the Koss clip-ons, NOT so with a product this expensive.

Comfort: If there is one thing that can be said, it's that the Yuin G1A is amazingly comfortable. They literally disappeared on my ears. The most important part of a clip-on in terms of comfort is the clips. If the clips don't feel good resting on your ears, that can be quite problematic. Thankfully, the Yuin's plastic clips are smooth and curved just right. They share a very similar form factor as the KSC-75's clips, which are both quite a bit better on the ears than the KSC-35's relatively sharp-edged clips. I also like that the clips are so smooth, they easily slide on my ears. The KSC-75's rubberized clips 'grip' on my skin, so it's a little harder to put on than the Yuin clips. They are both wonderful to wear, however. As mentioned before, the small form factor, secure fit, and super comfort make these practically unrivaled in terms of long sessions, relaxing, or physical activities. As usual, clip-ons may not be the best in comfort for those who wear glasses, as they have to share the same placement on the ears.

Accessories: The only accessories is a 3.5mm to 6.3mm (1/4\\") adapter (the same exact one found on the HE-400, coincidentally), as well as an extra pair of foams.

Isolation/Leakage: As with the Koss clip-ons, the Yuin G1A is open backed (though they actually LOOK closed). This means that they do not isolate well, if at all. External noise will come in with very little contention. I find this to be more good than bad for my Koss clip-ons, as I'd like to be able to hear things around me when I wear my clip ons at work. However, the G1A being hard to drive for such use (more on that later), as well as my fear of physically damaging them makes their very open nature not as beneficial, seeing as the GA1 is more content being used at home with a dedicated amp.

Amping: As I briefly mentioned, the Yuin G1A is a rare breed of clip-on, in that it has a relatively high impedance of 150ohm, and take advantage of that by being harder to drive than typical clip-ons (as well as lots of full sized headphones), which results in more refinement at the expense of versatility. They don't demand a LOT of amping, but amping is necessary nonetheless. Soundstage and overall positioning didn't change, but I feel the improvement in audio fidelity warrants using an amp.

Sound Signature: Before I get started on it's sound, let me state that all three clip-ons I have used can easily swap clips with the others (i.e. KSC35 with Yuin clips, G1A with KSC75 clips, etc). The problem I see with this, is that the sound signature of the headphones change quite a bit just by whatever clip you have equipped onto them. The reason being that each clip places the drivers at certain distances from the ears, which greatly vary the sound signatures. Even with the same clips, just a light bending of them will alter sound quality (easily done with the KSC75's clips). The Yuin clips can bend just a teeny bit, but be prepared to possibly break them in the process if you attempt to. The KSC35's clips don't seem to have any give whatsoever, so what you hear is what you get. For the purpose of this review, I will be rating the G1A based off it's stock clips, which I found to give the most balanced sound signature.

Now on to the sound itself. Upon first listen, the first thing I thought of was that the Yuin G1A sounded like a mini Q701. Well balanced, relatively neutral, with just a hint of warmth. Obviously lacking in soundstage, as well as being lot smaller in presentation of sound, but mini-Q701s is the best description I can come up with.

Bass: Starting with the bass, I can say that the Yuin G1A has neutral bass. The bass is neither strong nor weak. It's present, but not emphasized nor lacking. The KSC35 has more bass impact and presence by quite a bit, and the KSC75 has a slight lead in bass impact.

Mids: Really nice, balanced mids. Not forward or recessed, they sound natural and full. Some frequencies are ever so slightly forward than others, but overall, I find it well integrated with the rest of the frequencies.

Treble: Nice and smooth. SOMETIMES has some sparkle, but overall, it's presented quite naturally. A nice improvement over both the Koss clip-ons which sound grainy and unrefined next to the Yuin, especially in the treble.

Soundstage: Like the other clip-ons, the soundstage isn't big, but it's somewhat airy and spacious, still not rivaling a full-sized headphone's soundstage.

product_title: New Sony Sony Portable Radio Led Tuning Indicator Built In Speaker Earphone Jack Analog Tuner
review_body:
This is probably the best $10 pocket radio I've found, but it's $20 here. Details of this nice listening device...

Frequency range is 87.5-108 MHz in FM; 530-1605 kHz in AM. This is standard, and stations come in pretty clear. The antenna is for FM; it extends to about 18\\" long and folds into the left side of the radio. The antenna folds out, but it doesn't swivel around. I've found that reception is really good, and the antenna is necessary only in the basement. For AM, a ferrite bar antenna is built-in. Tuning is done with a dial scale; not digital. Fine-tuning with the dial is easy. A slide on the right side adjusts between AM and FM.

The radio has two speakers built in; one on the front and one on the back. They're 2-1/4\\" diameter each. Sound is nice and clear. You can use headphones, as a jack is provided on the left side. However, this radio uses monoaural for headphone use; you'll only hear sound from the \\"right\\" ear. I fixed this by buying an adapter from Radio Shack. Specifically, you're looking for a 1/8\\" (3.5mm) Mono Male to 1/8\\" (3.5mm) Stereo Female Adapter. They cost three dollars. This adapter isn't necessary for speaker use; only for headphones.

The radio runs on two AA batteries. Listed runtime is 40 hours on FM and 45 hours on AM. This is with intermittent use, as running the radio until the batteries die will significantly shorten runtime. For me, intermittent runtime was 42 hours on Duracell, 41 hours on Rayovac, and 37 hours on Energizer (FM). Runtime was 47 hours on Duracell, 46 hours on Rayovac, and 42 hours on Energizer (AM). Those runtimes are on standard alkalines; rechargeables will be a little less, while lithiums will be a lot more. Running the radio without turning it off will decrease those runtimes by half.

Size is 2-7/8\\" wide X 4-3/4\\" high X 1-3/16\\" deep (71mm X 118.5mm X 30mm). The radio weighs 7 ounces (202 g) with alkalines installed. Power output is 100mW at 10% harmonic distortion.

The tune indicator lights up in red, and serves as a low battery indicator when it dims. A wrist strap is attached to the left side, and is large enough for most users. I'm guessing it's about 10\\" long. The strap is made of shoestring-type cord; it's round, not flat. It's also pretty sturdy. I haven't tested my radio for drops or water resistance, but it feels like it would be operable as long as you don't throw it. The battery compartment is clearly marked for polarity and uses clean, quality springs. There's not a pull tab to remove the batteries, but it's not necessary. The battery compartment closes with a non-captive slide-on piece of plastic. It retains well, and shaking mine didn't pop it off.

In short, this is a great radio. The sound is excellent (considering the size) and it works every time I turn it on. The only reason I gave it four stars instead of five is because I had to buy an adapter for headphone use. This isn't just a defective unit; I have three more of these and they're all the same. Some users here have mentioned it on theirs as well. But, it's a $3 fix. Give this radio a try; you could do a lot worse for ten bucks./>

product_title: Yamaha RX-V373 Receiver
review_body:
Value
This was hard to beat, I got it on sale for one-seventy-seven. For somebody who doesn't care about 7.1 or 9.1 (5.1 is fine for me and I already had a 5.1 setup and don't want to buy new speakers), and doesn't care about advanced features like per-input settings or S-Video to HDMI video conversion, or tons of inputs (4 is plenty), this unit fills a nice spot in the middle market.

Sound quality
This thing sounds great, lots of midrange like all Yamaha's have had for years, but even better processing and a more even sound field than my old Yamaha RX-V795 from 15 years ago... YPAO probably makes part of the difference because it's setup perfectly (in a couple minutes). It sounds very clear throughout the room, no need to crank it to hear subtle sounds and dialogue. Speakers will make a difference but this thing will make good speakers sound better.

Features
Like I said, this is a basic 5.1 with HDMI, 4k pass-through, and all the latest Dolby/DTS codecs supported. Only 4 inputs, no per-input settings (but it sounds so great across all sources it wouldn't make a difference to most people to switch DSP settings, etc.), etc.

Quality Problems
Based on multiple other reviews mentioning audio drop-outs and pops/clicks this unit seems to have some quality problems. Mine isn't dropping out, but it pops/clicks at the start/end of audio streams and/or DD/Pro-logic switches (using an Xbox 360 and a PC). For now I'm putting up with it and the clicks seem to be getting less harsh over time... it's still better than the old unit that was shutting itself off while in use and sometimes had static on the center channel. I suspect you'd have less problems when opting for a unit in the higher end of the model line (with nicer electrical components), as this unit probably has a tiny profit margin and they probably cut costs on the components.

I suspect units like this are going to become more rare because the low end is going toward sound bars and sound projectors and the high end is going toward 7.1, 9.1, huge wattage, 4k upscaling, whatever-whiz-bang-feature-they-can-upsell-you-on, etc.

Bottom Line
Being able to get these under two hundies, it's pretty low risk if it doesn't last you that long (not in absolute terms, but compared to $650+ units this one is practically disposable). I feel dirty playing into throw-away culture, but we arrived there 20 years ago, so relax and enjoy the great sound (we can at least try to recycle it when it dies though)... besides, you don't want an iPhone that lasts 20 years, why would you want any digital equipment [that will be antiquated in a few years] to last that long?

product_title: Pioneer VSX-1022-K 560W 7-Channel A/V Receiver, Network Ready, Pandora, iPod/iPhone, Black (Discontinued by Manufacturer)
review_headline: Best bang for the buck receiver. Just about perfect in every way.
review_body:
I bought this receiver for $249, had it for 3 weeks, and couldnt' be more impressed with the way everything works in this receiver. While not an audiophile grade receiver, but for this price point, it is nevertheless just about perfect.

AIRPLAY works flawlessly. You can turn on the receiver and control volume on Airplay. Then again you have a iControl remote app for mobile devices. No longer you need a line-of-site or remote eye, or illuminated IR remote buttons.

Zone 2 playback is the best implementation I have ever seen in any of 7.2ch receiver. You can connect 7.1 speakers PLUS 2ch stereo at the same time. This feature is especially good for me. Other brands like Onkyo and Denon, you cannot even wire 7.1 and 2nd zone at the same time. You can only wire 5.1 + 2ch stereo. In this pioneer, you are limited to playing 5.1 + zone 2 simultaneously, but you can keep the wiring connected and choose to do either 7.1 or zone 2 stereo. Why does this matter? say you have a 7.1 ch setup AND 2ch stereo (i.e., computer speakers or different HI FI speakers).... you don't have to change wiring everytime you go from Zone 1 and Zone 2.

power is very adequate for nominal 8ohm speakers, like the manual says. No overheating. No distortion. I'd guess 6ohm speakers will make the amp run on the hot side, 4ohm speakers will overheat the amp. Read speaker's label and stick to the manual's recommendation. I often make this comparison - Yes your Honda S2000's engine can run up to 9000RPM but that doesn't mean it'll last for 100000 miles if you constantly asking it to rev at 9000RPM. Connecting 4Ohm speakers to this amp (or any other amplifiers that are not designed to be used with nominal 4ohm speakers - and believe me there are NO receivers in this price range that can deal with 7 channels of 4Ohm NOMINAL Load) it's like over-revving the engine the WHOLE TIME. and you complain your engine(receiver) overheats and goes into protection mode?

I have 7ch 8ohm nom. speakers + 2CH speakers. I play for hours and hours over days and days this receiver NEVER overheats. Cool to touch all the time.

HDMI inputs and output works flawlessly, passes 3D and XV deep color bandwidth. 1080p upscailing works very well (I have an old LD player) I wish it had a S-Video input but oh well.

I have a $20 1x2 HDMI splitter that feeds both my projector and monitor at the same time from this receiver. Works well.

Network playback feature is there but I don't use it. I listen to LOTS of music from all over the world (German, French, Japanese, Chinese, etc) and NONE of the fonts displays correctly in OSD, so I don't use it. (Even receivers 5x this price point, no UTF-8 font support... All these Japanese brands can't even display Japanese characters correctly. duh).

HDMI inputs, 7.1 ch + 2nd zone play, iPhone control, AIRPLAY, excellent sound quality and connectivities for $250? unbelievable.

* I have not done any jitter measurement (nor it's published in manual) but I'd like to believe it's not too bad. No it's not going to be 20picoseconds (Like Asynchronous USB), but it's quite pleasant sounding.
** I don't know what kind of EQ setting (e.g., no. of bands) it has. but you probably won't hear much difference anyway
