product_title: Sennheiser CX 300 II Precision Enhanced Bass Earbuds, Black
review_headline: Not even close to worth it.
review_body:
Thought I'd get myself some decent earbuds for listening to music at work. I spend a lot of time coding, working with equipment, and reading, so I needed a comfortable pair of earbuds that would have reasonably good sound.

The CX 300B MK II had decent reviews, a couple of audiophiles complaining they weren't good enough, and carried an excellent brand name. I thought I'd spring the little extra cash $27 for the pair when I bought them.

Initially, I was really confused about the unbalanced wire design before I realized that the short side goes directly to your ear and the long side goes around your neck to relieve tension. I ended up really liking that configuration.

What I didn't get was actually good noise. These buds aren't really worth it. I played around with different sized earbuds to get a comfortable fit (that's nice) and while the sound is acceptable for my needs, it's not better than a cheap $10 pair of earbuds.

The cable is also this incredibly grippy black rubber that sticks to everything: clothes, furniture, itself, and so it make it pretty annoying to thread the wires through clothing (e.g. to keep it from catching on anything). It feels substantial, but is not functionally useful.

The around-the-neck design does a good job of dampening cable noise to the far ear, but doesn't help with the close ear. The cable noise is definitely present as you jog or walk around. You can mitigate this by threading the cable through your clothing to minimize its movement.

The worst is the wind noise. When jogging, it's like a pulsing jet of air is swishing by your ears. I found that when walking, I'd get this "woosh" "woosh" "woosh" in time with my steps. I don't walk that fast, guys, that I should be generating wind effects. Just forget about wearing these while track biking.

It is tolerable, but this is what I expect from cheap earbuds. My old iPod earbuds (I used all the old versions, with and without rubber rims, remote control, etc) totally blow these out of the water. My old Skullcandy department store $6 earbuds performed just as well as these.

And finally, after about two good weeks of use, a small exposed piece of cable caught on a doorknob because of the extreme "stickiness" of the cable and gave them a good yank. The cable wire detached from the stereo connector, and my $27 was gone. Great. Won't be getting these again.

Pros:
1. Over-the-neck earbud design relieves some cable-bounce noise and cable tension.
2. Multiple earbud sizes is nice. I tried them all, stuck with the default medium size.
3. When seated correctly, they do a great job of isolating external noise.

Cons:
1. Expensive for their sound quality.
2. Cable noise is still an issue. Don't expect to job with these and have high-fidelity music.
3. Wind noise is absurd. I get wind noise from just walking.
4. All the advertisement about strong bass is hot air. They're no better than any other budget earbud.
5. Absurdly "sticky" cables make threading through clothes difficult and make cable catch on just about everything.

Conclusion:
These earbuds are just fine.... if they cost $10. They're really no better than any other cheap earbud and not worth the premium to have a Seinnheiser logo on them.the old versions, with and without rubber rims, remote control, etc) totally blow these out of the water. product_title: LG Electronics AG-F310DP Cinema 3D Dual Play Gaming Glasses (2 Pair) (Discontinued by Manufacturer)
review_headline: You don't need these if you have a couple extra pairs of regular 3d glasses
review_body:
So these are at a good price and are pretty nice glasses for gaming (thus the 4 star), but if you have bought a LG 3d tv and want to play games splitscreen but don't want to shell out the cash, here's how.

Simply pry open the regular glasses that came with your TV from the top. There is a lining you can probably see. Once you pop out the edges by the hinges, then you can pull out the flimsy lens part. Just do this to a left eye and then a right on another pair. Switch those 2 lenses you just removed to the other glasses and snap the plastic back together. Done. You now have 2 pairs of Gaming glasses.

Lots of companies will try to get you to pay $10-30 for a pair or 2 or 4 of these when you can make them if you have a couple extra pairs you aren't using. Mine came with 4 pairs, so I have 2 pairs for 3D viewing and 2 pairs for gaming. Just use fingernail polish or a permanent marker to mark the Gaming ones so you don't get them mixed up.

That said, these are a pretty decent deal and if I could not have done the above fix (or if I just didn't have more than 2 pairs) then I would have bought these.

Hope this review helps people.

product_title: HP MonsterPortable Power w/ USB 3 Outlets (HPM OTG300 USB ES) (Discontinued by Manufacturer)
review_headline: Essential for International Travelers - USB port works from 100-240V and outputs 1500mA
review_body:
I got this product ([[ASIN:B002RL9XRG HP Monster Portable Power w/ USB 3 Outlets OTG300 USB ES]]) for my recent business trip to Europe. It turned out to be a life-saver in several occasions, where there was only one AC outlet available but we needed to power two laptops. The built-in USB port was also handy for recharging my tablet and cell phone.

One important feature of this power strip is that: you can plug it into either 110V or 220V AC, and the USB port will work equally well. Strangely enough, this feature is not even advertised on Amazon product page. Although to be clear, this power strip does NOT do voltage conversion for its AC outlets, so whatever you plug into it better be rated for the input voltage. Fortunately, most portable electronics (such as chargers for laptops, tablets or cameras) are already compatible with universal AC voltage of 100-240V.

Another important spec that is missing is the USB port output current rating. There were a lot of confusions because earlier generation of this product was rated for just 500mA. On the package I received it says '1500mA', but on the power strip itself it says '1000mA'. Based on my own measurement with the [[ASIN:B005B9G79I VIZIO VTAB1008 tablet]] as load, this USB port is actually capable of supplying a maximum current of about 1600mA. This should be sufficient for recharging most portable electronics. One exception is that an iPad3 requires up to 2.3A. So if you try to recharge it through this USB port, your iPad may say \\"Not charging\\" even though it is still being charged at a slower rate.

I also have the [[ASIN:B003TXRTNG Monster Outlets To Go MP OTG300 LTOP 300]] which serves nearly the same purpose. It is more compact and has two USB ports, with a COMBINED output current of 1500mA. But when using one port at a time, the output current is limited to just 1000mA. So it will be even slower in recharging an iPad3 - not that it matters to me since I don't have i-anything. In any case, both products worked equally well and are highly recommended for international travelers.any case, both products worked equally well and are highly recommended for international travelers.

product_title: Denon AVR-4308CI Multizone Home Theater Receiver with Network Streaming and Wi-Fi (Discontinued by Manufacturer)
review_headline: Great Receiver but hard to use.
review_body:
I bought one of these 4 years ago and only now really have it humming. There are several bugs in the network/usb operation that Denon never addressed and never came clean on in the official Denon support page. After reading countless audio forums I fixed all the bugs and this unit really lives up to its potential as a knock out home theater hub.

Bug #1: The network function locks up after a few hours of operation and gives a \\"server disconnected\\" error. You must hard power cycle the unit to get it working again. The fix for this is to add a rule to your internet router to block the Denon 4308 trying to access the web address 207.188.0.25 This fix is buried in several discussion forums.

Bug #2: When using a wireless network connection and the internet radio station you are listening to goes down the Denon will disconnect from your LAN. You must go through a re-connection process to get it back on line. The only solution I know is to use hardwire ethernet connection then there is no problem.

Bug #3: When playing files from USB or a network server make sure the mp3 tags are not corrupt. The Denon 4308 will lock up and freeze on corrupt mp3 tags. It seems the Denon first trys to get the metadata and then plays the file. If the metadata is corrupt it goes no further even though the music file is fine. The only way to get the unit going again after a lock up is a hard power cycle. There is freeware you can download \\"Mp3tag\\" that can fix corrupt tags.

Two other complaints and then I'll get onto the pluses ....

a: Denon does not provide a remote control app for this networked unit .Fortunately there is one called \\"AVR-Remote\\" in the Google play store. It is free and very good.
b: The Denon manual is arcane and very difficult to understand. Fortunately there is a website called \\"Batpigworld\\" (no kidding) that does a great job of translating \\"Denonese\\" to US English.

Now having said all that ...I love this receiver and would not give it up. It handles and decodes all formats flawlessly. The sound is crisp and clean. The power more than adequate. The Audyssey processing is a big bonus. Even though it is a five year old model the only thing that is \\"outdated\\" is there is no \\"Audio return Channel\\" (ARC) on any of the HDMIs ... no big deal. This is a great product. It's a pity Denon didn't put more customer support behind it instead of the user community.

product_title: Comply Comfort PLUS Earphone Tips
review_headline: So much better than silicon - buy these
review_body:
Every time I get a new pair of earbuds I buy the matching Comply Foam tips. Because of the way the bass works on those in-ear phones you really need a tight seal and contact with the skin in your ear canal, and silicon or rubber tips just don't do the job as well as foam that compresses and expands to fill your ear. Also, they are more comfortable and provide better noise isolation.

These TSX-500 tips have a rather large tunnel and are meant for only certain headphones with matching barrels. I use mine with the Novero bluetooth earbuds and they also help them stay in place better than the included tips.

The downside is that the foam does wear out after a while, so you need the three-pack. Previously, the spherical tips only came in one size - I checked with the company and the M is the same as the old size. I seem to have pretty big ear canals, so take that as you will. If you have tiny ears I would deffo go with the small, but only if you are an elephant will you probably need the large size. Keep in mind that they squish and expand, rather than fold, so they fit a wider variety of ears.

The great things about these is that they include a wax-guard. There's a thin piece of mesh at the opening of the tube, so that when you replace the tip you get a fresh mesh, and no wax gets into the earphone. Most earphones have some sort of mesh of their own, but I have found they often get clogged and get ruined when I try to clean them - sometimes ruining the earbuds. This feature is definitely worth the extra money. Happy listening.

product_title: Outdoor Technology Tags Wireless Bluetooth Earbud Headphones
review_body:
Okay, I want to start off by saying that I am currently in Afghanistan as a contractor and work in and out of military vehicles. I got tired of my wired headphones catching on to different parts of the truck which would eventually destroy them. I looked online and found these for their awesome price. Once the headphones came in, I charged them and started using them with my new 7th Gen Nano. This was my first bluetooth device so I went through the directions and started playing with them. They connected quickly to my Ipod and the directions were awesome for a not-so-smart-guy. I also use these in the gym, it was just awesome not having a cable to get in your way or get caught on something. Another feature I liked about these headphones was that you can control the volume and go forward/backwards on your media device without having to pull out it out. I had my Ipod in my pocket while working out and it did not skip once! BUT... when I went outside, it began to skip, but I believe that was from being around all the military vehicles with their electronic counter measures on. At first, the medium sized plugs did not stay in my ears, but i swapped them for the larger ones and since then, the headphones have been staying in my ears! The day I got these, I charged them as soon as I got them out of the box, then used them for about 10 minutes, a few days later I had them on until the battery died. I was outside working from 945 a.m. to 3 p.m.. so I got around 5 hours with these headphones.

What I didnt like:
1. The ear clips: I'm not sure who designed those clips but would definitely like to talk to him about how horrible those fit around the ear. I wanted to take a star off for that, but decided not too, SINCE I do not use them, and will say that if you do decide to use the clips, they DO work but just didn't feel right for me.
2. The short usb charging cable: It would have been nice for it to be a wee bit longer...

Neutral:
The size of the headphones. Please do not under estimate the size of those ear pieces! They're not HUGE, but they will be bigger than what you expected, but this had no effect on me.

Great set of bluetooth headphones and would definitely recommend these to anyone looking for a pair.

review_headline: Increase the volume of your HDTV

HDTVs are notorious for having poor sound, even with the volume all the way up. It's even worse when streaming movies from Amazon or my PC.

I have wireless stereo headphones, which give me great sound, especially when I'm watching a movie or a program with music in it. But, I don't always want to wear them. I unplug the headphones from the HDTV and plug in this portable mini speaker to the same left and right audio out ports on my HDTV (I have an adapter at the end of the Y plug that holds the mic plug). The sound quality is amazing. I can keep the sound from the TV on, or turn it off and play only from the mini speaker. It makes a huge difference even though the cord only reaches out about two feet in front of the TV.

You can also use it for your Kindle Fire and any other tablet that has a speaker mic on it. Just plug it in to get louder sound. There is no volume control on it and the volume control on the device only makes a slight difference in the overall volume of the mini speaker. If it's up real high and you turn it down to half way, you will notice a difference, but if it's turned down in small increments, there is no real change in the volume of the mini speaker.

It would get five stars if it had a volume control.

review_body: I own an RV, and the interior plug for getting shore power inside the motorhome is finicky to say the least. When I first setup a computer on a power strip in the RV, the cord came out and my solid state drive failed to be recognized upon rebooting the computer. That was a total disaster, so I immediately researched UPS options as soon as I was up and running again. After a lot of reading, I settled on the CP1000PFCLCD because it had pure sine wave output, and the weight and power rating were right for my needs. In the time since it arrived, the plug has fallen out of the loose wall socket no few than 10 times... all without issue. Also, I didn't even realize before, but when I run my space heater, while connected to shore power, the incoming voltage drops to 108V... so the UPS kicks in and boost the power to around 118-120 in those times. You can download the latest version of Power Panel, and configure and monitor the UPS from your computer to see how many times it has kicked in in the past 30 days. And as if those aren't enough reasons to love this thing, it comes with a built-in "Kill-A-Watt" like meter, so I can measure my power consumption... which has proven incredibly helpful in planning my solar needs for an upcoming expansion I will be undertaking soon. All and all, this was the best purchase I've made to date for my RV. Shipping from seller was fast, and product arrived in perfect condition. I did follow the directions and leave it plugged in for 8 hours before attempting to connect any devices to it. I would recommend doing the same, since it has an auto-shutoff if undercharged.

product_title: Logitech 915-000144 Harmony Link - Black (Discontinued by Manufacturer)
review_headline: A Wonderful Remote by Logitech for the 99 Percent of Us
review_body:
My Harmony Link is a godsend. I have never been happier with a remote. Suddenly my wife's iPhone, my iPhone and my iPad tablet are all remotes that can control our TV, our TiVo, our Apple TV, our Blu-Ray player, our Audio Video Receiver and and our DVD player. And they control them in an elegant and straightforward way. They are easy to use, always available and simple to setup.

This product is designed for the 99 percent of us who want excellent function without having to become programmers. If you are comfortable with touch screens and soft controls and don't want to have another device on your table then use the Harmony Link with your iPad or your iPhone and enjoy not having to search for and charge another cumbersome remote.

With my iPhone I have buttons and sliders for all the appropriate device activities. And, on my iPad I have additional content displayed. Its background displays thumbnail pictures and icons of what programing is currently available by channel. You can constrain the display with one click to show only HD content, movies, sports or favorite channels that you have designated. You can also change the display to show a minimalist set of controls or a full set of buttons and sliders that will control every aspect of your devices with simple swipe of your finger.

Of course if you feel that you should be able to remove, add, change, or recolor every button then this is not your remote. If you want to enter hex IR codes or create macros to control your devices then this is not your remote. If you demand a hard push-button for every function then this is not your remote You need to get a Harmony One or a Harmony Touch or the Harmony 1100 or a Roomie remote or one of the many other programmable remotes on the market.

But, when I read the negative comments in some of the previous reviews I can only shake my head and wonder if these people were using the same Logitech Harmony Link that I have and adore. Setup?What could be simpler than signing onto the Logitech site and answering a few questions? Usage? Well it's all right there on your tablet or phone. And it works smoothly and well.

Now I must admit that I did some preparation before purchasing the device and before starting my install. I watched a number of YouTube videos on how to set up the product. I learned what to expect before I installed and configured it. I also read the reviews and manuals on my devices before beginning to configure the Harmony Link. In short, I did what anyone would do before driving off in a new car or starting up a new computer: I did my homework.

This is an excellent product for most of us and the price is phenomenal. What a great deal.

product_title: Sennheiser Digital Wireless Headphones
review_body:
I've heard very-high-end audio systems before (costing deep into five-figures), and I own a pair of Sennheiser HD 600 wired headphones, so I have experience with a good set of cans. That said, I wouldn't quite call the RS 180 audiophile grade. However, for anything less than highly critical listening, these headphones deliver clean, quality sound that should satisfy just about anyone.

I don't use these for listening to music, I use them with my TV when I want to watch a movie late at night. They allow me to mute the TV's speakers while listening through the headphones at whatever volume level I like without worrying about waking others in the house. I wasn't expecting much bass response, but they do have a respectable low end. Nothing that would match a good home theater system, but as much or more than what my TV's built-in speakers offer down low.

I debated whether to splurge and get the RS 220 or these. Reviews I read both at Amazon and elsewhere made me decide the RS 180 was the way to go. Many have reported having problems with static or broken signals with the RS 220, which, apparently, uses a different wi-fi system. I've had no problems with the signal using my RS 180. Sound quality is very clear and static free. My listening distance from the headphones' base is usually around 15 feet, but I've walked into other rooms while wearing these and found the signal remains clear and strong. The headphones are comfortable even after wearing them for several hours. Battery life has never been an issue. Sennheiser claims these can be used for up to 24 hours on a single charge (two AAA Eneloop rechargeable batteries are included). I've never even come close to testing that claim as I stop watching TV long before these things run out of juice. The RS 220, in contrast, only lasts up to 8 hours on a single charge, which could be an issue if multiple people were to use it during the day. The RS 220 reportedly does have slightly better sound quality, but you pay through the nose to get that little extra bit of quality. There's a point of diminishing returns with everything, and for my purposes, the RS 180 is the right balance of price and performance.

The only real niggle I have is with the volume buttons on the headphones. The volume-up button is actually bigger than the volume-down button. It's easy enough to find and press while wearing the headset. The button right next to it is the power button. It has a raised surface that aids in locating it by feel. The next button over is the volume-down button. It's notably smaller than the volume-up button (form over function) and can be a little hard to find when you're feeling for it while wearing the headphones. Sometimes I have to remove the headset to find it, although I'm getting better at finding it the more I wear these. It's not a huge deal since I don't have to adjust the volume often, but it's an area for improvement if Sennheiser ever decides to redesign these.

As others have mentioned, there is a very slight time delay in the wireless signal (emphasis on \\"very slight\\"), so if your TV's speakers are turned up while you're listening to the headphones, you can hear the slightest echo effect. If your TV's speakers are turned down enough relative to the headphones, you might not even notice it. The signal delay really is quite small, so the effect is minor, but, apparently, not all wireless headphone suffer from this, so it needs to be mentioned at least.

Despite these minor issues, I still give 5 stars to the RS180 for its solid performance at this price point.

[Edit: 12-1-13] Just wanted to update this review with a word about Sennheiser's excellent customer support. One of my kids knocked my headphones and its base off their shelf, which damaged them internally so that they would no longer produce sound. I sent them in to Sennheiser with a note about how they got broken. I acknowledgedthe existing warranty might not cover such abuse and stated I was willing to pay for the repair if needed. A couple weeks later, Sennheiser mailed me what looks to be a new (but is perhaps refurbished) unit and base with all of the needed wires (I had only mailed in the headphones and base unit without the wires). No questions asked, and no cost to me. First class customer service.

product_title: Monoprice Select Series High-Speed HDMI Cable
review_body:
Over the years, I have purchased over 20 of these cables at various lengths. I also own one from the Monster brand that was my first HDMI cable. The monoprice cables are clearly the better buy, but should you be concerned about reliability or performance? The answer is no. Back when analog cables were being used, the Monster brand made a name for itself, especially in the car audio segment. Now that we live in a digital world, the advantages they could once claim are no longer a factor. With digital, the quality of the picture is not determined by the cable itself (either the digital transmission makes it from the source to the destination, or it does not).

While you don't want to waste your money on an expensive brand like Monster, you also don't want to buy a cheaply made cable with poor shielding and reliability. Enter Monoprice, an affordable brand that has been around for years and considered by some to be the industry leader in this category. With Monoprice, you have the option of buying cables with or without ferrite cores. While the non-ferrite cores are slimmer and more attractive, I highly recommend getting cables that have them. This is especially important in situations where you have a lot of cables (power, video, sound, etc.) coming in contact with each other or close proximity. The ferrite cores help eliminate interference.

The particular cable I purchased from this seller was as described. Like other Monoprice cables I own, this one has performed well. For those not familiar with the brand, here's their main web site: [...]

product_title: Sony High-Resolution Noise Cancellation Audio Headset
review_body:
There are two major problems with this product. The first is that the reception is horrible. If you don't mind remaining in a set position like a statue I suppose this wouldn't be an issue, but if you plan on turning your head at any time during their use be prepared for a blast of static or loss of signal, even from a distance of less than 10 feet. I have owned T.V. wireless headphones of various types since they came out, but these number among the worst.

The second problem is the inaccessibility of the rechargeable batteries. The manual says they will stay charged for 23 hours, but cautions that the time may vary \\"depending on use.\\" Huh??? Since the headset can only be charged while resting on the base unit be prepared to wait the 3.5 hours for the headphones to charge back up in order to use them again once the charge runs out. I suppose the excitement of guessing when that might occur may be attractive to some, but I think I'll pass on that bit of unnessesary mystery. It seems to me that limiting the ability of the customer to use the product when they see fit is either a fatal design flaw or something which was done intentionally to force the customer to return the product for service once the rechargeable batteries are no longer functional. Batteries of this type are destined to reach their lifetime limit sooner than expected due the customer's habit of recharging them when they are not fully discharged, creating a memory in the batteries that make them non-functional over time.

At a cost of over $80, this product is grossly overpriced for what it delivers, and in my opinion, too expensive at any price.

They do not fall off, but I do have to be careful when bending my head down.

Volume control, track control and power button on the side of the right speaker is very easy to use and a great convenience.

Answering phone calls is a snap and I was worried from reading other reviews about the quality of the microphone when using the phone to call someone. I have talked to several people in the last two days and not once did anyone mention any issue with the sound quality. product_title: Logitech Harmony Touch Universal Remote with Color Touchscreen
review_body:
I have been a long time Harmony remote fan. I started with the 720 which I thought was perfect, moved to the 900 which somehow was even better, and now the touch. I gave it a try despite the poor reviews because my wife was not a fan of the 900. The screen kept needing to be reset by popping out the battery. It was annoying but it didn't really bother me. My wife however couldn't stand it. I got her the touch because it didn't seem to have this frequent reset need (and after weeks of use, I can confirm it definitely does not have this problem). I was expecting the touch to be average at best, possibly a disappointment (after seeing the scathing reviews), but I was shocked at how big of an improvement it was. I think Logitech took a page from the Apple playbook and tried to take a minimalist approach to what a remote really needs. I think they nailed it out of the park. The look and feel of the remote is the best yet, all my old settings programmed into the new online tool perfectly, and the new software is far easier to use than the old desktop client. I also love the favorite channels feature. I've played with this on old remotes and it was never quite right so I grew tired of it and stopped using it. They finally got it right on the touch.

I thought the missing DVR skip buttons would be annoying as well so I simply swapped them out for the hard FF and REW buttons. Blue and Yellow aren't used for anything (that I use anyway) on my satellite box, so I turned those into the FF and REW buttons. It is customizable after all, make it work for your needs.

product_title: Bose SIE2 Sport Headphones
review_body:
There's no disputing that these are good ear/headphones. I use them every day and am glad I have them because they have a couple of features that most of Bose's competitors' products don't. Specifically, the earphones, while oddly-shaped with soft pliable ear wings, are much more comfortable, yet much more securely fastened, than other top-range products that one has to stuff into his/her ear canal, that get waxy, and that pop out with mild jarring (e.g., while jogging). The Bose's stay put perfectly, and they let the right amount (for me) of ambient sound through, so you can hear traffic, a knock at your door, whatever. I also like the iPhone compatible microphone, pause button, and volume controls.

But there's also no disputing that these are not great ear/headphones. The sound quality is good, but no better than that -- nowhere near the quality one would expect for the price. Another disappointing bug (that Bose will surely argue is a feature) is the two-piece chord. At its short length, the chord is about 3" too short to use putting your iPhone in your pants pocket. [I'm 6' tall - it might be OK with 5'8" and under.] With the extension, the chord is about a foot too long, which maybe wouldn't be that bad, except that the connection between the basic and the extension chords adds significant weight to the chord and makes it dangle very awkwardly. My guess is that this dual-length design had the armband device-holder in mind, and the short length solo-chord probably is more optimally sized for that. But if you don't want to mess with an armband holder (which I can't imagine you would unless running), the chord is a design flaw. Another unfortunate oversight is that the mic/volume control doesn't have track-skip/forward-rewind capabilities.

Summary: I'm glad to have the SIE2i's, but, had I to do it over with the knowledge of their shortcomings, I would not purchase them again unless the price were cut by about 50 percent. It seems that's usually the case with Bose products. (And, therefore, it also seems I have a Bose "learning issue.")

product_title: Scosche Noise Isolation Earbuds with tapLINE II
review_body:
The sound is fine. The little thingamajig that makes the volume go up and down is fine. Being able to stop and start my audio books is fine. The microphone is fine. The fit in my ears is fine.

But ear buds should last more than 2 months!!!! They always break. Always. Every pair. And I'm really tired of it. This is not theoretical physics for cryin' out loud. I like my audio books and I listen to them all the time. So yes, they get used. But they don't get abused -- it's just normal wear on an iPod.

Sure I could fiddle around with the continuity tester which is somewhere in the garage and try to fix the darned thing. But dammit my hands are arthritic and it hurts. So I end up buying these things like cartons of cigarettes. Why can't they make these so that last for the life of the iPod? Is that really so unreasonable.

So I'm giving it 2 stars because I think that these things are all made so poorly that it smacks of planned obsolescence. In other words they're designed to break so that people have to buy them repeatedly thus increasing corporate profits.

But there's a product designer out there who might read this and decide to make a set of earbuds that don't break easily. And when you do you'll become wealthy because people like me will buy them. I think that there are a lot of people who are just as fed up with this as I am and we'd make great customers for a more robust product.

product_title: Sony BDVN790W Blu-ray Home Theater System (2013 Model)
review_body:
Don't let the size of the speakers fool you, this system is definitely a lot more to it than what you may think. I've always had a good experience with Sony products and this Blu-ray home theater system does not disappoint. The BDVN-790W Blu-ray Home Theater System really does follow the traditional quality product that Sony offers in its line of products, with sleek looks and good pricing from Amazon. Even with the good looks, it does not sacrifice quality of sound and performance. It has two main speakers, a center speaker, and two wireless rear speakers along with a subwoofer. If you own a PS3 or PSP or PS Vita, the home interface will be very familiar to you.
I use it to play music, watch Netflix, connects to my PS3/Xbox and TV with ease (as long as you have two HDMI cables), and to watch Blu-rays.

Pros:
- Very easy to set up, especially with the color coding of the connectors from the speakers/subwoofer to the Blu-ray player and wireless receiver
- Wireless receiver does not require batteries, it just plugs into a power outlet
- It includes a iPod/iPhone dock to connect to the system (Haven't used this yet as I don't own a iPod or iPhone. I'm not a big fan of Apple products...)
- Very sleek and stylish looking. The Blu-ray unit itself has a touch-interface for buttons such as Play, Stop, Skip buttons, Volume buttons, etc. (EXCEPT for the Power button, which is an actual button you can press)
- It includes FM radio as well
- The remote control has a dedicated red "Netflix" button (So awesome)
- There's an app on the Google Play Store to control the system from your Android phone (VERY handy when I'm in another room)
- Sound is just great, especially with the ease of the initial set-up with the included microphone to adjust the volume settings of the speakers. When the set-up is done just right, there is the bass you want, but not to the excessive point where you can't even hear the lyrics of a song or know what's even playing. (This is not like a sound system you will hear from a Honda Civic from back in the days, if you get what I mean...)
- Has popularservices like Pandora, and Netflix

Cons:
- The home interface seems outdated when compared to the UI of the PS3 (March 8th, 2013 at the time of this review)
- You can't have music playing in the background when you press the 'Return' or 'Home' button to navigate elsewhere in the system (The only exception to playing music in the background is when the screensaver kicks in)
- When I try to play music through an Android device (I have tried my Nexus 4, Motorola Xoom Wifi, and Galaxy Nexus, all had the same result) by connecting it via a audio cable (red and white connector with the opposite end containing the 3.5mm jack), the sound is horrible, even with the volumes on both device and system turned all the way up. The volume seems like it is less than half of what it should be at, and the quality of the sound is certainly downgraded compared to the sound quality of streaming music through Pandora or Sony's Music Unlimited program (NOTE: I have thought about buying a new audio cable to test if it's just the cable that isn't as good. Will update on this review when I try this out)
- Apps seem outdated when compared to other systems versions and UI layout (Examples are the Music Unlimited program, when compared to the PS3's version and desktop version. Another is the UI layout of Pandora, it also seems outdated.

product_title: APC PRO7T Surge Arrest Professional with Phone Cable
review_body:
I bought one of these same Pro 7 units 4 years ago and have used it daily since purchase. We live in an area that has frequent lightning storms and very unstable power surges that ruined one DVD and a flat screen TV using other surge protectors that had no light indicating whether active protection was working or not. After purchasing the Pro 7, I had no problems at all. Finally one day a few weeks ago the green \\"working protection light\\" stopped working for some unknown reason. I e-mailed APC/Schneider Electric and was promptly supplied with a new unit (after proving that, in fact, I DID own a Pro7 unit). They guarantee customer satisfaction and I can certainly vouch for that.

From past experience, though, don't buy a surge protector (particularly for a computer) unless it has a \\"Working Protection\\" LED light, plus protection circuits like the Pro 7's metal oxide varistors, thermal fuses, fast acting current fuses, and massive rod core inductors. As though that isn't enough, the on/off switch also acts as a circuit breaker. For an internet price of around $26, you can't buy any better protection.

product_title: C Crane Co CC2B Radio-2 AM FM/Weather and 2-Meter Ham Band (Black Mica)
review_body:
For some years now, I have been on a quest to find the best portable radio under $200.00. I've purchased more than a dozen radios, both new and used, ranging from the fine Sangean PR-D5, GE Super Radio II (a classic), Sony ICF-5 Mk2 (excellent, but expensive), CC Radio-EP (very good), CC Radio SW, Sony ICF-SW 7600GR, and several others, big and small. None perform as well as the CCRadio-2, overall.

AM reception is especially good with the station that broadcasts my favorite baseball team's games coming in strong. There is no drift, no surging, and no noise, even though the transmitter is well over 100 miles away. FM is very good, as well, and my preferred NPR stations all come in clearly. The CCRadio-2 also has a weather band that is supposed to work quite well, but I have not used this feature and I cannot comment on it. The digital tuner is very precise and it locks securely on stations, even weak ones, with little or no slop-over from nearby signals.

Sound quality is very good and the radio has bass and treble controls to adjust the sound to suit the listener's tastes. The CCRadio-2 has a limited number of memories (only five per band) which might be too few for some people, but it has not been a real problem for me. The radio has an alarm feature with snooze that is easy to set and use, too.

Build and material quality is very good. The CCRadio-2 is heavy, feels very solid, and has no loose bits or rattles. It provides a sense of quality that makes it a very satisfying radio to carry and to use. Another positive feature of this radio is, in contrast to other radios that offer a \\"wall wart\\" to plug into AC (if, indeed, they come with anything at all), the CCRadio-2 has a built in transformer and provides a cord that can be plugged directly into a wall socket. Happily, battery life has been surprisingly good, as well.

In summary, the CCRadio-2 does everything a radio should do and it does it very well, with no complaints, excuses, or glitches. In an era where radios are very nearly anachronistic, this radio hearkens back to an earlier time when this level of performance and quality was highly sought after and appreciated. Consequently, the CCRadio-2 has become my favorite radio for use around my house and when I go on short trips. I would not hesitate to recommend it to anyone. product_title: GOgroove AirBAND Wireless Bluetooth Stereo Headphones with Microphone and Onboard Controls - Compact & Adjustable , Sleek Headband Design , & 8 Hour Battery Life
review_headline: Solid product with decent sound for the price
review_body:
The main reason for me writing this review is that as someone who researched this quite a bit before buying, I just want to throw in my two cents based on the difference between what you're going to read about the product and the reality for the things that will matter most. So here are some highlights based on my experience so far keeping in mind that I primarily purchased it for working out.

Build quality: Relatively sturdy. Not worried about anything snapping or breaking, feels like it could take few drops, but I'm not going to test it.

Fit: I probably have a slightly larger than normal head, and when I first put it on it felt like a little too much pressure on my ears. But after using it for a couple workouts it feels totally comfortable. If you are moving around a lot during a workout, you may have to readjust from time to time for optimal sound, but it's barely an issue.

Sound quality: It's kind of hard to explain. It does have a full sound in many music scenarios, and it is probably on the top end of the spectrum considering it's wireless and under $50. But you should know that when there is a lot going on musically, it starts to break down a little at higher volumes. Which is to say it's not quite as crisp when the music is more simple. Otherwise the sound balance is pretty good. Good bass, but not too much. Good highs, but not piercing.

Of course headphones are always such a person preference, but I think for the under $50, you can't really do better than this.

product_title: Sanus Systems LL11-B1 51 x 80-Inch Ultra-Thin Flat Panel Mount for TV
review_headline: One of the best BIG SCREEN mounts...but may need slight modding
review_body:
I love this mount simply because of it's width which I believe was 36" (writing this review long after i bought, so i forget)

My only problem with this (hence no 5 star, cuz everything else is pretty awesome) is what has been previous commented on...the lack of proper holes. This unit is wide enough to hit 3 (yes THREE) studs, BUT....not with the current hole drillings that come on this unit. I used a drill press and drilled a hole on top/bottom in the middle AND on the FAR left and FAR right. This allowed mounting to 3 studs. Some may say that that's not necessary, but I was mounting a 65" plasma which was very expensive. I want the extra protection. This thing isn't going anywhere on three studs

Other factors: It's ultra-thin. I like this feature but some may find it TOO thin. The arm bracket's lock onto the wall plate very nicely. The material of the build feels good. Has convenient string on bottom of brackets to unlock from wall plate. AND....one of my favorite features was a fine-adjustment on the bracket arms. There is a screw that, when used with an alan wrech (While the TV is mounted) can fine-tune the height of the mounted tv. What this means is, if you mounted the wall plate and even though you were careful, it came out slightly crooked....these screws will fine tune it. But only has like 1.0" to go either up or down.

I would recommend this to anyone mounting large flatscreens. Looks beautiful if done well

product_title: TDK Life on Record Sound Cube Audio System
review_body:
I bought one of these having read prior reviews and learning about a potential battery issue. When I received it I mustered up 12 D cells and populated the battery compartment, but stuck a current meter in series with the batteries. It read that the unit was drawing 60mA from the batteries continuously, even when 'switched off'. I plugged in the power adapter. It STILL drew 60mA from the batteries even though it was powered externally. This makes no sense and defies it's use as a portable unit. The batteries would be exhausted in a few days, even not being used.
As I had bought it to be used as a portable unit, this defect really bugged me. I concluded I needed to add a power switch to the unit, so I could isolate the batteries independent of what the unit was trying to do. I contacted TDK, that confirmed the batteries would be drained if left in the compartment, told me I could not obtain a service manual and if I modified it, the warranty would be voided.
I could not take the thing apart - the four exposed screws in the base do not allow it to be separated once removed. Their is an internal bracing bar that runs top-to-bottom inside the unit and the screw that holds it together is hidden.
I eventually found I could gently edge-out the rim around the rear passive woofer with a flat knife. Once removed the screws holding the passive woofer in place were accessible, and on their removal I could take out the passive woofer (it has no wires) and gain a 5 inch access port. I drilled a hole in the rear of the case, cut the red wire to the battery compartment and added a switch in-line (this also required some almost-blind soldering; but I was determined). Now it works the way a user would like it to.
PROS
Sounds good, a little boomy indoors but great outdoors.
Runs on a large set of batteries so it lasts quite a while truly as a portable
Has a USB port - I use micro USB memory sticks, that do not even protrude out of the recessed rear connector panel, so one can be left in permanently.
Top leather handle so easy to pick up and move around
Sturdy, feels robust
Two powered speakers (left and right) with concentric tweeters
Two passive woofers to increase bass.
Loud
Nice and clear display

CONs
The battery power drain issue is a big one for a portable. If you are not adept at soldering and don't want to insert a switch, but want a portable unit, this one is not for you.
Exposed drivers require you take care and can easily damage them
Left/right tweeters are side firing and no Hi-Fi guy would accept the dispersion limitations this results in, but it is perfectly fine for casual outdoor listening
Limited USB music management. It handles hierarchical directory structures, but for some reason will only shuffle within the lowest directory. So if you copy music onto a stick in the usual format - Artist - Album - Tracks, then it will only shuffle the tracks on one album. What use is that? You have to put all tracks in one directory to shuffle them. I cannot make sense of that, but can live with it.
No remote, or Bluetooth.

Did I say it looks and sounds good outdoors. It most certainly does. It is impressive as a sound box and has more potential than TDK took advantage of. They designed in some pretty basic flaws, but once you figure out how to get around them, hardware mods and warranty voided, it is quite a nice machine.

It also has a guitar input for those budding buskers!

review_body:
The Waterfi Shuffle was a present. I had been shopping for a waterproof music player and before I could buy one, this came a gift. I am glad the decision to buy it was out of my hands because I had been leaning towards the SwimP3. I can't say if this is better or not, only that it is everything I want.

I clip this to my bathing suit strap and bundle the excess ear bud wire into the top of my suit (securing the extra length with wire wrap, with a little bit of waterproof sports tape to blunt the edge of the wire wrap). I also wear a bathing cap and that helps keep the ear buds in. As the instructions say, put them in before you shower down. I believe one advantage to wearing the unit on your front, is it's easier to operate and people see it (so they are less likely to talk to you -- since you can't hear them well). I can't see much without my glasses on and once I'm in goggles -- so not having a display is a non-issue (and I don't think any of the waterproof units on the market offer much in the way of this).

The player itself never gives me a problem but every so often, the rubber cover of an ear bud will slip out of place. Make sure that you take it out in the shallow end of the pool - or when you are out of it! Also, it wouldn't hurt to have a blunt set of tweezers with you in case you have a hard time pulling a separated rubber end out of your ear. If you have a small ear canal, that might be an issue.

This seems to be a tough little unit and it's compact size is ideal. I am super careful about where I keep it (so I don't lose it) and make sure my ear bud wires are untangled before I put them away in a plastic eye glasses carrying case. I also rinse the unit and ear buds off after each swim to get the chlorine off them and once I get home, set them out to air dry. I like this Shuffle so much, I want it to last forever!

product_title: Grado Headphones
review_headline: Written Review of the Infamous Grado Prestige Series Model No. SR-60i (5 Stars)
review_body:
Personally, I wouldn't trust written reviews. The overall rating is usually inaccurate. This is due to the age old principle that people \\"complain before they praise.\\" So the overall rating is usually really .1 to .3 stars higher than the one on amazon, or sony.com or wherever there are reviews. I would go to Youtube and search for the product reviews there. That is much more helpful and usually can help make your mind over faster than written reviews can.

Well, here is the information I would look for in a written review.
The grado SR60i is a huge bargain. That is a fact. I compared them with the original Bose OE headphone at Sam's Club in Michigan. The Grado SR60i sounded better with an fm recording on a 40 dollar mp3 player than the bose oe sounded with the music they themselves provide at their displays. I also have been able to compare the Bose AE2 with the Sennheiser HD-203 through the same audio source. The Sennheiser HD-203, although being 100 dollars less, sound a little better to me. I would steer clear of bose, seriously. Back to the grados. They are not perfect headphones. They are open, which means that sound leaks to the fullest extent possible. That also means that liquids are a more significant danger around these headphones. They are huge, which means that they are not portable. Candidly, I have tried everything to make them portable. They have the unfortunate ability to swivel endlessly in one direction because of the alien antenna-like silver pole that connects the cans to the headband, so that means a lot of time will be spent undoing the tangled Y cord that results from the swiveling. The speaker cone cannot handle a lot of bass or volume without tearing. within two months after they arrived, the right speaker cone ripped because I was experimenting with volume and the equalizer(hey, I was 19, autistic and finally had my first audiophile headphone, what can i say?) Now more positives. These dont sound perfect, but they sound verysatisfying in an almost sensual way. They regularly gave me shivers down my whole body because of the excellent audio quality. They are not entirely ugly. They do look cheap, but the audio quality will still have you wearing them around your neck with your ralph lauren blazer. They are a great way to brag too. Show these to anyone who has any other headphone under 300 dollars and you will get your karma points immediately. WHat else can I say in an either positive or negative light? Well, they used to be 79.99! People have ideas as to why the price was raised so much, but we don't really know. Honest buyers will say they do not know why the price rose, because we don't. I do hope you buy these, but I would advise paying the price that you find on the grado website. You have to buy them from third party, but the price at gradolabs.com should be the authority for you. :-)as swaggy looking as beats, and they aren't as preppy looking as Bose, but they have the sound to make up for it. If there is one thing that is negative, it is the sound leak, but that cannot be fixed, so If you buy these, you are going to have to put up with that, not gonna lie there.

EDIT EDIT EDIT EDIT EDIT

EDIT: I went to the mall and couldn't help myself, I had to see how the grados measured up. I went to the best buy outlet and tried a few headphones.
1. Some huge, swaggy, 299.00 dollar headphones from sony
2. Those beats solo(the HD edition)
3. Some 150 dollar skullcandys
4. DNA's
5. at another store was a quietcomfort Audio Technica that i tried

I tried them all with 2 songs,
A. Luther Vandross
B. Urban Music

All of them suck except for the sony's which were VERY nice, almost better than expected, BUT, the sony's were Bass heavy and almost harsh in the bass. The sony's had a V-shaped audio response as all urban cans do(bose also has this, whether you realize it or not), All in all, EVERY headphone i tried, regardless of price, fell short of the 80 dollar grados performance. The Sony's are worth 300, though, i will say that much for them. The model number is MDR-X10 I tried the red ones. But the grados still had better balance.

The only complaints I have are that the turn on/turn off sound seems much louder than necessary. Also, the response to commands comes out a bit on the booming side. But these are small issues.

The [[ASIN:B008MF3X8G Monster Clarity HD Micro Bluetooth Speakers, Black]] is a great accessory for your iPad or mobile phone that let's you hear music or make speaker calls clearly and with ease.

product_title: Logitech UE Smart Radio
review_headline: Logitech UE way better than Mondo Grace for podcasts
review_body:
I'm an NPR freak, and especially love listening to This American Life, Wait Wait Don't Tell Me, and Radiolab, among others. I wanted to be able to listen to these on demand and not have to wait for when my local station aired them, and I originally tried the Mondo Grace internet radio. The organization of podcasts on the Mondo was completely illogical and cumbersome, and the Reciva service was spotty at best, meaning that most of the time no podcasts where available at all, and sometimes even when they were they would stop suddenly in the middle of playing. Also, strangely enough, it was impossible to pause, stop, rewind, or fast-forward a podcast, so if you needed to step out of the room you'd miss something.

The Logitech UE's podcasts worked immediately out of the box. I could find what I was looking for easily, and the podcasts played smoothly and seamlessly. I could also pause them mid-play! It also actually comes with a rechargeable battery pack, whereas the Mondo doesn't and charges you another $50 to get one.

The Pandora and last.fm features on the Logitech are not yet working with our VPN service (says we're out of country), which we are working to troubleshoot, but they work fine with the VPN turned off, so I wouldn't hold this against the radio. (The VPN was not a conflict with the Mondo.) The Logitech's screen is a bit smaller, it doesn't show the time when turned off, and it doesn't have a remote (as opposed to the Mondo on all of these items), but these things are small potatoes considering I can actually use the Logitech in the way I wanted, which I can't do with the Mondo.

Very happy with the Logitech UE, and sorry Mondo, but we're returning you immediately.

product_title: Mount-It MI-310B Heavy-Duty Full Motion Articulating TV Wall Mount for 32 to 60-Inch TVs, VESA Standard up to 750x450mm, 175 lb Weight Capacity (Black)
review_body:
Do you have a stud finder? A tape measure? Go check the wall you want to mount your tv on and find out how far apart on center your studs are, then come back... I'll wait...
Got that info? Ok, keep reading.

The mount itself is exceedingly well made. It's very solid in constructions and heavy as all heck, having Amazon Prime saved a ton on shipping. Therein, however, lies my problem. I received the mount after looking for one that would support my 48inch Samsung and decided to go with overkill for making sure it stays on the wall and doesn't drop. I receive it and had planned to get it mounted this weekend. TV is pulled out away from the wall along with it's stand, cables moved around, area cleaned, brackets put on back of the TV to hold it. Studs in the wall are located and their centers found. Then I go to mount the plate against the wall only to find that the plate is too short! My studs are 24inch on center apparently and this mount WILL NOT work with 24inch on center studs. Mount-IT! does sell one that works with studs set that far apart and I did order that one, however I'm stuck with this mount as it would be prohibitively expensive to send it back for what I paid for it due to shipping. No where in the description did it say it WOULD NOT WORK with 24inch on center stud walls.

The only fault with the product is the description needs to be more clear so I can't really take more than two stars off. Not every one is going to think to measure how far apart their studs are BEFORE purchasing this. Live and learn, but sometimes mistakes are expensive.

Moral of this story is measure. Then measure again.

product_title: Logitech UE Smart Radio
review_headline: Former Logitech streaming radio users abandoned, future support of UE Smart Radio questionable
review_body:
- In September 2012 Logitech announced that it was dropping the Squeezebox line of internet radios, to be be replaced by the UE Smart Radio. Unfortunately since that time Logitech has given no indication of how long they will support the Squeezebox players, the Logitech Music Server software used with Squeezeboxes, or the mysqueezebox server. I personally have two Squeezebox Booms, a Touch, and a Classic that have been abandoned by Logitech.

- The new Logitech streaming software, UE Music Library, is not compatible with any of the previous Squeezebox products except the Squeezebox Radio. Those with Squeezebox Touch / Boom / Duet / Classic / Transporter units are out of luck. In addition, UE Music Library has not been officially provided for Unix (only Mac and Windows), so those wanting to run UE Music Library on their NAS (as I did with Logitech Music Server) are on their own. (There are unofficial Unix builds available, but no indication by Logitech that these will ever be supported.)

I mention the above because I want to make it clear how the Squeezebox community of users has been abandoned by Logitech, and that potential purchasers of the Logitech UE Smart Radio need to understand that they could be abandoned just as quickly if Logitech decides to once again move in a different direction. And at least for my Squeezebox units they will still be able to stream my music collection if the server is turned off; from all indications if the UE Smart Radio servers go away this radio becomes a doorstop.

product_title: Belkin Pivot Surge Protector with 6ft Cord and Telephone Protection
review_body:

The grounded and protected lights are a good feature. It has a coax protector for cable but most experts recommend you don't use that feature - instead you want to have a good surge protection device on the main coax line when it comes into the house, grounded to true ground. Amazon sells a good one here: http://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B0016AIYU6/ref=oh_details_o01_s01_i00 - any surge protector coax linkup will degrade signal and doesn't provide near the protection of a dedicated device like that.

Keep in mind that if you hook ANY piece of your home theater equipment up to any line that is not surge protection, and it is connected by any cable to the rest of the equipment, then the entire system will get knocked out by a surge - a surge will travel down any line that conducts electricity. Make sure you don't plug in half of your stuff.

product_title: Evervue SP 32" Waterproof Mirror HDTV
review_headline: The worst television buying decision I have ever made.
review_body:
I own a custom audio/video company in Central Texas and I bought one of Evervue's waterproof flat panel's for a customer of mine as I thought the concept was great. This is the worst television company I have ever dealt with. I sell major brands like Sony, Samsung, Toshiba, Panasonic, and Elite and have never received such atrocious service and poor quality as I did with Evervue. I would not recommend anyone buy this TV, you can get a much better product by buying a 32\\" tv from a major brand, get a piece of di-electric glass, and some silicone and do it yourself. You will also save a large chunk of change. An account of my experience is below.

Once the TV was installed by me following Evervue's instructions, there seemed to be an issue with it. Anytime someone walked near it and tapped the wall the picture would flicker. I called them to have it serviced or replaced. I spoke with the receptionist (I only assume that, she is the only person I ever got to speak to on the phone) and she said that I could send the TV back and they would repair it which would take about thirty days, or I could pay $800 for a new TV. I told them this was unacceptable and did get a replacement TV. About six months later the TV starting having issues with the video again. I called and spoke with the receptionist who told me I could send the TV in for repair and I had to pay $50 for shipping (they say that is in their warranty, but in emails I sent asking what their warranty is and on their website there is no mention of it). I sent the TV off in packaging of my own using FEDEX (I did not have the original packaging anymore) and it made it to them in good condition. They told me a few days later that they had run \\"tests\\" and found nothing wrong with the tv and that they could send video proof. I asked for the proof and it was a VERY short video shot from the receptionists iPhone. I decided to have them ship the TV back to me as I could tell I was getting no where. Theydelayed shipping it for about a week as they said they needed to get \\"special\\" packing for it as it was not in the original packaging. They used their carrier (UPS) to send it back, when it arrived one of the corners of the TV were shattered. I immediately called them and demanded a new TV because I did not want a TV that had suffered a large enough impact to bust the glass. First they tried to blame it on FEDEX because they apparently can not keep track of who they ship with. I told them they shipped with their carrier and that this was their problem. Again their solution was for me to spend $50 to send the TV back to them and have them put thicker glass on the TV. We got a lawyer involved as they did break a law by not honoring their warranty. Their response to this was \\"The only way to resolve this is that the customers sends back the TV to us, shipping prepaid, and we will repair the TV for free and ship back to him. We will not communicate about this anymore with you or the customer because we already tried to explain the situation this several times.\\" This is from their tech support/owner/manager.

As for the TV, I dissected it just to see what was in it and it has been recycled for spare parts. Lesson learned.

product_title: Etymotic Research Noise Isolating In-Ear Headset and Earphones for iPad, iPhone, iPod Touch
review_body:
First, the good: Sound and sound isolation is up to snuff for Ety. If you like in-ear, isolating headphones, these do the job well like all Ety products. And for those who don't like the provided buds/sleeves, check out Comply Foam. If you aren't using Comply products with your in-ear headphones you're totally missing what the product can be. Also, the \\"Awareness\\" app is a nice accessory to the product line.
But the reason for the low rating is that these phones are entirely inappropriate for any sort of exercise. They are not moisture sealed and the tiniest bit of sweat will wick into the control piece and cause the set to fail. Volumes will move randomly--including jumping to highest volume to blast your ear drums into bits of sonically powdered dust. Then, the controls will become inoperative. The only choice is to unplug.
I emailed Ety to describe the problem. I got a quick, abrupt response, telling me the MC3 probably wasn't the best option for workouts since sweat gets into the microphone hole. Gee. Thanks. I thought I'd attempt a fix and tape over the mic hole. Nope, still the same problem. The moisture gets in where the wire enters the control piece, too. Tape over that area solved the problem temporarily. But be advised, if you get sweat into a control mechanism like this just once, it's shot. The salt, urea and other chemicals in sweat will coat the workings and corrode them, just like road salt will kill your car. The residue is hygroscopic, meaning it will continuously absorb moisture from the air, causing the corrosion to continue until the product fails completely.
Ety has lost me as a customer because of this crappy product and worthless customer service.
If a product is this unsuitable for an obvious and widespread use like working out, it should say clearly that the product is unsuitable. Yes, they include the pitiful lawyers warning of not using it while running or jogging since you can't hear what's going onaround you, but it should say \\"Even on an elliptical or treadmill this product will fail within minutes.\\"
For travel use, go for it. These will be fine as long as you stay out of the rain and never sweat. But if you'd ever wear them while exercising--forget it.

product_title: Onkyo TX-NR515 7.2-Channel Network A/V Receiver (Discontinued by Manufacturer)
review_body:
To paraphrase the science and technology advisor to the White House, who recently responded to a petition on whitehouse.gov: we are in the future. I understand how my electronics work, more or less, but I just recently made some massive upgrades and got myself caught up to 2012. Let me say this: my cell phone can control my surround sound system. I said, MY CELL PHONE TALKS TO MY SURROUND SOUND SYSTEM.

Sorry. This was literally science fiction when I was a kid. The Onkyo Remote software works pretty decently. Not quite as straightforward as the Sony TV remote software app that I use so MY CELL PHONE CAN TALK TO MY TV. *Ahem* (Slipped again. Sorry.)

Anyway, the remote software has some nice features and graphical tools, such as slider bars, for some settings. There's a slight delay when the commands are sent, but probably no longer than 0.5 seconds. Maybe less. It's fast enough for me. (What do I want? My cell phone can talk to my receiver.) The receiver is connected via cat5e cable to my wireless router in the other room per the manual's recommendation for maximum signal stability, so I can't say anything about its wireless performance.

There are tons of bad reviews about this thing due to its glitchy initial firmware. Everyone seemed ok after they updated to the firmware issued in the autumn of 2012, so I took a chance and bought one when there was a brief drop to ~$300 at The Egg around the end of December. It arrived packaged only in its Onkyo box, announcing its contents to the world. *Shrug* Oh, well. So did my Polk Monitor 30's. The box seemed sturdy enough to have survived and protected its cargo, given that I found no damage to the receiver.

One of the first things I did, after getting the basics set up, was to upgrade its firmware. Onkyo wasn't kidding when they said to put the files at the root of the drive with nothing else on the drive, so I cleared off a Patriot 16 Gb flash drive and loaded them up. Once the update began, there were two phases that, combined, ate about 45 minutes to an hour while I found other things to do.

As an aside, it wasn't actually *quite* that simple. Clearly, Onkyo's customer support was busy this past holiday season; I was on hold for slightly over an hour before I got a hold of someone. The person was very patient and helped me figure out that I was a moron and that I had failed to put the files in the correct (root) folder. Regardless, I can confirm that if you have enough physical and phone minutes to spare, there's a good chance you'll be able to contact someone knowledgeable there.

I finally ran Audyssey a few days ago. MUCH better clarity. Detected the fact that I had only 3 front full-range (L/R/Center) speakers connected and calibrated accordingly. Maybe this is old hat to many other consumers, but I was thoroughly impressed with the program.

The sound quality keeps getting better as both the receiver and the speakers get properly adjusted and broken in. Disclaimer: I'm no audiophile and my living room has terrible acoustics on account of being adjacent and completely open to the kitchen. The fridge is loud, and the HVAC unit makes noises, too. All that said, I can finally understand the words that come out of actors' mouths during quiet parts of shows, and the the music I've played sounded great. The compressed music optimizer, accessed via button on the front panel of the receiver, works reasonably well. Not sure how to qualify it, but its effect reminds me of the \\"loudness\\" button on an old car stereo I had.

If other things come to mind about this unit (cons, perhaps), I'll try to remember to get back on here and update my review. Otherwise, for now, I think the bottom line is that I love the TX-NR515, and I think it was well worth the ~$300 - ONLY because there's properly working firmware available.

review_headline: Very nice sounding subwoofer for music and movies - not too boomy
review_body: I was going to hide this in a corner, but it sounded better on a front/side wall, angled with the port facing the couch.  I have watched movies like Pirates of the Caribbean, and the cannon fire was awesome - freaked my kids out a little to feel the floor vibrate.  It takes a bit of tweaking with the volume and surround cut-off frequencies (that, I mostly control at the receiver), but I have it at the perfect balance.  Got an HDMI adpater for the Wii, and the increase in sound depth is excellent.  I have also listened to digital music, mostly 80's and 90's new wave/alternative stuff, and I think it sounds great.  I'm not into rap, and I don't want a subwoofer that overpowers the music/dialogue.  This subwoofer does a very decent job at a very decent price-point.  If you want to damage your walls and windows (and hearing), you'll want a bigger, more expensive box.  This is not a tiny subwoofer, but it's more than plenty for me, and I do like to turn it up (to "adult-loud" levels).  My wife surprisingly didn't mind the box being in the open (it's got a nice sleek black finish), and yes, the light is a little bright. but it's blue, and both of us think it looks cool.  It also reassures you that the subwoofer is on.  This has an automatic mode, unlike some of the others, so you can plug it in, and forget it.  When some bass comes through, it will spring to life, and I think it adds plenty of life and depth to both movies and music.

review_body:
How many of you have likely spent hundreds of dollars buying one cheap pair of earbuds at a time, only to have them break or blow out after a period of use? Well I know I have for years now. This just makes the point that buying quality the first time will doubtlessly save you money and frustration in the long run.

I purchased these last week, and have been very happy with them. Here is a breakdown of what I like about, and possible concerns if you're thinking about a purchase:

1.) The fit is different than that of other earbuds you have tried. They buds themselves are constructed of a very comfortable silicon, and I have yet to have any comfort issues. The way they work is by sitting more shallow in the ear than other earbud style headphones. They have a small piece that inserts deeper into the canal for ideal sound quality, but the the majority of the bud sits in the outer ear canal. They also have a "wing" I will call it that fits along the upper contour of your ear, keeping the bud in place. Now at first you might have trouble getting it to fit perfectly in your ear, this is ok and can be resolved in a few way. Firstly try just replacing the silicon bud cap with one of the other two sizes that come in the packaging, After a few minutes of frustration trying to get the medium size that come on the buds to fit I replaced them with the smalls and they fit great. the other issue is that you just don't have the wing properly resting in your ear. Once you get this all figured out you can headbang to that techno drop all you want without worrying about your earbuds flying out of your ears. All in all, the comfort of these once you get used to them is superior to others I hav tried. Since they rest shallow in the ear you ear canals don't become fatigued after prolonged use.

2.) the audio quality of these earbuds are very nice, the base is rich and the high notes are reached fluidly without straining the speakers. I give these 5 stars alone for the quality of audio, you will not regret them for that.

3.) Overall quality is very nice, the cords are a bit thicker and seemingly more robust than i was expecting, very nice feel. the little things were considered when making these, for instance: The 3.5mm jack is set at an angle out of the peg so the the cord doesn't not bend at the contact, making sure that the cables aren't strained at that point of wear. This will greatly prolong the period of usage of these headphones. Again, excellent quality.

In summary, these are a great buy if you spend a decent amount of time with headphones on. product_title: Cheetah APTMM2B TV Wall Mount for 20-75" TVs up to VESA 600 and 165lbs, and fits 16” And 24” Wall Studs, and includes a Tilt TV Bracket, a 10' Twisted Veins HDMI Cable and a 6" 3-Axis Magnetic Bubble Level
review_body:
I bought this hoping it would work for me given the price of other mounts out there (especially at the retail stores). I have a 46\\" LED LCD TV that I wanted to mount above me fireplace (I know, I know, not supposed to do it but it was the only place for it in the room). Anyway, I took note of some of the negative reviews about making sure all the parts were there and placed my order. First off, not sure if something has changed in terms of the directions or packaging but my mount arrived with every large part individually labeled with a letter that corresponded to the instructions. Additionally, all of the screws and small parts were in a long bag with individual pockets that were also lettered and corresponded to the instructions. Total build time - about 10-15min to make sure it was all tight and ready to rock. Wall installation couldn't be easier - just make sure your hole marks are perfectly straight before you drill. Check this with a tape measure and level since it's easy to mark the drill spots in different locations on the left and right side and end up with one side a little higher than the other (I did this). The only complaint I have is since it mounts the TV so close to the wall, the bottom set screws are impossible to get to unless you have a very long flat head screwdriver. That being said, for flush mounting against a flat wall, they aren't really necessary and I haven't seen any issues with not having them screwed in. Otherwise, for the price, you can't beat this mount!

Couple of edits from notes I've seen.
- There is more hardware supplied than you will need. This is because Cheetah is nice enough to provide many types of mounting bolts to secure your TV to the mount. Since you only need 4 bolts to mount to your TV, you won't need all of them.
- Check to see if you need any special adapters to use your TV with a mount that wasn't made by the same manufacturer. For instance, I have a Samsung TV and they provide special adapter discs to put in the holes to space the tv properly if you're using a VESA standard mount that Samsung didn't make. Otherwise the bolts would have been too long and the mount wouldn't line up properly with the back of the TV.

product_title: Bose QuietComfort 15 Acoustic Noise Cancelling Headphones (Discontinued by Manufacturer)
review_headline: Perfect for traveling or around the house
review_body:
I finally took the plunge with Bose and got these for my girlfriend. She loves technology but isn't necessarily tech savvy, so I wanted something that had a good background of quality and comfort. Trying these on myself, I can say that on those two fronts the QC15s are great. We took this with us on a recent trip to Paris and had them on for hours so I can safely say that they are quite comfy. The sound reproduction is also fantastic. They aren't the most bass heavy of headphones, so if you do listen to a lot of low-end-heavy music, there are perhaps better options (Monster and Klipsch come to mind). But for the majority of music and movies, the sound you get out of them is full and consistent over its frequency range. You do get the feeling that the QC15 has been worked on and tuned to merit the somewhat hefty price tag.

Of course, the major selling point with these particular headphones is the noise cancelling. Like is stated elsewhere, you only get sound out of them if the noise cancelling is turned on. Turn it off, the headphones do nothing. When turned on, the noise that gets cancelled is what most would call "ambient noise". The general drone of the world around you. Think, the sound a plane makes when inside it. Speech isn't cancelled as aggressively, so you'll still take notice when someone starts talking to you. I'd say this is more of a good thing actually, as you can wear them when around other people and still respond to them.

If you've never used a pair of noise cancelling headphones, then don't expect the ambient sound to just vanish. Instead of cancelling, think of it as lessening. It's there but is drowned down to the point where the music or whatever you're listening to is no longer impaired by it. Think something akin to how earbud headphones work. When you pause your music with earbuds on, you can still heard the world, but turn the music back on and it is no longer audible.

I can't speakto the battery life yet as the original batteries haven't died yet. That being said, thus far they've lasted for many hours (10+).

The general build of the headphones is solid. The battery compartment has a door that swings open but stays connected to the set, so that's nice. You don't notice its there when it's closed, and in fact it was a little hard to find when I initially got them. The 3.5mm cable unplugs from the set and can be stored separately, which is a nice touch. Don't worry though, the connection doesn't feel loose so you aren't in danger of it coming unplugged accidentally. You also get an extra iPod cable, with music controls and an plane adapter.

Overall, the QC15 are a great pair of headphones but only if you need or want the noise cancelling, since they don't work unless you turn it on. For travel, there's really nothing better. Combine the quality, comfort, and noise cancelling and it's almost a must have.
