product_title: Creative WP-350 Wireless Bluetooth Headphones with Invisible Mic
review_body:
Let me start with this. I am an audiophile. I have several very high end wired headphones with separate compatible amps. When I want to seriously listen to music I use those setups. Now that is stated let me review the WP350.

I own at least 6 pairs of Bluetooth headphones. Two pairs of Sony, a Motorola, Samsung and a few other brands. My favorites had been the Sony BT101. I thought they sounded the best of the bunch and had good controls. Plus they charge from a mini usb plug. That is important to me.

Sound quality BT headphones will never equal my high end setup. But can they sound good enough?

Well the Creative WP350 (WP300 (same as 350 minus the mic)) can and do. They have an impressively smooth sound with exceptional bass. They are also comfortable to wear. I dont want to wear them for hours but an hour or so they are just fine (frankly I dont want to wear any headphone more then an hour or so). Also I have a very large head and they are fine. Plus my wife can wear them too. So speaks to good design.

The sound quality really impresses me. The real test is since I have bought these (I now own 2 pairs) I have not used my high end rigs at all. I generally use them with my iPad. Bought them for watching video's youtube and music. They work great but again I am most impressed on how well they sound on music.

These hp's have a unique design. They have a ported bass enclosure. You will notice 2 little holes in the hp's. This allows for their impressive bass response. Block them and the bass goes away. They also sound muddy when you do that too. This creates a bit of a problem for me because the holes are on the backside of the phones. Therefore when I lie on a pillow when in bed it can block the holes. So I have to position my head and pillow such that it doesnt block the holes.

They sound so much better then any other phones I own again I was shocked. I bought them initiallybecause I wanted another set that I would like and they use a micro usb charge cable. I am done with proprietary cables and such. Too much of a pain. But when I got them and used them I was hooked.

Their controls are where you would expect and function as you would expect. And I think the build quality is very good.

I highly recommend these headphones.

product_title: Denon AVR-3313CI Networking Home Theater Receiver with AirPlay and 3 Zone Capacity (Discontinued by Manufacturer)
review_headline: Small Foot Print; Monster A/V Performance!!!!
review_body:
I swapped my Onkyo TX-NR809 with Denon AVR-3313. Before Onkyo, I was using Yamaha RX-V3900 and I just wasn't satisfied with the power output of Yamaha. My speakers are Klipsch (RF-82 II, RC-62 II, RS-52 II, SUB-12, and a DIY subwoofer as mid-bass module).
Now over to the Denon AVR-3313; it is my first ever Denon and I'm all sold on it and a Denon fan forever.

VIDEO
There is hardly any difference in video performance between Onkyo 809 and Denon 3313. Video chipset used on Denon is at par with that on Onkyo 809.

AUDIO
Audio is the main performance area where Denon 3313 will chew alive the 37lbs heftly Onkyo 809, though Denon only wieghs in at 26 lbs. I am in awe as to how much power this little monster is pumping out. The difference is not in the heavier power supply of Onkyo; it's rather in the discrete circuitry (HammerHead SHARC 192Khz/24 bit Audio DACs on all 7 channels) and shorter audio path between the pre and pro section in Denon 3313. They collectively reduce noise and reproduce sound with bare minimum distrotion. The result is outstanding audio reproduction both in movies and music. Denon offers surprisingly tremnedous amount of power, deeper and wider soundstange, fantastic and most accurate channel seperation, and really immersive sound for movies and music alike. The highs have weight and do not sound thin. It's sort of like you feel the guitar strings in your chest with each pluck of string.

Make sure you run full 8 point Audyssey setup. My speakers are crossed at 80hz on avr. Also, remember your speakers can sound as good as they are. If you feed them bad recordings; they will sound terrbile. If you feed them good recordings, they will sound as good as they are. So, the trick is to process the source materail as accurately and as cleanly in the AVR as possible. I used same source material (FALC for music, and 1080p DTS/DD MKV files for movies) on Onkyo and Denon. Denon simply blows Onkyo outta the water. Denon has livened up my Klipsches to another level with no hint of distortion even beyond reference levels.

Fantastic and most accurate sound reproduction both in movies and music ...... DENON fan forever.

So, to me the headphones sound a bit lifeless at the high end without a bit of equalizer compensation.

However, others in my family with better hearing, don't have this reaction and find the audio quality without equalization to be the best they have ever heard. Even given my hearing limitations, I can tell that the sound is extremely detailed and very well balanced. These headphones are ultrasmooth and very pleasant to listen with. They are also quite comfortable to wear for extended periods.

My only issue really is a minor one: the default plug is the big kind for a standard preamplifier and you need an included adapter to get a mini-plug that fits an ipod or pc. Having two plugs in a row for the most common use these days is a bit awkward.

product_title: Sony MDR-V6 Monitor Series Headphones with CCAW Voice Coil
review_body: I used to use a set of these headphones back when I did some minor video production work, and was always impressed by their full range and sound quality. I have been plodding along with some old Koss headphones on my gaming rig, and they were clearly at the end of their long life.  I have a nice little 5.1 surround setup for my computer to play games with, but when the wife goes to bed, I have to plug in the ear cans.  Going from all of the glorious booms and rumbles I get with the sub attached to my 5.1 system to the lack luster sound of my old headphones was jarring.  Well I can say that this is no longer a problem with these Sony headphones.  These produce a full range of sound that makes me forget I am wearing headphones instead of listening to my full speaker set.  Not overpowering on the low end, and not too tinty on the high.  As for the comfort on the head, some have said they dislike them, but I have no complaints.  I wear glasses, which can be problematic for extended periods of time with some headphones, but so far, these don't bother me at all, even after 3-4 hours of continuous wear.  If anything, the only problem I have with these, is that they block out the sound so well around me, that I can't hear when my wife comes into the room.  She was trying to talk to me the other night, and I had no idea she was speaking, which may get me in trouble one of these days.

product_title: VideoSecu ML531BE TV Wall Mount for most 22"-55" LED LCD Plasma Flat Screen Monitor up to 88 lb VESA 400x400 with Full Motion Swivel Articulating 20 in Extension Arm, HDMI Cable & Bubble Level WP5
review_body:
For the price, this is a great wall mount for a flat screen TV. I got it for a 32\\" flatscreen that I bought for my wife's craft room (Christmas present). I was impressed by all the different screws and fittings that comes with the mount to attach it to the wall (need to find a stud) and to screw the universal fit plate to the back of different TV's. If I was going to mount a TV to cement block or to a cement wall, I would use metal butterflys (cement block) or metal expansion bolts and glue for solid concrete. I wouldn't trust a plastic expansion sleeve (comes with the mount) to hold my expensive TV several feet above the floor. There are even fittings to adapt the flat plate to fit a curved back TV. As some reviewers have noted, the articulating joints are stiff. I think they will loosen up as the TV is swiveled with use. I have another wall mount same design, different company that has loosened up with use.

I especially liked this mount's design that quickly allows you to lift, fit and hold the TV to the arm without having to hold the TV in place while you try to screw in a bolt. After the TV is held in place, a small nut safely secures the plate to the arm.

The mount is made of thick stamped steel that is welded where needed. It appears to be powder coated in bright gloss black. I thought the mounting instructions were adequate.

This mount also comes with a small torpedo level and HDMI cable. While I didn't need another cable, I did use the level.

Error is the same in all cases - \\"Invalid Write Address\\" shortly after 50% of disc capaсity. I'm guessing it's the layer break point. If anyone is interested in my opinion - go with BD-RE (rewritable) media for now if you don't want to waste an awful lot of money.

review_body: I added one of my old Radio Shack passive sub-woofers to my Polk Monitors in my office, fed by a Yamaha AV receiver, some years ago. The speakers, recycled AV receiver and DVD player are used in my 11ft x 12ft home office to listen to my CDs as I peruse the web. My LR HDTV has a better system - including an inexpensive 10\\" Sony subwoofer. I ordered the 12\\" Polk to replace it, sending it to my office. Sadly, the new subwoofer wouldn't fit in the LR - but just fit perfectly in my office... go figure! The new Infinity speakers I also received in that order easily displaced the old Monitors. Wow! Great improvement - such classics as Paul Simon's 'Graceland' and 'The Rhythm of the Saints' albums came alive with real bass... as did several display items on shelves around the room. Several items hit the floor, adding to the experience. I'll admit that the sound level was 'significant' - but the bass was clear and unmuddied, if that's an appropriate term. The only negative I can think of affects me as a short wave radio listener. The sub-woofer's power supply, a switching type producing a rich and strong source of radio frequency interference. The noise is there as long as the subwoofer is plugged into the wall. I remedied that with a switchable outlet box, with added transient protection. An odd problem, it joins the myriad of consumer electronics in my home that must be disconnected before I can do some serious shortwave listening. Aurally, the Polk PSW505 deserved 5 stars.

review_headline: Great starter setup for either new or just returning to Vinyl
review_body:
I have now owned the Debut Carbon for about a month. So far I'm very pleased and it sounds great. I haven't owned a turntable in about 15 years and my old record collection was given away when I got rid of my turntable, no loss there since it was all 80's Pop. I also had purchased the Pro-Ject Xpression III and fitted with the same cartridge, I could not tell a difference between it and the Carbon. That being said, I would have kept it but I had a problem with the sub-platter, it had a bad wobble to it so I returned it and kept the Carbon and spent the extra money I saved on some new vinyl (and the spent some more, and some more again).

I wanted to share a few things that I learned so far in my vinyl journey:
1. Put on a decent album, preferably new and you'll be stunned how much bigger vinyl sounds on your system. The soundstage is just huge compared to digital. (Diana Krall Live in Paris is highly recommended)
2. Unless your ready to spend two to three times more money, you are not going to get a huge step up in sound quality from the Carbon. It's in the sweet spot of price vs performance.
3. $400 for the turntable is just a drop in the bucket, plan on spending double to triple that to get EVERYTHING you need. Nice phono preamp, carbon fiber brush, alignment tools, decent plastic lined sleeves for all that new vinyl you about to buy, tweaks, gadgets, cleaning supplies, etc......
4. Skip the Speed Box, it might be convenient but watch out for rumble/woofer pumping. I tried it on both the Carbon and Xpression III and as soon as I removed the Speed Box, the rumble went away and my woofers are happy again!
5. The only thing the tonearm is missing on this turntable is VTA adjustment. Don't worry about it and just get a Ortofon 2M Blue Stylus and put it on the 2M Red Body and that should be all the cartridge you need with this turntable. (The 2M Red and 2M Blue use the same body, just a different stylus).
6. The Acrylic platter upgrade is really only necessary if you are going to use a MC cartridge. I found that the Steel/Felt combo actually sounded better with standard vinyl. Audiophile 180/200G I would say it's a tie, maybe a little tighter base on the Acrylic. It does look cool though and is a little less prone to static. I did keep it.
7. Plan ahead and budget for a record cleaning machine, after you own a few albums you will want it. Even brand new sealed vinyl has dust and will crackle and pop.
8. When buying new vinyl, shop around, prices are all over the place.
9. 50 year old used records sound like.........50 year old used records.......
10. This will become an addiction and is a VERY expensive hobby, don't be shocked when you get that first credit card bill, you've been warned.

Update 11/02/2012
I no longer own the Debut Carbon, I have moved up to the Music Hall MMF-5 and can say it was a nice incremental upgrade. I really like the split plinth design and it seems much quieter with background noise. I was able to get one with the Goldring 1012GX cartridge and it's a departure from the Ortofon 2M series, very mellow and laid back. At some point I will try the 2M Blue on the Music Hall but want to give the Goldring time to break-in. That being said, at twice the cost, I can't say the Music Hall sounds twice as good but definitely sounds better. I still feel the Debut Carbon offers allot of bang for the buck in sub 1K turntables.Acrylic platter upgrade is really only necessary if you are going to use a MC cartridge. product_title: RCA RC117V Dual USB Radio with Alarm Clock
review_headline: Love it! Low Tech meets High Tech
review_body: First off let me say, I love this radio/alarm clock. It is exactly what I was looking for and it delivers. After doing a lot of online research for a nice looking clock radio, I was frustrated by all the negative reviews. Seems that regular low tech clock radios are going by the way side and I found it difficult to find any in stores that you could put your hands on first. RCA has been making radios since they were first invented and they do a good job of putting decent sound in a bedside radio/alarm clock. What I like about this model is that it is simple, sleek design which fits nicely on the bed stand. The top tray which has a felt like material will protect your phone while you are charging it or it is a good place to put any other item that you want within reach, rings,pen,fingernail file etc. The digetal clock is plenty readable and soft on the eyes with its light blue background and darker numbers. Yes it has 3 levels: high, medium and off. and it is a little bright but I would much rather have the soft blue than that hideous alien green you see so often. If it is too bright, I just turn it off, I can still see it in the morning even with my older eyes. As I said the sound is very good for bedside radio, stations come in clearly. The snooze button is handy and even turning off the alarm altogether is easy as it is first button on the right. What I like best about this is that I was able to set the time and the alarms in about 10 minutes. The last one I bought a few years ago,I threw away cause I couldn't figure out how to program it and I waited too long to return it.  There is something to be said for low tech. simple instructions and it performs the functions it is supposed to. Personally, although I have used computers for years, I have not gotten on the ipod/smart phone band wagon and dont have a clue how to hook those up to be alarms. And I didnt want that. I wanted a simple clock radio that looked good and sounded good and was easy to set up and this model delivers. I also like the fact that it has a usb charger as I know I can grow into that when I am ready without compromising the other features. The usb chargers are hidden by the top shelf so if you dont use them you wont miss them. Other models I looked at looked incomplete without a phone stuck in it. This looks like a clock radio with an indented felt shelf on top. It looks like what it is with the chargers hidden under the nice little shelf on top.  Although the retail price for this was $44.00, I got it for $28.00, which I thought was a very good price/value. So if you are looking for an old fashioned clock radio/alarm clock that looks nice on the bedside, sounds good, nice display, is easy to set up and will also charge your cell phone, this is the model for you. Oh and for you techies, the box says it is compatible with ipod, iphone, ipad, mi3 audio in and android phones. Like I said low tech meets high tech in a mutually compatible format.

product_title: Antennas Direct C2-V-CJM ClearStream 2-V Long Range UHF/VHF Indoor/Outdoor DTV Antenna with 20-Inch Mount
review_body:
I had experimented with several OTA antennas (indoor) to bring in the major networks. I tried 5 different antennas, from an inexpensive RCA rabbit ears type to the \\"Leaf\\" as well as two different amplified RCA products. All would bring in two local channels with no problems. With a great deal of maneuvering, resetting, etc., I could bring in two more channels, so I could have CBS, NBC, PBS, Fox. It was a pain and no ABC, no matter what, since the ABC tower didn't even show up as available on antennaweb.org I decided to try an attic location because I did not want to mount outdoors for several reasons. I took the cheap RCA I had and put it in the attic and ran the connection. I was able to set it to bring in the 4 previously mentioned with no maneuvering. I decided to make one last try and ordered the ClearStream 2.

I received it yesterday and installed it this morning in the attic location. With one adjustment, I was able to bring in the previous 4 channels with great quality AND ABC showed up! The ABC tower is about 40 miles away, as near as I can tell, although I cannot reference that, for sure. Needless to say, I am very pleased. It was relatively easy to put together, although the \\"U\\" bracket for attaching it to the mast was a little unclear on the instructions, but with a little common sense, it went together well. I really think you will be happy with this antenna. I sure am, at this point!

product_title: FiiO E6 Portable Audio Headphone Amplifier
review_headline: Works Great with Cowon D2 and Sony MDR-V6's
review_body:
I have a pair of Sony MDR-V6 headphones[[ASIN:B00001WRSJ Sony MDR-V6 Monitor Series Headphones with CCAW Voice Coil]]that I use with an older Cowon D2 mp3 player. When I added this Fiio E6 to the mix I realized that I had been only scratching the surface of what those 'phones could do. When paired with my Koss SportaPros[[ASIN:B00001P505 Koss SportaPro Stereo Headphones]] or KSC 75's[[ASIN:B0006B486K Koss KSC75 Portable Stereophone Headphones]]the Fiio doesn't make much of a difference. The same goes for when I've used it with my HTC EV0 (One X) smart phone. If you turn off the Beats enhancements and use a better audio program like JetAudio you can hear the more of a difference, but ultimately this product is for using with a good mp3 player and larger headphones.

I showed it to my audiophile step-father and he was intrigued enough to buy the E11 [[ASIN:B004QVPGXK FiiO E11 Portable Headphone Amplifier With Micca Accessory Pack (Wall Charger and Extra Battery Pack)]] and L9 cable [[ASIN:B004QVNNI0 FiiO L9 L-Shaped Line Out Dock (LOD) Cable For iPod and iPhone]] to use with his iPhone 4. He was impressed too, and this is a guy with Peachtree headphone amp at home. If you are going to use it with an iPod or iPhone definately get the L9 cable too. We tried it both ways and the sound is much better using the L9 cable with either the E6 or E11.

If you are trying to decide between the E6 and E11 I would say the biggest benefit to the E11 is that is easier to operate and the battery life is much longer. The E6 dies after about 5 hours of being turned on. Sometimes I forget to turn it off in the morning after I get off the bus and by the time I leave work it is dead. The E6 also dies abruptly. The E11 has double the battery life and an indicator light for life. When my E6 dies forever I will be stepping up to the E11.

product_title: MEElectronics Wooden In-Ear Headphones for iPod
review_body:
Introduction:

MEElectronics does one thing better than almost any other headphone manufacturer, they always pack a ton of value into an affordable price. CW31's not any different.

Meelectronics describes CW31 as \\"Clarity Series In-Ear Headphones Crafted for audio perfection, the CW31's wooden housing resonates with the music, giving a natural touch to the clean and clear sound, while the small size and light weight allow for easy insertion and long-lasting comfort\\", these earphones are designed to be a relatively inexpensive choice for users who are accustomed to clearer more analytical sound signatures

Specifications :

Driver: 9.0 mm dynamic drivers
Housing: Wooden housing with angled nozzle
Frequency Response: 20Hz - 20KHz
Sensitivity: 99 dB
Impedance: 16 ohms
Maximum Power Input: 30 mW
Connector: 3 pin stereo 3.5mm gold plated 45° plug
Cable: Designer black 135 cm cable (53 in) with attached shirt clip

Accessories: 1) 5 sets of silicone ear tips (small/medium/large Single Flange, 1 double-flange, small triple-flange)
2)Round zipper hard nylon case

Packaging : CW-31 ships in a rectangular plastic box, the earphones and the case are resting inside a tray. The new case provided is slightly thicker than the clamshell case that comes with M series earphones. The case is solid black except for the glaring purple zipper which might be an eyesore to some.

Build Quality : The CW31 housings are made of wood and plastic which are sturdy. Strain reliefs are made of hard rubber and ends with a lower-profile 45-degree plug. The earphones feature two vents, one at the rear of the housings and one, very tiny vent next to the nozzles with the nozzles being oval shaped

Cable: The cable is the typical gray MEElectronics cable. It is strong and low on microphonics

Microphonics: None unless you really really try. Excellent cable.

Comfort: These IEMs are very comfortable to wear,being an oval shaped insertion design that allows these to pretty much disappear in ones ears. Deep insertion levels as well as wearing them over the ear are not possible due to the oval shape.

Isolation: Isolation is average since deep insertion is not possible, but the included Double Flange/Triple flange improves it a bit.

Sound Quality:

Burn-in: Its been burned to 100+ hours before the evaluation.

Amped / unamped: Not much of a difference, these are drived easily by even low power sources

Signature : The sound signature is mostly neutral in character and frequency response or in short analytical

Lows: It isnt bass heavy as its basically neutral, but it still packs a decent amount of bass enough to be enjoyable for most music

Mids: The midrange is nice and smooth, very slightly forward and linear with superior detail.

Highs: It has pleasant harshness and treble response, is similarly linear and rolls off gradually as you approach the top end.

Soundstage: Sound stage is average but slightly better than M series IEM's

Final Conclusion : Meelectronics CW31 comes at 39.99$ which is great for a balanced IEM's with a good touch of neutrality and a bang-for-buck indeed. I rate CW31 as a great IEM in meelectronics series above all M series IEM's and below Balanced armatures A151 and A161P in SQ. They outclass many contestants in its range and undoubtably one of the best balanced IEM's around 50$. CW31 is for those who want to experience clarity, detailing and neutrality at a affordable price.

Pros:

1) Strong and low microphonic cable
2) Nice improved case
3) Comfortable for long sessions
4) Intro to neutrality at a Very good price

Cons:

1) Mediocre Isolation

review_headline: Audio is okay but this is NOT what I paid for
review_body:
Admittedly, I might have been a bit careless when purchasing this item. I searched for replacement cables for my beats since the original cable gave in. Most of the ones available on amazon were under $10 and these had the best review. The price was also middle-of-the-pack, so I thought it was a good enough choice. I mean I'm not going to spend more than a few minutes researching about something that only costs $7.

Much to my disappoint, the cable does NOT include iPod control - a fact that is not immediately obvious in the photos or description. If you're saying \\"Audio Replacement Cable for Headphone Monster Solo Studio 1.2m\\" then I expect it to do the EXACT SAME THING as the original. Ok, build and audio quality might be slightly poorer since it does only cost $7, but the whole point of getting a replacement cable for the Beats (and not just a plain audio cable I could've bought for $3 over here) is that I want to have the same experience with the original cable. I live in the Philippines and had to use a forwarder to get the package, it would be cheaper to buy another cable than to send this one back for replacement.

As far as audio quality goes, I can't tell a difference, so this does a good job there. But overall, I think this product is poor because it fails to deliver a significant part of enjoying owning these overpriced headphones which is iPod control.

product_title: Sony Budstyle Headphones
review_body:
1. Reliable
I am always skeptical while buying Sony products as they don't last long for me but I am using these headphones for more than 6 months now and they are still going solid (considering I am not good at taking good care of such small things).

2. Good sound quality
When I first got these, sound was terrible and I thought I made a mistake buying these but they do break-in. I am no audiophile but I feel sound quality has been really good after 2-3 weeks

3. Nice volume levels
Maximum volume level of these headphones is really good. Sometimes videos have inherently low volume or music doesn't reach the level you want, but I use these headphones in such scenarios and never got disappointed.

4. Comfortable fit but not interchangeable buds for different ear sizes
These headphones do look somewhat uncomfortable but they are not. They fit perfectly for me and almost never fell out. I don't even feel the discomfort other mentioned, even after hours of wearing them. The only minor discomfort I have is when I sleep with them on as protruding end keeps pushing the headphones in.

5. Tangle-free
Not a big deal but these are the first headphones whose wires do entangle in my pocket.

I do watch a lot of movies and mostly listen to music while studying, working or sleeping. These headphones help me enjoy movies/music without disturbing others around me. I would recommend these to anybody looking for pocket-able, sturdy, good sound quality, cheap headphones.

product_title: RCA ANT121Z Durable Passive Indoor Antenna
review_body:

And I have it set up in the middle of our first floor living room near the center of our brick house. I know that nothing about where it is set up is optimal. but I did not have much choice given the layout of our home. So far the best I've been able to do is get one channel well and several that are spotty. I may try it on our second floor once I get an adapter for the cable (our 2nd HD TV we bought when living overseas and its antenna hook up is not consistent with what the RCA ANT121 came with.

So for the $13 I paid for it, I'm giving it 5 stars because it seems to do what it is supposed to. As a novelty for us it works fine. He tried the adapter with his stereo headphones and it worked fine.  So your satisfaction may depend on why your purchasing it; might work for stereo headphones, but I wouldn't count on it for a single cell phone earpiece. product_title: Audiovox Surface SURF60N 60ml Small Screen and Lens Cleaner with Microfiber Cloth
review_body:
Well, I have a ton of smudgy electronics with screens that need cleaning, like most people. I've used lemon juice, vinegar and windex on TV screens, and they all left streaks behind. So much so, that I try to actively avoid cleaning the TV screen because the streaks are often worse than the smudges were. My 3DS screen gets smudgy frequently and I usually clean that by wetting a microfiber cloth very lightly and wiping at the screen. This works pretty well.

Still, I've always thought it'd be nice to actually have a spray that doesn't streak things and works well on those tricky electronic screens. So, I decided to try out this spray on a variety of screens. I tried it on the TV first, and it did much better than the Windex used to, but not perfect as there were still a few small streaks that needed buffing. Next, I tested it on my phone's screen, and it did quite well. Then I tried it on my 3DS, and it did excellently - no streaks at all. I also tried it on an ipad and a computer monitor. That left a bit of streakage behind, despite buffing.

Overall, I'd say this spray is decent at what it does, but not perfect. It's certainly better than other options I've tried, such as the Windex. As for the packaging, I like it. It's quite clever with it's nice cap that holds a microfiber cloth. I do wish the spray was TRULY streak-free, but maybe that's an impossibility. Either way, it's at least a decent option for anyone out there looking for a screen-cleaning spray.

product_title: Bose Lifestyle Unify Remote Control
review_body:
We all know that Bose equipment is not inexpensive. That being said, where else are you going to get a RF remote that does not require line of sight?? You can use this as well as the expansion remote for additional zones with an SA2 or SA3 amp from any reasonable distance.

What I LOVE about this specific unit is its two-way LCD read out, particularly when operating its dedicated IPod dock. From anywhere, if you want to know what's playing, just press a key on the remote and you get artist name, then song title, and then album name.

IN MY OPINION, THIS WITH TWO-WAY RF COMMUNICATION IS BY FAR THE BEST IPOD DOCK REMOTE ON THE MARKET, SHORT OF PERHAPS A SONOS SYSTEM CONTROLLED BY AN IPAD FOR A LOT MORE MONEY.

The expansion remote RCPMC III provides the same two way read out.

BOSE LIFESTYLE

The one thing I do not care for with the Lifestyle v25 or v35 is that rather than having a dedicated Bose CD/DVD player it depends upon third party vendors products. This would be OK, if like prior Bose Lifestyles the product set up included the codes to make the remote compatible with many other vendors products. Instead, the RC35T-L is a learning remote. Bose provides almost NO documentation in its users manual for how to \\"Teach\\" the remote, other than to go to the Unify set-up and select \\"Teach\\". When you do this, the on screen menus are not terribly descriptive/informative.

I hope my review is helpful to another consumer.

The mix that works best for me are Large \\"earbuds\\" and Medium \\"clips\\".
You really need to spend some time at the beginning to figure out the right combination that works and fits best for you.
You might find your ears are not the same size and you need to have different sized clips or buds in each ear.

If the buds are too loose, you get zero base, yuk.

Any way, they're great for jogging and don't fall out. The cord or wires are not as thick or as heavy as iBeats, which is good from a weight standpoint, but these don't have the same resilience as IBeats. But I do like the iSport sound. Clear crisp sound throughout the entire sound range.

product_title: V-MODA Crossfade LP Over-the-Ear Headphones
review_body:
I purchased these headphones for a great price on a lightning deal the other day, and really wanted to like them. They come with 2 detactable kevlar cables (one of which has a remote and mic for iDevices), they include a great hard case, have a good warranty, are (arguably) quite stylish, and the minute you pick them up you can tell they are very solid and well built.

The problem is that the sound isn't up to par for headphones in this pricerange. I have many pairs of on-ear headphones in the $100 range, from brands like Audio Technica, Grado, and Sony, and these don't even come close in terms of sound quality. The Crossfade LP's have solid bass, but it is muddied, and overpowers the mids and treble. Everything sounds hollow and flat. Occasionally, the underwhelming highs and mids will shine, but only until they are drowned-out and distorted by the sloppy bass. And don't misunderstand, I do enjoy bass-heavy headphones, but only when it's done right, like with the similarly-priced ATH-M50's. I would compare the overall sound of these headphones to what I would expect out of a $15 pair of earbuds.

After the first 24 there was a slight improvement (or maybe my expectations were just lower), and in the following 2 days I heard no improvement at all.

I gave these headphones 3 stars because I understand that some people with less discerning ears would probably be perfectly satisfied with the sound quality, and would really enjoy the quality with which these headphones are made, and the nice accessories that come with them. If you like the sound of Beats headphones, for example, I would say these offer a similar sound, but are better made and cost less.

However, If you are the type of person that makes an evening of listening to high bit-rate audio through a dac and headphone amp, these will dissapoint. There are far better choices for pure listening enjoyment than these. Mine are going back to Amazon today.

review_headline: Very Good Product for the Google Nexus 7 - Two Issues - Use of Mini Versus Micro USB Connector & Lack of Vendor Support
review_body:
Update To Review - My initial review gave the product (4) stars. I would like to take this opportunity to update a review I wrote earlier about the product. Since my review - just under a year later - the device just stopped working. It will no longer connect to my tablet (Google Nexus 7). The most most unfortunate part, however, is that I have been unable to get in touch with the vendor. Its listed email does not appear to work and its website is useless. I gave a favorable rating on the product after first purchasing and giving a good run through on functionality. Given, the experience with vendor support, I would advise against purchasing the product.

=============================================

Purchased the Rii Touch N7 for use with a Google Nexus 7. In summary, for the Nexus 7, the device performs as advertised and it performs well. Pairing and connecting via bluetooth is straightforward. The touch pad works well. The virtual mouse wheel works. The virtual wheel takes some practice in using and understanding how it works with user interfaces.

The auto sleep and wake functions to extend battery life work well. I've fully charged the battery once and have used it off and on for the last seven days without seeing a low battery indication. Please note that I am not typing several hours a day with the device; probably, on average, about 30 - 40 minutes per day, at most, at this point.

For the Nexus 7 all but one of the keys with additional functions activated by the function modifier key perform as designed. The one function that did not elicit a response from the tablet; the one to completely turn off sound. There are, however, function activated keys to incrementally increase or decrease the tablet's speaker volume. There is a Print Screen function key, and F1 - 11 keys. Those are applicable for PCs.

Finally, the back light for the keyboard generally works well. Lighting on some keys is a bit brighter or dimmer depending on location of the keys relative to the light source. Please note, though, that in a dimly lit or dark room, one will be able to readily see the keys. In essence, the level of illumination does the job.

The only drawback from a typing perspective - upon first using the keyboard, capitalizing letters can be a little bit cumbersome. With continued use, however, most people will adapt.

The device would have rated 5 five stars, but for one item - the use of a mini USB connector rather than the popular micro connector for power charging. With the exception of Apple devices, many vendors have moved to the micro USB connector for charging/data data connections where possible - some would now call the mini-USB a universal connector. There appears to be no description about the type of USB connector on the Amazon web site.

Overall, as mini keyboards go, the this model of the Rii used in combination with the Google Nexus 7 is a good value for the price.

product_title: Onkyo TX-NR717 7.2-Channel Network A/V Receiver (Discontinued by Manufacturer)
review_headline: A great upgrade of my 12 year old Onkyo!
review_body:
I don't write a lot of reviews, but this model is new enough, I thought I should give my $.02. For starters, the TX-NR717 replaced an Onkyo TX-DS777 that I bought exactly 12 years ago. The 777 has been and still is a fantastic receiver, aside from idiosyncrasies due to it being outdated (more details below). If it hadn't been for those issues, I wouldn't have been in the market for a new receiver, but since I've never had a single problem with it, I went with Onkyo again.

I initially planned to get the TX-NR515, but after reading sour reviews from people having HDMI issues (having to unplug the unit every day), I started looking at the 616, only to find it had the same issues. Finally, someone posted that their 717 didn't have the HDMI issues, so even though it was about $250 more than the 515 at the time, I gave it a closer look. I compared the 717 to the Denon AVR-2113CI, which was identically priced at the time. After several weeks of poring over the specs of the Denon and 717, I finally settled on the 717 because of the dual HDMI outputs (the Denon only has one). The ONLY reason I almost went with the Denon was that it included Audyssey MultEQ XT (also available on the far more expensive Onkyo 818).

Sound and video-wise, I don't think I could be more happy! I have it paired with 5 Polk satellites, a Polk subwoofer, and an LG 47LW5600 HDTV. I'm hearing things (especially ambient) like never before, a single HDMI cable to the TV saves a few button presses & wires, and the video upconversion is nice (see below).

I admit it - I'm one of those guys that prefers to read a manual cover to cover before plugging anything in. That said, I only read through 20 pages of the 100 page PDF before I got impatient enough to start using it. If it had been a printed manual, I probably would have read it in bed before plugging it in. I'll finish reading it over the next week or two, and I might print it out since I'd like to have it at my fingertips...there's just way too much cool stuff going on with this thing to figure it all out \\"by accident\\" (see network example below).

A few people have noted problems with the Audyssey 2EQ auto-setup. The \\"how to\\" on Audyssey's website clearly states something like \\"do not hold the mic...set it on a tripod at ear height. Then for the 2nd position, move it 2' to either side; for the 3rd position, move it back 4' to the other side.\\" I did that, and setup was a breeze...I love the little chirping sound. :) The mix is beautiful; the only thing I noticed was it set the subwoofer a little quieter than I like it. It's easy enough to fix temporarily, but I haven't figured out how to make it remember my setting.

There are so many options for the sound, and I'm sure it's mostly subjective, but initially I wished I knew which was \\"best\\" for what without having to play with the settings mid-listen. After a couple weeks, I settled on straight Dolby for 5.1 TV & movies, Dolby TV Logic for 2-channel/stereo TV, and Dolby PLII Music for CDs, network streaming, and 2-channel music DVDs. The PLII has fantastic separation, and music sounds awesome! One of my favorite things is the 717 allows me to set the output audio for every different incoming stream (mono, stereo, Dolby 5.1, DTS, etc.), and it remembers and auto-switches if the incoming stream changes! So if I'm watching a stereo broadcast, then flip to a 5.1, it automatically changes to the output setting I last used for that format.

I've gone into the main setup multiple times over the past couple weeks, just playing with the different options; I still need to read the manual (which is actually quite well written) to truly understand a couple options, but the menus are setup pretty well, and there are one line descriptions of each option - acceptable for most, but not all options, so I DO recommend reading or at least skimming the manual.

Unlike the 515 & 615, the 717 upconverts ANY signal (including 480p, 720p, etc.) to 1080p or even 4k (if you have a projector, etc. that displays 4k). The 515 & 615 only upconvert 480i. Nice of them to sneak that one in. I don't have a Blu-Ray player yet, but I can honestly say the DVDs (using component cables) look noticeably crisper with the upconversion to 1080p. It really looks fantastic!

Gone are the A/V sync issues we used to have with our DVR. While watching TV, my 777 played the (optical) audio nearly half a second before the LG HDTV could process the (HDMI) video, no matter how much I fiddled with the TV's settings, and it drove us crazy while watching people talking or dancing. The 717 sound is synced perfectly with the video since everything is passing through the AVR & same cables.

Gone also are the weird A/V sync and lag issues we had with the Wii. The Wii always worked fine on my SDTV, but when we got the LG HDTV, it made playing games where timing is important nearly impossible to play. Yes, I had the TV set to all the \\"game\\" options...it didn't help. The 717 solved the sync & lag issues completely, and now we're playing the Wii much more again! Even the Wiimote seems to have better responsiveness, although I don't know how. :)

Gone also are the weird audio cutouts while watching certain broadcasts (like Comedy Central). With the 777, using an optical audio cable (even brand new AND coax audio), the sound would cut out for a second or so three or four times per hour, then come back in much louder or much quieter. It was VERY annoying, and it hasn't happened AT ALL with the 717 via HDMI. YAY!

I was pleasantly surprised that I can watch one source (e.g., Game) while playing the audio from the TV/CD source. I often prefer to listen to a CD while playing Wii games, so this is a nice plus for me. It only works if the video source is HDMI and the audio source is analog, which makes sense.

When I initially viewed the network options, I liked that it had Pandora and DLNA, but I thought, \\"man...I wish somehow I could tap into DI.FM (a streaming electronic music website).\\" After digging a little further into the manual, I found the \\"My Favorites\\" section in the network options. The receiver has a built-in html page (just browse to the receiver's IP address from any computer on the network) that allows a user to program up to 40 network streams (M3U, PLS or other playlists). Excited, I tried entering one of the streams from DI.FM into the web link. I ran back into the family room, went to My Favorites, clicked on the link, and it immediately started buffering; within seconds, DI.FM was playing in simulated 5.1 surround (via the PLII Music setting). AWESOME!!! This could be my favorite thing about the receiver!

One evening, about two weeks after setting it up, we were watching CSI. There was a scene in the morgue, and my wife out of nowhere said, \\"WOW...the sound is way better; it actually sounds like a big, echoey morgue.\\" Hearing her comment without me asking made me realize for sure that I made a great purchase. :)

DLNA on the 717 still isn't as simple as it seems like it should be, but it definitely does a way better job with DLNA than my LG TV. It also means I can listen to music via DLNA without turning on my TV. For ALL the network options, the display on the receiver is really nice. I just wish it could do video over DLNA, instead of just audio. :(

I'm not a fan of the remote, especially compared to the 777's remote, which was truly programmable. I spent 10 minutes or so trying to get it to recognize my DVD player, CD player, TV, and DVR, but I think only one of them worked in the end since it's code-based \\"programming.\\" So, we still use the 777 remote and only use the 717 remote to change the sources and audio settings. I may end up programming those buttons into the 777 remote and abandoning the 717 remote altogether. :)

I've briefly played with the Android Remote app; it's decent, but not great. It's nice when listening to Pandora since it lets me see the song info no matter where I am in the house, although trying to use the virtual \\"rocker\\" to do thumbs-up/thumbs-down is impossible. For that matter, the virtual \\"rocker\\" is pointless for anything; it's just too tough to find the up/down/right/left sweet spots vs. \\"enter.\\" When I get around to utilizing zone 2, I'll probably use the app a lot more. Having said that, it can't see the 717 if the unit is turned off, unless it's in hybrid standby, which uses more power (see below) and is a significant trade-off. However, it probably needs to be in hybrid stand-by to use zone 2 or 3 anyway, but I haven't tried or read about it yet to know for sure.

I tried plugging a video camera into the USB slot, and nothing happened (or maybe I at least got audio). Like DLNA, I guess it doesn't support video; only audio.

The last thing I'll point out is the power usage. I measured it with a Kill-A-Watt meter, compared it against my 12-yr old TX-DS777, and got the following results:
* Standby: 0W (nice); my 777 used 1.5W
* Hybrid standby: 2.1W (keeps the network connection & HDMI pass-through active)
* On, but not doing anything: 65W initially, then 75W after using it for something; my 777 used 79W
It also has an auto-standby, which shuts off the unit after 30 mins of being idle; this is really nice in case someone accidentally leaves it on. If you don't like the auto-standby, you can shut it off.

There are a couple things I haven't tried yet (when I do, I'll update): Zone 2 or 3; 2nd/sub HDMI out, USB direct connection for iPods, etc.

PROS: See most of above

CONS (some also mentioned above):
* Remote is so-so; it should have been a programmable/learning remote
* Only Audyssey 2EQ instead of Audyssey MultEQ XT (I suppose they needed a carrot to get people to buy the 818)
* Subwoofer level via auto-setup is a little quiet for my tastes, although this could be the proximity of the setup mic to the back wall. The manual may have a way to permanently set it higher...I just haven't looked yet
* Can't play video via USB or DLNA (probably a lot to ask for an AVR)
* As someone else mentioned, HDMI initialization time is 10-15 seconds. It doesn't really bothered us, but it's definitely noticeable.

All things considered, I'm SUPER happy with this unit!

For that matter, the virtual \\"rocker\\" is pointless for anything; it's just too tough to find the up/down/right/left sweet spots vs. \\"enter.\\" When I get around to utilizing zone 2, I'll probably use the app a lot more. Having said that, it can't see the 717 if the unit is turned off, unless it's in hybrid standby, which uses more power (see below) and is a significant trade-off. However, it probably needs to be in hybrid stand-by to use zone 2 or 3 anyway, but I haven't tried or read about it yet to know for sure.

I tried plugging a video camera into the USB slot, and nothing happened (or maybe I at least got audio). Like DLNA, I guess it doesn't support video; only audio.

The last thing I'll point out is the power usage. I measured it with a Kill-A-Watt meter, compared it against my 12-yr old TX-DS777, and got the following results:
* Standby: 0W (nice); my 777 used 1.5W
* Hybrid standby: 2.1W (keeps the network connection & HDMI pass-through active)
* On, but not doing anything: 65W initially, then 75W after using it for something; my 777 used 79W
It also has an auto-standby, which shuts off the unit after 30 mins of being idle; this is really nice in case someone accidentally leaves it on. If you don't like the auto-standby, you can shut it off.

There are a couple things I haven't tried yet (when I do, I'll update): Zone 2 or 3; 2nd/sub HDMI out, USB direct connection for iPods, etc.

PROS: See most of above

CONS (some also mentioned above):
* Remote is so-so; it should have been a programmable/learning remote
* Only Audyssey 2EQ instead of Audyssey MultEQ XT (I suppose they needed a carrot to get people to buy the 818)
* Subwoofer level via auto-setup is a little quiet for my tastes, although this could be the proximity of the setup mic to the back wall. The manual may have a way to permanently set it higher...I just haven't looked yet
* Can't play video via USB or DLNA (probably a lot to ask for an AVR)
* As someone else mentioned, HDMI initialization time is 10-15 seconds. It doesn't really bothered us, but it's definitely noticeable.

All things considered, I'm SUPER happy with this unit!

*** FEB 2, 2013 UPDATE: I finally got around to connecting my iPod directly to the USB port. The iPod music menus (Playlists, Albums, Genres, etc.) and functionality are all replicated on the TV screen (if you have it on), receiver display, and Android remote. I was able to easily find and play music via the receiver's display with the remote since it truly mirrors the iPod's menus. Having said that, the Network streaming and iPod USB connection is where the Android remote REALLY excels since the display is larger and you don't need a direct line of sight. It's nice to not have to reach for the iPod to change songs or playlists or the check song info. Of course, the sound is excellent since it's digital via the USB.

Speaking of remotes, we almost never use the 717's remote; instead we still use the 777's remote, which is what I expected. The fact that the new one isn't a learning remote is the only reason.

product_title: Velodyne vPulse In-Ear Headphones (Classic Black)
review_body:
I've owned many headphones over the years and typically done research on what magazines have recommended as the best choices under $100 or less. The ones I've owned have included the Ultimate Ears 500vi, the Klipsch S4, and the Shure SE215. To be honest, I've liked aspects of all the headphones that I tried, but none really captured everything that I wanted it to do.

The Ultimate Ears 500vi had a great control system compatible with the latest phones as well as a multitude of ear pieces to ensure a great fit. The sound, to me, however, wasn't particularly great and I had a hard time discerning a noticeable difference between those headphones and ones much more affordable.

The Klipsch S4 are also highly recommended and I liked the convenient controls they had as well and found the earbuds easy to put in and take out. Sound was good, but build quality was definitely a bit less than some of the nicer headphones in the same range.

The Shure SE215 were my most recent pair and I was most happy with their excellent sound. The cable felt strong and high quality and the sound reproduction was awesome. Sad part was that they were hard to put in and out as they involve a rather involved over the ear style that you see musicians use. They also lacked the inline control of the other two models.

That leads me to the Velodyne. They have the highlights of every headphone above. They come with in-line control. The cable is high quality and flat, preventing cord tangle. The sound is fantastic, especially if you love bass and is equal to the Shure SE215 to my ears. And finally, they are very comfortable and easy to put in and out as well as coming with a multitude of ear tips as all the high quality manufacturers now provide.

Wirecutter (and former Gizmodo editor Brian Lam) has chosen this as their new $100 choice and I can't disagree. I'm very happy with them.

product_title: URC R6 Learning Remote Control (Discontinued by Manufacturer)
review_body:
First, I apologize for the cheesy subject line of this review...
Second, if you're looking for a universal remote, you could do far worse than this.
I purchased this thing because I make a point to have a remote with a "learning" function, that way it will ALWAYS work with
your electronics if you have the original remote handy. I went to Walmart first before shopping here on Amazon, and it was
a waste of time and effort. The closest thing they have to this remote ran about $30, and lacked the back-lit buttons feature.

If you're unfamiliar with how the "learning" feature of universal remotes works, here's a quick run-down:
If you own a an electronic device that is perhaps obscure or outdated, many of these universal remotes will not have
the pre-programed coding to properly work your device. If that happens to be your situation, pop the remote into the
learn mode. Once there you simply line up your device's original remote with this new universal one, so that they are
facing each-other. You are then able to teach the universal remote each button function as it works on your old remote.
(For example, you hit the "channel up" button on your old remote, while holding the "channel up" button on the universal remote).
Once the universal remote reads the signal, it will blink at you to state that the code was learned.
You can then move on to other buttons. It may sound tedious, but using this method I programmed
my girlfriend's TV and surround sound system within ten minutes.

~Rusty

So, as an alternative to the cheap in-ears you can get for a few bucks and wear out quickly, as they tend to be cheaply made, these offer a mid-range alternative to the bottom-line ones and the audiophile ones for a lot, which again can be fragile as they suffer the same cord-tension-jack problems across the board.

Not everyone can or should wear the \\"cans\\" that seem the rage. I do on a plane or at home, but they aren't travel friendly. These Monsters do have a diminished sound, and I don't hear enough of the massive bass the blurb touts. But, my ears are not the most sensitive to the ranges that more discerning listeners enjoy, so they'll do for a small size and the handy pouch with alternate sizes (large and small but medium default as installed is fine for me). They do stay in, too!

Obviously, for active wearers who are meant as the ideal audience, these are better. They keep out more sweat and moisture as the sound hole is not straight at the end of the flange, as in IEMs, but angle downward more sharply. This allows I assume less gook from the ears to get in. The upper tip does look strange, but it anchors the gizmo in each ear (small letters on the top of each tell you which is which side) snugly.

I am used to such, but wearers of buds may find these at first a bit more invasive in the ear: it takes a bit to get used to the placement. They are a halfway compromise between the deep IEM and the shallow earbud that pops out. They are not as sonically sharp as IEMs, but better than the earbuds that lack an anchor.

The cord is green and light. The thickness of a rubber band and the appearance of a noodle, it may not win style awards. There is a talk button for a microphone if you need it. Monster is known (as are Sennheiser and UE) for quality.

product_title: Sennheiser CX 890i Headset
review_headline: The finest in-ear headphones I've ever used
review_body:
After extensive testing, adjusting, comparing, and listening, I have come to the conclusion that these are the best headphones I've ever owned. I own three pairs of over-ear Sennheisers, and have owned multiple pairs of Klipsch headphones as well. I've used the Koss PortaPro, and more cheap and mid-range pairs of headphones than I care to try to even to count. True, these are the most expensive headphones I've ever owned, but I don't think that's causing any bias...

Sennheiser in General...

I became a huge fan of Sennheiser on the day when they sent me a brand new pair of headphones (for free!) when when wife broke the expensive ones that I gave her and I sent them in to be repaired. True, I was already a fan of their enormous sound quality for their $30.00 and $40.00 over-ear headphones (which I use for listening while on break at home, during late night gaming, and for general computing use), but when a company gives a complete stranger five star treatment on the first-call, well that's the stuff that makes lifetime fans. I recommend Sennheiser to anyone, whether they are looking for a good $20.00 pair of headphones or have money to burn.

Break-In Period

Other people will tell you to NOT listen to your headphones while you break them in, but personally I get a kick out of seeing headphones open up and start to really sing after a week or two. Hearing the tinny sound of vocals, the shrill sound of strings, and the screech of horns morph into warm detailed vocals, tender heart-string pulls, and epic fanfares that make the heart swell is an experience that I greatly enjoy. And once you give these headphones a week of play...sing they certainly do.

The Music Is In the Details

The bass is punchy, but clean, warm and strong. Not the deep thumping that a pair of Beats or some other Bass specialty headphone would give you, but the kind of bass enjoyed by enthusiasts of orchestra music and jazz.

Vocals, strings, and horns shine on these headphones. Voices have texture, detail, and become very distinct. Strings are given a separation and clarity that make every finger-slide and tap distinct. Horns are clear as a bell and have great power. I mention each of these things because while these headphones are excellent, these areas in particular shine.

Some people might find the sound of these headphones a bit cold (as opposed to warm), but the detail and overall CLEANNESS of sound is absolutely outstanding. I tested everything from pop music to Broadway musicals, and used by favorite kind of music (orchestral recordings) as my ultimate benchmark. And during my testing something happened I didn't expect. I got GOOSEBUMPS while playing some of my orchestral favorites with the sound turned up. The effect of these headphones on a great orchestral recording is absolutely ELECTRIFYING.

Initially I was concerned that these headphones might not handle flat recordings well, as while they were breaking in some old mp3s of pop music sounded quite flat. I am exceedingly pleased to say that when they are fully broken in these headphones have no such weakness. While exceptionally mastered recordings (anything by the Prague symphony orchestra) will be absolutely mind-blowing, even plain-Jane regular recordings will get a massive boost from these headphones by the excellent definition of vocals and bass in particular.

Functionality

It took me a while to find the right fit with these phones (apparently one of my ears is bigger than the other), but once I established a good fit the seal is tight (not so tight you can hear NOTHING outside, but then again I think that may be a problem more than a feature on other headphones I've tested). You'll know you have a good fit when the source of the sound seems to disappear and you are simply in a blanket of sound (if they sound faint or tinny you have either not broken then in or have a bad seal).

I tested the volume controls on my iPod touch and they work perfectly. I find the controls on the device much easier and more intuitive than the controls on the iPod touch so this is one feature I like a great deal.

Some people have complained about the length of the headphone cord on these headphones, which quite simply is totally ridiculous. For Sennheiser's over-ear headphones 9 foot cables make sense as they expect you to attach them to a desk/amplifier/speakers. These headphones are clearly deigned for use with your iPod or other mp3 player, and as such their length is perfect.

Initially I had thought to mark these headphones down slightly for audio issues and design choices, but with further testing I have found my fears unfounded (audio issues were resolved after full break-in period and any design flaws are too minor to subtract from such a superior product). The carrying case may be an odd choice (I believe I am using it correct wrapping the headphones AROUND it rather than putting them IN it), but it's functional. The directions oddly explain things that should be obvious and skip things that aren't (how to use carrying case). But in the end...

Simply The Best

These headphones are beautifully designed, wonderfully functional, and work EXTREMELY well for the use they were designed for. They were clearly carefully optimized to give you the best sound possible out of an iPod product. They are beautiful, well made, and sound fantastic. If you are a skeptic, or prefer your sound with lots of bass or very warm, you may want to comparison shop first, but if you are a Sennheiser fan who likes in-ear headphones you absolutely cannot go wrong with buying these headphones.

review_headline: Best full range driver for the money
review_body: If you are looking for something that performs exceptionally well, do not judge this driver by its low price. I have used this driver in transmission lines, back loaded horns and it sounds fantastic.  It provides a very big sound.  It has fairly high power handling and has great clarity and transient response.  The mids and highs are excellent, great choice for jazz, vocals, small ensembles, big band with brass and woodwinds. However, in order to bring out the bass, this driver needs a good cabinet design with either a transmission line or back loaded horn to fully bring out but when done properly, the results are phenomenal.  A very simple folded transmission line can be easily made and provide very nice results.  You will be hard pressed to find a better driver for 3x the price.  This same driver is specified in many high end ($$$) commercial systems that use line arrays.  Give it a try and you will not be disappointed.  Do a search on DIYAudio.com for this driver and you will see that it is used in a lot of HiFi projects with great results and is highly regarded by all who use it. product_title: Belkin Conserve Socket Energy-Saving Outlet with Timer
review_headline: Saves electricity, pleasant to use, and best of all, it's grounded
review_body:
It's hard to find a single switch plug that is actually grounded. My ACE Hardware only carries switch plugs without a ground, and for most appliances and electronics, that's pretty useless. I was very happy to find this grounded power switch on Amazon.

I have several large surge protectors, and sometimes I just want to be able to turn off ONE thing on it, like the microwave in the kitchen, and like my cell phone charger by the bedside. Now I just reach over and click it off, instead of wasting watts or needing to turn off the entire strip.

Using the plug with a surge protector means I don't have to reach over, hunch down, or crawl behind anything to actually use the switch. My life is simpler with this power switch.

It's even elegant looking. Not that I need that in something I stick in an outlet, but it does make it more pleasurable to use. The switch glows a nice green and feels good to the touch when you rock it.

Belkin usually impresses me with their useful, attractive, thoughtful products, and I'm happy to include this power switch to that list. At around six dollars, it's a good buy, and saves money in the long term.

NOTE: I love the idea of conserving watts whenever I can. With a lot of attention to my electrical practices, I've been able to get my electric bill down to the point where my electric company sent me a letter asking if there was something wrong with my meter. Seriously. So this switch is part of my arsenal. :-)

review_body:
I received my Bose SoundDock 10 a couple of hours ago and have been playing with it ever since. I was surprised when Fedex delivered the box, because its heavy. But even with the music blasting, it was still crisp and clear.

The system has a video output and aux input for using this with other pieces of equipment. I tried the video output using my son's IPOD and we listened to the audio on the Bose unit and watched the video on our projection screen. The sound is as good as our older model home theater system with six speakers surrounding the room. I think the Bose unit may become our new home theater speaker system.

I could not be happier with this unit. I have a few other Bose speaker units and I have always been impressed with their quality. I think this one steps that quality up another notch.one steps that quality up another notch.

product_title: Coby 8 GB 1.8-Inch Video MP3 Player with FM Radio
review_headline: For $5 more you can get one a LOT better
review_body: I bought two, a red one and a blue one, because it seemed like a good deal and the reviews looked promising.  I wanted one to carry in my car (we live in the mountains with only one radio station) and one to leave in my bedroom.  They were nothing short of terrible.  After pushing the ON button, it takes several seconds for a response of any kind.  So much so that I wonder if it even recognized that I pushed the ON button, so I push it a few more times.  After consistently doing this each and every time I turn it on, I assume it must be the way it was manufactured.  It takes approximately 10-15 seconds to turn on, either way.  10-15 seconds might not seem like a long time, but I invite you to sit there and count to 15...waiting...just waiting...  Trying to skip songs is just as painful.  It takes at least 5 seconds to skip forward.  You're not sure if it picked up on you pushing the skip button, so you push it again, still no response...then 3-5 seconds later it skips forward 3 songs...but you only pushed the skip button twice...  Really, the main problem with this unit is the response time.    Other cons:  Not expandable --  no microSD card slot  Every time you turn it on, it resets itself and starts on the first song uploaded.  I find that annoying and want it to start playing the last song I was listening to.    Luckily, I also bought another MP3 player (completely different brand, MUCH better quality) that I picked up from Staples.  The one from Staples was $5 more, but infinitely worth it.  I like it so much better.  It is sturdier with a metal case, not cheap plastic.  It has a MicroSD slot and is expandable.  It has a camera (not that I'm likely to use it.)  Lastly, and mainly, the response time is much better.  My only complaint is it doesn't hold a charge indefinitely when it's not in use.  I charge it, put it in a drawer and expect it to still be fully charged a couple of weeks later, but it often drains itself.  Then again, I do have 4 kids, so it could just as easily be them playing with it as the battery itself.  (Eclipse brand, 4GB, [...])

My only problems with this receiver are VERY insignificant/small, mostly personal issues:

product_title: One-Mount Plasma / LCD Wall Mount for 23"-84" Screens
review_body:
I bought this mount after looking at several others from Chief, Premier, Omnimount and others. I needed to mount a 125 lb., 65\\" plasma TV, pretty much flat on a wall. And, this mount was a pretty good fit for the job.

The mount is heavy duty & quite versatile in configuration to fit many types of large TV/monitors. This mount will allow some up & down tilt, but no left/right placement, and no ability to pull away from the wall without removing the TV from the mounting rails. The distance from the rear of the TV to the wall can be as little as a couple inches. Nice!

Pros:
1. This mount is VERY versatile, and also comes with a plethora of fasteners for all kinds of TVs!
2. It's pretty cheap for such a heavy duty mount.
3. It was easy to put together & easy to mount the TV once the rails are mounted to the wall.
4. The directions are good!

Cons to this mount are few, but worth mentioning:
1. The fit of the wall rail system is pretty loose. You have to carefully tighten all of the mounting hardware with a level close at hand. The loose fit causes the side pieces to sag.
2. There is no leveling adjustment after the TV is mounted in place. This is a pain since the rails fit loosely and can shift with the weight of the TV.
3. (Not necessarily a con) The tight spacing to the wall makes connections difficult. I actually wanted the tightest spacing possible for aesthetic reasons.

I like the mount & will use it again.

product_title: iHome Android Alarm Clock Speaker Dock
review_body:
I previously had an iHome alarm clock for my iPod touch. This current Android model is definitely an improvement over what I used to have. A few other reviewers have complained about some of the features, but they are actually some of my favorite things about this clock/radio.

PROS:
1)It has a flexible charging cord/audio input cord. Some reviewers said that they thought it decreased the attractiveness of the clock when you have cords poking out, but I actually really appreciated the way the phone charged. I have another Android alarm clock from another brand that actually docks directly into the phone, but since I use a thick protective case on my phone (I've got toddlers in my house), I was never able to connect my phone directly to the clock unless I completely removed the protective cover. With the iHome clock I can plug directly into my phone without needing to remove my case.

2)The phone can be positioned either vertically OR horizontally. I've actually used the horizontal feature to watch a show on Netflix while I was laying in bed. My other docking android phone does not have this capability (it only allows me to use the phone vertically.

3)There are a few different settings for brightness. The highest setting is really too bright for me, but I find that the lowest illuminated setting is about the same light output-wise as a standard illuminated digital alarm clock.

CONS:
1)The sound is not great. It sounds a bit tinny. Very little bass, poor sound quality.
2)The buttons on the top of the clock are not really upraised at all, making it somewhat difficult to know if you're fingers are on the correct buttons (this can be even more challenging if you're half asleep at the time).

I really like this alarm clock. It also has an FM feature (although there is no way to preset or program stations - I usually keep it on the same station all the time, so that's not really an issue for me.)It has all of the features I need on an alarm clock, plus it charges my phone at the same time.of the features I need on an alarm clock, plus it charges my phone at the same time.

product_title: RCA 4 Device Big Button Remote
review_headline: Simplicity is strength - put in the hands of little kids and visitors
review_body:
I like this remote more than expected and apparently more than others. Simplicity is strength. Nobody has to stare at an unfamiliar remote with multi-colored keys. They're less likely to accidentally order things or some other mischief.

My 3-yr olds use it. Grandparents use it; visitors use it. It works as well as the regular remote for my big Panasonic TV, with regard to the limited operations so visible on the remote. Anybody can channel surf.

If you want a primary remote to fully operate a TV, this isn't the one. That's not its niche.

Pitch the directions

Throw out the directions if you want. Throw out the code list too. RCA keeps the manual and code list on its site (RCA website). Use the search function on the site's homepage. Search rcr4258n (type that in the search box). Now zoom the manual at 200%. From that view the programming instructions are not intimidating at all.

Brand Code Program Method

There are four ways to operate this remote to search for the TV or other device you want to program. For me the best way is the Brand Code Search. This method requires the code list (see above paragraph).

How to Program this Remote

Since my TV is Panasonic, I located the six codes for that brand on the Code Sheet (per RCA's website or per the Code Sheet that came with the product). Per the instructions, I pressed and held the TV key and the POWER key at the same time. The light goes on the remote so let go the keys. Enter the code number in the numeric keypad. Pointing the remote at the TV, press POWER key and wait 2 seconds. If the TV turns off, it's the correct code. When the code is correct, press STOP key and the programming is all done.

Big and Friendly

My experience: This remote works and is super-easy to program. The manual says it can be programmed for 4 devices. I only use it for 1 TV and I have not tried to program any other device. I like seeing my 3 yr olds use the TV with ease, and others as well. It's big, friendly and works on the one device that I programmed.device. I like seeing my 3 yr olds use the TV with ease, and others as well. It's big, friendly and works on the one device that I programmed.
