product_title: SDMX22-004G-PAR
review_headline: Disapointed by this unit: poor firmware design and bugs. Screen went out too.
review_body:
Disappointed by this unit: poor firmware design and bugs. Screen went out!

Sorry this is so long, but at least I will be thorough.

This is my third Sansa player. I have been very satisfied with the quality of their products, their compact size, extensive format compatibility and low cost. As you may know SANSA are not some third-rate market nobody, they are responsible for the very excellent SD Flash memory format. Being somewhat of a nerd, I enjoy sporting a SANSA over the equivalent iPod which is aimed squarely at the undereducated average consumer, and so devoid of many features.

Like my previous player, the SANSA Fuze (which was unfortunately stolen) this one has a lot going for it:

o A voice recorder. It eats battery fast, and is limited to an hour and a half of contiguous recording, but the sound quality from accross a small room is excellent
o A chronometer
o The ability to resume playback
o The ability to speed up or slow down playback for Audiobooks / Podcasts (main usage for me - very helpful)
o A radio with good reception / StationID features
o A uSD slot allowing you to cheaply expand the storage capability. I have a 32gb card in mine, and it supports up to 64gb. The uSD card content is well integrated into the file manager, unlike other models that artificially separate the 2 kinds of memory.
o Relatively low price

The player used to look quite stylish (see below). The color screen, a first for the Clip Zip and the ultimate reason why I went with this model over larger ones, is well suited for browsing through your library and navigating the menus. It displays track information effectively, even if the scroll rate, which is not adjustable, is somewhat slow.

The battery in this SANSA is excellent, and a great improvement over other models I've tried. I am able to go about 4 days without recharging. I listen for about 1.5 hours a day on average, butsometimes a lot more. The battery charges very very quickly. You can get enough juice to last you several hours by plugging it in in the morning for literally 5 minutes (while you brush your teeth).

However, not only did Sansa make several very poor decisions for the file management, but there were bugs in the original firmware, which is quite unacceptable for an experienced manufacturer and a mature product line.

Additionally, the nice new color screen that swayed me into buying it has now ended up malfunctioning, 6 months after purchase with gentle use. That all is very disapointing.

Here are the issues I have had with the unit, starting with the most irritating:

o The \\"white noise\\" bug at the beginning of a song. The new firmware corrected for this, but I have used Mp3 players since they were an exotic item in the now distant year 2002, and only at the dawn of the Mp3 era could you expect errors like this!

Imagine listening to quiet relaxing music. The track switches, and suddenly you hear a blast of white noise, AT MAXIMUM VOLUME, lasting for a half a second. How do you like that? It happens on LAME CBR mp3s (majority of my collection) that I encoded personally, and that I have never had any issues with on any other players. This kind of oversight - allowing an error like this into production - is completely unacceptable, given the overall high sound quality that SANSA is well known for, and their supposed experience putting out mp3 players. Apparently the team that wrote the firmware for this unit was managed very poorly, and apparently the QA people failed dramatically as well.

o The navigation system is flawed. It depends on every file being correctly ID3 tagged. It is not possible any longer to play the files in order in the way they are placed and numbered in the folder. I do not understand what kind of thinking resulted in this design. Numbering tracks and placing them in a folder is the simplest way of organizing music! Why complicate it?! ID3 tags are useful and convenient, but you will have to spend lots of time editing the ID3 info on many of your tracks to get them to show up correctly and play in order. This really is much more of a headache than you would think, especially if you are like me and have a large collection that you've ripped long ago without using CDDBs. What am I supposed to do - re-rip everything??? The new firmware sidesteps this issue by repairing M3u playlist support. Now wait a second... why was this not functioning properly when the unit was first released? M3u has been around since 1995 and is the STANDARD playlist format for Mp3s. It is not too difficult or expensive to implement.

o These software problems can probably be resolved by installing an alternative firmware such as RockBox. But this reverse endineering automatically voids your warranty, is not supported by the manufacturer, and can permanently break your unit, which is why I have not done it. But I have been tempted.

o The screen broke after 6 months of use. What a bummer! I turned the player on on Monday and about 1/3 of the screen on the left side is completely dark, and the backlight is dimmer than it was before on the part that does still light up. This saddens me, as my Fuze lasted me almost 2 years, and was going strong when it was nabbed. I was hoping to get a reliable product here that I could use for a few years. To my surprise SANSA, which I expected to be reliable has dissapointed me. Perhaps in future I will need to look for a better manufacturer...

product_title: GE 23298 RF Modulator Video Converter (Discontinued by Manufacturer)
review_headline: Nice video Channel 3 or 4 analog modulator
review_body:
I'm using this modulator to send Direct TV satellite modulated audio/video to a TV in my detached garage workshop. (Our Direct TV Receivers don't have modulated RF outputs on them; only HDMI and RCA video/audio.) The garage is about 100' away from the house, and the cable run is about 125'

For set-up all I had to do was connect video and audio jumpers, select the desired channel for RF output, attach my RG-6 cable connection going out to the garage, and plug in the wall wart power supply. The modulator gives you the option of using either TV analog channel 3 or 4 for output.

The audio and video in my garage is crisp and clear; and shows no sign of noise, shadows or ghosting. I've had this setup going for ~3 months now, and haven't had any problems, including audio popping due to signal drop-out.

The key to a good setup with any remote audio/video/composite RF signal, is to use good cable and avoid routing your cables near noise sources. So try to avoid routing next to florescent lighting, large power cables, etc. In my case I'm using good quality Quad Shield RG-6 cable, crimp connectors (not twist-on connectors), and most of the run is routed through a buried conduit that connects between the house and garage.

product_title: Unibrak UNB 550 Dual Arm Articulating Cantilever LCD Plasma LED LFD TV Wall Mount Extends 33 inches 42" 50" 58" 65" 70" Extra Heavy Duty Sony LG Panasonic Samsung Sharp
review_headline: Just a great overall TV mount!
review_body:
I'm giving this mount 4 stars instead of 5 only because, as other reviewers have mentioned, the arms are a little stiff. Pulling the tv out from the wall is pretty nerve wracking for me as I usually push it back almost all the way to the wall until the kids go to bed. Once that happens, I pull it out gently and extend it to almost the full length (which is a long way and the reason I bought this one!) and turn it towards my seating position for gaming, etc. I have heard my set creak just a tiny bit as I'm extending the mount towards me, even though I'm careful to only grab the back of the part that is attached to the tv and not the set itself. I'll probably lube up the arms here pretty soon to combat this

I have a 55' ES 2012 series Samsung LED by the way and because of my kids I wanted to install it pretty high on the wall which was a beast to do even though the tv was listed as only being around 40 pounds. NOTE: If you have the same type of set with the U shaped mount (not the 4 spider legs) you can actually leave the stand on and mount the set, and then take the stand off last)

It took me and my dad hoisting it up near shoulder level while my wife was on the other side tightening down the 4 screws that attach the two separate parts of the mount (Theres one piece of the mount that goes to the tv, and one piece with the arms pre-attached that goes on the wall first)

The nice thing about the actual mounting part is that the piece that is attached to the tv goes up and hooks downs/sets down into the 2 \\"open top\\" top holes of the square attachment plate. This makes it easier to screw down those 2 top bolts and start on screwing down the bottom 2 bolts to attach the set to the other part of the mount (I took us a bit of trial and error to figure this out so remember this when you hoist the tv up to actually attach it to the other piece)

Beware the instructions do suck as everyone else oh so helpfully mentioned (Engrish anyone?) but you will rike this tv mount regardless of how bad the instructions are ;) Also beware of anyone saying that you can do this with one person. If you want to mangle your tv or have a small set then go ahead and try. If you are a videophile and are worried about tightening down every screw too much which can cause light bleed etc. on an LED, then you would never go so far as trying to manhandle a big led screen by yourself to hang it up. I would recommend 3 people for the hanging part if you want to be careful with your set, and only having 2 people is possible but would be pushing it (for sets 26\\" and up, mine is a 55\\")

The quality of the mount itself is perfect. The included screws and even the washers will work fine (regardless of what other reviews may say). If you have a Samsung with recessed holes, the tv itself usually comes with the 4 pieces that sit down into those recessed holes to make them flush with the back of the tv (But if you lost them, don't worry this kit includes some too). I also needed to use 4 of the spacers included in the mount's kit right on top of those (be prepared to use the spacers also if you need to)

Overall I would definitely highly recommend this mount to anyone. If you are looking for ease of installation over cost then go buy a Sanus mount at Wally World, etc. for 3x the price if you need good instructions/online videos of how to do it. If you would rather get a great mount for a little over a hundred dollars and don't mind figuring some things out for yourself then go for it!

product_title: Cerwin-Vega Home Audio Center Channel Speaker
review_body:
UPDATE: Thanks to G. Green (see his ugliness below), I'll add this update (I'd forgotten I even reviewed them here): After breaking these CV's in, the bass has a more natural sound and the primary objection I have is the lack of highs. CV's choice of cross-over points is unconventional but does manage to handle a variety of music well, below 1 KHz. I'm driving them with a Rotel RB-1070, so no power shortage and they handle the power and deliver the sound. But, the high mid to tweeter range needs some help and as a result ends up sounding very much like a PA speaker with great low end. These are play speakers for me, but I have not gotten around to significant modifications, which I believe could save them from their short-falls. What I've done instead is add a pair of Boston Acoustic bookshelf speakers (driven by a separate RB-1070) and used an equalizer to pull out the bass and let the mids and highs from the BA's augment the sound of the CV's. Everyone that has raised an eyebrow to this setup becomes a believer when I drop out the BA's and let the CV's stand on their own. One day I plan to do a tweeter transplant to see if this will make the XLS-15 an acceptable hi-fi speaker all by itself. Please note that my initial complaint stands, in that the overall quality of construction and materials used in these speakers is on par with white box units.

Original Review:
These 'throw back to the '70s' are boomy with an overall very cluttered sound. They will make lots of noise with moderate power, but even at $500, they are not great. But, sound is like beauty ... What my comments are really addressing is build quality: mediocre at best. One mid-range was not working when I received mine (not from Amazon), so I pulled it apart to see if a wire had popped off of it. It's a big empty box with a sloppily applied 1/2\\" if \\"wool\\" on all walls and no bracing. Turns out the wires were in place, so I powered just the driver and it was fine. Checked connections to the crossover. No problem there, so it had to be the crossover itself. I put it all back together, and while I applaud the robust metal grill, design and application are poor!

For you nay-sayers that will dismiss this because 'no one would open up a brand new and warrantied speaker', I frequently take brand new things apart even when the are working just fine, at least to the point that I am confident the warranty is in tact.

Going 'round back, I pulled the crossover out and gave it a visual. I was surprised to see a missing capacitor! They apparently have quality control issues here, since all components are glued to the circuit boards and some are even tie wrapped to the boards. So, there it was - a nicely curved impression in the glue that was supposed to hold the capacitor in place through all the vibration that might break the leads or the solder joint. But this didn't even make it through shipping! So, back to the big box I went an stuck my hand through the hole where the crossover was feeling around for the missing cap. I couldn't feel it, so I took out the woofer for better access and ... yep ... there is was tucked in the wool. This is BAD, folks. Really bad. But a little cleaning and re-soldering and all is well. hmmm ... All but my astonishment at how lame these are. I will invest the time to break them in, but I do no have very high expectations at this point.

I sold a pair of vintage Rectilinear IIIa's that would have put these to shame. My mistake. If you like that 70's sound, you may like these. But beware of poor design and quality.

review_body:

However, each time I hit volume now (for the soundbar) the TV displays a message (forget the exact wording) for basically stating that internal speakers are off. That is annoying. I understand this is not the soundbar, but a $600 soundbar would have a better solution/option.

Now for the bigger issue. My unit for some reason keeps shutting off. So I could be watching a movie or Cable TV and after about 5 minutes, the thing just shuts off! I then manually shut it off then turn it back on, and the unit is supposed to pick up the source automatically. It doesn't. So then I hit the source button few times thinking one of the sources will pick up the audio. And still it doesn't. I've tried different devices (blu-ray, cable tv box, PS3, dvd player, direct connection w/ MP3 player) and still same issue.

Contacted support and they came to a conclusion that the unit was defective. It was covered under warranty to be replaced. Now comes the hard part, I had to pay for shipping. And this unit is huge so I ended up paying $65 to ship the item back. They at least replaced it but haven't had a chance to hook it up.

Again, a $600 unit should sound great and work flawlessly. The sound is great but the working flawlessly part could use major improvement.

EDIT Update: Harman shipped me a new soundbar w/ a new Subwoofer. The original issues I was facing have gone away. I think that they updated the soundbar from the original one. So I am glad I contacted them.

product_title: Philips SHE5105BK/28 CitiScape Downtown Headphones
review_headline: Comfortable to Wear & Clear Sound Reproduction
review_body:
COMFORT
Philips CITISCAPE headphones achieve something few sealed ear headphones ever do. They fit comfortablely for hours at a time. Sealed ear headphones both block out external noice, while increasing the bass response from the headphone's drivers. These models tend to be the heavier headphones, so fatigue often sets in, after an hour or so of wear, pinching the ear, or putting uncomfortable pressure across the skull. I didnt run into that problem with these CITISCAPE DOWNTOWN headphones. Unlike the open foam headphones, which let sound in and out, the tight seal of the memory foam around your outer ear mutes moderately loud urban enviorments, tho these headphones dont have ambient noise cancelation technology. So you will still be bothered by jet engines, loud horns, sirens, etc. On the other hand, your music isnt going to leak out from the headphones, so youll be able to enjoy even loud music, without bothering anyone within hearing distance. Also, since these headphones fit snug and secure around your head, I could walk, dance, jump, shimmy, whatever, and they didnt slip off my head. That's pretty important if youre walking, dancing, jumping or shimmying thru an urbal Citiscape.
SOUND REPRODUCTION
I compared these headphones to my old KOSS headphones, which are an open ear model. (Open ear headphone models dont form a tight seal against the ear, to create the bass response.) I listen to folk music, jazz, trip hop, electronica/alternative, reggae, and across the board, found the sound reproduction to be detailed, precise, with especially distinct clarity in the upper ranges. Acoustic guitars had ringing overtones, reggae snare drum/hi hat work was crisp and full, and vocals were rich. The bass response was flat, distinct, without any boom or pop. Bass heavy music, like reggae and trip hop, reproduced the bass end with richness and depth. I wasn't sure how detailed the upper register was, until I compaired a CD mastered off a vinyl record, against my old KOSS headphones. These CitiScape headphones reproduced every hiss, pop and needle distortion you get from vinyl, sound which was invisible on the KOSS headpohnes. This crisp, detailed sound reproduction was why I could hear distinct backround vocals, drum cymbals, or 12 string guitar overtones.
CONCLUSSION
I found the Philips Citiscape headphones to be quality audio equipment. These headphone's sound reproduction is noticably flat, so your music isnt colored by weak high frequency response, or boomy bass. If you intend to wear these for several hours, they wont become uncomfortable. Nor will they slip off your head, if you are running across the street, or dancing to your music. Altho earplugs are less noticable, they simply can NOT reproduce high end audio. If your MP3 player or computer employs LOSSLESS audio, MP4 or WMP formats, which reproduce music with greater realism and articulation, you wont hear that audio improvement unless you listen with high quality headphones. review_headline: Good only within a narrowly defined, standard set-up
review_body:
If you're using popular brand model devices in a standard cable/satellite configuration then these remotes will probably be all you need. If your model is not on the list and you have to use the generic code for your manufacturer, or if you are using devices not within the standard set up (Roku, over-the-air-TV converter box).

One of the remotes is touted as capable of handling six devices, TV, DVD, Blu-ray, VCR, SAT, CBL and DVR. It didn't work out too well for me. My set up includes a Sony Bravia TV and Sony wireless Blu-Ray player and Sony DVD/VHS combo. Those were easy to program and worked fine. The issues came when I wanted to use one of the other unused keys for an additional (regionless) Philips DVD player. It appears to allow only one DVD player - regardless of how many keys are available.

The other remote is capable of handling three devices. The remote should be capable of handling a TV with a built in DVD player, which I have. Unfortunately, mine is a Maxent. There is no code for my model, only a generic code for Maxent. I tried entering the generic code under the programmable buttons for both the TV and the DVD player. The remove will power up the TV, but it will not operate the DVD portion.

In addition, I could not get either remote to work with a DISH box for over the air TV or a ROKU player. So, I still have to keep separate remotes for those.

I was hoping a six device remote would eliminate the need for some of my other remotes, but was disappointed by the inability to handle anything outside a very narrowly defined, standard set-up.

Well, after a few years of no TV except for what I could get with a Roku that I purchased for Netflix, Hulu Plus, and the occasional Amazon streaming movie I decided to purchase a [[ASIN:B004QK7HI8 Paper Thin Leaf Indoor HDTV Antenna - Made in the USA!]] and a [[ASIN:B001DVZXC0 Zinwell ZAT-970A Digital to Analog TV Converter Box (for Antenna Use)]] through Amazon thinking that if I did not get any reception then I could return them easily enough. To my surprise and amazement, I got about 12 useable channels, then moved it closer to the outside wall and got even more channels including PBS, ABS, NBC, FOX, the CW, and some of the Spanish Language channels (though I lost 1-2 of the independent channels - kinda odd to me). But I was floored at the clarity being shown on my 20 year old tiny TV. The only reason that I did not immediately move these to the big TV (that has my Roku on it already) was that it was about 11:00 p.m. when I hooked everything up to try it out. When I get home from work today I am moving these to the big TV (hopefully in time to enjoy the Bears game tonight!). I also ordered a [[ASIN:B000F28DP2 PCT 1-PORT BI-DIRECTIONAL CABLE TV HDTV AMPLIFIER SIGNAL BOOSTER WITH PASSIVE RETURN PATH]] that has yet to show up, but once I get that I fully expect to get every Chicago station (with the possible exception of the CBS affiliate since Channel 2 has notoriously bad reception in this area even before digital) plus the Rockford IL stations (which should net me the CBS affiliate).

Long story short - if you are at all considering getting this product do yourself a favor and get it. product_title: SanDisk Sansa Fuze+ 16 GB MP3 Player
review_headline: Sansa fails with thier new Fuze+
review_body:
I have the predecessor of the Sansa Fuze+, the Sansa Fuze, had gotten it refurbished. This new version lacks the functionality of the older model in a few ways. I had some misgivings seeing that the Fuze+ lacked a wheel to navigate but figured it should work fine.

It is sluggish and slow to respond, the layout of the UI interface is quite complicated, the touch pad is unresponsive and not well defined. Often the touch pad is too sensitive and difficult to work. If you want to skip a song you have to tap twice (once to wake it up, once to FF) and hope you aren't pausing it (the play/pause tap area is right above the FF area). The lack of a tactile sensation makes it difficult to use the Fuze+ without looking. I like to bicycle around, looking at my player just to skip a song is dangerous!

The auto lock feature is maddening. If you want to rate a song you must hold down the forward touch area for several seconds. On my Fuze it's just scroll, click, scroll, click. A matter of a few seconds, tops, not 5+ seconds. Also it seems to default to seeing your music as a subset of ten artists and only one song from each! You have to tap over to songs to make sure it will shuffle all the songs instead of a select 10 songs and do it every time you switch from the radio you will have to do so.

I had purchased a 32gb microSD to use with this player but it didn't recognize the sd card (said it wasn't formated correctly). It also was unable to format the SD card making it a useless purchase. I took the 16gb microSD from my old Fuze and put it into the Fuze+ and the Fuze+ still didn't like it (same result). My old Fuze saw the 32gb just fine.

I had managed to record a radio program I wanted to listen to but when it was finished I had a devil of a time finding it. Again the touch pad was inprecise enough for it to be a struggle to choose the right menu. product_title: HH54VP series
review_body:
Bought this a couple months ago as we got into storm season. It has alerted twice, only for severe thunderstorm warnings, but it works. Where we are, Wx broadcasts are not strong, so I keep it in the charger on a window sill in my home office to make sure the signal gets to it. Outside the signal is fine. You need to read the manual to program it with your S.A.M.E. codes, but it is a snap once you look them up and do one of them. The loud beep others complain about can be turned off (but not down), but it's not so terrible, just providing affirmative feedback on all button pushes if you leave it on.

The display is clear and readable. The alert method is configurable: tone, tone-then-radio sound or just turn on the radio sound. Everything is via easy to use menus on the screen.

If traveling, you can put it in an \\"any code\\" mode where any alerts it can hear will set it off, so you don't have to keep programming it. I look forward to having it with me on my boat in the nearby lake this summer, so any sudden violent shift in the weather will be alerted.

At home, you might think you're covered with TV or radio, but how much \\"live and local\\" TV do you watch these days? Between DVR-delays, national \\"cable\\" channels and watching DVD's you may have a lot of time you're NOT \\"on the grid\\" to receive warnings like this when you think about it. Having this or another silent monitor listening-in all the time is cheap insurance that you'll hear about something unexpected.

Get the cradle and battery pack version. It's compact, works well and a lot easier than messing with your own batteries all the time, but have some extra alkalines that fit ready in case you're without power for an extended period.

product_title: Cowon S9 Video MP3 Player with Touchscreen
review_body:
Pros:
Well let me tell you folks, I'm so happy with this thing, that I'm writing this review about 2.5 years after my initial purchase in March of 2010. I have listened to this thing continuously, nearly on a daily basis with at least an 8 hour workday. At first, I worked at a desk, and bought this to replace a Creative Zen: Vision M that I had owned for about a year or two. The battery on my Creative wasn't holding up, the screen was scratched and the buttons were broke. It also froze up allot. So I ordered this Cowon S9. Oh my goodness! Loved it!

The touch screen works wonderfully and it is made of an almost indestructible gorilla glass surface that has held up strong through numerous drops, skids across the floor, tumbles onto concrete, off shelves, beat on poles and everything else imaginable. It has only one scratch and I don't know where it came from. But this thing has been really hardy and taken allot of abuse (not on purpose, of course). The touchscreen worked exactly where my finger touches is and I have no trouble with it whatsoever. The screen is an extremely bright LED, though to conserve battery life, I normally keep the display brightness set a few notches down. Which brings me to another topic, the battery.

The battery, well what can I say? I've had this S9 for about 2.5 years and I honestly have not seen any depletion of the battery condition. I listened to it all day at work, which was an 8 hour day, and I still have a full charge on the battery. Yes, a complete, full charge after a full days work. I no longer work at a desk, I'm actually in a warehouse now so I don't tinker with the screen as much as I did before, but a full charge still... now that's awesome.

The sound is spectacular and is so great, the Apple iPods can't even compare to this. It has an amazing graphic equalizer and digital processing that I have NEVER experienced on ANY other mp3 player. This thing has hands down, no competition, the BEST sound you will ever find. It can even add Reverb and echo effects. It can slow the music or speed it up and still keep the same pitch (or not, if you prefer). The clarity is incredible on this thing. The presets are very nice and if that's not enough for you, you can set your own sounds, up to 4 savings, customizing everything from bass to treble, echo to reverb, even widen the deepness of the stereo or narrow the sound channels. Seriously, this thing rocks.

You can change your backgrounds, watch detailed movies, read txt books, you can even watch Flash! It ha sa sound recorder a calculator, notepad, typewriter thingy, recorder, clock, even a game lol. A calendar, radio, post it thing and a really cool gravity sensor so if you turn the player to the side, it switches to a side view. If you don't want it to switch, you can lock it to one view. But wow!

What can it play? WMA, MP3, FLAC, just about anything you want. A few video formats it won't support, but that's no biggie. It supports the most popular. Syncs well with Windows Media Player and Media Monkey. I could go on and on and on and on.

Cons: After 2.5 years, it still hasn't broke yet, so I don't have any excuse to go shopping for a new player. :( Not really a con, but it's all I could think of. Oh, there seems to be a small bug with playing FLAC files. For some reason, it won't display the album art of my FLACs and the txt of the song is displayed in japanese... Not really sure what that's all about, but it plays fine.

Other Thoughts: It can be kinda techie and getting used to messing around with all the different settings and features to get the hang of everything it's capable of. There are even aftermarket operating systems and things you can upload into your player to change the way it looks and all, though I've never really messed with any of that.

When I do finally go hit the market for a new MP3 player, I will definitely be buying another Cowon product. Far superior than Apples Ipods, which sell only because of the familiarity of the name. Trust me, the Cowon devices are much better. If you want incredible sound and durability, you can't lose.efinitely be buying another Cowon product. Far superior than Apples Ipods, which sell only because of the familiarity of the name. Trust me, the Cowon devices are much better. If you want incredible sound and durability, you can't lose.

product_title: Monster Diamond Tears On-Ear Headphones, Black
review_headline: Great sound, so so comfort and polarizing design
review_body:
The sound quality of these headphones is amazing. I played music from different sources and did a side-by-side comparison of Diamond Tears, standard Apple iPod head phones, and low-end Sennheiser MX400. In the sound quality department Diamond Tears wins hands down. With Diamond Tears I could hear every detail and the bass was the best of the bunch.

Diamond Tears' ear pads are soft, comfortable and pivoting, so the fit and noise isolation are absolutely top notch. Materials used seem to be of a very high quality, and headphones have good weight to them, but are not too heavy, in my opinion. However, it seemed to me that the headband lacked sufficient cushioning and created an uncomfortable pressure point on top of my head, so I had to move the headband periodically. My wife also thought Diamond tears were a little too tight, but we attributed that to them being new.

Diamond Tears come with a storage pouch and three cables: a simple 3.5mm to 3.5mm cable, a 3.5mm to 3.5mm cable with controls for Android, and a 3.5mm to 3.5mm with controls for iPod/iPad/iPhone. Cables are interchangeable and can be plugged into either left or right earphone as both have a 3.5mm port. When headphones are folded to be placed in the storage pouch, one of the ear pads touches the \\"diamond\\" on the other, which may cause additional wear and tear on the ear pad.

Diamond Tears' design can be described as \\"love it or hate it\\". My wife uses them at work, and she says that she loves them. However, quite a few people who saw the headphones expressed more of the latter feeling. Although, everyone agrees the sound quality is great.

Overall, these are great sounding headphones if you do not mind the design and the price, and if you find them comfortable.

product_title: Mohu Leaf 30 TV Antenna, Indoor, 30 Mile Range, Original Paper-thin, Reversible, Paintable, 4K-Ready HDTV, 10 Foot Detachable Cable, Premium Materials for Performance, USA Made, MH-110583
review_body:
A buddy at work was raving about this antenna. He lives in the city, and I live in the suburbs on the other side of a large hill. I didn't expect I would get much of a signal having tried large and expensive antennas for HD before cable finally offered HD.

Today, I:

1) Opened the box,
2) Taped the leaf to the wall (white side out) behind the flat screen (about 12 inches of distance between the TV and the wall).
3) Connected the 75 ohm connector
4) Changed the tuner to 'air' and had it auto program.

It found 28 digital channels. 7 of those channels are High Def, the others are standard def digital.

No antenna I tried ever pulled in this many channels.

I supposed your location will make a difference, but it works in my situation very well.

Now I need to go find some push pins and attached it properly to the wall - it is a keeper.

product_title: Leaf Plus Amplified Indoor HDTV Antenna (Discontinued by Manufacturer)
review_body:
The Leaf Plus is very close to amazing. The antenna is the thickness of a laminated sheet of paper. Opened the package (which arrived in 5 days w/ free shipping!). Read the easy to understand instructions. Temporarily Scotch taped the antenna to the south wall. Hooked the coax and USB cables to my TV. Within 5 minutes of opening the package, I was watching as my TV searched for AND FOUND 43 digital channels and 1 analog channel. I applied the included Velcro strips on the south wall. Reception was great with the exception of one of my favorite channels. To solve this, I added a couple of additional Velcro strips that I had lying around the house on the west wall. Ta-daa! When I want to watch that particular channel, I simply move the antenna. The Leaf Plus works much better than the Terk amplified antenna that I had been using. Additionally, it's made in the United States... just like me. I'm a happy camper.

I live in the Fort Lauderdale, FL region and all the stations received are within a 29 mile radius.

UPDATE: (9/9/12) I have since purchased two more Leaf Amplified Antennas for a total of three. The first one, as stated above, was great. The second one was useless and had to be returned (no reception... zip... nada... zilch). The third one is not as good as the first but, has acceptable reception. Apparently I was lucky with the first one.

review_body:

You can set the remote so that the volume and mute keys are controlled by the mode you're in, or by another mode. For example, my cable box actually has its own volume function, but I'd rather the volume and mute keys control the TV volume and mute. Instead of having to toggle back and forth from \\"cbl\\" to \\"tv\\" to change the volume then back when you want to change channels, you can set the remote so that the volume and mute keys control the TV even if the remote is in \\"cbl\\" mode. You can set each mode independently to let volume and mute be controlled by that device or by a different device, such as the TV or a receiver. I like this versatile feature.

product_title: SkipDr DVD and CD Manual Disc Repair System
review_body:
I bought the older version of this some years ago and it still works fine. The version I have is the motorized version, but I believe the manual version works just as well. This device is designed for minor imperfections on the disk that make the disk skip or unplayable. It's not going to fix deep scratches. I remember reading about a device that would fix most scratches as well as cracks but it was expensive and I don't know how well it worked.(this expensive device heated up the plastic that covers the disk and melted it. You then added a bit of solution to it to help fill in any scratches and cracks. The device then smoothed out the plastic surface, cooled it, and the disk was supposed to be like new again....as if you had just placed a new plastic covering on the disk.)

The SkipDr. doesn't do this, it just basically polishes the disk to remove minor scratches and stains on the disk. I bought it because I get DVD movies from Netflix and I frequently find that the DVDs are dirty or scratched and they won't play properly. By using this device on those disks, I would say that I can clean the disk so that it's watchable in about 95% of the cases. The remaining 5% are disks that have deep scratches that this device will repair somewhat, but not enough to be usable.

It's a shame that DVD makers don't use the more expensive scratch resistance plastic on their DVDs instead of the cheap plastic that they now use, if they did, the DVDs and CDs would be less prone to scratching and could endure more abuse. At least with a product like SkipDr., we can save some of these scratched or dirty disks.

product_title: Audio Technica ATH-ANC23 QuietPoint Active Noise-Cancelling In-Ear Headphones
review_body:
I bought an MP3 player for the first time, and the earbuds that came with it, of course, were less than stellar. If purchased separately they probably would've
been priced at $8.99. So, I decided to upgrade the earbuds and decided that noice-cancelling ones would be ideal with a portable device. I chose the Audio-Technica ANC23 Quiet Point model. They deliver on the noise reduction ( via an in-line battery pack unit). AND they deliver on the audio as well. They sound excellent with my MP3 player....but the \\"amazing\\" part is that I used them with my home theater reciever to watch a BLU-Ray of \\"Snow White & The Hunstman\\" this weekend, and I was blown away by the depth and clarity of these little guys. Not only were the sound effects, such as exploding fireballs and the huge , menacing Troll brought on with unbelievable impact...James Newton Howard's dazzling orchestral score with blazing brass and massive strings sounded fabulous as well. I live in an apartment and can't really enjoy the full merits of my modest surround speakers...but with these earbuds in , I'm able to enjoy a pretty loud volume, without disturbing a soul! Here's the real kicker. They're only $47 ! They sound as good as my $250 pair of Sennheiser HD590 monitor phones ( no exagerration! ), and they're far lighter
and easier to move with as well. I never would've expected this kind of quality for the price point. Thank you Audio-Technica!

I was using an old pair of Sony's that had to be smacked to work any longer. When the Sennheiser headphones arrived I fully charged them and was surprised that I had a terrible hissing/static noise. I thought they were defective until I went to the Sennheiser site and downloaded the instruction sheet. I found out that there is a lever on the base that adjusts up to three different frequencies. I moved it over a notch and voila! the noise went away. I've suggested to the sellers that they include that sheet with the headphones to avoid confusion about this feature. While there is the faintest hiss in the background, it does not affect the sound. So I am very satisfied with the quality of these headphones and would definitely recommend them to others.

product_title: Hi Capacity UPS Replacement Battery for APC BX900R (2) 12V 7ah Batteries Beiter DC Power …
review_body: I have the [[ASIN:B000NDA5E0 APC BACK-UPS RS BR1500LCD 1500VA/865W UPS System]] since June 2007. When the original batteries died in 2010, I bought the APC replacements. Those only lasted 2 years, so I decided to try an aftermarket battery. So far, so good. I'll try to remember to update or add a new review when these die. Initial runtime tests show that these batteries have as much capacity as the OEM versions. But these are much cheaper. I recycled the APC batteries for free at my municipal recycling center.    UPDATE April 15, 2013: The first set of batteries I bought has died, I replaced them with another set, shipped by Battery Supersite.  The first set of aftermarket batteries lasted approximately 1 year with very few transitions to battery power (probably less than 10) and a total time on battery of less than 30 minutes. I'm disappointed with the longevity of the batteries, but again they are so cheap, I'm willing to try again, so I bought another set.    UPDATE August 20, 2014: The second set of batteries has started acting flaky, the UPS shows the batteries as disconnected and then connected and the charging seems to be not working correctly. Again, I've had very little runtime on these batteries, probably less than 30 minutes total over the last 15 months. I have replaced the UPS since it was 7 years old. I left my review at 4 stars because I was using the batteries in an old UPS and it isn't clear if the UPS is bad or if the batteries are the problem. However, I am disappointed that the replacement batteries appear to be only lasting around a year versus 2-3 years for the APC branded batteries.

product_title: RCA Bathroom Clock Radio
review_headline: Good clock radio. NOT for the shower
review_body:
Most of the poor ratings of this clock radio are from folks who were expecting a shower radio--one that can be deluged with water and survive. Not this clock radio--this works perfectly as a radio that sits on your bathroom dresser to keep you company while you are getting dressed in the morning. It will not provide accompaniment for popstar wannabes when belting out tunes while bathing.

The radio is well designed--it looks very much like an upright shampoo bottle, so it is discreet in appearance which works for a bathroom. We own the green one, and the entire radio--including the buttons--are of the one color tone. The screen light, when the backlight button is pushed, has a purplish glow. All the buttons are slightly recessed, which I assume, provides protection against moisture and small amounts of wetness. The battety compartment is screwed down, and must be removed with a screwdriver (I assume for the same reason the buttons are recessed), so make sure you use some long-lasting batteries.

The AM/FM radio uses a digital tuner, which is great--no turning dials to find stations. You can save stations as presets, so no worries as to the radio getting accidentally bumped and your station getting lost in the bathroom shuffle. There is no external antenna, but the radio picks up our local NPR station clear and strong. the speaker is more than adequate for a bathroom--it actually can get quite loud. We aren't a household of bubble-bathers, so we don't use it for an extended period of time. There is no alarm function, so it is not designed to be a bedside radio.

A great clock radio--recommended. Just don't bathe with it.

product_title: Creative ZEN X-Fi3 32GB Bluetooth MP3 Player
review_body:
I have owned two other Creative MP3 players. I loved both of them, but upgraded as I outgrew the storage space. I now need an MP3 player with at least 32GB of space, so I ordered another Creative MP3 player.

The first thing that frustrated me was the packaging. Others noted this, but let me repeat it, because it's absolutely worth understanding that you nearly need a stick of dynamite to get the player out of the packaging. Fortunately, [[ASIN:B000IHHOVI I have a tool for opening packages]], but even with that it was truly a challenge. One could not simply cut away the plastic that sealed in 3 sides. The only way to get into the package was from the bottom and one really needed a tool to cut away at it. I do not know how I would have opened if I didn't have that tool.

It came fully charged. That was nice.

The instructions are virtually non-existent. There is a tiny piece of paper with the most basic information. Perhaps that's not too unusual these days, but there isn't even a good on-line manual!

I connected it to my PC and began to copy the 2000+ songs I have to the player. I did that using Windows Media Player, as I had done with my other Creative Players. Much to my surprise, though, the play lists did not copy to the player. Of course, the \\"instructions\\" are useless.

So, I went to the Creative web site to see if there was something about this. There was. The solution involves saving your existing play lists manually in .m3u format. What a pain for most people! They do provide instructions on Creative's site (if you can find them), but they are not terribly friendly. Even so, I did what they said and it worked. However, it's not a good solution. Every time I get get new songs, I have to manually go update these special play lists before I sync.

For the tech savvy, you'll be happy to know this MP3 player does not need Media Player. You can just create your m3u files using whatever tool you like and copy music and play lists directly to the player. (So, I have this fully automated now.)

Next, it's time to give the player a try. The first time I started the player after loading it with music, it took what seemed like forever as it (I assume) indexed all of the music. I just left it alone to run for a while.

It finally finished, but each time I start the media player, it still takes 18 seconds to start. Others complained about this to Creative, I found, and Creative defended it saying the player has to go look for new music. Perhaps, but 18 seconds!?!? My other player did not take that long after I added new music.

Anyway, I plugged in earphones and ... oh, the sounds was horrible! People said the X-Fi is wonderful. I found it to be quite the opposite. It distorts the sound of the original MP3 file and not in any good way. Fortunately, I could (and did) turn that X-Fi feature off.

When you play a play list, it gives you a \\"shuffle\\" option. You can also (painfully) scroll down the list of music. There is no search feature. It's not a good user interface. For those who like to pick a specific song to play, forget it if you have very many songs at all. My old Creative Player at least had some basic features (e.g., old player would allow me to go to the letter 'P') to help me find the song or artist.

Anyway, I selected \\"shuffle\\". The first song that played, to my amazement, was the first one: it was not a random one. I did that several times. It always plays the same song at the start. Subsequent songs are randomly selected, but not the first song. It's always the same. So, you have to select shuffle and then manually skip over the first song (unless you love hearing that same first song every time). Again, a pain. This looks like a software error.

So far, some pain, some good points, but the worst was the fact that I only have access to about half my music! Recall I mentioned I have over 2000 songs. Well, I pushed the arrow to go to the next song many times, but NEVER did the X-Fi 3 select a song that was higher than 1015. It never played song #1364 or #1875 or #2001. Every time it selected one at random, it was between 1 and 1015. So, I believe that is software error #2. And this is a serious one. I bought an MP3 with with 32GB of space so I could load it with a lot of music. This is a major failure. (Smaller play lists with, say, 400 songs works just fine, though. I tested that out, too.)

The next gripe is about the \\"touch\\" interface. I really do not need a touch interface on my MP3 player, but do not care if it's there. However, this one is bad. I have to touch it several times sometimes before it recognizes a touch. I'm wondering if this is really touch or push pretending to be touch. Whatever the case, I don't like it. Really bad interface. It's absolutely not \\"touch\\" like you get on an iPod or Android phone. It's more like \\"touch\\" with... oh, heck, the buttons on my refrigerator are more responsive.

There are other gripes that are less important, but nonetheless demonstrate software quality issues. For example, sometimes the screen does not redraw correctly. Call that bug #3, though it does rarely happen.

Overall, I'm not very impressed. I've contacted Creative about the fact I cannot play songs higher than 1015 in a play list. If they have a solution to that, I'll report back. Otherwise, this player is going back. I consider this a major \\"fail\\".

UPDATE: I did hear back from Creative after a few days. The fact the player always starts playing randomly from the same song was acknowledged behavior. No hint about why the player will only play half of the 2003 songs (due to never selecting a random number above 1015). In any case, given this issue and the others noted, I decided to return it. My previously Creative player was much better than this. There's simply no comparison here. I appreciate Creative finally replying, but it was too little too late for me.

product_title: SplashBudz Water Resistant Bluetooth Headphones / Headset - Sweatproof Sport-style - Great for Running in the Rain, Hands Free Phone Calls, and More - Great Sound Quality, Black/Gray
review_headline: Mine have held up to daily use.
review_body:
I've used these for 6 months while exercising, and they're still going strong. I like them a lot.

Compared to Motorola S9-HDs: These are comparable in fit and comfort, but the splash buds are obviously more water resistant. (Important to me, as I'm a sweater, and have killed 3 S9-HDs.) Splashbudz win.

Compared to the Motorola S10-HDs: The S10's pinched both my ears and skull and were very painful. (Perhaps I have a larger than normal skull?! Thanks, Motorola, for bringing this so painfully to my attention.) Despite being labeled sweat resistant, my S10s died from sweat in the first several days and were returned. Splashbuds tolerate my sweating without issue, so far. Splashbudz win.

Compared to Jaybird JF3 Freedoms: I like the JF3s. They fit and are reasonably comfortable, although the wire draping on my sweaty neck is distracting. (I usually, however, tuck it into my hat, so it doesn't bother me.) The Splashbudz can be angled so they don't touch your neck, and hover behind your head. The JF3s don't fit securely to my ears unless I also use over-the-ear hooks and outer-ear-form-fitting-honeycomb-mesh, however, with those, they fit very securely, more so than the Splashbudz. The Splashbudz are therefore easier/quicker to put on, for me. The JF3s, because they're in-ear, sound better and block out more sound. (I'm not sure the latter is desirable when outside exercising.) But the Splashbudz reach greater volume levels, which actually gives them an edge overcoming wind-noise over the JF3s. (Wind-noise is comparable for both, but signal to noise ratio goes to Splashbudz.) Talking to iPhone 4S' Siri definitely works better with the Splashbudz compared to the JF3s. I also like the placement of the buttons on the Splashbudz better than the JF3s, even though they're at a slightly more awkward angle, but the JF3s require you to press the driver into your ear canal to depress the pause/power button, which is uncomfortable.Overall, I give the Splashbudz a slight advantage, even more if you consider their lower price.

I'm not entirely sure, but I think the Splashbudz may drain my iPhone battery faster than any of the other three headsets. This may not be true, however, as I often leave the splashbudz idling when I forget I'm wearing them.

Given the other negative reviews, it seems possible there are intermittent quality issues with the product, but my unit has been stellar, and I might buy another just to have one always charged.

\\"This item cannot be returned \\". I purchased CP1350AURLCD from Amazon and received a defective product. product_title: Amazon Kindle Replacement Power Adapter Works with 6 - Inch, 9.7 - Inch Display, 2nd and Latest Generation Kindles
review_body:
This charger works well with any e-reader Kindle and with any 'low power' gadget (not tablets) that charges through a USB port. It charges Kindle Fires too but only very, very slowly. It can be used just about anywhere in the world (100-240V) for as long as you have the proper plug adapter.

Amazon's adapter is more versatile than most because you can use it with devices that charge through either a Type B, Mini B or Micro B port for as long as you can supply the USB cable. I'm using it to charge my old Blackberry Torch, a couple of other phones and the kids charge their MP3 players. And the reverse is also true: most other USB chargers will work with your Kindle. One good example is the Blackberry's.

It's worth noting that Amazon's e-readers can be charged through most generic USB adapters. Amazon's may cost a couple of dollars more than a generic but it comes with Amazon's logo and some peace of mind. For anyone going 'generic' and looking to closely match the specs, here are the Amazon adapter's specs:

INPUT (AC): 100-240V, 50/60Hz
OUTPUT (DC): 4.9V, 0.85A

Prices fluctuate so I'm not going to discuss 'price' but it's always a good idea to search Amazon for alternatives before placing an order.

_____________________________________________

NOTE:

Kindle e-readers can be charged in several different ways:

- Off a laptop or PC through one of their 'powered' USB ports (you will need a laptop or a PC)
- With this (Amazon branded) adapter (you will need the Amazon-supplied or any generic USB cable)
- With a third-party, branded or generic USB charger (search Amazon for either 'kindle charger' or 'usb charger')

product_title: SanDisk Sansa e250 2 GB MP3 Player with microSD Expansion Slot
review_body:
After a disappointing experience with the Creative Zen Stone MP3 player, I wanted to find one that I didn't have to throw away after the rechargeable battery died, but I didn't want to spend a lot of money. After some research, I discovered the Sansa C200 and E200 series. These players are just what the doctor ordered! These players can still be found for around $25 to $50 dollars on the internet, although they are getting a little scarce and the prices are climbing. The rechargeable battery is easily accessible (with the c200 series, you don't even need a screwdriver!) and, as an added bonus, the memory is infinitely upgradable with readily available MicroSD cards (Recommended card size: 4 gig maximum). Some have criticized the sound quality, but these players sound great to my family and me as long as you invest in some decent ear-buds or earphones - the ones that are supplied with the player are not-so-good. Their capabilities and interfaces are also expandable and changeable with the addition of Rockbox software (although, as of this writing [30 Dec 2010], the c200v2 series is classified as unstable - works fine on my C240 though).
I have purchased 5 of these players for myself and my children and they have all worked great with the Rockbox software. I only have 2 problems with the player. First: the original operating system software that comes with the player is a little glitchy - the installation of Rockbox takes care of this. Second: SanDisk, in their infinite wisdom, decided to go to players without replaceable batteries - good, perhaps, for their bottom line but bad for us who have a problem with pointless waste.

The Logitech UE wireless speaker with AirPlay, made in China with a black plastic outer shell and black mesh fabric on the front, uses your Wi-Fi network to communicate to your iDevices instead of using Bluetooth like most wireless speakers. Using a Wi-Fi network allows for greater range and less interference than using a Bluetooth connection. Included in the box are the Air Speaker, AC adapter, and user documentation.

Setup is straight forward and simple to complete as long as you have a Wi-Fi network, and an iPad, iPod Touch 2nd generation or greater, an iPhone 3G, 3GS, 4, and 4S with iOS 4.3 or greater, or a computer with iTunes 10.2 and later. All connecting devices must be using the same Wi-Fi connection. Docking the iDevice to the Logitech UE wireless speaker's retractable dock shelf installs the automatically configured app. The iPhone 5 should work with the Logitech UE wireless speaker wirelessly, but will require a 30-pin/Lightning connector adapter for docking. Then playing audio on the Logitech UE wireless speaker is just a matter of connecting to and selecting it.

The simplistic UE Air app includes treble and bass slider settings, a signal strength indicator, plus help and setting information. There are no preset audio settings or a way to create your own. Fortunately, the Logitech UE wireless speaker produces pleasing audio with the powerful front speakers and rear bass pipes.

The visually obscured top includes power and mute buttons plus a volume dial for manual control. Other audio devices can be used as well by connecting a 3.5 mm audio cable (not included) to the auxiliary port on the back. Additionally, the Logitech UE wireless speaker can be connected to your network using the port on the back.

Every now and then, I can connect to the speaker without any issue. Most of the time, I have to either redock my iDevice or reboot the speaker to reestablish a wireless connection. Additionally, audio can skip on the Logitech UE wireless speaker when connected wirelessly and traffic volume is high.

Connecting by Wi-Fi is the Logitech UE wireless speaker's strongest feature. I also have a [[ASIN:B005KSZ430 Philips DS8530]] which has an app with more functionality and great sound, but doesn't get used as much due to Bluetooth connectivity and proximity during use.

Overall, I enjoy using the Logitech UE wireless speaker which I have set in a central location where I can listen from several rooms. This has proved beneficial during small gatherings and for indoor guests at pool parties when used for background music. For these situations, I typically dock my iDevice, but it's nice to know I can carry my iDevice with me and not worry about losing the connection as long as I'm in the proper Wi-Fi zone. If you're looking for a wireless speaker with mobile freedom, the Logitech UE wireless speaker with Airplay is worthy of consideration.

review_body:

You can control the mic/guitar volume separately from the main volume, so it's easy to control how much of your voice is mixed in with the music. The shoulder strap makes it easy to carry. Overall it's just a really well engineered piece of equipment. JVC left no stone unturned. It does pretty much everything I could ever want it to do and more. It's just so versatile it makes it perfect for parties, flash mobs, chilling out, whatever. It makes me wish boom boxes never went out of style because it's just so awesome. One tiny little problem I should note. It is not hot-swappable between AC power and battery power. It turns itself of when you switch from one to the other. Other than that, no complaints here.

product_title: Philips ShoqBox SB72 Bluetooth Wireless Speaker
review_headline: Military Chic with Great Sound, but...
review_body:
I read the description and product inserts thoroughly, and Phillips was very careful to never use the word \\"stereo\\" anywhere in their description or literature, except to say, that a second Shoqbox could be added for stereo sound. Instead, they describe the 2 speakers in this military style case as \\"Two neodymium speaker drivers...\\" which just means this Shoqbox contains 2 speakers that have neodymium magnets inside them. All speakers use magnets to help drive the speaker cone and push out sound waves. Neodymium magnets are amongst the strongest magnets around, which undoubtedly goes a long way in making this tiny speaker sound so good. But that in and of itself, does not make this a set of stereo speakers. It's just a really good mono speaker, and if you want true stereo sound, you'll need to buy a second pricey Shoqbox; which also adds up to double the bulk and weight to carry around too. And using 2 of these at home wouldn't necessarily be convenient either, since the speakers shut off after 15 minutes of non use; which means you'll constantly be turning them back on when you want to use them. It's not exactly a heavy chore, but it isn't convenient either; particularly if you listen to music throughout the day.

Easy Pairing & Setup

I like to try and operate my tech toys without reading any of the instructions first. My theory is, that a well designed piece of tech should be self-explanatory; be it a tablet, cell phone, bluetooth speakers, or whatever. If you can't make it go right out of the box, then the design engineers didn't do their job. This Shoqbox was very easy to setup and pair with my Thrive tablet right out of the box. No hiccups and nothing complicated, just as it should be. Though after a couple days, I did have to re-pair them all over again. Not sure why, but worth mentioning; somehow they disconnected themselves entirely from my tablet all on their own.

Nice Volume Dial

There's a large silver colored volume dial on one end of the speaker casing and it takes up almost the entire surface area. This is nice, because it makes the volume dial easy to find and use; though personally, I'll probably leave it maxed out and use the volume on my tablet.

Great Sound

This Shoqbox sounds pretty good considering the size; nice, rich fidelity without any distortion. Undoubtedly, that's the benefit of neodymium magnets. Don't expect to rattle any walls with deep bass or anything; nothing this small can compete with a full-sized sub-woofer. But compared to other speakers in this class, this Shoqbox sounds great and is better than most. The 2 speakers are quite close together, so even if they were independent left and right channels, you wouldn't get much stereo separation given their proximity to each other. Having said that, the design of this Shoqbox actually helps create a full, dynamic effect. So the sound really has some breadth and depth, and sounds much fuller and richer than any other compact speakers I've tried.

Volume Boost

As good as these sound, I still wasn't impressed with the overall volume. So I tried these out with a volume boosting Android app called [[ASIN:B004YLWL0I Volume+]]. The app boosts audio up to 20 decibels. Just be careful if you use this app, because you CAN damage your audio components if you over boost the volume to levels the device's speakers can't handle. I boosted my Shoqbox a full 20db. and it definitely started to come apart at the seams, so to speak, as far as fidelity and clarity. A 10db boost was about all the boost this Shoqbox could handle, which brought the overall volume to a more acceptable level.

Gimmicky Motion Sensor

The Shoqbox has a motion activated sensor for track forward, reverse, play and pause; just swipe your hand over the sensor to activate the controls. Sounds cool, but I kept accidentally changing tracks which got annoying really fast. I'd much rather use the controls on my tablet, so I just put a sticker over the motion sensor to eliminate the problem entirely. For me, it's just a gimmick that doesn't work well and adds more aggravation than functionality to this speaker.

Industrial Strength Build Quality

This is the type of speaker Tom Cruise would have clipped to his belt loop while scaling a steep vertical rock-face with his bare hands; funky soundtrack blaring while he looks ultra cool behind his chic shades. And Phillips definitely intended the association; so much so, that even the included carabiner clip had a tiny warning sticker on it that said \\"not for climbing.\\" The Shoqbox is sturdy, compact with a thick rubberized casing that assures this speaker would survive any drops, bumps, or intentional hurling across the room.

Bottom Line -- this Phillips Shoqbox sounds really good considering the size. The design is cool, but beyond that, it helps throw the audio to create the illusion of much fuller and dynamic sound. And the neodymium magnets are a great touch. But personally, I have a little problem with the hefty price point for a set of mono speakers, no matter how decent they sound. Linking 2 of these together would undoubtedly sound fantastic, but still nowhere near as good as my home stereo system. So at roughly $350 for a pair, this Shoqbox is unquestionably overpriced. Overall, it's a great little speaker, but you might be better off looking elsewhere or waiting for the price to drop.. product_title: Merax 510 Disc Capacity Black Aluminum-Like Hard Plastic CD DVD Storage Case
review_headline: Solid, safe, compact, long-term CD/DVD disc storage solution
review_body:
First, I only store discs in mine, no disc art work, so I cannot comment on how well or poorly this design may or may not accommodate both CD/DVD disks AND artwork.

Although largely plastic, this CD/DVD disc storage case has metal to stiffen the box and lid, along hinges and locks, all where most needed. Metal edging line the opening to both box and lid and its use provide a solid feel when opening, closing and locking the lid. Each of the three storage channels supports are also made of painted metal, both in the box and lid. Closing the lid gently \\"locks\\" the hanging sleeves into each of their respective channel supports, thereby reducing (or, hopefully, eliminating) shifting when moving or storing the closed, locked box. Keys are even included should you wish to lock the box.

Although I was concerned that the manufacturer did not use metal hanging supports for the double-sided disc hanging sleeves before purchase, I now realize that given the negligible weight of two discs that this would have been design overkill. Also, metal-on-metal would have likely damaged the black finish of the channel supports. The choice of plastic supports for hanging the disc sleeves appears sufficient. Still, they are fragile and demand some caution when in use so as not to break off the support hooks ends.

This box can comfortably accommodate more than 510 discs, perhaps 560. It is possible to purchase extra sleeves. I do wish that alphabetized tab cards had been included as my storage is alphabetical and not numeric as they provide.

The hanging discs are lined with a non-scuffing dividers so as to eliminate scratching from wear and tear while stored. If you are sensitive to fresh-from-the-factory plastic odors the plastic sleeves require some off-gassing, easily accomplished by them exposed to open air, or preferably exposed to a bit of sun for a day or two.

I would recommend this for those who need a solid, safe, compact, long-term CD/DVD disc storage solution.

product_title: Philips Bluetooth Soundbar Speaker with Subwoofer Black
review_body:
I just bought this soundbar from a competitor and wanted to give people a heads-up that it will NOT work with a Philips 40PFL4706/F7 TV! It makes no business sense whatsoever, unless Philips' goal is to encourage people to buy TVs made by other manufacturers!

I bought the TV a couple of weeks ago. The picture is pretty good but the audio is TERRIBLE. The speakers are on the back so unless you're standing to the back of the TV or to the sides, you get a tiny, almost mono-like sound quality and you have to turn up the volume WAY up to hear anything. Yes, I did try various settings on the TV, to no avail.

In desperation, I decided to buy the Philips CSS2123 Soundbar to try and improve the sound. I figured that by buying the same brand, I would avoid any connection problems. What a mistake!

1) This TV does NOT have digital optical audio output (the soundbar does have that).
2) This TV does NOT have analog audio outputs connection either (confirmed by a Philips Audio technician).
3) The only audio output this TV has is for Coaxial Digital Audio.
4) This TV does NOT have the option to change the audio to \\"PCM\\" or \\"Standard\\" as it required for the Philips sound bar to work. It only has its default Dolby Digital setting.

5) Connecting the soundbar to the TV with a coaxial digital cable may or may not work. I didn't even bother trying because:
a) the Dolby Digital might cause the soundbar to hum loudly while playing the audio (according to various Philips sources, including the Philips Audio technician)
b) I watch over the air TV (I don't have cable so I don't have the option to connect the soundbar to a cable box or anything) and was told by Philips Audio technician that some over the air stations only broadcast in Dolby Digital so I would NOT getting audio on those channels at all (though the soundbar which only plays \\"PCM\\" or \\"standard\\" audio).

So in the end, this 2011 Philips TV willnot work with a 2012 Philips soundbar. How does this even make any business sense?

I am returning the soundbar and will probably return the TV too. I didn't buy them through Amazon but since most people come here to check the reviews, I figured I'd put in my 2 cents and try to spare the same experience to someone else.

It's really too bad because the low profile of the soundbar is awesome. I sat right under my TV, on the same surface, and didn't block anything.

Information I gathered while looking for solutions online:

* You do have to use the soundbar remote to control the soundbar. It's a very tiny remote (think very small pocket calculator), which would be very easy to \\"lose\\". Some people reported online being able to get a universal remote that controls both the soundbar and the TV.

* There is no volume bar that will appear on the TV when you use the soundbar remote. You really \\"play it by ear\\".

* The lights telling you which mode you're in (coaxial, digital, analog, Surround) are on the top and back. I'm not sure why because unless the bar is placed on the floor, then you can't see them. What's the point of even having them then?

* You need to remember to turn OFF the soundbar independently from the TV if you want to save electricity :)

product_title: Winegard HDTV Antenna
review_headline: Worked well for me, after a LOT of re-positioning...
review_body:
Apparently I live in an area where it's difficult to pick up VHF stations -- even though I'm only 15 miles away from the broadcast antennas. The hills around here apparently create a great deal of interference...

I bought this antenna, and it got excellent reception of all the local UHF channels, but very poor reception of the VHF channels -- signal strength around 25% or less, no picture on those channels. I then bought a Winegard GS-2200, because it was supposedly better at receiving VHF signals -- still no luck.

It took multiple attempts over several days, but I finally got this FV-30BB positioned just right, and am now picking up the VHF stations that I was trying to get. (There is one VHF station that's 21 miles away that I'm still not picking up, but I'm not concerned about that one -- it's not a channel that I watch regularly.)

So, overall, I'd have to say that this antenna is probably excellent in an area with few or no hills. If I were closer than 10 to 15 miles away from most of my stations, it would probably have been easier to get it positioned correctly to get all the channels. But due to the hills around here, the listed 25-mile range on this antenna is completely wrong -- it's more like 10 miles when you take into account the terrain.

But, if you live in a flat area, or closer than 10 miles to your broadcast towers, I highly recommend this antenna. If you don't, get a good Yagi-style antenna and save yourself some trouble. I did finally get this antenna to work for me in my particular location, but it was an awful lot of trouble.

product_title: Sanyo R227 WiFi Internet Radio (Black) (Discontinued by Manufacturer)
review_headline: Good idea, spotty execution, unintuitive controls
review_body:
UPDATED AUG. 5, 2012:

To my surprise I got the radio to come back to life by plugging it in while holding the Standby (On/Off) button down for several seconds. It came back up, connected to my new higher speed network, and downloaded the new Reciva station list. After I registered it on the Reciva web site through my account there, it also downloaded the personal preference stations I had set up. So it is now a functional radio again... but it still has the unsatisfactory volume problem that it had from day one. There is no way to turn the volume up high enough to hear from more than a few feet away. The volume indicator bar needs to be at 60% length before whispers can be heard from the speakers, and at 90% before it is at a good level for same room listening. The solution to this is to use powered plug-in stereo speakers, of which most people will have a spare set around. But why wouldn't the company produce a device that could hit satisfactory volume levels on its own?

I upgraded this evaluation from one star to two. The Grace radio that was this radio's replacement is still a far better unit.

EARLIER REVIEW BELOW THIS LINE

This is an obituary rather than a review, because this model is now out of production and can no longer be purchased except perhaps in remaindered lots at close-out operations. I would be sorry if any are still out there to tempt buyers, because I have to give it a pretty low evaluation. Remainder buyers beware.

I bought this in 2009 when it first came out and was fairly happy for a few months. But the volume control was never reliable and I eventually just started listening to internet radio on a laptop rather than a dedicated unit. Every so often I would retry the Sanyo and eventually began getting connection problems. Recently I turned it on and got the fast-flashing blue screen indicating a fried circuit. So much for that. Still thinking that a separate internet radio was a good idea and ever optimistic, I bought a Grace unit. I hooked it up the other night, and except for some buffering problems because my ISP couldn't deliver the up and down speeds my contract calls for (Verizon, if anyone is interested), the new unit works fine.

In retrospect, I think the Sanyo R227 was simply not ready for prime time. The Grace radio has better input/output options, better speakers and equalization capacity, and more intuitive controls. So far so good on that one. I'll review it on its own page when I think I have used it long enough to form a careful opinion.

Order of shows is basically the order in which they were copied into the directory. You might want to find a \\"Folder Sort\\" utility if you want it to look more like you'd see it on a PC. Having an expansion card is a nice feature compared to the sealed products from Apple.

I cracked the screen by putting the device in my pants pocket and went climbing and sliding with the toddler in the playground. So after surviving several drops, and impressing passers-by with my trust of my toddler with my \\"phone\\", it's off to e-cycling.

I ordered the Onda VX570 to replace it, and I have to say that the Onda is a more polished device and I enjoy using it more. Main downside is that it's only 4GB. But 16GB Micro SD cards are now under $10, so not as big a deal as it used to be.

review_body:
I recently had an opportunity to try out these RHA MA-350 earbuds and received them just as I was leaving for a weekend trip out of town. I was the passenger on a 4 hour car ride with someone who's music tastes differ from mine. I brought along my Kindle Fire loaded with MP3's and about an hour or so into the trip, I plugged in the earbuds and started listening to music while I read. Right away I noticed the sound isolating features. The country music that was playing on the car's stereo was blocked out and I was able to hear my music clearly.

The next day while waiting in the hotel for a few hours for someone, I again pulled out my Kindle and started reading. It was mid-morning and all around me were the sounds of housekeepers vacuuming and cleaning. I turned on the TV try and drowned it out, but found it difficult to concentrate on reading with the TV up so loud. Then I remembered I still had the earbuds in my travel bag. Putting them on and turning on my music completely blocked out the surrounding sounds and I was right back to my reading.

The cable/cord has a fabric braid over them, which I find adds quality and durability to electronics. The cords tend not to get pinched or cut as easily with this braided fabric. Also it slides smoother over clothing. So when you are wearing the earbuds, the cord lays flat against anything you're wearing instead of getting bunched up when you move around, like what happens with earbuds that have the rubber outer coating.

These earbuds come with 3 sizes of silicone tips, which I always appreciate, as I wear the smallest size. My ears get sore/tender when I wear earbuds with too large of tips. Happily these come with interchangeable different size tips, so I get no ear discomfort at all when wearing them with my correct size.

Because of their sound isolating features and the way they play music, I think these would also be great for audio books. The words are clear and with background sounds blocked, concentrating on the story would be quite easy.

Great quality earbuds with attention paid to even the smallest details. review_headline: WORKED GREAT AT FIRST BUT THEN BROKE :(
review_body:
I purchased this remote and used it to connect my entire media center together. So no longer did I need the four remotes that I would constantly have in front of me.

I have been trying for a very longtime now to find the perfect universal remote and have went through about five different ones so far including this one. This one being the most expensive one that I bought for myself. You can say that I am a little OCD about this. I need things to be just absolutely perfect.

So first of all the most interesting thing about this remote is that it makes your life so much easier. For example you can choose on the remote itself using its color touchscreen that you want to watch TV. The remote will then automatically turn on your TV, your cable box, and your audio system. No longer do you have turn on all three things on their own. You can group certain activities with certain devices and the remote will do the rest.

The remote activates from the moment you pick it up, it is motion sensitive. Also if you hate using touchscreens the remote has many regular buttons that you can use instead. I happen to like the touchscreen but my boyfriend can't seem to figure out how to use it exactly.

I was very happy with this remote for about 5 months and then the touchscreen just broke. I really don't know what I did wrong exactly but it just would no longer turn on. This takes away a lot of the functionality of this remote control. After the amount of cash I spent on this device you would think that it could last me for a few years at least. I am going to look into getting it replaced I am sure there has to be some kind of warranty but it truly is a hassle because I have everything already set up how I like it.

The remote itself is great but mine broke :(

Perhaps I just got unlucky?
