I received this unit as part of the Vines program, so it was free and I don't have a bone to pick with Logitech. I was unsure that this was a product I would find useful, especially with my spouse bemoaning the fact that we have 'another' remote to contend with. I sort of wanted to prove her wrong. As you'll see I wasn't entirely successful.

The pros:
Packaging was excellent...this could have been an Apple-branded product from the way it was packaged. Even the inside of the box had some foam padding glued to the top (for some reason), but I was impressed. The unit can be seen in the photos...very streamlined and unobtrusive.
Setup can be easy, if you have an existing Harmony remote for your system. I just opened the software on my computer and copied the device information into myHarmony.com online setup. The only problem I had was finding the setup site, since you first have to hook up the unit, via USB to your computer, then create a new account. Once you do this, the site recognizes the device, and leads you through the setup. Very easy.

Downloading the app to the iPad and iPod Touch was also very easy. When you synch the app to the device, after it is placed in your viewing room, it asks for your password, and the synch proceeds with no problems here. The iPad app is different than the iPod app. I would only use the iPod app in an emergency and find very little benefit from using it.

The IR blaster works!! We positioned the small receiver under the stand of our TV, then put the pod unit in the cabinet and closed the doors. The blaster transmitted the signal (via a thin wire) to the pod unit and controlled the TV with no problems. I wish our Harmony One could do that!

Actual use observations:
First off, this is not a replacement for your universal remote. It can duplicate the functionality for simple things, like watching TV, watching a DVD, listening to the radio, listening to CDs. But if you have special functions on your TV, you will run into trouble. The problem arises in this type of case: You need to use the TV remote buttons for special functionality, but want to control the volume of your system with your receiver. Harmony remotes let you program for this type of instance, but Harmony Link does not. You can use the iPad app to view the buttons on your different device remotes, but you need to slide the panel on the app to the far right to view them. Then you need to scroll thru all the choices and pick the button you want. My TV (Samsung) has a special function called Smarthub that provides an internet portal to Netflix, Vimeo, game, web, etc. To use it, I need to use the functions on my Samsung TV remote, yet control the volume with my receiver. This is very difficult to do with the Harmony Link.
I also found a bug in the remote that turns off my AppleTV when I hit the Select/OK button on the iPad remote app. This is not good and should be fixed.

Now the interesting part of the app, and probably the only reason we would use Harmony Link. When you set up the app with your cable provider (which worked well for us....we use Uverse), it streams all the programming available at the current time and 24 hours in advance. You can quickly scroll through the program icons (many of which have descriptive logos/designs on them), and find which program or movie you want to see. Touching the icon gives an info screen about the program, how much time is left, etc. You can hit the Watch Now button, and it will select that channel. Many times we want to find where the US Open is being broadcast, and by scrolling through the icons you can find it without channel surfing. Also, you can select pre-defined filters to find News, Sports, Movies, Kids, etc. The downside, is that all the channels for your package are shown, even the ones you don't subscribe to. You can also select a program and add it to 'Favorites', sort of a personalized filter.

Another downside is that scrolling is limited by a buffer and stops while it is being filled, so it is not as smooth as I'd like. It is not fun scrolling through 575 channels and having to wait as the buffer fills up.

What would improve Harmony Link:
1) More flexibility with Activity setup; giving the user functionality comparable to Logitech Harmony remotes.
2) Allow the user to drag remote buttons onto a template to create a customized remote with needed actions and user-designed placement. This would be really awesome.
3) Allow users to create filters on the app, so that programs are defined according to a user's tastes rather than pre-sets from Logitech, e.g. CNBC doesn't appear in the News filter preset, and I would want it there.

The nice thing about this product, is that it depends on the software for most of the functionality. product_title: Sony Stereo Bluetooth Headset
review_body: If you answered \\"hell yeah\\" to that question, but you live with your parents and rockin' out loud at maximum decibels isn't permitted, or maybe you just happen to be a librarian that wants to get yer groove on at work?, or maybe you run a noisy ass jackhammer all day long?, maybe your college roommate is a sex machine and you've had enough of listening to his / her freaky escapades night after night, and you have no where else to go?, maybe you just want to listen to music you like while sitting in you office or cubicle and your boss is a \\"noise nazi\\", or you just want to tune the boss out entirely, and all your annoying co-workers too? or maybe you are in the frequent flier clique and you most definitely don't want to hear anything but your zen meditation \\"muzak\\".  IF YOU ANSWERED \\"YES\\" TO ANY OF THESE QUESTIONS THEN YOU SHOULD GET THIS Sony DRBT50 Stereo Bluetooth Headst!!!!!!    I bought this headset used at about half retail price, it came without any instructions of any kind, (but in a nice leather carry pouch!)  In the month since I bought this headset, I have used it every day, for anywhere from 90 minutes to 10 straight hours. They charge quickly and I've yet to have the battery run out on me. (My IPhone might need 2 or 3 charges just to \\"keep on rockin'!\\") I regularly listen to them while walking my dogs on sidewalks along busy streets congested with traffic and noise. I recently put the \\"phones\\" to a particularly grueling  test: wore them for about 10 hours straight, liostening to my ipod while running a floor sander all day long.  Dust, noise, being dropped on the floor repeatedly... this headset made a believer out of me, never stopped the music, no bluetooth signal loss even among swirling sawdust, plenty of volume to easily be heard over the noise of the big sander, no pinched, uncomfortable ears even after 10 straight hours! These phones did waaaay more than just survive all the punishment I could dish out that day, they passed with grade A playback quality.    In fact the only problems I've had are not the fault of the phones, but issues with my IPhone:    1. If this is not your first bluetooth headset (as was the case for me) the wireless bluetooh signal may be VERY weak with extremely limited range from the iphone.  If this is the case for you, try \\"resetting\\" (restarting) your I-device, then re-establish the connection with the headset. Once I reset my iphone and cleared its' memory of my previous headset, the signal strength was was enormously improved.   2. If my IPhone battery drops below 20%, the bluetooth signal from the phone gets much weaker, resulting in more signal \\"dropouts\\" (gliches in music playback), but again the fault lies with the IPhone - not the headphones.                   Those are the biggest negative issues I've experienced as of yet.  Pairing with my Iphone is fairly easy, the controls on the headset are easy to use, although, I still have yet to figure out how to use the headset during phone calls - I have no instructions on that and I don't talk on my phone all that much.  While the phones are slightly bulky, and heavier than most headsets, they are are still comfortable to wear for long periods of time, and the volume and sound quality just blows away that of my first bluetooth set. I have not worn my headphones while walking through a rainstorm yet, nor am I willing to ruin a good thing by putting them through that test. I do know that they have more than enough volume that I've adjusted the EQ setting on my phone from \\"Flat\\" to \\"X-tra Bass\\", and the bass heavy setting still sounds great through the headset.     Overall I'd give these phones an \\"A\\" grade approval, and yes, I would not hesitate to buy another pair (if needed), although I still don't think that I would pay full price for them... Mostly because I couldn't afford it right now.    IF YOU'RE LOOKING FOR GOOD BLUETOOTH HEADPHONES, STOP LOOKING, AND CLICK \\"BUY NOW!!!\\"

review_headline: card might be ok, but software that comes with it is bootlegged
review_body:
First, the software that comes with this card, \\"Pico2000\\" is bootlegged from China. First hint is the lack of decent instructions on how to install it, and the document that comes with it is in such terrible English, it's hard to tell. Third, it that unless you run this \\"English Pack\\" file it comes with, it's all in Chinese. product_title: Comply Foam Premium Earphone Tips - Isolation T-100 (Black, 3 Pairs, Large)
review_body: Comply claims that these foam tips are thirty times softer than your standard silicone tip, and at first, thirty times sounds a wee bit ridiculous as most of us have experienced memory foam in some form such as headband rests, ear pads or wrist rests, which are pretty soft, but the Comply foam is softer than Sean Penn's heart. Imagine a gooey chocolate chip cookie for your ears... Just not as messy.    I didn't find the outside noise isolation to be notably better than the included smaller Monster triple-flange, which I received a good fit from, but comfort increased and so did the actual fit. I found with the Monster triple-flange that if I smiled or started laughing, the tip would loosen its hold, but with the Comply T-400, I was free to any facial expression I could ever want! Another bonus I found was the actual removal of the tip from my ear canal, where with other tips I would experience some discomfort or even find in a few cases that the tip was removed from the IEM and left in my ear, the Comply tips could be removed even more easily than when they're inserted. While walking or riding my stationary bike, I found the fit to hold up just fine and I'm confident that these would remain comfortable and in place through intensive exercise. Comply also gives you an option to customize your order with different colours and your choice of sizing or, what I'd recommend, the mix of the three different sizes.    In regards to sound quality, I found the bass to be more prominent than with the Monster triple-flange, indicating that the seal was definitely better than what I was previously experiencing; nothing really noticeable on the mids or highs.    If you're buying a pair of even basic hi-fi IEMs that you'll be using on the plane, bus, walking, at the gym, office or even at home, I can't see why you wouldn't spend that extra $15 for the added comfort and the perfect fit-- absolutely recommended to those who hate IEM tips and fit. Dang it, Comply, you've made a returncustomer out of me!    Super-conclusion: 8.5/10, they're like pillows for your ear canal!

product_title: Sennheiser Headphones
review_headline: These headphones will give you multiple EAR-gasms.
review_body:
PROS:

+ Provides clarity and increased bass.
+ Gives an immersive music and movie experience.
+ Very comfortable earpiece and headband coverings.
+ Comes with 10 feet of cord, and an adapter for standard 1/8 headphone jacks.

CONS:

- Other people can hear if you crank up the volume.
- Pricey, but they're worth the price.

OVERVIEW:

I won't pretend to know what Eargonomic Acoustic Refinement (E.A.R.) technology or an internal surround reflector is: I'm just an average guy who likes his music and movies, and doesn't enjoy feeling like his ears are drowning in sweat after taking the headphones off.
After using these, I can say that they not only gave me superior sounding bass, but they allowed me to hear sounds in music and movies that I've never picked up before. Plus, the coverings kept my ears free and clear from sweat.

Here's a few of the quality tests I performed:

MUSIC TESTS:

The Prodigy - Firestarter: This was the first song that jumped to mind when I heard these headphones give great bass, and the bass line was positively delicious. Anyone who's heard this song knows how powerful the bass line is...it thrummed through these headphones loud and clear without any feedback.

Soundgarden - Spoon Man: Another song that came through clear as crystal - the bass was a perfect balance with the lyrics - One didn't overpower the other.

Reek Da Villain Feat. Busta Rhymes & Swizz Beatz - Mechanics: This was a suggestion from a fellow coworker when I asked \\"What's the best song for a bass test as well as musical clarity?\\" Oh, how right he was. Each lyric sounded as crisp as a celery stick being snapped, and the pronounced bass only made the song sound better.

MOVIE TESTS:

I had to see how these headphones could handle some of my favorite action sequences!

Déjà Vu (listening through my PC) - I had to pick one of my favorite Tony Scott films. The chase scene with the \\"goggle rig\\" took on new layers of enjoyment with these headphones. I could head the crescendo and decrescendo of the music much clearer than I ever have before; it was as if I could hear individual pieces of debris flying off cars during impact.

The Replacement Killers (listening through my PSP) - This was an unexpected bonus. I rarely watch any movies on my PSP because the sound is very tinny. With these headphones, the dance club music was louder, the gunshot audio was more pronounced, and the bass was (for lack of a better word)...thicker.

The Matrix Reloaded (listening through my PSP) - Having seen this movie more times than I can count, I was amazed to hear the first segment of \\"Matrix code\\" during the credits channeling from my left ear to the right. I never noticed that before, but these headphones made it crystal clear. I could also hear the sound of individual cups and utensils hitting the floor during the fight scene with Seraph, and I've never heard that before either.

CONS:

When I turned up the volume on these, my spouse asked if I was actively TRYING to blast my eardrums apart. They're good for private listening but if you turn up the volume, other folks might hear. They're also a little big for portable use, so you won't find me plugging these into an iPod for my afternoon jog.

The only other con I found to these headphones was the price - but if you want to enjoy levels of sound this crisp and clear, it won't come cheap.

FINAL THOUGHTS:

I enjoyed these headphones very much. They enriched the entire audio spectrum (especially the bass), and also brought some lesser-heard tones to the surface. They made movies sharper and music clearer. review_headline: RSW15 is a bargain for such great performance
review_body: Sound and Vision rated the Klipsch the best subwoofer they ever tested that was under 10,000 dollars!! (The Epic and the Genelec come to mind)  It will hit 97dB at 20Hz and will play at 113dB from 25 to 63Hz with ONLY +/-3dB of varitation (with less than 10% distortion). Yeah, there are subs that will play louder at 20Hz but none of them can equal the flat frequency response of the RSW15. I have owned this subwoofer for 4 years now and it has amazed everyone that has ever had the pleasure of hearing it. Besides, it is beautiful, relatively small compared to an ***, and is built like a tank. It will play louder than anyone I have had in the room can stand. It is not all about peak dB but how flat it can play. It does not get much magazine page space and that is fine with me. I would not trade it for anything.

This is simply not true as the scrim cloth is so thin it cannot be removed in one piece and the adhesive is still left behind and must be removed.  I contacted Yamaha to see if they could send me new scrim cloths for the speakers after I painted the grills and explained the instructions are completely wrong when it comes to how to paint the grills.  After about a week of calls and emails someone from Yamaha eventually did contact me only to say that they didn't have just the scrim cloth.  They also agreed that this part of the instructions needs to be revised as it was almost impossilbe to remove and reuse any part of the scrim cloth.  They ended up sending me another set of grills which I'll keep in a safe place should I need to replace in the future.  I ended up painting the grills and made my own scrim cloths out of material I picked up at a fabric store.

product_title: Sony SSF-7000 Floorstanding 4-way Speaker (Pair)
review_headline: Audiophile quality at a very affordable price
review_body: I have owned speaker brands such as Celestion, DBX, Magnepan, Definitive Technology, JBL, NHT, Acoustic Research and others over the last 20 years. This speaker is exactly what others say here, a true bargain.  This is part of Sony's project to improve their image and in fact, some of the technology incorporated in this product has been developed for the new line of high-end speakers.    My musical preferences go from Contemporary Classical to Fusion Jazz, Brazilian and Pop. In all these genre this speaker performs with excellence. The bass is solid and clear and for music aficionados no subwoofer is required. Maybe the A/V folks will decide to add a subwoofer, but unles it is a 12\\" plus subwoofer the gains are not going to be significant. This speaker excells in its transparency, attribute that I have usually enjoyed after paying three  times as much. You can easily follow the individual instrument lines and the transients are fast and clean.    No system is perfect and what I have found is that for critical musical listening placement is very important. Leave at least one foot on the back and do not exceed about 8 -9 ' of separation between speakers.  The soundstage is B+ in definition and depth. The drivers tend to be get slightly congested in the upper-mids but nothing distracting.  Bass never boomy.  The tone can be dramatically impacted with knobs. A [2] change in any direction WILL have a major impact in the speaker response. So, play with frequency response. product_title: 5.8 GHz Wireless Speaker Kit, Model 1600
review_headline: Don't see the point of this in a true HD system
review_body: Bought this. Good price and whatnot, but I'm running HD programming via HDMI from satellite to the TV, which only has one audio output, and that's optical. Running that to my receiver.    This Amphony unit is hooked up with the surround left and right outputs going via 16g speaker wire to the Amphony inputs. The thing doesn't pick up a signal. No indicator light saying that a signal is being detected at all, and the indicator and power are working because it does it's self test at initial plug in without problems. My receiver doesn't have RCA line out plugs that will output signal regardless of source. Each channel has its own outputs, so I can't simply connect the optical cable to the receiver and then send the output out via RCA.    When I pulled the Amphony out of the system and hard wired the surround speakers directly to the outputs, they work perfectly as usual. I went online and had to hunt all over before I found a review that casually mentions the fact that this Amphony unit cannot send digital audio to rear speakers, so if you are running HDMI or HDMI to optical this will not work.    Nowhere in their entire website product description, nor in the user's manual, does it make any mention of this limitation. Instead, the website claims the Amphony can accept \\"almost any input\\". Multiple e-mails with their support personnel went nowhere, as they were hellbent on figuring out which unit was \\"faulting\\" between the receiver and Amphony and ducked no less than five direct attempts to verify that the Amphony cannot detect and use a digital signal coming from a receiver.    It appears that to use this product under these circumstances, I will have to purchase an additional $100+ digital to analog decoder, which would allow me to plug the optical cable from the TV into it and then take two analog cables to the receiver's TV channel IN. But I can't verify that this will work, because Amphony will not confirm that the signal type is incompatible, and so I could end upbuying the converter and it still doesn't work.    This is deceptive advertising to me. If it doesn't work with digital audio then wouldn't people really want to know that up front, considering most people trying to set up home theater are doing so with high end TVs and intentions of using Dolby Surround sound with as high a quality (digital) as possible? What exactly is the point of a wireless surround kit that cannot detect signals from the high end devices it is likely to be paired with?    Unless you have a receiver with every connection type known to mankind, or are using it with a non-HD television or without digital cable/satellite, this is a useless product. I'd love to be wrong about this but unless someone comes back with verification that this is untrue in a comment, I'll never know where I'm wrong, because the manufacturer will not answer the question frankly.

product_title: Zeo Personal Sleep Manager
review_body: I've done no \\"testing\\" to determine how accurate the device is.  So, I can't rate the device based on accuracy, only on how well it seems to work and how easy it is to use.    =====  Overall Rating =====  4 out of 5 stars  There are 2 main items that keep it from being 5 starts.  1 - I have no way to tell if the data is accurate or not.  Not sure there is any \\"fix\\" for this.  2 - There are waaayyy to many buttons on the device and the on device menus/user interface are not well designed.    I've only used it for 4 nights so far.  So, I'll try to update this review after longer use.    Knowledge is power.  Understanding what your body does while you sleep is critical to helping you improve your sleep. I've been looking for a device like this for years.   I've never found any other device that does close to what this device does for sleep analysis at home.  Especially at this relatively low price.  From that point alone I'd recommend the device.    =====  Me  =====  Techie in early 40s with history of sleep issues.  I've read up on sleep in general most of my life and have tried many things to improve my sleep.  I think I know a lot about sleep and sleep issues.  And I know a fair amount about hardware & software design.      === Hardware Design ===  Overall - 3 out of 5, buttons 2 out of 5  The device itself seems well made and in general well designed.  The headband mount is magnetic, keeping the hadband in place while it charges (very nice).  The unit size is good, not too big, not too small.  The brightness of the display is easily adjustable.  Which is important to me since I like a dark room at night.    The buttons and user interface I'd rate a 2 out of 5.  I realize there is a lot this thing does.  But there are 6 buttons on the top, not including the 4 directional buttons to step through menu (total 10).  2 of the buttons are double wide with 2 icons but don't seem to be rocker buttons.  Having the double label just confuses things. All buttons are the similar in size and all small (even the double wide buttons are small).  They are evenly distributed across the top and are very close together.      The snooze button is a double wide button on the far right and is the only one with raised bumps.  So, they attempted to make the snooze button easy to find.  But in my opinion they failed.  A good alarm clock should have a big Snooze button, usually in the middle, that is touch discernible from the other buttons.  And it should be difficult to accidentally press a non-snooze button when reaching for the snooze half asleep.  This is not true here.  It's easy to hit a non-snooze button when reaching for the snooze.  So, I'm not using the clock for an alarm clock yet.  I might in the future, once I'm more familiar with the device.    The headband fits well, stays on and is comfortable.  I got used to it quickly but I used to wear a CPAP.  So, I'm used to having things strapped to my head when I sleep.  One other note, I don't move much when I sleep.  So, it's probably less likely that any device would come off when I sleep.    ==== On Device Software & Menus ===  3 out of 5 at best  The many buttons and many menus you have to step through make the device more complex to use than it should be.  It's difficult at times to determine what button you're supposed to push when stepping through the menus.  And it's easy to choose the wrong item.  The problem seems to be how they chose to display the menu/instructions on the screen as you step through using the arrow buttons.  But even with all the features and settings of this device, this is something they can easily improve.      ==== Online Software =====  6 out of 5, yes 6  I work for a very large internet company.  So, I'm very familiar with online software in general.  And I have to say they have done a GREAT job here.  The software is very easy to use and provides lots of great features.  There are many ways for you to look at your sleep data.  The software interface is very easy to step through the various options and views.  The graphs are very clear.  The interface buttons are few and well labeled.  Again, I can't get over how great the software is in  user interface design and functionality.  This takes the device from a 3 overall rating to a 4+ rating for me.    =====  Privacy concerns with online software =====  3 out of 5 - I'm not happy but not overly concerned    They do ask for a lot of personal and a few questions that they should not need to ask, birthday for example.  They should only need to know the year of your birth for sleep analysis.  Or possibly the month and year at most.  So, this question is a bit of a security risk and should be corrected by Zeo.  But, you are not forced to put in real data.  And with any site asking for personal information, you should not put in real data if you're uncomfortable with it (Sorry Zeo).    They ask for address, phone number and other data that is clearly to collect information to market to us later.  While I don't like this.  You're not forced to put in real data (again, sorry Zeo)    And in Zeo's defense.  Their online software is VERY nice and it's FREE.  It costs a lot of money to setup all the hardware and develop the software to run an online service like they have.  And just like with Microsoft, Yahoo, and other companies that offer free internet services, to get something for free you need to be willing to allow them to market to you in exchange.    So, again, Zeo, please improve the security of some of your questions.    And, again Zeo users, Their online software is REALLY GREAT and it's FREE.  Giving them some basic information for them to market to us seems like a fair trade.    ==== Note to Zeo ====  Thanks for producing this device Zeo!  I'd be happy to help you improve your 2.0 version and would happily volunteer as a beta tester.

review_headline: Look elsewhere if you're hard on your headphones
review_body: I remember about 5 yrs ago when Shures made the top end headphones and after having a pair of Shures for awhile, I heard about a new company named Etymotic that also made some really good headphones.  3 years ago, I was back in the market for a new pair of headphones so I decided to give the Etymotic brand a chance.  I do agree that the sound is great, but in the 3 years that I've had these headphones, I had to return them 3 times within the 2 yr warranty period and the last set that I got from the warranty currently does not work.  I've since had to go back to Shures.  While I can't fault Etymotic for quality or customer service, I'm giving the 2 stars for the build quality.  I do admit that I am quite rough with my headphones.  I usually use them in the morning for an hour commute to work and then it's in my pocket for the next 8-10 hrs until I get off work.  I untangle the headphones when I'm on my way out the door and then use it until I get home, I understand this is hard on the headphones, but I find it unacceptable that they are only good for 6-8 months before they break.   You can't even consider it a fluke b/c it happened consistently 4 times.  If you are not that rough on your headphones, then I would probably give these 4 stars, but considering the price I would expect it to have a good build as well.

They were an absolute breeze to hook up and Mission even included a pair of white gloves so as not to get any fingerprints on that beautiful finish during installation.  Wall mounts were included but I just use the provided desk stands.  I use them both as computer speakers hooked up through a usb port and also as a system for my iPod (Mission includes the cable necessary for iPod integration).  The real appeal though is that classic warm Mission sound.  The little digital amp puts out some pretty impressive power and the m-ispheres deliver with a crisp and bright sound that really resembles more of a pretty good set of bookshelves.  Amazingly, there's a bit of real soundstage to them, which is something I've never experienced with any portable, computer or docking station set-up.    All in all, a great product from a company that has given me excellent sound for a number of years.

product_title: iLive iS809B 30-Pin iPod Speaker Dock
review_headline: Terrible build quality and horrible service
review_body: The base unit blew a transisitor practically on the last day under 90 day warrenty.  I called for service and they wanted close to $100 for a replacement base unit.  Do not buy this unit, and do not buy any product made by this company.  ---below is my original review-----  I don't always write reviews but when I do its because I am either really happy or pissed about the product. In this case, I was impressed with the iLive wireless speaker system.  The speakers are paired with the base unit out of the box, which I didn't know so I unpaired them by accident.  Pairing them again was simple following the instructions.  I placed one speaker out back on the patio, the other in the living room, and the base unit in the kitchen.  Plugged my iPhone 4G in the base station and tested the sound.  At first I thought it was low in volume, but I found the analog volume knobs on the speakers and put them on max.  The sound I thought was a little flat, but I noticed on the remote there are bass and treble controls - so that fixed that problem.  I also experimented with the aux-in by outputing my Bose Wave stereo to input FM to the iLive. I kind of prefer the aux-in method since you can get some volume boost from the output device.  The remote control is also nice in that it doesn't use IR, so you don't need line of site to use it.    All in all, I had a party with 50 people a few nights later and the sound generously filled the room, and when people went out back the music was there to follow.  It not the best sounding speakers in the world, but I feel that the iLive lives up to what it advertises.  Its nice to be able to walk to different areas of the house never missing a note.  I've been using them everyday for 1 month with no problems.

product_title: Ultra High Performance HDMI Switcher, 3to1 Switch
review_body: Real quick review.    first: the setup is a DVD/HDD player and a Sony Blu-ray, both with 6 foot cables into the unit.  another 6 foot cable on output into the TV.    second: it selects the input fairly successfully, but, it might need to be selected manually, even though the input is already selected.    third: it seems like it is underpowered for my configuration.  Not enough power gets through for the switches and the image may not get through.  If I turn on both units, there seems to be enough draw to make the signal get through.  The Sony wouldn't show anything other than boot up until the HDD was turned on.  During the HDD playback, the signal got lost twice, for ~ 3 seconds, over a one hour play time.  the image turned into digital snow (not pixilated images) during those times.  The HDD playback, once rewound, would show the proper image.    Gut feeling is that in most short cabling solutions would work fine with this.  But, with 6 foot cables, the signal might degrade so that it can't leech power from the cables well enough to get the signal out.    Still playing with this.  The end result might be to get a 5V plug for this, to help the signal boost of the repeater.  But, for my limited needs, I don't mind turning on the other products for power support.  But, once we get used to our new HDD recorder toy, this could be come tiresome without the 5V adapter.

product_title: Sennheiser Sports Earbud Headphones
review_body: Make no mistake, these headphones are designed specifically for sporting, be it running, working out, or other activity. Earbuds fall out, tug on your ears, tangle up and are generally a nuisance but have the desirable form factor. Spendier in-ear buds also suffer the problem from seals, sure they block out noise but often your own footsteps become deafening thuds.  Previously, my go to work out earbud was the classic Shure e2c, relatively decent priced ($80), and they featured a few desirable traits not found in many earbuds: a unique earwrap design,  slightly reduced dynamic range, foam earbuds that worked well at reducing cord and footstep noise and a good price point. Their durability, however, was subpar as I killed a few over years from running in all sorts of weather and general abuse. Shure later changed their headphones, favoring a more traditional earbuds which left me out in the cold. Sure there were other headphones but nothing as high quality as the Shures for exercise.    I own the [[ASIN:B001GT185K Sennheiser  PMX80  In-Ear Sport Series II Behind the Head Earphones]] the precursor to the Adidas repackaged Sennheiser PMX-680, and lost them (only to find them days before my order arrived) and currently the PMX-680s. First off, neither of these headphones are high end. In fact, the redesigned Apple earbuds included with the iPhone 4 have more tighter bass, better articulation in the mids and cleaner highs, but unlike the Apple earbuds, Sennheiser understands our ear holes aren't circles. (Yes, as much as everyone loves to hate the Apple Earbuds, they've improved over time. The iPhone 4G buds are not bad, seem  to be on par with a few earbuds I've tried in the $25-40 range). Both the PMX-80s and PMX-680s are well designed for workouts. First off the cable is consolidated to one cord, meaning less tangle. The wrap gently presses the earbuds in but doesn't violate one's ears, and the over the ear wrap design lets the headphones rest gently in the ear. Overall its a well done design, but not exactly perfection. The PMX-680s also include a volume knob on an extension cord. This also functions as a break-away cord so if you catch your cord, the headphones will disconnect at the volume dial, saving wear and tear on your MP3 player's headphone jack. This gets extra kudos, although ut could break away a little easier. Also the PMX-680s feature a slightly more stylish design thanks to Adidas and a very nice carrying case.    Sound wise, the PMX-680s are lacking, they're good enough. They won't offend your ears but they're not exactly great sound either. Also, without foam tips that insert into your ears, they lack noise blocking capability. This is bad as you have to turn up your music louder to drown out a noisy gym or environment. There's a significant lack of detail to the highs and bass. The bass also is slightly muddy, undefined and lacking the attenuation for workouts. For the average bundled earbud with an MP3 player, these headphones (considering sound quality only) are a lateral upgrade. The real prize here is ergonomics.     Updated:    Are they worth it? Short answer: yes and no.     Despite the short comings, these headphones are decent however its the older PMX-80s feature considerably better mid and highs. After going for a run using the PMX-80s, there's quite a large difference, the highs on the 680s are muffled, and lack clarity and the bass is over bloated, even when working out.  I originally cited these as the headphones to get, but I rescind. Get the PMX-80s over the 680s. They may lack the volume knob and spiffy adidas case but they're considerably better. I still prefer the defunct Shure E2cs, that combined the magic of earwrap design, foam tips and higher quality sound but these are less than 1/2 the price, designed from the ground up to be used for active wear    Maybe in the future we'll see these get a substantial upgrade, until then, go for PMX-80s. I've linked them in this review.

review_headline: Seems to work but time will tell.
review_body: Ok, so I was looking for an alarm clock for a long time.  Why?  Well I am sensitive to light at night and many of today's alarm clocks, although they may use night friendly colours such as blue, have to high a contrast.  Their LCD contrast produces an impressive glow in some cases.    My gf and I needed a replacement for her aging alarm clock but we needed one where I did not have to sit up to see over her (the clock is on her side of the bed).  Enter the Emerson. review_body:

Also, one thing that wasn't mentioned is that you cannot preset any radio stations. They are digital, but are switched with a dial on the side of the radio.

Now to the positives. The best thing about this radio is that fact that you can hook up your mp3 player or in our case, the mp3 players on our phones. We use this feature all the time. It was also easy to install since they give you a template to follow to drill the holes. I personally thinks it looks nice - it isn't an eyesore. It is slim as well.

Granted, this radio does has its downfalls, however the reason I decided to give it 4 stars out of 5 is because it is simple: you get what you pay for. If you are looking for an inexpensive under-the-cabinet radio this one is just fine. If you want awesome sound - obviously this one isn't for you. I would recommend it if you don't want a radio with all the bells and whistles, but something simple to play some music while cooking or eating dinner.

product_title: RCA ANT1650F Flat Digital Amplified Indoor TV Antenna
review_headline: Works Great for Me, but Depends on Your Area...
review_body:
When I received this antenna, I attached it first to my TV and set it flat near the TV. I was able to get some channels, but very few. Then, I set it up near the window on its end and rescanned. This time, I was able to get about forty-five channels. I proceeded to attach a splitter so that I could use it with the TV in my bedroom and my living room.

The picture quality is great on most of the channels (better than my old cable service), and although I won't use most of the channels (Spanish etc...), I do like the quality of Fox, PBS, NBC and ABC which is what I was going for. A plus is that the digital setup tells me what is playing and gives me a short description (like cable), and I don't have to watch the show for a few minutes to see if I am interested.

However, if you are concerned about the poor reviews on this site, be aware that the quality and number of channels you receive will depend on your proximity to local stations and where you place the antenna. As I said before, I received few channels on my first try, but once I moved the antenna, I received more channels. I do live in an apartment building and am surrounded by tall buildings (which hurts reception), so it may actually be easier for you to receive the programming you want.

I recommend going to the website [...]. Although they don't recommend indoor antennas, they will tell you where your local stations are located, so you will have better luck with positioning your antenna to pick them up.

Oh yeah, and in case you are wondering, you do not need a digital convertor box to use this antenna if you already have an HD TV.

product_title: SMK-Link PS3 Blu-Link Universal Remote Control
review_headline: It's a good, cheap, universal PS3 remote with one draw back
review_body: As a new PS3 owner and an owner of many electronic devices with remotes(DirecTV DVR, TV, Surround sound), I was soon in the market for an all in one universal remote. I found out that the PS3 cannot be controlled by just any remote, but by remotes that use Bluetooth technology. This greatly narrows the field of available universal remotes compatible with all of my devices AND the PS3. Either spend $100+ on a computerized remote or give this little guy a shot.     Is this remote capable of controlling all of my devices? Yes, and it has all of the buttons I need to control them.    If the remote doesn't have the same button as the original remote, is there a work around? Yes, it has a learning feature that allows you to program a certain button on the remote to carry out the same feature as the original one.    So what's the con? Like many users have experienced, the remote tends not to be responsive with the PS3 after anywhere from 30 min's to 2 hours. If this happens, you will have to release the batteries and reprogram the remote to your PS3. I have found a work around for this. After using the remote for the PS3, if you simply press a button for another device, like TV, you should not lose programming with your PS3. Although this may not be idea for many users, your choices are either dish out the extra cash for one of the alternative remotes, or use the PS3 controller and use the other remotes you currently have.     I hope this review helps.

review_headline: An easy to use, inexpensive, portable music player...
review_body:

Sansa Clip Review:
I've never used an ipod or ipod mini, but I don't see the need for those expensive devices to play music, when the Sansa Clip does everything I want it to. You can build playlists, or just play music based on the album, genre, or even the artists name. It has an FM tuner as well, and I think you can record voice (but I've never used it for that). It has a lock switch, so that you do not accidentally alter your music player, and all the controls are intuitive. I've owned the Sansa clip for over a year, and it has performed well in that time. 5 Stars.

Earphone Review:
When I bought my Sansa clip, I removed the stock earphones for another pair I bought some time ago for my phone (knockoff ipod earphones), because I thought the stock earphones would be inferior. However, for the gym, the earphones I bought were not that good, because it was difficult to hear the music in a noisy area, even when the volume is at the maximum level. I recently ordered a new pair of earphones to exercise with, but needed to wait for delivery. I was without earphones and used the ones that came with the Sansa, and woah, was I wrong about it being inferior. The earphones that come with the Sansa are AWESOME! They provide great fidelity, and I hear bass and subtle sounds in my music that I never heard with my \\"for ipod\\" earphones. The foam sponge surrounding the buds fit well in my ear, are comfortable for moderate use and do not remove themselves easily unless I pull or tug at them with adequate force. The foam also serves to provide some noise isolation, but the earphones are not for this purpose. They do however create a good seal so that you hear mostly the music from your music player, compared to ambient noise. 5 Stars.

product_title: ZVOX 430 High-Performance Single-Cabinet "Sound Bar" Surround Sound System (Discontinued by Manufacturer)
review_body: The ZVOX 430 is simple to set up and is easier on the eye than bigger home-theater setups.  Primarily, you can think of the 430 as a speaker box with incredible range and fidelity.  Surprisingly, it performs excellently for music and movies alike.  If you want a system that will rumble the floor and give you excellent surround sound, this is probably NOT it.  If you want something that will delivery rich, full sound at low to moderate volume levels, this is the ticket.    First, for a speaker bar this size, it really does push out impressive sound.  The bass is tight and accurate, so while it produces deep, low bass frequencies, it won't be a boomy floor-rattler.  It'll still do enough to upset the neighbors in an apartment building, but you won't mistake it for a dedicated high-power sub.  The box produces great midrange and subwoofer and treble adjustments are available to adjust the basic EQ.  Your television probably also has a basic output EQ that you can use to supplement as needed.  One of the few week spots I've noticed is that higher frequencies are just a tad weak.  With treble all the way up on both the speaker and tv EQ, it still doesn't quite capture some of those high-frequency cracks and gunshots.  My guess is a lot of people would describe the top end as warm, but again, it doesn't perform poorly, just not up to the standard it sets for itself in other areas.    Vocals are wonderfully pronounced when watching tv - one area where many systems falter.  There is no need to increase the volume to attempt to overcome poorly mixed tracks - just click up the treble a little and reduce phasecue and the vocals will stand out at any volume.  The phasecue does an acceptable job of simulating some level of surround.  I'm not big into surround, so you'll have to depend on other reviews to assess the performance in that area.    Besides the slight knock I had on the treble, the only other major 'con' I can think of is the remote.  It is poorly made (and appears likewise).  Also, the remote uses outdated, somewhat rare universal codes.  The stated codes did not work for my remote, but a little fishing around and I found something that worked.  ZVOX would do much better to provide a better remote and use universal codes that are more common.  The fit and finish is excellent, the only flaw I found was that the gloss end pieces aren't finished on the inside.  While most of this area is hidden, there is a small exposed edge where you can see the unfinished side.  A small gripe, but worth mentioning as it sticks out compared to quality of the rest of the box.    Overall, this is a very impressive product.  It is so good, that I'm sure I would have been happy with one of their smaller models.  Despite all of the adjustments I detailed above, one of my favorite things about the system is that it is fairly transparent - I don't find myself constantly tweaking levels and EQ - only every once in a while and usually because a program is poorly mixed.

review_headline: Great value at the price point
review_body: I've lived with this thing for a year.   Overall, I'm very pleased with it.   I have a fairly typical 100% HDMI 5:1 setup.   Panasonic Blu Ray and Motorola digital set-top box as inputs.   I stream a lot of Netflix through the internet connection on the Blu Ray player.   I listen to music from an iPod or Pandora through the Blu Ray player.   I drive four vintage Polk Audio Monitor 10 floor speakers, a newer Polk center, and a Polk sub for audio. Video is a 50\\" Panny G20 plasma.   If you are 100% HDMI and use an iPod all the time, this gets you everything you need without spending premium dollars for analog to HDMI conversion and video upconversion features you don't need.  I don't notice any interference with the HDMI signal.   I don't notice any audio distortion at normal listening levels.    My gripe list:    You need to hit a button twice to wake up the remote control.   I suppose this prevents accidentally hitting a button but after a year, I'm still annoyed by it but not annoyed enough to buy and program a universal remote.    The only control interface for setting up the AV receiver to the TV is NTSC analog video.  The man-machine interface is 1970's Radio Shack TRS-80.   I live in an HDMI universe.   If I want to control the iPod or set things up on the AV receiver, I'd like to do it over HDMI, pleeeze.   I borrow the cable off the subwoofer and run it to the plasma the rare times I want to reconfigure the unit and do most minor things through the front panel display.      The iPod interface works well but you can only shuffle the whole iPod, not an artist or a play list.     I'd like it to charge the iPod even when I haven't selected it as the source.  The connector for the iPod cable is in the front.  The cable is attached permenantly so I would much prefer it in the back.  Since the video output to control the iPod is only NTSC, I have to use the wimpy little display on the front panel of the AV receiver to select artists and songs on the iPod.   It's painful finding an artist on a 16 gig Nano.  Almost useless on a 160 gig Classic where it's quicker to unplug the iPod, select the artist I want, and plug it back in.    I guess I'm old school but the power output specs are nothing like I'm used to.   In 1980 terms, it puts out about 30 watts per channel.   More than adequate for a small room and fairly efficient speakers but the claimed 110 watts per channel should have the police knocking on my door.

product_title: Maha Powerex Wizard One MH-C9000 Advanced Battery Charger and Analyzer - Deluxe Accessory Storage Case Included
review_body:
While there are a few folks that have a bad opinion of this charger, I have not had any problems whatsoever.

I have a 100% success rate in charging NiMH batteries from several different manufacturers... but they were new batteries.

I suspect the problems many are claiming with the charger may perhaps be with old batteries?

The charger has a mode that you can use to recondition batteries, and it has not often been clearly stated by those complaining this charger did not work whether or not they tried to recondition the batteries (Refresh/Analyze or Break-In/Forming mode).

If a battery is marginal, I suppose that if this charger won't charge the battery, it should tell you to either recondition the battery or throw it out.

Other criticism has been the number of key strokes it takes to setup the charger for a battery. But if you don't do anything when inserting batteries, it will default to CHARGE mode using a 1A charge rate (2 hour charge rate for typical 2000mAH AA batteries).

Perhaps there should be an easier way to setup the charger, but I don't see that as something preventing it's use. This is NOT a basic (nor cheap) charger, it's a Charger/Analyzer. If you want a basic charger, you can buy one far cheaper than this one. The intended purpose of this charger is to maintain your batteries in good working order with variable charge/discharge modes. So I suppose some degree of setup is required to use the features of the charger (and it's certainly easier to use than a West Mountain CBA-3 analyzer).

I am not going to badmouth the LaCrosse charger as I don't own one, but my general opinion of LaCrosse products over the years (mostly their weather instruments) has been less than stellar - which is why I bought the Maha charger in the first place.

One observation I will make between the two chargers is that the Maha/PowerEx C9000's Break-in/Forming charge is in compliance with International Standard (IEC-61951-2.7 - Testing NiMH batteries.) while the LaCrosse BC-900 is not. While that may or may not make much difference in conditioning the batteries, the C9000 is at least going to provide more accurate test results of the battery.

If folks are having issues with batteries failing the Break-in charge from the C-9000 charger, then one could conclude their batteries are not meeting the battery performance found in the IEC standard... in other words, their batteries are bad.le the LaCrosse BC-900 is not. While that may or may not make much difference in conditioning the batteries, the C9000 is at least going to provide more accurate test results of the battery. If folks are having issues with batteries failing the Break-in charge from the C-9000 charger, then one could conclude their batteries are not meeting the battery performance found in the IEC standard... in other words, their batteries are bad.

review_body:

What's in the box?
* The Nyrius Dock, model NiC708
* AC Adapter
* Remote Control
* RCA Cables

The dock is very compact and will easily fit on just about any table or surface. It is approximately 5 ½ \\"wide by 4\\" deep and only 1 inch high.

The only output connection for a TV is RCA, but since we are talking about iPod media, you don't need any Hi-def cables anyway. If you have a need to keep the dock more than a couple of feet from the TV, you might want longer RCA cables. These are about 3 feet, 9 inches from end to end.

The unit includes an SD slot and a USB port, as well as an `aux in jack' so you can access media through those as well.

Like most docks, the Nyrius charges your iPod while you are using the dock.

Set up is easy. Simply plug it in to a wall outlet, and connect the RCA cables to the dock and to your TV.

The remote control is pretty generic. With buttons to power on/off, mute, switch between inputs (labled iPod, Card, and USB), and perform other basic functions. Such as Play, Stop, Rewind, Fast Forward, etc.

If you are looking for a TV Dock for your iPod this product is decent.

product_title: NuForce - Icon - Integrated Desktop Amplifier (Black)
review_headline: Excellent product. Well packaged and sounds great.
review_body: My on-board PC audio was very poor. It suffered from noise crossover from all the other kit in the PC and the drivers were crap. The sound was muddy and distorted.     The problem with internal PC audio is they often have  cheap digital to analogue converters (DACs). The DAC is the critical part that converts digital audio into an analogue signal that comes out your headphone/line out port. I confirmed this by bypassing my amp and plugging my headphones directly into headphone socket. The sound quality was appalling and all the amp was doing was making it a little louder and adding its own deficiencies.     So, what to do? First thing I decided was that I needed a better quality external DAC to eliminate the noise problems. There are a few available - but they don't come cheap. And I had a secondary problem of how to drive my external speakers - so I still needed an amplifier as well. Oh and I wanted to use my headphones still - especially at night. What I needed was something that had an external DAC, integrated amplifier AND a headphone socket. Turns out such a combination is rare indeed.     The Nufoce Icon integrated amplifier and DAC is one solution. It connects to your PC via USB, has an internal DAC, headphone socket and pumps out 15 Watts per channel (peak). This may not sound like much but I am not talking about running a rave party here - I want to LISTEN to music at my computer as I type. 15W is plenty when your speakers are no more than a meter away from your ears. The reviews I read were impressive to say the least.     The device is about the same size as an old external USB drive and has only two knobs - one for volume and one for source selection. You can select from USB (using its own DAC), 3.5mm stereo socket, or RCA. So if you just want to plug in an analogue source (like a phone) you can. There is a little blue power LED and a 3.5mm headphone socket also on the front.     The back panel has a power socket, 3.5mm audio, USB, RCA, and a line out socket (apparently you can use it as a DAC/preamp only or use this socket to drive a powered subwoofer). The weirdest thing is how the speakers are connected. Nuforce have decided to use standard RJ45 (yes ethernet) sockets for this. Its a bit strange but at least they give you two one meter speaker cables with banana plugs as part of the package. The nice thing about this arrangement is that if you want a longer cable you can just use standard cat5e straight cable and a cheap RJ45 cable joiner - thats what I have done as my speakers are more like 3m total from the amp. Or if you want you can make up your own cables using the wiring diagram on the website. But its worth noting that they seem to use 4 wires for positive and 4 wires for negative. This means that you have the benefit of 4 x AWG24 of a standard cat5e wire - the equivalent of a single AWG18 cable. But don't get me started on speaker cable...    The important thing is how the thing sounds and on that score, it's just brilliant. I have plugged it into my 10 year old Krix Brix bookself speakers and they have NEVER been driven like this before. No need for a subwoofer, the bass is fantastic and the high end is audible for the first time. At volume set to 12 noon, the sound is about comfortable listening level. Set it to 3 o'clock or 4 o'clock and the sound comes alive! Clarity I have NEVER heard before. Max it out and the room starts to vibrate with only slight distortion (bookshelf speakers remember).     With the multiple inputs, its possible to run direct comparisons between the internal DAC and the on board audio on my PC. The difference is noticeable - if not glaring. First off for some reason, the signal from the on-board audio is MUCH LOUDER - maybe 5 - 10 dB. But in this case, louder is not always better as the onboard audio is still muddier and clouded with mid range bass. The high end seems to be lacking and of course the noise is still there is quieter bits.     On the headphone front the device performs admirably but I think I may have to upgrade from my Sennheiser CX300s to really appreciate it.    Its worth noting that Nuforce have recently released an upgraded Icon-2 Amp. Its 50% more expensive. The main differences is doubling of power (to 30Wpc) and a 32 bit integrated DAC. The extra power would be nice but as I do not have any 32-bit source material (has anyone?) I doubt I'd hear any difference.     All in all, an excellent and much worthwhile upgrade to any desktop audio system - especially if you already have some good, high sensitivity speakers and are looking for something to drive them.

review_headline: High end receiver at an unbelievable price
review_body: I bought this receiver having waited years for B&K to offer high resolution codec decoding on their receivers.  That never happened and I've heard B&K is bankrupt.   That left me looking for an up-to-date receiver that had enough horsepower to handle a 7.2 system 100% Martin Logan electrostats.  The Martin Logans are great speakers but require a lot of juice and the ability to handle impedance loads 4 ohms and below.   I am happy to say that the Onkyo TX-NR5008 has the chops to do that.  The sound is definitely different from what I had with my old B&K AVR307.  The B&K can produce amazingly open sound with my MLs.  The Onkyo maybe just a little less so.  In exchange, however, the detail and stage presence with the Onkyo is just amazing.  Imaging is amazing and on most recordings whether music or high res Blu Ray movies the best way I can describe the sound is 3D.  The receiver has a phono input.    I had been using an old DBX decompression hardware with my turntable that helped bring my old vinyl up to similar dynamic range as CDs.  I found out with the Onkyo that I did not need the DBX  unit.  In fact it made the phono sound worse.  The phono in THX music mode sounds amazing.  My only two complaints about the receiver are its weight (of course you get some great power supplies because of that weight) and the fact that it won't accept spade connectors for the speaker hook ups.  I had to cut off all of the spade connectors from my speaker leads to hook up the speakers.  Anyway, you won't be sorry with this purchase.  Highly recommended.

product_title: TDK Life on Record 77000015378 USB Belt Drive Turntable (Discontinued by Manufacturer)
review_body:
This turntable works fine for converting vinyl records to mp3 or other preferred digital formats. However there are a few things that keep it from being a 4 or 5 star product.
1. The assembly. The mechanics of this turntable are very basic. I still have a 30 year old Denon turntable that has superior construction to this. It seems that when CDs took over the music business that there was not much call to build turntables any more so all you can get now are basic units. At any rate, this turntable comes with a leather covered top, which is nice but odd. I would have preferred acrylic so I can lower the lid while the record is playing. If you do that here you can't tell what's going on. Also, you have to loop the rubber drive belt around the motor spindle. The belt comes attached to the platter, similar to a gasket. You have to pull the belt away from the platter and drop it over the drive spindle. I couldn't believe I had to do that or that the belt is exposed when you play. I've owned numerous turntables in my time and the belt has always been within the motor housing. The belt is flush against the platter and is made of rubber so you have to be very careful in pulling it away from the platter so you can loop it around the spindle. I used a bent paper clip to get behind it to minimize the risk of tearing the belt and this seemed to work fine.
2. The software. The software that comes with this turntable is called Vinyl Recorder. It works ok but has 2 problems. First, it's only a 30 day trial version so if you want to keep using it you have to pay after the expiration. This struck me as a rip off. Had I paid for the turntable I would have expected a software version that at least worked well enough for me to use the turntable without shelling out more bucks. I installed Audacity, a superior, and free, piece of software. Also, when I used Vinyl Recorder to rip from my records I had to find the correct setting for the record to play through the speakers while I was ripping it. When I switched back to listening to music through iTunes, it wouldn't work. I had to disconnect the turntable from the USB port to resolve this. Might be just my system but worth mentioning.
3. The price. I did not pay for this turntable, having received it through Amazon Vine. However, if I were looking for a turntable to rip my vinyl records I'd pass on this as too expensive. I think for what you get a reasonable price is about 25% of what it's listed for. Again, that's just my opinion but the simplicty of the materials and basic functionality of the item don't warrant the listed price.pping it. product_title: Sanyo Eneloop AA NiMH Pre-Charged Rechargeable Batteries - 4 Pack (Discontinued by Manufacturer)
review_headline: Works as advertised! Long shelf life, much longer than standard NiMH
review_body:
The problem with traditional NiMH rechargeable cells has been their self-discharge rate. Expect 3 months maximum before those batteries depleted to the point they are no longer usable in a device (under 1 VDC). Fully charged, NiMH cells stay at around 1.3-1.32 VDC. The Eneloop batteries come out of the box around 1.3 VDC and I have found that they drop only 0.001-0.01 VDC every month.

The negative aspect of the Eneloops is their capacity. While they have a long shelf life, they aren't as high capacity as standard NiMH cells, but that is acceptable with many of the low-demand electronic devices. If you have a digital camera or a flash light, chances are you won't really need the long stand-by life of the Eneloops.

Pros: Slow self-discharge rate, charges in NiMH chargers, affordable

Cons: Lower capacity than most modern NiMH cells

Overall: 5/5 stars

product_title: JVC Noise Cancelling Headphones - Black
review_body:
I originally arrived at Amazon planning to order the Sennheiser PXC 250-II, but read the reviews of this product and saw its cost, so I ordered it too in order to do a head to head comparison.

The JVC headphone covers much more of the ear than the Sennheiser. It also has a removable cord, which makes it easier to use solely for noise reduction. It also comes with a 1/4\\" adapter, if you need one of those.

Ultimately I decided to return it. Why?

1. The PXC 250-II is much, much lighter -- 65g, as opposed to 150g for the HA-NC250. On long trips the top of my head gets tender where the headphone rests. Much of the weight difference is because the PXC 250-II has its battery in an in-line enclosure on the cord. You clip it to your shirt/blouse to keep the weight off of your head.

2. The PXC 250-II in its case is about 1/2 the size of the HA-NC250.

3. The PXC 250-II does a better job of reproducing musical detail. I used as my test \\"Live: Brad Mehldau Trio\\". In more subtle, quieter moments, the PXC 250-II hands down had more detail than the HA-NC250. This won't matter if all you listen to with these headphones is poorly done MP3 rips, or the music is hot, highly-produced material. But for subtle jazz it was the difference between a muddy brush on a snare and being able to imagine it moving around the head.

review_headline: Mobi Headphonies - Cute design and booming sound
review_body:
Mobi Headphonies are adorable, useful and reasonably priced!

When I read magazines, I love to tear out and keep pages of things that peek my interest. So while I was leafing through a magazine one day, I came around a totally too cute personal music player speaker called Headphonies. They caught my eye because of their unique designs. So I tore out the advertisement to keep so I could learn more about the speakers.

While I was attending the Consumer Electronics Show (CES) in Vegas, I could not believe it when I happened upon the Mobi booth. The Headphonies looked just as good in real life as they did in the magazine.

Mobi Headphonies are micro speakers that are just 3 inches tall and weigh only 4 ounces each. Inside the head of each character is a tiny speaker that uses digital signal processor circuitry to produce music with clear bass and without the distortion found in most speakers of this size.

Mobi sent me the Sunny Headphonies for review and it is too adorable in that pink polka dot bikini. When I unpacked the Sunny, I followed the instructions and charged the battery using the enclosed USB charge cable. Headphonies contain a lithium-ion battery that provides four hours of play time per charge. After I charged the battery, I connected the Sunny to my smartphone using the enclosed audio input cable. I would never know by listening to the music that the great sound was coming from such a small speaker.

Headphonies come with a clip-on tether so you can attach the speaker to a cord to wear it around your neck or clip it to a music player or gaming device like a Nintendo DS.

One con of the Headphonies is that you have to remember to keep the battery charged. You are suppose to use the speaker until the battery is completely drained but it does charge fairly quickly within 20 minutes. Another thing is that the speaker grill is on the back of the character's head which means you have the turn it backwards to hear the music. Although the back is the speaker is also cute, it would be better to have the grill on the front so that you can still see the character's cute face while playing music.

Mobi Headphonies are available on Amazon.com ranging in price from $9.99 to $29.99 depending on the character design. These cute speakers with the booming sound would be great for anyone from kids to adults which is why I included it as part of my Valentine Day Gift Guide.

product_title: Logitech 915-000139 Harmony IR Extender System - Black (Discontinued by Manufacturer)
review_body: Ok so I bought this to wall mount a TV, hide my DVR (Comcast) in the closet, and still use the Comcast remote.  I'm using a 35 FT audio extension cable to reach the cable box.  After some \\"fiddling\\" (See below) the product works great!    After initially installing I was receiving major IR interface from multiple sources that rendered this device useless.  The main sources being CFLs and the LCD TV.    Logitech customer service was not helpful since I was not using this with a Logitech remote.  So I spent a few days researching IR interference and found a post on a forum suggesting to use a piece of electrical tape to cover most (not all) of the IR receiver.  The tape acts as a filter and blocks out most of the weaker IR signals and allows only the strongest ones (ie remote signal) to get through.     Since placing the tape over the IR receiver the device works perfect!     Hope this helps!     Phil

product_title: Terk VR1 Automatic TV Volume Controller
review_headline: works pretty well with a standard TV and Roku player
review_body: The older I get, the more annoyed I am with painfully loud sounds on TV, especially when the dialogue seems a faint murmer in contrast. When listening to a TV with externally connected, high quality, speaker systems, it's much less of a problem. However, when I connected a Roku player to my old tube TV (with just the TV's onboard speakers), it was nearly impossible to make out speech without excessively cranking the volume, and this would inevitably be followed by a virtual nuclear bomb of sound when music or background noise came on. It is my understanding that this is due to compression of sound done by the digital player. This Terk device pretty effectively fixes that, and does it at a minimum of expense. The other reviews that mention pops and clicks are correct, there will be an occasional pop when the unit starts to suppress sound, but for me it is a small price to pay not to have my ears blown out, or frantically toggle the volume up and down. There also is a slight degradation of quality. However, it does a pretty good job of leveling out the sound to a reasonably stable level. If you are an audiophile, you will probably not be happy with it, but I suspect if you are that picky, you have an expensive external speaker system that handles sound far better than standard TV speakers anyway. If you are like me, and just want to enjoy a movie on a plain, old, TV without fighting the volume, you will like this product very much. There is nothing else out there that works, for this amount of money. Setup takes seconds, literally, and you don't even need the included instructions.

review_headline: Good product - with a few caveats
review_body: It's great to be able to hide the cables in the wall when mounting the TV. I was originally going to run all the cables including the power cable down the wall, but then decided to do it to code. (The code people think that the power cord is going to fail in the wall, and the romex cable won't.)    The instructional video online shows you how to do it yourself, and the instructions are quite adequate so that anyone can really do it. But the instructions do say something to the effect of \\"Should be installed by a professional.\\" (Must be a legal liability thing.) It doesn't say what kind of professional, and I'm a professional real estate broker, so I've got that professional thing covered.     The biggest drawback that I find is that the power cord that plugs into the bottom assembly is so large that it pushes my furniture away from the wall. The female plug extends about 2-1/4 inches away from the wall, so be prepared for that. I was going to cut a hole in my entertainment unit where the plug bumps it, but the unit cost $1532 and my wife would freak out if she saw me with a hammer and chisel behind the unit.     The other issue is, if you have a tv that provides you with a flat type plug, that works against you using this system because you can't get a flat plug into the small space in the box. Another work-around situation. You can get a straight plug extension cord and plug the tv into that.    My quick and easy installation ran about 5 hours including 3 trips to the hardware store for work-arounds.  That shouldn't be your experience though. For some reason the spot where I need to mount my tv has studs every 6 inches for a distance of about 4 feet. I actually had to squeeze this thing into a vertical position. I couldn't find a sixteen inch on center pair of studs except beyond the edge of where the TV ends. But that's a bit unusual. You probably won't have that issue.    The kit comes with everything you need to do the job, though.
